    • Microscopic Detection of Leishman-Donovan (LD) Bodies: Giemsa-stained smears of splenic aspirate (highest sensitivity \(95 ext{–}98\%\), but requires caution due to haemorrhage risk), bone marrow aspirate (\(70 ext{–}85\%\) sensitivity), or lymph node aspirate (\(50 ext{–}60\%\)). Amastigotes are oval (\(2 ext{–}4\ \mu ext{m}\)) with a large purple nucleus and a distinct, perpendicular rod-shaped bar kinetoplast.
    • rK39 Immunochromatographic Rapid Dipstick: Recombinant 39-amino-acid kinesin protein antigen of L. donovani; sensitivity and specificity \(>98\%\) in acute symptomatic visceral leishmaniasis.
    • Formol-Gel (Napier's Aldehyde) Test: Add 1 drop of 40% commercial formaldehyde to 1 mL patient serum. Immediate complete solidification/gelification like boiled egg white within 1–20 minutes indicates high serum gamma-globulins.

3. Blood and Lymphatic Microfilariae (Filarial Nematodes) (Cheesbrough pp. 270–274)

Filarial nematodes are tissue-dwelling roundworms that produce motile embryos (microfilariae) that circulate in peripheral blood or skin tissues:

Species & Disease Vector & Periodicity Sheath & Dimensions Diagnostic Tail Tip Nuclear Architecture
Wuchereria bancrofti
(Bancroftian Lymphatic Filariasis)		 Mosquitoes: Culex quinquefasciatus (urban), Anopheles, Aedes. Strict Nocturnal Periodicity (\(22:00 ext{–}04:00\)) (except diurnal subperiodic in South Pacific). SHEATHED; graceful, smooth sweeping body curves (\(240 ext{–}300 imes 7.5 ext{–}10\ \mu ext{m}\)); cephalic space length = width (\(1:1\)). Tail tip is completely CLEAR and FREE OF NUCLEI (terminal column of nuclei stops short of the pointed tail tip). Causes hydrocele, lymphangitis, and gross brawny elephantiasis of lower limbs and genitalia.
Brugia malayi
(Malayan Lymphatic Filariasis)		 Mosquitoes: Mansonia species (associated with aquatic water lettuce *Pistia*) and Anopheles. Nocturnal Periodicity. SHEATHED; stiff, irregular, crinkled kinky body curves (\(175 ext{–}230 imes 5 ext{–}6\ \mu ext{m}\)); long cephalic space (\(2:1\)). Sheath stains bright pink with Giemsa. TWO SEPARATE TERMINAL NUCLEI: Tail tip tapers to a bulbous swelling containing one subterminal nucleus and one isolated terminal nucleus at the extreme tip. Causes elephantiasis below the knees.
Loa loa
(African Eye Worm / Loiasis)		 Day-biting Chrysops deerflies / mango flies (Chrysops silacea, C. dimidiata). Strict Diurnal Periodicity (\(10:00 ext{–}14:00\)). SHEATHED; stiff, undulating body curves (\(250 ext{–}300 imes 6 ext{–}8\ \mu ext{m}\)); short cephalic space. Sheath stains poorly with Giemsa. CONTINUOUS COLUMN OF NUCLEI EXTENDING TO THE VERY TIP OF THE BLUNT ROUNDED TAIL: Large, crowded, irregular nuclei run in an unbroken line to the extreme caudal margin. Causes transient Calabar swellings (angioedema) and subconjunctival adult worm migration across the cornea.
Mansonella perstans Biting midges / gnats (Culicoides species: C. austeni, C. grahamii). Non-Periodic (circulates equally day and night). UNSHEATHED; small, slender (\(100 ext{–}150 imes 4 ext{–}5\ \mu ext{m}\)); actively mobile. Nuclei extend to the very tip of the blunt, rounded, truncated tail. Usually benign or causes mild eosinophilia and serositis.
Mansonella ozzardi Biting midges (*Culicoides*) and blackflies (*Simulium*). Non-periodic (Americas). UNSHEATHED; slender (\(160 ext{–}200 imes 4 ext{–}5\ \mu ext{m}\)). Tail is sharply pointed and completely free of nuclei.

Standard Blood Concentration Techniques for Microfilariae & Trypanosomes

1. Knott's Concentration Technique:

Collect \(1 ext{ mL}\) of venous blood and mix thoroughly with \(9 ext{ mL}\) of 2% (v/v) formalin in a centrifuge tube. Formalin lyses all red blood cells and straightens microfilariae. Centrifuge at \(500 ext{ g}\) for 5 minutes. Decant the supernatant, transfer the sediment to a glass slide, allow to dry completely, and stain with Giemsa.

2. Polycarbonate Membrane Filtration Technique (WHO Gold Standard for Surveys):

Draw \(1 ext{ mL}\) of venous blood into a syringe containing \(9 ext{ mL}\) of 10% Teepol or saline. Attach a Swinney filter holder housing a \(3\ \mu ext{m}\) pore size polycarbonate membrane filter (e.g., Nuclepore). Pass the lysed blood through the filter, flush with \(10 ext{ mL}\) of distilled water followed by air, remove the membrane filter, mount on a glass slide, fix with methanol, and stain with Giemsa. Recovers 100% of microfilariae in \(1 ext{ mL}\) of blood.

Section 5.8 Interactive Examination Bank (8 High-Yield Clinical MCQs)

Test your diagnostic competence on trypanosomiasis staging, Leishmania LD body identification, microfilarial tail nuclear anatomy, and Babesia differentiation:

Question 5.8.1 (Q305): A patient from rural West Africa presents with intermittent fever, extreme daytime somnolence, and non-tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy (Winterbottom's sign). Microscopic examination of a Giemsa-stained lymph node aspirate reveals actively motile hemoflagellates with a central nucleus, small posterior kinetoplast, undulating membrane, and free anterior flagellum. What is the diagnosis and the primary screening test for this condition?
Correct Answer: A (Trypanosoma brucei gambiense; screened by CATT)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 263–265 & Fig. 5.28: Trypanosoma brucei gambiense causes chronic West African sleeping sickness transmitted by riverine tsetse flies (Glossina palpalis). The hallmark early physical finding is Winterbottom's sign (enlargement of posterior cervical lymph nodes). CATT is the standard mass field screening agglutination assay for T. b. gambiense antibody detection.
Question 5.8.2 (Q306): A blood specimen collected at midnight (\(23:30\)) from an immigrant with gross brawny leg elephantiasis is processed via Knott's concentration technique. Giemsa staining reveals sheathed microfilariae measuring \(280\ \mu ext{m}\) with graceful, smooth body curves and a tapered tail whose terminal tip is completely free of nuclei. What organism has been identified?
Correct Answer: B (Wuchereria bancrofti)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 270–273 & Fig. 5.31: Wuchereria bancrofti microfilariae are sheathed, have smooth graceful body curves, display strict nocturnal periodicity (\(22:00 ext{–}04:00\)), and are definitively characterized by a tail tip completely clear and free of nuclei. In contrast, Brugia malayi has two distinct terminal nuclei in the tail, and Loa loa has nuclei extending to the very end of the rounded tail.
Question 5.8.3 (Q307): A missionary returning from Cameroon presents with transient, painful, non-pitting subcutaneous swelling on the forearm (Calabar swelling) and reports having observed a thin white worm crawling across the subconjunctival space of the eye. A daytime blood film (\(12:00\)) reveals sheathed microfilariae with nuclei extending in an unbroken, continuous column to the extreme tip of the rounded tail. What is the diagnosis?
Correct Answer: C (Loa loa / African Eye Worm)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 272–274 & Plate 5.54: Loa loa microfilariae are sheathed, have strict diurnal periodicity (\(10:00 ext{–}14:00\)), and possess a continuous column of crowded nuclei extending all the way to the blunt rounded tip of the tail. Adults migrate through subcutaneous tissue causing allergic Calabar swellings and frequently migrate across the anterior subconjunctival sclera. Transmitted by day-biting Chrysops deerflies.
Question 5.8.4 (Q308): A Giemsa-stained splenic aspirate smear from a patient with high remittent fever, massive splenomegaly, profound pancytopenia, and hypergammaglobulinaemia demonstrates numerous small, intracellular, oval bodies (\(2 ext{–}4\ \mu ext{m}\)) inside reticuloendothelial macrophages. Each body possesses a distinct spherical nucleus and a perpendicular, rod-like bar kinetoplast. What organism has been detected?
Correct Answer: B (Leishmania donovani / LD bodies)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 268–271 & Plate 5.50: Visceral leishmaniasis (Kala-azar) is caused by Leishmania donovani, which multiplies within host macrophages as non-flagellated amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies). The pathognomonic feature on Giemsa stain is the presence of two distinct internal organelle structures: a large purple spherical nucleus and a smaller, dark, perpendicular rod-shaped kinetoplast.
Question 5.8.5 (Q309): An asplenic patient from the northeastern United States presents with hemolytic anaemia, high fever, and hemoglobinuria. A thin blood film reveals intraerythrocytic pleomorphic ring trophozoites resembling Plasmodium falciparum, but the rings lack malarial pigment (haemozoin), extracellular rings are observed, and characteristic tetrads of 4 budding pyriform merozoites forming a "Maltese Cross" are identified. What is the diagnosis?
Correct Answer: D (Babesia microti / Babesiosis)
Cheesbrough Reference p. 278 & Plate 5.56: Babesia species are tick-borne (*Ixodes*) intraerythrocytic piroplasms. While their ring forms can closely mimic P. falciparum, Babesia is definitively distinguished by: 1) Complete absence of malarial pigment (haemozoin) at all stages; 2) Presence of extracellular naked rings; and 3) Pathognomonic "Maltese Cross" tetrads formed by cruciform division of 4 daughter merozoites attached at their pointed ends.
Question 5.8.6 (Q310): What pore size is specified for the polycarbonate membrane filter used in the WHO standard membrane filtration concentration technique for the quantitative recovery of blood microfilariae?
Correct Answer: A (\(3.0\ \mu ext{m}\) polycarbonate membrane)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 273–274 & Plate 5.42: The standard membrane filtration technique utilizes a \(3.0\ \mu ext{m}\) pore size polycarbonate membrane filter (Nuclepore). When \(1 ext{ mL}\) of lysed venous blood is forced through the filter, red cell debris and water pass freely while all microfilariae (measuring \(5 ext{–}10\ \mu ext{m}\) in diameter) are quantitatively retained on the membrane surface, providing 100% recovery.
Question 5.8.7 (Q311): A South American patient from an endemic triatomine bug region presents with chronic congestive heart failure, complete heart block, severe dysphagia, and massive colonic dilatation. What is the pathological mechanism of this condition?
Correct Answer: B (T. cruzi amastigote destruction of myocardium and myenteric plexuses)
Cheesbrough Reference p. 265: In chronic Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi), pseudocysts of multiplying intracellular amastigotes trigger persistent chronic myocarditis, fibrosis of the bundle of His/Purkinje fibers (leading to right bundle branch block and apical aneurysms), and progressive denervation of the enteric autonomic nervous system (Auerbach's plexus), resulting in massive smooth muscle flaccidity: megaoesophagus and megacolon.
Question 5.8.8 (Q312): A blood specimen collected without timing restrictions reveals small, actively motile, unsheathed microfilariae measuring \(120\ \mu ext{m}\) in length. On Giemsa staining, the nuclei extend in a solid column to the very tip of the blunt, rounded, truncated tail. What is the species?
Correct Answer: A (Mansonella perstans)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 272–273 & Fig. 5.31: Mansonella perstans is an unsheathed microfilaria, is small (\(100 ext{–}150\ \mu ext{m}\)), displays no periodicity (circulates equally day and night), and is definitively identified by having a blunt, rounded, square-cut tail tip packed with nuclei to the very end. Transmitted by Culicoides biting midges.
Home > Chapter 5: Parasitological Procedures > 5.9 Blood Exam for Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas Disease)
PART 1 • CHAPTER 5 • SUBUNIT 5.9 • PP. 266–271

Examination of Blood for Trypanosoma cruzi (American Trypanosomiasis / Chagas Disease)

Comprehensive district laboratory procedures for diagnosing acute and chronic Chagas disease, Strout and Hoff blood concentration techniques, Romanowsky differential diagnosis with Trypanosoma rangeli, xenodiagnosis, blood donor screening, and serodiagnosis according to Monica Cheesbrough.

Diagnostic Stages: Trypomastigotes (Blood) • Amastigotes (Pseudocysts in Muscle) Vectors: Triatomine Cone-Nosed Bugs (Triatoma, Rhodnius, Panstrongylus) Endemic: Central & South America (Mexico to Argentina)

1. Etiology, Distribution & Vector Transmission

Trypanosoma cruzi is the causative protozoan hemoflagellate of Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis), endemic throughout 21 tropical and subtropical countries of Central and South America (ranging from Mexico down to Argentina). WHO estimates approximately 13 million individuals are infected, with over 3 million presenting symptomatic disease.

T. cruzi Complex & Vectors

  • Strain Lineages: Divided into T. cruzi I (sylvatic/domestic cycles) and T. cruzi II (associated with severe parasitaemia, chronic megadisease, and severe myocarditis).
  • Primary Insect Vectors (Subfamily Triatominae, Family Reduviidae):
    • Triatoma infestans: Major domestic vector in Southern Cone (Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Peru, Uruguay).
    • Rhodnius prolixus: Principal vector in Colombia, Venezuela, Central America, Mexico.
    • Panstrongylus megistus: Brazil and Southern South America.
    • Triatoma dimidiata: Central America and northern South America.
    • Triatoma brasiliensis: Semi-arid north-eastern Brazil.

Modes of Transmission & Reservoir Hosts

  • Stercorarian Transmission: Transmission occurs NOT by vector bite, but via contamination of bite wounds or mucosal membranes with infectious vector feces containing metacyclic trypomastigotes passed while the bug takes a blood meal.
  • Blood Transfusion & Organ Transplant: High risk in endemic urban areas; mandatory serological donor screening is legally enforced.
  • Congenital Transmission: Transplacental transfer from asymptomatic infected mothers; causes premature birth, low birthweight, hepatosplenomegaly, or stillbirth.
  • Animal Reservoirs: Dogs, cats, opossums (Didelphis), armadillos (Dasypus), rodents, bats, and guinea pigs.

2. Clinical Spectrum: Acute vs. Chronic Chagas Disease

The pathogenesis is characterized by an acute phase of high parasitaemia followed by an indeterminate latency and a debilitating chronic phase dominated by destruction of autonomic ganglion plexus networks:

Clinical Phase Pathophysiology & Tissue Sites Key Physical Signs & Symptoms Laboratory Diagnostic Yield
Acute Chagas Disease (1–4 Months) Metacyclics invade local histiocytes and muscle fibers → transform into intracellular amastigotes (dividing by binary fission) → form pseudocysts → rupture into bloodstream as trypomastigotes. • Chagoma: Painless inflammatory skin induration at inoculation site.
• Romaña's Sign: Unilateral, painless bipalpebral edema and conjunctivitis with regional preauricular lymphadenopathy (pathognomonic after conjunctival entry).
• High fever, acute myocarditis, hepatosplenomegaly, meningoencephalitis.		 HIGH PARASITAEMIA:
• Direct wet preps • Thick/thin Giemsa films • Strout & Hoff concentration techniques.
Indeterminate / Latent Phase Parasites disappear from circulating blood; sequestered intracellularly within myocardium and smooth muscle cells. Immune response controls parasitaemia. Completely asymptomatic; normal ECG and radiology; can last 10–30 years or throughout patient lifetime. Blood microscopy NEGATIVE.
• Serology (ELISA, IFAT, IHAT) persistently POSITIVE.
Chronic Chagas Disease (10–30% of Patients) Autoimmune-mediated destruction and inflammatory fibrosis of myocardial conducting fibers and intramural autonomic nerve plexuses (Auerbach's and Meissner's plexuses). • Chronic Chagas Cardiomyopathy: Right bundle branch block (RBBB), ventricular arrhythmias, apical aneurysm with mural thrombi, sudden cardiac arrest (leading cause of heart failure in Latin America).
• Digestive Megadisease: Megaesophagus (severe dysphagia, regurgitation) and Megacolon (intractable constipation, fecaloma, volvulus).		 Direct blood microscopy is USELESS (subpatent parasitaemia).
• Confirmed by paired serology (ELISA + IFAT) • Xenodiagnosis • Specialized PCR/Blood Culture in reference labs.

3. Direct Microscopic & Concentration SOPs

In acute Chagas disease, immediate detection of circulating trypomastigotes is essential because early treatment with benznidazole or nifurtimox cures infection and prevents irreversible cardiac and digestive denervation.

BIOSAFETY ALERT: High Inoculation Risk

Live T. cruzi trypomastigotes can penetrate intact mucous membranes, conjunctiva, and minor skin abrasions. Staff MUST wear gloves and eye protection. NEVER break microhematocrit capillary tubes to retrieve blood for smears; use Strout or Hoff concentration instead.

Strout Concentration Technique SOP

Standard concentration method using clotted whole venous blood:

  1. Collect \(5 ext{–}10 ext{ mL}\) of venous blood into a clean dry glass tube without anticoagulant.
  2. Incubate for 1 hour at \(37^{\circ} ext{C}\) (or room temperature) to allow complete clot retraction.
  3. Carefully transfer the separated serum (containing freed trypanosomes) into a conical centrifuge tube.
  4. Centrifuge at low speed (\( ext{RCF }pprox 400 ext{ g}\), \(pprox 1,500 ext{–}2,000 ext{ rpm}\)) for 5 minutes.
  5. Discard supernatant; place a drop of sediment on a slide, coverslip, and examine with \( imes 40\) objective for rapidly moving flagellates.
  6. Spread remaining sediment into thin smears, fix in absolute methanol, and stain with Giemsa or Field's stain.

Hoff Concentration Technique SOP

Ammonium chloride red cell lysis concentration method:

  1. Collect \(2.5 ext{ mL}\) of venous blood into EDTA anticoagulant and mix gently.
  2. Dispense \(6 ext{–}7 ext{ mL}\) of buffered ammonium chloride lysing solution (Reagent No. 8) into a conical centrifuge tube.
  3. Add the EDTA whole blood, mix by inversion, and allow 3 minutes for complete red cell lysis.
  4. Centrifuge for 15 minutes at medium speed (\( ext{RCF } 400 ext{–}500 ext{ g}\)).
  5. Discard supernatant; tap tube to homogenize sediment and examine wet preparation and stained thin films.

4. Microscopic Differentiation: Trypanosoma cruzi vs. Trypanosoma rangeli

In Central and South America (especially Venezuela, Colombia, Brazil, Panama, and Guatemala), human blood may be co-infected with Trypanosoma rangeli. T. rangeli is a non-pathogenic hemoflagellate transmitted by the salivary bite of Rhodnius prolixus that produces long-lasting parasitaemia. Stained thin blood films must be carefully scrutinized to prevent false-positive Chagas diagnoses.

Plate 5.53 (Textbook p. 270): Giemsa-stained thin blood film comparison.
Right: Trypanosoma cruzi (classic curved C-shape, centrally placed nucleus, large prominent terminal kinetoplast).
Left: Trypanosoma rangeli (longer, slender form, small subterminal kinetoplast, nucleus situated in anterior third).
Morphological Feature Trypanosoma cruzi (Pathogen) Trypanosoma rangeli (Non-Pathogen)
Typical Shape in Fixed Films Characteristic curved 'C' or 'U' shape; short, stout body. Gracefully curved, undulating, elongated slender form.
Total Length \(12 ext{–}20\ \mu ext{m}\) (average \(pprox 16 ext{–}20\ \mu ext{m}\)). \(26 ext{–}34\ \mu ext{m}\) (significantly longer and thinner).
Kinetoplast (Size & Position) VERY LARGE, round/oval, dark-red staining; situated at the extreme posterior tip. SMALL, dot-like; situated subterminally (distance from the pointed posterior end).
Nucleus Position Centrally placed; stains red-mauve. Situated in the anterior third of the body.
Posterior End Blunt, truncated wedge shape. Tapered, long, pointed posterior end.
Transmission Route Stercorarian (infective feces rubbed into bite/mucosa). Salivarian (transmitted directly via bug saliva during feeding).

5. Chronic Diagnosis, Blood Bank Screening & Serology

Xenodiagnosis & Blood Culture

  • Xenodiagnosis: Laboratory-reared, pathogen-free 3rd/4th instar triatomine nymphs (starved for 2 weeks) are allowed to feed on the patient's arm for 30 minutes. Ingested parasites multiply into epimastigotes in the bug gut; fecal drops are examined microscopically at \(30 ext{–}60 ext{ days}\).
  • Blood Culture: Inoculation into specialized Novy-MacNeal-Nicolle (NNN) or liver infusion tryptose (LIT) blood agar; incubated at \(25 ext{–}28^{\circ} ext{C}\) and examined after 14–21 days.

Donor Screening & Blood Prophylaxis

  • Mandatory Serological Screening: All blood donations in endemic zones must be screened by at least two distinct serological tests (e.g. ELISA and Indirect Hemagglutination - IHAT or IFAT).
  • Gentian Violet (Crystal Violet) Chemoprophylaxis: In resource-limited regional blood centers where blood cannot be discarded, gentian violet (\(125 ext{ mg}\) per \(500 ext{ mL}\) blood, \(1:4,000\) dilution) is added and stored at \(4^{\circ} ext{C}\) for 24 hours to lyse trypanosomes prior to transfusion. (Causes transient skin/mucosa staining).
  • Congenital Chagas Diagnosis: Detection of infant-specific IgM antibodies (which do not cross placenta) or direct microhematocrit buffy coat examination at birth.

High-Yield Board Exam MCQs • Section 5.9 (Q313–Q320)

Eight rigorous clinical scenario questions with instant answer validation, scoring, and Monica Cheesbrough rationales.

MCQ 313 • Transmission Mode & Pathophysiology
A 7-year-old child from rural Bolivia presents with unilateral bipalpebral painless eyelid edema and conjunctivitis (Romaña's sign) following an insect bite sustained while sleeping in a thatched-roof house. How is Trypanosoma cruzi primarily transmitted from the triatomine bug vector to humans?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: Trypanosoma cruzi is transmitted via the stercorarian (posterior station) route. While feeding on host blood, the triatomine bug defecates; infectious metacyclic trypomastigotes present in the feces are rubbed into the bite wound, mucosal surfaces, or conjunctiva by the patient scratching the pruritic bite.
MCQ 314 • Microscopic Differential Diagnosis
A medical laboratory technologist examines a Giemsa-stained thin blood film from a febrile patient in Colombia and observes hemoflagellates measuring \(16\ \mu ext{m}\) with a characteristic curved 'C' shape, a central nucleus, and a prominent, very large round dark-red kinetoplast at the posterior tip. Which species is identified?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: The classical morphologic hallmark of T. cruzi trypomastigotes in thin Romanowsky films is their curved C-shape, length of \(12 ext{–}20\ \mu ext{m}\), central nucleus, and characteristically very large, terminal, dark-staining kinetoplast. In contrast, non-pathogenic T. rangeli is longer (\(27 ext{–}32\ \mu ext{m}\)), slender, has an anteriorly displaced nucleus, and a small subterminal kinetoplast.
MCQ 315 • Concentration Techniques: Strout vs. Hoff
Which of the following correctly describes the Strout concentration technique for detecting T. cruzi in acute Chagas disease?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: The Strout technique involves collecting \(5 ext{–}10 ext{ mL}\) of venous blood without anticoagulant, incubating at \(37^{\circ} ext{C}\) for 1 hour for clot retraction, and transferring the serum (which harbors liberated, active trypomastigotes) into a conical tube for low-speed centrifugation (\(400 ext{ g}\) for 5 minutes). The sediment is examined wet and stained.
MCQ 316 • Hoff Concentration Technique Mechanism
In the Hoff concentration technique for Trypanosoma cruzi diagnosis, what chemical reagent is added to EDTA blood to selectively lyse red blood cells prior to centrifugation?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: The Hoff technique mixes \(2.5 ext{ mL}\) of EDTA blood with \(6 ext{–}7 ext{ mL}\) of ammonium chloride lysing solution (Reagent No. 8). After 3 minutes of erythrocyte lysis, the tube is centrifuged at \(400 ext{–}500 ext{ g}\) for 15 minutes to concentrate intact, motile trypanosomes in the sediment.
MCQ 317 • Chronic Chagas Pathogenesis & Megadisease
A 52-year-old immigrant from Brazil presents with severe dysphagia, regurgitation of unchewed food, intractable constipation, and an ECG showing right bundle branch block (RBBB) and apical left ventricular aneurysm. What is the fundamental cellular mechanism responsible for these chronic gastrointestinal manifestations?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: Chronic Chagas megadisease (megaesophagus and megacolon) is caused by irreversible inflammatory and autoimmune destruction of intramural parasympathetic ganglion cells within Auerbach's and Meissner's autonomic plexuses, leading to loss of peristalsis, achalasia, massive organ dilatation, and muscular wall thinning.
MCQ 318 • Laboratory Safety & Capillary Tube Handling
Why does Monica Cheesbrough explicitly warn laboratory staff NEVER to break microhematocrit capillary tubes when harvesting concentrated blood buffy coat for Trypanosoma cruzi smear preparation?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: Breaking capillary tubes carries a catastrophic risk of puncture injuries and micro-aerosol/splashing to eyes and skin. T. cruzi can establish life-threatening infections through minuscule abrasions or intact conjunctiva. Strout or Hoff concentration in capped tubes must be used instead.
MCQ 319 • Blood Bank Chemoprophylaxis
In endemic areas of Latin America where blood transfusion transmission of Chagas disease is a severe threat, what substance and storage protocol has been historically utilized to treat donor blood units when infected units cannot be discarded?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: Addition of gentian violet (\(125 ext{ mg}\) per \(500 ext{ mL}\) of whole blood, \(1:4,000\)) followed by refrigerated incubation at \(2 ext{–}8^{\circ} ext{C}\) for 24 hours reliably kills circulating T. cruzi trypomastigotes in donor blood, though it reversibly discolors the patient's tissues.
MCQ 320 • Xenodiagnosis Protocol
What is the standardized biological principle of xenodiagnosis used for parasitological confirmation in chronic Chagas disease?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: In xenodiagnosis, clean laboratory-reared triatomine bugs (starved for 2 weeks) feed on the suspected chronic patient. Ingested subpatent trypomastigotes multiply within the insect midgut into epimastigotes and metacyclics, which are demonstrated by microscopic examination of rectal drops/feces at \(30 ext{–}60 ext{ days}\).

PART 1 • CHAPTER 5 • SUBUNIT 5.10 • PP. 271–279

Examination of Specimens for Leishmania Parasites (Kala-Azar, Cutaneous & Mucocutaneous Leishmaniasis)

Comprehensive district laboratory procedures for diagnosing Visceral Leishmaniasis (VL / Kala-Azar), Cutaneous Leishmaniasis (CL), Diffuse Cutaneous (DCL), and Mucocutaneous Leishmaniasis (MCL / Espundia). Microscopic identification of Leishman-Donovan (LD) amastigote bodies in splenic, bone marrow, and lymph node aspirates, slit-skin smears, rK39 immunochromatographic rapid dipsticks, Direct Agglutination Test (DAT), Formol-Gel aldehyde screening, Montenegro skin test, and NNN culture according to Monica Cheesbrough.

Intracellular Stage: Amastigotes (LD Bodies, \(2 ext{–}4\ \mu ext{m}\)) Vector: Female Phlebotomine Sandflies (Phlebotomus & Lutzomyia) Key Species: L. donovani, L. infantum, L. tropica, L. major, L. braziliensis

1. Principal Leishmania Species, Complexes & Clinical Spectra

The leishmaniases are vector-borne protozoan parasitic infections caused by obligate intracellular hemoflagellates of the genus Leishmania. Endemic in 88 countries across Africa, the Indian subcontinent, the Middle East, the Mediterranean basin, and Central/South America, placing 350 million people at risk with over 1.5–2 million new cases annually.

Clinical Entity Species Complex & Etiological Agents Vector & Geographic Endemicity Primary Diagnostic Specimens
Visceral Leishmaniasis (VL / Kala-Azar) • L. donovani: Anthroponotic; severe epidemics in India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya.
• L. infantum (syn. L. chagasi): Zoonotic (canine reservoirs); Mediterranean, Middle East, Brazil, Central/South America.		 • Old World: Phlebotomus sandflies (P. argentipes, P. orientalis, P. martini).
• New World: Lutzomyia longipalpis.		 Splenic aspirate (\(95 ext{–}98\%\) yield), Bone marrow aspirate (\(64 ext{–}86\%\)), Lymph node aspirate (\(55 ext{–}64\%\)), Buffy coat smears, rK39 RDT, DAT serology.
Post Kala-Azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL) Sequela of L. donovani occurring months to years after treated/untreated VL (\(5 ext{–}10\%\) in India; up to \(50\%\) in Sudan). Hypopigmented macules, papules, erythematous butterfly facial nodules. Major reservoir for epidemic anthroponotic transmission during inter-epidemic periods. Slit-skin smears from nodular lesions; dermal punch biopsy (contain abundant LD bodies in monocytes).
Cutaneous Leishmaniasis (CL / Oriental Sore) • Old World CL: L. tropica (urban dry anthroponotic), L. major (rural wet zoonotic desert rodent reservoir), L. aethiopica (highlands).
• New World CL: L. mexicana (chiclero ulcer), L. peruviana (uta), L. guyanensis (pian bois), L. panamensis.		 • Old World: Phlebotomus sergenti, P. papatasi.
• New World: Lutzomyia spp. (forest dwelling).		 Slit-skin scrapings from active raised ulcer borders; needle aspirates from base of induration; Montenegro skin test.
Mucocutaneous Leishmaniasis (MCL / Espundia) • L. braziliensis (Viannia subgenus) and L. panamensis. Metastatic hematogenous/lymphatic spread leading to destructive necrosis of nasal septum, palate, pharynx, and larynx. South and Central America (Amazon basin, Bolivia, Peru, Brazil). Biopsy/scrapings of mucosal lesions (amastigotes scanty; marked cellular infiltrate); Montenegro skin test strongly positive (\(>95\%\)).

2. Transmission Cycle & Dimorphic Morphological Stages

Intracellular Amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan Bodies)

  • Habitat: Obligate intracellular parasites within the phagolysosomes of macrophages and monocytes of the reticuloendothelial system (spleen, liver, bone marrow, lymph nodes, dermis).
  • Morphology: Small, round to ovoid bodies measuring \(2 ext{–}4\ \mu ext{m}\) in diameter.
  • Romanowsky Staining (Giemsa / Leishman):
    • Cytoplasm: Pale sky-blue.
    • Nucleus: Large, round, staining dark reddish-mauve.
    • Kinetoplast: Distinct, dark rod-shaped or dot-like organelle lying perpendicular or tangent to the nucleus.
    • Flagellum: Non-emergent internal root (axoneme) visible under high oil immersion.

Extracellular Flagellated Promastigotes

  • Habitat: Midgut and proboscis of female sandflies; also the stage proliferating in artificial cultures (NNN agar).
  • Morphology: Slender, elongated spindle shape measuring \(10 ext{–}15\ \mu ext{m}\) in length by \(1.5 ext{–}3.5\ \mu ext{m}\) wide.
  • Flagellum: Single anterior free flagellum (\(15 ext{–}20\ \mu ext{m}\)) providing active, rapid, darting motility.
  • Transmission: Inoculated as infectious metacyclic promastigotes into the skin when the female sandfly takes a blood meal. Phagocytosed by dermal macrophages → transform into amastigotes within 12–24 hours.

3. Clinical Microscopy Atlas: Diagnostic Amastigote Plates

Plate 5.54 (Textbook p. 276): Leishmania amastigotes inside a circulating monocyte in a Giemsa-stained peripheral buffy coat blood film from a Kala-Azar patient.
Plate 5.55 (Textbook p. 276): Giemsa-stained Leishman-Donovan (LD) amastigotes showing dark mauve nuclei and distinct rod-like kinetoplasts inside reticuloendothelial macrophages.

4. Diagnostic SOPs for Visceral Leishmaniasis (Kala-Azar)

Tissue Aspirates: Sensitivity & Safety Rules

  • Splenic Aspiration (Positivity: \(95 ext{–}98\%\)): Highest diagnostic sensitivity; gold standard.
    Mandatory Safety Pre-requisites: Must check prothrombin time (\( ext{PT} \le ext{control} + 5 ext{ s}\)) and platelet count (\(>40,000/\mu ext{L}\) or \(>40 imes 10^9/ ext{L}\)). Spleen must be palpable \(\ge 3 ext{ cm}\) below costal margin. Monitor bed rest, pulse, and BP for 6 hours post-aspiration to detect internal hemorrhage.
  • Bone Marrow Aspiration (Positivity: \(64 ext{–}86\%\)): Iliac crest (adults) or sternum/tibia (children); safer in patients with severe bleeding diathesis or thrombocytopenia.
  • Lymph Node Aspiration (Positivity: \(55 ext{–}64\%\)): Inguinal or cervical lymph nodes; particularly sensitive in East African (Sudanese) VL and Mediterranean canine leishmaniasis.
  • Staining SOP: Thinly smeared, methanol-fixed for 2 minutes, stained with Giemsa (1:10 at pH 7.2 for 25–30 min) or rapid Field's stain. Examined under \( imes 100\) oil immersion (\(>1,000\) fields or 15–20 minutes before reporting negative).

Serodiagnosis & Formol-Gel Aldehyde Test

  • rK39 Immunochromatographic Rapid Dipstick: Detects high-titre circulating IgG antibodies to 39-amino-acid recombinant kinesin-related antigen of L. infantum/donovani.
    • Sensitivity: \(98 ext{–}100\%\) in Indian subcontinent; \(85 ext{–}92\%\) in East Africa.
    • Result in 10–15 minutes with 1 drop (\(20\ \mu ext{L}\)) of whole blood or serum.
    • Note: Remains positive for months/years post-cure; cannot be used for test-of-cure or distinguishing relapse from reinfection. In HIV/VL co-infection, sensitivity drops to \(60 ext{–}75\%\).
  • Direct Agglutination Test (DAT): Freeze-dried, trypsin-treated, Coomassie blue-stained whole L. donovani promastigotes in V-bottom microtitre plates. High sensitivity (\(95 ext{–}99\%\)) and specificity (\(98\%\)).

Formol-Gel (Aldehyde) Test SOP & Interpretation

A rapid non-specific screening test reflecting marked polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (elevated IgG) characteristic of visceral leishmaniasis (\(>3 ext{ months}\) duration):

  1. Dispense \(1 ext{ mL}\) of clear patient serum into a small test tube.
  2. Add 1 drop (\(50\ \mu ext{L}\)) of commercial concentrated formalin (37–40% w/v formaldehyde).
  3. Mix thoroughly and observe at room temperature for up to 20 minutes.
  4. Positive Reaction: Solidification and opacification like the white of a hard-boiled egg within 3–20 minutes (indicates serum IgG \(>30 ext{ g/L}\)).
  5. Negative Reaction: Serum remains liquid and transparent. (Note: Also positive in multiple myeloma, trypanosomiasis, and advanced cirrhosis).
Plate 5.56: Left: Positive opaque clot (+) • Right: Negative liquid (-)

5. Diagnostic SOPs for Cutaneous & Mucocutaneous Leishmaniasis

Slit-Skin Smear & Ulcer Border Scraping SOP

  1. Clean the ulcer border thoroughly with \(70\%\) ethanol; crusts must be removed. Secondary bacterial infection must be treated first.
  2. Pinch the active indurated margin of the lesion firmly between thumb and index finger to blanch the tissue and stop bleeding.
  3. With a sterile scalpel blade (No. 15), make a small \(2 ext{–}3 ext{ mm}\) superficial slit into the dermis at the inside margin of the lesion border.
  4. Scrape the sides of the slit to collect tissue juice and dermal pulp (avoiding gross blood contamination).
  5. Smear thinly onto a clean slide, air-dry, fix in absolute methanol for 2 minutes, and stain with Giemsa (Plate 5.57).

Montenegro Leishmanin Skin Test & NNN Culture

  • Montenegro (Leishmanin) Skin Test: Delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) skin test using \(0.1 ext{ mL}\) suspension of killed promastigotes (\(5 imes 10^6/ ext{mL}\) in phenol saline) injected intradermally on the volar forearm.
    • Read at \(48 ext{–}72 ext{ hours}\). Positive reaction: induration \(\ge 5 ext{ mm}\).
    • Positive: Uncomplicated CL and MCL (\(>95\%\)).
    • Negative: Active Visceral Leishmaniasis (due to T-cell anergy) and Diffuse Cutaneous Leishmaniasis (DCL). Becomes positive 6–12 months after successful treatment of VL.
  • Novy-MacNeal-Nicolle (NNN) Blood Agar Culture: Rabit-blood enriched biphasic agar overlayed with physiological saline containing penicillin and streptomycin. Incubated at \(22 ext{–}26^{\circ} ext{C}\) (never \(37^{\circ} ext{C}\)) and examined weekly for motile flagellated promastigotes for up to 4 weeks.
Plate 5.57 (Textbook p. 278): High-power photomicrograph of a Giemsa-stained slit-skin scraping from the active border of an Oriental sore showing numerous intracellular and ruptured extracellular Leishmania amastigotes.

High-Yield Board Exam MCQs • Section 5.10 (Q321–Q328)

Eight rigorous clinical scenario questions with instant answer validation, scoring, and Monica Cheesbrough rationales.

MCQ 321 • Parasitological Yield & Splenic Aspiration Safety
A 28-year-old male from Bihar, India presents with prolonged irregular fever, marked cachexia, massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia, and hypergammaglobulinemia. Which tissue aspiration site provides the highest diagnostic sensitivity for demonstrating Leishman-Donovan (LD) bodies, and what mandatory hematological criteria must be satisfied prior to the procedure?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: Splenic aspiration yields the highest diagnostic sensitivity (\(95 ext{–}98\%\)), compared to bone marrow (\(64 ext{–}86\%\)) and lymph node (\(55 ext{–}64\%\)). Because of the catastrophic risk of fatal splenic capsule laceration, strict pre-conditions must be verified: platelet count \(>40 imes 10^9/ ext{L}\) (\(>40,000/\mu ext{L}\)), prothrombin time within 5 seconds of control, and spleen palpable \(\ge 3 ext{ cm}\).
MCQ 322 • Amastigote Microscopic Morphology
Under oil immersion (\( imes 100\) objective), a technologist observes intracellular structures within reticuloendothelial macrophages in a Giemsa-stained bone marrow smear. Which description definitively identifies Leishmania amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies)?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: Leishmania amastigotes (LD bodies) are small intracellular organisms (\(2 ext{–}4\ \mu ext{m}\)). In Romanowsky stains, they demonstrate a pale blue cytoplasm, a large spherical mauve nucleus, and a pathognomonic dark rod-like or dot-like kinetoplast lying adjacent to the nucleus. (Option A describes Toxoplasma gondii; Option D describes promastigotes).
MCQ 323 • rK39 Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) Characteristics
Which statement regarding the rK39 immunochromatographic rapid dipstick test for Visceral Leishmaniasis is clinically and methodologically accurate?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: The rK39 test is an antibody-detection dipstick (detecting high-titre IgG against a 39-amino-acid repeat kinesin antigen). It gives results in 10–15 minutes with \(>98\%\) sensitivity in South Asia. However, because anti-rK39 antibodies persist for months to years after successful cure, it CANNOT be used as a test-of-cure or to distinguish relapse from reinfection, and its sensitivity is compromised (\(60 ext{–}75\%\)) in HIV-coinfected individuals.
MCQ 324 • Formol-Gel (Aldehyde) Test Mechanism
In district laboratories where specialized serology is unavailable, what biochemical phenomenon is responsible for a positive Formol-Gel (Aldehyde) test in a patient with chronic Kala-Azar?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: The Formol-Gel test is a non-specific screening test. Chronic visceral leishmaniasis stimulates massive polyclonal B-cell activation, elevating serum IgG levels (\(>30 ext{ g/L}\)). Adding 1 drop of commercial formalin to \(1 ext{ mL}\) of serum results in rapid protein cross-linking, producing a solid, opaque gel resembling boiled egg white within 3 to 20 minutes.
MCQ 325 • Montenegro (Leishmanin) Skin Test Interpretation
What is the expected result of the Montenegro (Leishmanin) delayed-type hypersensitivity skin test in an untreated patient suffering from active, florid Visceral Leishmaniasis (Kala-Azar)?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: During active Visceral Leishmaniasis (and Diffuse Cutaneous Leishmaniasis), specific cell-mediated immunity is suppressed (marked T-cell anergy), making the Montenegro test negative. Following successful antiparasitic cure, cell-mediated immunity recovers and the test converts to positive (\(\ge 5 ext{ mm}\) induration at 48–72 hours). In contrast, uncomplicated CL and MCL patients test strongly positive throughout active disease.
MCQ 326 • Slit-Skin Smear Technique in Cutaneous Leishmaniasis
When preparing a diagnostic slit-skin scraping for suspected Cutaneous Leishmaniasis (Oriental sore), why does Monica Cheesbrough specify that the sample must be obtained from the active indurated margin/border rather than the center of the ulcer?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: The necrotic floor of an ulcerated lesion contains dead tissue, polymorphonuclear leukocytes, and secondary bacterial invaders, resulting in very low diagnostic yield. The active, indurated, raised outer border contains intact, parasite-laden histiocytic macrophages. Pinching the margin to arrest blood flow and scraping dermal tissue juice yields the highest concentration of amastigotes.
MCQ 327 • NNN Culture Medium SOP
Which incubation temperature and morphological transformation occur when tissue aspirates containing Leishmania amastigotes are inoculated onto Novy-MacNeal-Nicolle (NNN) blood agar medium?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: In vitro cultivation of Leishmania mimics the poikilothermic vector insect gut. Inoculation into biphasic NNN agar must be maintained at \(22 ext{–}26^{\circ} ext{C}\) (incubating at \(37^{\circ} ext{C}\) kills the organisms). Within 7 to 21 days, amastigotes transform into slender, motile, flagellated promastigotes (\(10 ext{–}15\ \mu ext{m}\)) demonstrating darting motility in the liquid phase.
MCQ 328 • Post Kala-Azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL)
A 35-year-old Sudanese farmer treated for Kala-Azar 2 years ago presents with widespread hypopigmented macules and nodular skin eruptions on his face and trunk. What is the clinical diagnosis and epidemiological significance of this presentation?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: Post Kala-Azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL) is a dermatological manifestation that follows treated or subclinical L. donovani visceral leishmaniasis. The nodular lesions harbor numerous viable amastigotes. In anthroponotic regions (India and Sudan), patients with PKDL are the primary reservoir maintaining parasite transmission to feeding Phlebotomus sandflies during inter-epidemic periods.

PART 1 • CHAPTER 5 • SUBUNIT 5.11 • PP. 280–291

Examination of Blood for Microfilariae in Lymphatic Filariasis and Loiasis

Comprehensive district laboratory procedures for the identification, concentration, staining, and quantitation of blood-borne microfilariae: Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, Brugia timori, Loa loa, Mansonella perstans, and Mansonella ozzardi. Microfilarial periodicity schedules, capillary sampling, Saponin lysis, Polycarbonate Membrane Filtration, Delafield's hematoxylin staining, NOW ICT Filariasis circulating antigen card test, and DEC provocative screening according to Monica Cheesbrough.

Sheathed vs. Unsheathed • Tail Nuclei Architecture Periodicity: Nocturnal (\(22:00 ext{–}04:00\)) • Diurnal (\(10:00 ext{–}14:00\)) • Non-periodic Concentration: \(5\ \mu ext{m}\) Polycarbonate Membrane Filtration • Saponin Lysis

1. Filarial Species, Endemic Distribution & Periodicity Timing

Microfilariae are the pre-larval embryonic stages produced by adult filarial nematodes dwelling in lymphatic vessels, subcutaneous tissues, or body cavities. Because microfilarial release into peripheral circulation follows strict rhythmic periodicity, blood collection MUST coincide with the peak circulation window of the suspected species:

Filarial Nematode Clinical Disease Entity Microfilarial Periodicity Optimal Sampling Time Primary Insect Vectors
Wuchereria bancrofti (Sheathed) Bancroftian Lymphatic Filariasis (Hydrocele, retroperitoneal lymphangitis, elephantiasis of legs/genitalia, chyluria). Nocturnal periodic (majority)
Subperiodic diurnal (Polynesia)		 \(22:00 ext{–}04:00 ext{ h}\) (night)
\(14:00 ext{–}18:00 ext{ h}\) (Pacific)		 Culex quinquefasciatus (urban), Anopheles spp. (rural Africa), Aedes spp. (Pacific).
Brugia malayi (Sheathed) Malayan Lymphatic Filariasis (Elephantiasis below knees; genital sparing; acute adenolymphangitis). Nocturnal periodic (rural open swamps)
Subperiodic nocturnal (forest swamps)		 \(22:00 ext{–}04:00 ext{ h}\)
\(20:00 ext{–}22:00 ext{ h}\)		 Mansonia spp. (swamp vegetation), Anopheles spp.
Brugia timori (Sheathed) Timor Filariasis (Severe recurrent lymphadenitis, draining abscesses, lower leg elephantiasis). Nocturnal periodic (Timor & Lesser Sunda Islands, Indonesia). \(22:00 ext{–}04:00 ext{ h}\) Anopheles barbirostris (rice fields).
Loa loa (Sheathed) Loiasis (African Eye Worm, transient fugitive Calabar swellings, subconjunctival adult worm migration). Diurnal periodic (daytime) \(10:00 ext{–}14:00 ext{ h}\) (midday) Chrysops deer flies (C. silacea, C. dimidiata — mangrove/rainforest daytime biters).
Mansonella perstans (Unsheathed) Mansonelliasis (Adults in peritoneal/pleural cavities; mild eosinophilia, arthralgia, pruritus). Non-periodic (found day or night) Any time (day or night) Culicoides biting midges (C. austeni, C. grahamii).
Mansonella ozzardi (Unsheathed) New World Mansonelliasis (Adults in body cavities; mostly asymptomatic; joint pain, headache). Non-periodic (Caribbean, Central/South America). Any time (day or night) Culicoides midges and Simulium blackflies.

2. Comparative Morphology: Diagnostic Tail & Sheath Features

Definitive species identification in stained thick films or membrane filters depends on four core morphologic criteria: (1) Presence/absence of a sheath, (2) Size and gracefulness of body curves, (3) Nuclear column packing, and crucially (4) Tail tip nuclear arrangement:

Plate 5.58c: W. bancrofti tail (No nuclei in tip)
Plate 5.58f: B. malayi tail (2 terminal nuclei)
Plate 5.58g: Loa loa (Kinky body, continuous nuclei)
Plate 5.58j: M. perstans (Small, blunt tail)
Plate 5.58 Comprehensive Textbook Atlas (p. 287): High-power microscopic identification of blood microfilariae in Giemsa and Delafield's hematoxylin stained blood preparations.
Species Sheath Staining Length & Body Curve Nuclear Column Tail Architecture & Nuclei
Wuchereria bancrofti Sheathed (Stains poorly in Giemsa; clearly in Delafield's hematoxylin). \(240 ext{–}300\ \mu ext{m}\); graceful, smooth sweeping curves; cephalic space \(L:W = 1:1\). Regular, distinct, discrete nuclei easily counted individually. Pointed tail; TERMINAL TIP CLEAR OF NUCLEI (no nuclei in the posterior \(10 ext{–}15\ \mu ext{m}\)).
Brugia malayi Sheathed (Stains bright deep pink in Giemsa). \(180 ext{–}240\ \mu ext{m}\); stiff, crinkled, angular kinky curves; long cephalic space (\(L:W = 2:1\)). Dense, tightly packed, overlapping, blurred nuclear column. Tapered tail with TWO SEPARATE TERMINAL NUCLEI (one subterminal, one isolated at extreme tip).
Brugia timori Sheathed (Sheath does NOT stain in Giemsa; unstained space). \(290 ext{–}320\ \mu ext{m}\) (longer than B. malayi); elongated cephalic space (\(L:W = 3:1\)). Discrete nuclei; less confluent than B. malayi. Tapered tail with two terminal nuclei; sheath remains unstained in Giemsa.
Loa loa Sheathed (Unstained in Giemsa; stains pale blue-grey in Delafield's hematoxylin). \(250 ext{–}300\ \mu ext{m}\); coiled, undulating, kinky rigid curves; short cephalic space (\(L:W = 1:1\)). Coarse, irregular, crowded nuclear column. Blunt rounded tail; NUCLEI EXTEND CONTINUOUSLY TO THE EXTREME TAIL TIP.
Mansonella perstans UNSHEATHED Small: \(100 ext{–}150\ \mu ext{m}\); slender, graceful curves; short cephalic space. Prominent, densely packed nuclei. Distinctive BLUNT TRUNCATE TAIL filled with nuclei to the end.
Mansonella ozzardi UNSHEATHED \(160 ext{–}200\ \mu ext{m}\); slender body with smooth curves. Compact, uniform nuclei. Long, thin, TAPERED POINTED TAIL WITH NO NUCLEI IN TIP.

3. Standard Concentration & Staining Protocols

Saponin Lysis Concentration SOP

  1. At the scheduled periodicity window, collect \(100\ \mu ext{L}\) (\(0.1 ext{ mL}\)) of capillary blood into a conical tube containing \(1 ext{ mL}\) of saponin-saline solution (Reagent No. 51).
  2. Mix gently and allow 2 minutes for complete red cell stromatolysis (remains transparent red).
  3. Centrifuge for 5 minutes at low-to-medium speed (\( ext{RCF } 300 ext{–}500 ext{ g}\)). Warning: Avoid high speed to prevent microfilarial unsheathing artifacts.
  4. Discard supernatant; transfer sediment to a slide, add a drop of methylene blue-saline, cover with \(22 imes 40 ext{ mm}\) coverslip, and count active motile microfilariae under \( imes 10\) objective.

Polycarbonate Membrane Filtration SOP

  1. Load a \(25 ext{ mm}\) diameter, \(5\ \mu ext{m}\) pore-size clear polycarbonate membrane filter (Nuclepore) into a Swinney filter holder.
  2. Draw \(1 ext{ mL}\) of EDTA/citrated venous blood into a \(10 ext{ mL}\) syringe followed by \(9 ext{ mL}\) of distilled water or \(1\%\) Teepol; invert to lyse red cells.
  3. Attach the syringe to the Swinney filter holder and push the hemolysed blood steadily through the filter.
  4. Flush with \(10 ext{ mL}\) of distilled water, then push \(5 ext{ mL}\) of air to clear fluid.
  5. Remove filter with fine forceps, place flat on a microscope slide, stain with hot Delafield's hematoxylin or Field's stain, and examine under \( imes 10\) and \( imes 40\) for absolute microfilarial quantitation per mL.

Delafield's Rapid Hematoxylin & DEC Day Provocation

Delafield's Rapid Hematoxylin Staining SOP:

Romanowsky (Giemsa) stains fail to color the sheath of Loa loa and W. bancrofti. Delafield's hematoxylin specifically stains microfilarial sheaths pale blue-grey and nuclear columns deep blue-purple. Methanol-fixed smears are covered with Field's B + A (1 min), rinsed in buffered water pH 7.1–7.2, and stained with heated Delafield's (1:10) for 5 minutes.

DEC (Diethylcarbamazine) Daytime Provocation Test:

Used when nocturnal blood sampling for W. bancrofti is culturally or logistically impossible. An oral dose of \(100 ext{ mg}\) DEC (or \(2 ext{ mg/kg}\)) is administered during the daytime. Microfilariae are provoked out of pulmonary capillaries into peripheral blood within \(30 ext{–}60 ext{ minutes}\). CONTRAINDICATION: Never administer in areas co-endemic for Onchocerca volvulus (severe Mazzotti reaction) or heavy Loa loa infections (fatal encephalopathy).

4. NOW ICT Filariasis Circulating Antigen Rapid Test

The NOW ICT Filariasis Card Test (Binax Inc.) is the WHO gold-standard rapid immunochromatographic diagnostic assay for Bancroftian filariasis elimination programs:

  • Antigen Target: Detects soluble, circulating circulating filarial antigen (CFA) released by adult Wuchereria bancrofti worms (AD12.1 monoclonal antibody gold conjugate).
  • Daytime Feasibility: Because CFA is released continuously by adult worms regardless of microfilarial periodicity, blood can be collected ANY TIME OF DAY OR NIGHT.
  • Volume & Timing: Requires \(100\ \mu ext{L}\) of fingerprick whole blood or serum; read through the viewing window at 10 minutes (Plate 5.59).
  • Interpretation:
    • Positive (2 Lines): Test line (T) + Control line (C) indicates active adult W. bancrofti infection (even in amicrofilaremic/latent cases).
    • Negative (1 Line): Control line (C) only.
  • Specificity: 100% specific for W. bancrofti; negative for Brugia spp., Loa loa, Onchocerca, and Mansonella.
Plate 5.59: NOW ICT Filariasis rapid test card showing positive dual pink lines (T and C) at 10 minutes.

High-Yield Board Exam MCQs • Section 5.11 (Q329–Q336)

Eight rigorous clinical scenario questions with instant answer validation, scoring, and Monica Cheesbrough rationales.

MCQ 329 • Blood Sampling Timing & Periodicity
A district laboratory technologist in coastal Kenya is requested to examine blood for suspected nocturnal periodic Wuchereria bancrofti microfilariae in a patient presenting with scrotal hydrocele. What is the scientifically recommended blood collection window to achieve peak diagnostic sensitivity?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: Microfilariae of nocturnal periodic Wuchereria bancrofti are sequestered in the deep pulmonary capillaries during daylight hours and emerge into peripheral blood exclusively between \(22:00 ext{ and }04:00 ext{ h}\), coinciding with the peak biting activity of nocturnal vector mosquitoes (Culex quinquefasciatus and Anopheles spp.).
MCQ 330 • Microscopic Tail Differentiation
Examination of a Giemsa-stained thick blood film from an expatriate missionary returning from Gabon reveals sheathed microfilariae measuring \(270\ \mu ext{m}\) in length with coarse, crowded nuclei that extend in an unbroken column continuously to the very tip of the blunt tail. Which filarial species is confirmed?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: The key diagnostic characteristic of Loa loa microfilariae is that its dense nuclear column extends continuously to the extreme tip of its rounded/blunt tail (Plate 5.58h). In contrast, W. bancrofti has a terminal tail space completely devoid of nuclei, and B. malayi has two distinct terminal nuclei.
MCQ 331 • Brugia malayi Morphologic Hallmark
Which distinct morphological feature definitively differentiates the microfilariae of Brugia malayi from Wuchereria bancrofti in a Romanowsky-stained blood smear?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: Brugia malayi is characterized by stiff, angular, irregular body curves, a prominent long cephalic space (\(L:W = 2:1\)), a sheath that stains intensely bright pink with Giemsa, and a tail that tapers with two distinct separated terminal nuclei (one subterminal and one at the tip).
MCQ 332 • NOW ICT Filariasis Diagnostic Principle
What fundamental biological advantage enables the NOW ICT Filariasis card test to detect Wuchereria bancrofti infections in blood collected during normal daytime clinic hours?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: The NOW ICT Filariasis test detects soluble circulating filarial antigen (CFA) produced by living adult Wuchereria bancrofti. Because CFA circulates in the peripheral bloodstream 24 hours a day at steady concentrations, diagnostic blood sampling can be performed conveniently during daytime hours without requiring nocturnal venipuncture.
MCQ 333 • Polycarbonate Membrane Filtration Technique
What pore size of polycarbonate membrane filter is specified by Monica Cheesbrough for the quantitative concentration of microfilariae from hemolysed venous blood?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: The membrane filtration technique employs a \(25 ext{ mm}\) diameter clear polycarbonate membrane filter with a pore size of \(5\ \mu ext{m}\) (or \(3\ \mu ext{m}\)). Lysed blood erythrocytes pass freely through the pores, while intact microfilariae (width \(5 ext{–}9\ \mu ext{m}\), length \(150 ext{–}300\ \mu ext{m}\)) are retained quantitatively on the surface.
MCQ 334 • DEC Daytime Provocation Test Contraindications
A health center in Nigeria plans a daytime survey for Bancroftian filariasis using diethylcarbamazine (DEC) provocation. Under which clinical circumstance is the DEC provocation test STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: DEC administration causes rapid destruction of microfilariae. In individuals co-infected with Onchocerca volvulus, it provokes a severe life-threatening inflammatory reaction (Mazzotti reaction) causing blindness and collapse. In patients with heavy Loa loa infections (\(>8,000 ext{ microfilariae/mL}\)), DEC precipitates severe destructive fatal encephalopathy.
MCQ 335 • Mansonella perstans Diagnosis
In a non-periodic daytime blood sample from Uganda, a technologist observes small unsheathed microfilariae measuring \(120\ \mu ext{m}\) with densely packed nuclei and a characteristic blunt, rounded, truncate tail filled with nuclei to the end. What is the diagnosis?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: Mansonella perstans is a small (\(100 ext{–}150\ \mu ext{m}\)), unsheathed microfilaria found in tropical Africa and South America. It lacks periodicity and is distinguished by its blunt, truncate posterior end packed with nuclei right to the tail margin (Plate 5.58j).
MCQ 336 • Delafield's Rapid Hematoxylin Purpose
Why is Delafield's rapid hematoxylin staining specifically utilized when Romanowsky (Giemsa) staining proves inconclusive during the microscopic evaluation of blood microfilariae?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: The sheaths of Loa loa and W. bancrofti frequently fail to take up Romanowsky dyes (remaining completely clear or faint). Delafield's hematoxylin stains the sheath a distinct pale blue-grey and the somatic nuclei a crisp deep blue-purple, allowing precise differentiation of sheath presence and terminal nuclear positioning.

PART 1 • CHAPTER 5 • SUBUNIT 5.12 • PP. 291–295

Examination of Skin for Onchocerca volvulus Microfilariae (River Blindness / Onchocerciasis)

Comprehensive district laboratory protocols for the detection, harvesting, and quantitation of dermal microfilariae: Onchocerca volvulus and Mansonella streptocerca. Standard bloodless skin-snip biopsy techniques (needle & scalpel vs. Walser corneoscleral punch), physiological saline incubation, microscopic motility evaluation, Giemsa morphological differentiation, Mazzotti DEC patch testing, nodule palpation (onchocercomas), and microfilarial density quantitation in epidemiological surveys according to Monica Cheesbrough.

Dermal Stage: Unsheathed Microfilariae (\(220 ext{–}360\ \mu ext{m}\)) Vector: Simulium Blackflies (S. damnosum s.l., S. neavei, S. ochraceum) Clinical Hallmark: Onchocercomas, Sclerosing Keratitis, Chorioretinitis (River Blindness)

1. Etiology, Vectors & Clinical Spectrum

Onchocerca volvulus is a filarial tissue nematode causing onchocerciasis (River Blindness), endemic across 30 African countries, Yemen, and localized foci in Central and South America (Guatemala, Mexico, Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Brazil). WHO estimates over 18 million infected individuals, with nearly 1 million visually impaired or blind.

Vector Biology & Transmission Cycle

  • Blackfly Vectors (Family Simuliidae): Transmitted by female Simulium blackflies that breed exclusively in fast-flowing, well-oxygenated rivers and streams ("River Blindness").
    • Simulium damnosum sensu lato (major African vector).
    • Simulium neavei (East Africa).
    • Simulium ochraceum and S. metallicum (Central/South America).
  • Adult Worms (Macrofilariae): Inoculated third-stage larvae (\( ext{L}_3\)) mature over 10–12 months into adult worms living encapsulated in fibrous subcutaneous nodules (onchocercomas) for 10–15 years.
  • Dermal Microfilariae: Gravid female worms produce thousands of unsheathed microfilariae daily that migrate actively through interstitial dermis and ocular tissues (lifespan 1–2 years). They do NOT enter peripheral circulation in significant numbers.

Clinical Manifestations & Pathology

  • Subcutaneous Onchocercomas: Firm, painless, non-tender fibrous nodules (\(0.5 ext{–}5 ext{ cm}\)) over bony prominences.
    • African Savannah: Predominantly on pelvic girdle, iliac crests, greater trochanters, ribs, and lower limbs.
    • Central America: Predominantly on the scalp, skull, neck, and upper torso (due to S. ochraceum biting habits).
  • Onchocercal Dermatitis: Severe pruritus, papular onchodermatitis, chronic atrophy ("lizard skin"), patchy depigmentation ("leopard skin" over shins), and hanging groin (loss of dermal elasticity with inguinal lymphadenopathy).
  • Ocular Lesions & Blindness: Dying microfilariae in ocular tissues induce severe chronic inflammation: punctate keratitis (snowflake opacities), sclerosing keratitis, anterior uveitis, chorioretinitis, and optic atrophy leading to complete irreversible blindness.

2. Standard Operating Procedure (SOP): Bloodless Skin Snip Biopsy

The definitive parasitological diagnosis of onchocerciasis is the demonstration of living O. volvulus microfilariae emerging from a bloodless skin snip. Capillary bleeding must be strictly avoided to prevent contamination with blood microfilariae (e.g., Loa loa or M. perstans):

Plate 5.60 (Textbook p. 293): Standard needle and scalpel technique for elevating and excising a \(1 ext{–}2 ext{ mm}\) bloodless epidermal cone.
Plate 5.61 (Textbook p. 293): Unstained wet saline preparation under \( imes 10\) objective showing motile O. volvulus microfilariae actively wriggling out of the submerged skin snip.

Needle & Scalpel Elevation Method

  1. Anatomical Selection: Clean skin with \(70\%\) ethanol; allow to dry.
    • Africa: Posterior iliac crest / buttocks / calf (highest microfilarial density).
    • Central/South America: Outer scapula / deltoid / neck.
  2. Insert the tip of a sterile 23G/25G needle superficially into the epidermis; elevate a tiny skin cone \(1 ext{–}2 ext{ mm}\) in diameter without puncturing dermal capillaries (Plate 5.60).
  3. With a sterile scalpel blade (No. 11 or 15) held flat against the skin, slice off the peak of the tented skin cone. The snip should weigh approximately \(1 ext{–}2 ext{ mg}\) and appear bloodless.
  4. Immediately immerse the skin snip into \(1 ext{–}2 ext{ drops (approx. } 50 ext{–}100\ \mu ext{L})\) of physiological saline in a microtitre well or on a microscope slide.

Walser Scleral Punch & Survey Quantitation

  1. Walser / Holth Corneoscleral Punch: Used in standardized epidemiological surveys to collect uniform skin snips of exactly \(1.0\ \mu ext{m}\) depth and \(pprox 1.0 ext{–}2.0 ext{ mg}\) weight. Disinfected in \(70\%\) ethanol for 15 minutes between patients.
  2. Immerse each standardized snip into \(200\ \mu ext{L}\) of physiological saline in flat-bottom microtitre plate wells.
  3. Cover plate to prevent evaporation; incubate at room temperature for \(3 ext{–}4 ext{ hours}\) (or overnight in a moist chamber). Over \(90\%\) of microfilariae emerge within 4 hours.
  4. Count emerging microfilariae using an inverted microscope or \( imes 10\) objective. Calculate Microfilarial Density (MFD) as: \( ext{MF per mg skin weight}\) or \( ext{MF per standardized snip}\).

3. Microscopic Differentiation: O. volvulus vs. Mansonella streptocerca

In West and Central African rainforests (Nigeria, Cameroon, Ghana, D.R. Congo), skin snips frequently contain Mansonella streptocerca. Because M. streptocerca causes mild non-blinding dermatitis transmitted by Culicoides midges, definitive microscopic differentiation in Giemsa-stained smears is critical:

Plate 5.62a: Onchocerca volvulus (Straight/gently curved, pointed tail clear of nuclei)
Plate 5.62b: Mansonella streptocerca (Smaller, characteristic shepherd's crook hooked tail with nuclei to tip)
Plate 5.62 Textbook Atlas (p. 294): Giemsa-stained skin microfilariae under oil immersion (\( imes 100\) objective).
Morphological Feature Onchocerca volvulus (River Blindness) Mansonella streptocerca (Streptocerciasis)
Sheath Presence UNSHEATHED UNSHEATHED
Length & Breadth \(220 ext{–}360\ \mu ext{m}\) long; \(5 ext{–}9\ \mu ext{m}\) wide (larger). \(180 ext{–}240\ \mu ext{m}\) long; \(3 ext{–}5\ \mu ext{m}\) wide (noticeably smaller).
Tail Curvature Straight or gently curved; tapered to a fine point. Distinctive SHEPHERD'S CROOK (HOOKED TAIL) bent into a sharp 'J' curve.
Tail Nuclei Distribution TERMINAL TAIL TIP CLEAR OF NUCLEI (final \(10 ext{–}15\ \mu ext{m}\) is anucleated). NUCLEI EXTEND IN A SINGLE ROW TO THE VERY END OF THE HOOKED TIP.
Head / Cephalic Space Slightly spatulate head; cephalic space \(L:W = 1:1\). Rounded head; long cephalic space.
Vector & Habitat Simulium blackflies (riverine); adults in subcutaneous nodules. Culicoides midges (rainforest); adults in dermal connective tissue.

4. Mazzotti Reaction & Non-Invasive DEC Patch Test

The Systemic Mazzotti Reaction

Administration of oral diethylcarbamazine (DEC, \(50 ext{ mg}\)) in onchocerciasis causes rapid microfilarial destruction, triggering an acute, massive inflammatory response (Mazzotti reaction) within 2–6 hours: intense generalized pruritus, urticaria, high fever, tachycardia, hypotension, painful lymphadenopathy, and severe ocular flare with permanent retinal damage.
Systemic oral DEC is strictly obsolete for routine onchocerciasis diagnosis due to life-threatening toxicity.

Transdermal DEC Patch Test SOP

A non-invasive, highly specific field screening test avoiding systemic Mazzotti complications:

  1. Prepare an occlusive adhesive dressing containing \(1\%\) or \(10\%\) DEC in Nivea cream or petroleum jelly.
  2. Apply the patch firmly to the skin over the iliac crest or upper torso for 24 hours.
  3. Positive Reaction: Appearance of intense local erythematous papular rash and microvesicular dermatitis limited strictly to the patch contact area at \(24 ext{–}48 ext{ hours}\).

High-Yield Board Exam MCQs • Section 5.12 (Q337–Q344)

Eight rigorous clinical scenario questions with instant answer validation, scoring, and Monica Cheesbrough rationales.

MCQ 337 • Skin Snip Biopsy Technique & Safety
Why is it mandatory that skin snip biopsies collected for the parasitological diagnosis of Onchocerca volvulus be strictly bloodless?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: A skin snip must be strictly bloodless. If the dermal capillaries are punctured, blood enters the saline droplet, introducing circulating blood microfilariae (such as Loa loa or M. perstans in co-endemic zones of Africa), which causes false-positive misidentification.
MCQ 338 • Microscopic Differential: O. volvulus vs M. streptocerca
A technologist in Cameroon examines a Giemsa-stained smear prepared from an emergent skin snip preparation and identifies unsheathed microfilariae measuring \(210\ \mu ext{m}\) with a characteristic sharp 'J'-shaped hooked tail (shepherd's crook) containing nuclei in a continuous single row to the very tip. What is the diagnosis?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: Mansonella streptocerca microfilariae are unsheathed, smaller (\(180 ext{–}240\ \mu ext{m}\)), and possess a pathognomonic hooked tail bent like a shepherd's crook with nuclei extending to the extreme tip (Plate 5.62b). O. volvulus microfilariae are larger (\(220 ext{–}360\ \mu ext{m}\)), straight/gently curved, with a pointed tail completely clear of nuclei.
MCQ 339 • Anatomical Sampling Sites in Africa vs Americas
Why are diagnostic skin snips primarily taken from the pelvis, buttocks, and iliac crests in Africa, whereas in Central America (Guatemala and Mexico) they are taken from the outer scapula, shoulders, and neck?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: The anatomical distribution of onchocercomas and microfilariae reflects vector feeding habits. African Simulium damnosum flies feed close to the ground, biting predominantly on the legs and pelvis. In contrast, Central American Simulium ochraceum bites high on the body, resulting in nodules and highest microfilarial densities on the upper torso, neck, and head.
MCQ 340 • Incubation Time in Saline
According to Monica Cheesbrough, how long should a bloodless skin snip be incubated in physiological saline in a moist chamber to allow over \(90\%\) of living Onchocerca volvulus microfilariae to emerge into the fluid?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: While some microfilariae can be seen emerging within 15–30 minutes, \(3 ext{–}4 ext{ hours}\) of incubation at room temperature (or overnight storage in a moist container) is required for \(>90\%\) of the microfilariae to wriggle out of the dermal matrix into the saline droplet for accurate quantitative counting.
MCQ 341 • Walser Corneoscleral Punch Standardization
What is the specialized function of a Walser (or Holth) corneoscleral punch in onchocerciasis field control programs?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: The Walser punch is an ophthalmological corneoscleral punch adapted for epidemiological surveys. It takes uniform, calibrated, bloodless skin snips weighing approximately \(1.0 ext{–}2.0 ext{ mg}\) with minimal patient discomfort, allowing direct calculation of microfilarial density (MFD per mg of skin).
MCQ 342 • Transdermal DEC Patch Test
Which response characterizes a positive transdermal DEC patch test used for the non-invasive screening of onchocerciasis?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: The DEC patch test applies \(1\%\) or \(10\%\) DEC cream transdermally. Local absorption kills dermal microfilariae in that specific patch zone, creating a localized Mazzotti reaction (pruritic papular erythema and microvesicles) at 24–48 hours without inducing systemic collapse or ocular damage.
MCQ 343 • Microfilarial Morphology of O. volvulus
Which morphological profile accurately describes Onchocerca volvulus microfilariae in a Romanowsky-stained slide?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: Onchocerca volvulus microfilariae are unsheathed, measure \(220 ext{–}360\ \mu ext{m}\) in length, lie in smooth gentle curves, and feature a tapered pointed tail whose terminal \(10 ext{–}15\ \mu ext{m}\) tip is completely clear of nuclei (Plate 5.62a).
MCQ 344 • Vector Breeding Environment
What unique environmental and aquatic breeding requirement of Simulium blackflies explains why onchocerciasis is colloquially referred to as "River Blindness"?
Monica Cheesbrough In-Depth Rationale: Simulium blackfly larvae require high oxygen saturation to breathe through external gill filaments. Consequently, breeding is strictly restricted to fast-flowing, turbulent rivers, rapids, and cascading streams. Human communities residing in fertile river valleys suffer intense vector biting, leading to high parasite loads and endemic blindness.
