Media Taxonomy Formulation Chemistry

1. Classification & Functional Categories of Culture Media

A culture medium must supply essential nitrogen (peptone), carbon/energy, mineral salts, water, appropriate buffering (\(\text{pH}\ 7.2–7.4\)), and a solidifying agent (agar-agar, melting at \(95–100^\circ\text{C}\) and solidifying at \(42–45^\circ\text{C}\)):

Functional Category Definition & Mode of Action Key Examples in District Formulary Target Microorganisms & Clinical Use
1. Basal (Simple) Media Non-selective supportive media containing basic nutrients (peptone, meat extract, NaCl, agar). Nutrient Agar, Nutrient Broth, Peptone Water. Subculturing non-fastidious organisms and preparing basal media for biochemical sugar tests.
2. Enriched Media Basal medium supplemented with highly nutritious blood, serum, or egg to support fastidious pathogens. • Blood Agar (5–10% defibrinated sheep/horse blood)
• Chocolate (Heated Blood) Agar
• Lowenstein-Jensen (LJ) Medium (egg-based) 		Streptococci, *S. pneumoniae*, *S. aureus* (shows alpha/beta/gamma hemolysis);
*Haemophilus influenzae* & *Neisseria meningitidis* (releases Factor X & V);
*Mycobacterium tuberculosis* isolation.
3. Selective Media Contains inhibitory substances (bile salts, dyes, antibiotics, high salt) that suppress commensal flora while allowing target pathogens to grow. • Thiosulfate-Citrate-Bile Salts-Sucrose (TCBS)
• Modified Thayer-Martin (MTM) Agar (vancomycin, colistin, nystatin, trimethoprim)
• Mannitol Salt Agar (7.5% NaCl)
• Xylose-Lysine-Deoxycholate (XLD) / DCA 		*Vibrio cholerae* (high pH 8.6 + bile salts);
*Neisseria gonorrhoeae* (VCNT inhibits Gram-pos, Gram-neg coliforms, and yeast);
*Staphylococcus aureus* (halotolerant);
*Salmonella* and *Shigella* enteric isolation.
4. Differential (Indicator) Media Contains fermentable carbohydrates and pH indicators to visually distinguish bacterial species by colony color. • MacConkey Agar (Neutral Red indicator)
• CLED Agar (Bromothymol Blue indicator)
• Eosin Methylene Blue (EMB) Agar 		Lactose fermenters (LF = pink/red colonies) vs Non-lactose fermenters (NLF = pale/colorless);
Urine culture without *Proteus* swarming (electrolyte deficient);
*E. coli* greenish metallic sheen.
5. Transport & Enrichment Broths Non-nutritive holding media (preserves viability without multiplication) or liquid selective broths (multiplies target pathogens). • Cary-Blair Medium (enteric transport)
• Amies / Stuart Medium with Charcoal
• Selenite F Broth & Alkaline Peptone Water (APW) 		Fecal stool transport (*Vibrio*, *Shigella*);
Urethral/cervical fastidious swabs (*N. gonorrhoeae*);
Liquid enrichment of *Salmonella* and *V. cholerae*.
QA Protocols Sterilization Methods

2. Media Sterilization, Pouring & Batch Quality Control SOP

1. Autoclaving Standard

Autoclave at \(121^\circ\text{C}\) at \(15\ \text{psi}\) (\(103\ \text{kPa}\)) for \(15\ \text{minutes}\). Required for Nutrient, Blood agar base, MacConkey, and CLED. Exception: TCBS and DCA agar must NEVER be autoclaved (heat only until completely dissolved; autoclaving destroys sodium deoxycholate and selective inhibitors).

2. Inspissation (Fractional Heating)

Used for protein-rich media containing whole eggs or serum (Lowenstein-Jensen, Loeffler serum). Coagulated and sterilized at \(85^\circ\text{C}\) for \(45\ \text{minutes}\) in an inspissator. High autoclave heat causes egg protein boiling and destruction.

3. Membrane Filtration (\(0.22\ \mu\text{m}\))

Used for heat-labile supplements (antibiotic mixtures for MTM agar, urea solutions for Christensen urease medium, sugars, and serum). Passed through sterile cellulose acetate/polycarbonate membrane filters (\(0.22\ \mu\text{m}\) pore size) that mechanically trap all bacteria.

Plate Pouring & Batch Quality Control Checklist

  • Blood Addition Temperature: Cool sterile melted agar base to \(45–50^\circ\text{C}\) before adding 5–10% defibrinated blood. Adding blood to hotter agar (\(>55^\circ\text{C}\)) lyses RBCs and turns it into chocolate agar.
  • Dispensing Volume & Depth: Pour \(15–20\ \text{mL}\) of agar per \(90\ \text{mm}\) Petri dish to achieve an exact agar depth of \(4.0 \pm 0.5\ \text{mm}\). Flame surface briefly with a pilot Bunsen flame to pop air bubbles.
  • Drying Poured Plates: Store agar plates inverted with lids slightly ajar in a \(37^\circ\text{C}\) incubator for \(15–30\ \text{minutes}\) before use to remove surface condensation moisture (prevents confluent bacterial swarming).
  • Batch Sterility & Performance QC: Incubate 3–5% of each freshly prepared batch at \(35–37^\circ\text{C}\) for \(48\ \text{hours}\). Test growth and selective properties with ATCC control strains (*E. coli* ATCC 25922, *S. aureus* ATCC 25923).
Streaking Mastery Textbook Diagrams

3. Standard Inoculation Techniques & Streaking Patterns

Fig 7.6: Primary Quadrant Streak Plate (Cheesbrough p. 63). Sequential dilution streaking with loop flaming between quadrants to obtain discrete single colonies.

Fig 7.9: Half-Plate & Multi-Sector Inoculation (Cheesbrough p. 65). Cost-effective section plating for multiple diagnostic specimens.

Fig 7.11: Butt & Slope (TSI/KIA) Inoculation (Cheesbrough p. 66). Stabbing deep butt with straight wire followed by serpentine surface streak on slope.

Quadrant Streak SOP for Single Colonies

  1. Primary Well (Quadrant 1): Inoculate specimen onto first quadrant (\(25\%\) of plate) with sterile wire loop or swab in close parallel zig-zag lines.
  2. Flame & Cool Loop: Heat loop red-hot in Bunsen flame from handle to tip; cool against sterile agar margin.
  3. Secondary Streak (Quadrant 2): Turn plate \(90^\circ\); pass loop 2–3 times through edge of Quadrant 1, then streak parallel lines into Quadrant 2.
  4. Tertiary & Quaternary Streaks: Flame and cool loop again; streak into Quadrants 3 and 4, ending with a loose tail to deposit single isolated bacterial cells.

Quantitative Urine Inoculation SOP

  • Calibrated Loop (\(0.001\ \text{mL}\) / \(1\ \mu\text{L}\) or \(0.01\ \text{mL}\)): Dip vertically into uncentrifuged, well-mixed urine.
  • Primary Centerline Streak: Draw a straight line down the center of a CLED or Blood Agar plate.
  • Perpendicular Lawn: Without flaming, streak closely spaced perpendicular lines back and forth across the entire centerline to distribute bacteria evenly.
  • Quantitation: \(1\ \text{colony on}\ 1\ \mu\text{L loop} = 1000\ \text{CFU/mL}\) (\(10^3\ \text{CFU/mL}\)). A count of \(\ge 100\ \text{colonies} = \ge 10^5\ \text{CFU/mL}\) (Kass criterion for significant bacteriuria).
Atmospheric Control Anaerobiosis Validation

4. Incubation Atmospheres: Aerobic, Capnophilic (\(CO_2\)) & Anaerobic Systems

1. Standard Aerobic Incubation

Standard ambient air (\(21\%\ O_2\), \(0.04\%\ CO_2\)) at \(35–37^\circ\text{C}\) for \(18–24\ \text{hours}\). Used for Staphylococci, Enterobacteriaceae, *Pseudomonas*, and uncomplicated urine/pus cultures.

2. Capnophilic (\(5–10\%\ CO_2\)) System

Essential for fastidious capnophiles: *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*, *Neisseria meningitidis*, and *Haemophilus influenzae*. Created using a Candle Extinction Jar (smoldering smokeless wax candle consumes \(O_2\) until extinguished, generating \(3–5\%\ CO_2\)) or commercial \(CO_2\) generating chemical packs.

3. Strict Anaerobic System

Required for *Clostridium* spp., *Bacteroides fragilis*, *Fusobacterium*. Utilizes an Anaerobic Jar with Gas-Pak and cold palladium catalyst pellets (\(2H_2 + O_2 \xrightarrow{\text{palladium}} 2H_2O\)). Validated with a methylene blue redox indicator strip (turns completely colorless within \(2\ \text{hours}\)).

Plate 7.4: Anaerobic GasPak Container & Jar System (Monica Cheesbrough Part 2, Page 61). Gas generator sachet produces hydrogen and carbon dioxide; palladium catalyst removes residual oxygen.

Macroscopic Examination 8-Point Standard

5. Systematic Macroscopic Characterization of Bacterial Colonies

Colonial Feature Descriptive Morphological Terms Diagnostic Pathogen Signatures
1. Size & Elevation Pinpoint (\(<0.5\ \text{mm}\)), small (\(1–2\ \text{mm}\)), large (\(3–5\ \text{mm}\)); Flat, raised, convex, dome, umbonate (draughtsman). • Streptococcus pneumoniae: Umbonate / draughtsman colonies with depressed center due to autolysis.
• Enterobacteriaceae: Large, convex, smooth colonies.
2. Margin & Edge Entire (smooth circular), undulate (wavy), crenated, rhizoid, filamentous ("Medusa head"). • Bacillus anthracis: Rough "Medusa head" irregular interlocking filamentous edges.
• Staphylococcus aureus: Perfectly entire smooth circular margins.
3. Consistency & Texture Smooth (S-type), rough (R-type), mucoid/slimy (viscous stringy capsule), dry/friable. • Klebsiella pneumoniae: Extremely mucoid, sticky colonies stringing \(>5\ \text{mm}\).
• Mycobacterium tuberculosis: Rough, crumbly, buff/cream "breadcrumb" colonies.
4. Pigmentation & Odor Golden-yellow, blue-green, red, black; Sweet grape-like, foul putrid, bleached ammonia odor. • Pseudomonas aeruginosa: Blue-green pyocyanin pigment + sweet grape/corn-tortilla odor.
• Serratia marcescens: Red prodigiosin pigment at \(25^\circ\text{C}\).
• Proteus mirabilis: Concentric swarming rings + pungent fishy/ammonia odor.
5. Hemolysis on Blood Agar Alpha: Partial lysis with greenish-brown zone.
Beta: Complete clear transparent zone of lysis.
Gamma: No lysis/discoloration.		 • S. pneumoniae: Alpha-hemolytic.
• S. pyogenes & S. aureus: Beta-hemolytic.
• Enterococcus faecalis: Gamma-hemolytic (usually).
Board Examination Section 8 Active Interactive MCQs

Section 7.4 Board Review Questions (MCQ 377 – 384)

Test your mastery of culture media formulation, sterilization protocols, streaking techniques, and colonial interpretation:

MCQ 377 • Heat-Labile Culture Media Sterilization
Which of the following culture media formulations must NEVER be sterilized by autoclaving because high autoclave temperatures destroy its selective bile salt inhibitors and caramelize sugars?
A Nutrient Agar
B Blood Agar Base
C Thiosulfate-Citrate-Bile Salts-Sucrose (TCBS) Agar
D MacConkey Agar
Correct Answer: C — Thiosulfate-Citrate-Bile Salts-Sucrose (TCBS) Agar. TCBS agar is formulated for the selective isolation of Vibrio cholerae. It contains high concentrations of sodium thiosulfate, sodium citrate, bile salts, and sucrose at alkaline pH (8.6). Autoclaving destroys these selective inhibitors and caramelizes the sucrose; TCBS must only be brought to a boil until completely dissolved and poured directly into plates.
MCQ 378 • Blood Agar Preparation & Temperature Control
When preparing 5% Sheep Blood Agar, why is it mandatory to cool the sterile melted nutrient agar base to \(45–50^\circ\text{C}\) before aseptically mixing in the defibrinated blood?
A Adding blood at \(<40^\circ\text{C}\) causes bacterial contamination.
B Adding blood to agar hotter than \(55^\circ\text{C}\) thermally lyses the erythrocytes and denatures hemoglobin, turning the medium into Chocolate Agar.
C Higher temperatures neutralize the peptone nitrogen sources.
D Sheep blood coagulates into solid clots below \(50^\circ\text{C}\).
Correct Answer: B — Adding blood above 55°C lyses erythrocytes and denatures hemoglobin, converting it into chocolate agar. Intact red blood cells are required to observe true alpha, beta, and gamma hemolysis. If blood is added to an overheated base (\(>55^\circ\text{C}\)), the heat immediately lyses the RBCs and oxidizes hemoglobin to brown hematin (producing chocolate agar instead of blood agar).
MCQ 379 • Primary Quadrant Streaking Purpose & Execution
What is the fundamental technical reason for flaming and cooling the inoculating loop between each successive quadrant streak during the primary isolation of bacterial pathogens?
A To incinerate excess residual bacteria on the wire, ensuring that each new quadrant streak mechanically dilutes the bacterial population to deposit individual single cells that develop into discrete isolated colonies.
B To heat-activate bacterial spore germination on the agar surface.
C To burn off toxic agar condensations along the streak path.
D To convert aerobic bacteria into microaerophiles.
Correct Answer: A — To incinerate excess bacteria, ensuring progressive dilution to obtain single isolated colonies. Without loop flaming between quadrants, thousands of bacteria remain on the wire, resulting in a continuous dense, overgrown lawn across the entire plate. Isolated discrete colonies are essential for pure subculturing, biochemical identification, and disc sensitivity testing.
MCQ 380 • Calibrated Loop Semi-Quantitative Urine Bacteriuria
A calibrated \(0.001\ \text{mL}\) (\(1\ \mu\text{L}\)) inoculating loop is used to plate uncentrifuged urine onto CLED agar. After 24 hours of incubation, 150 yellow colonies are counted on the plate. What is the calculated bacterial concentration per milliliter of urine?
A \(150\ \text{CFU/mL}\)
B \(1,500\ \text{CFU/mL}\)
C \(15,000\ \text{CFU/mL}\)
D \(150,000\ \text{CFU/mL}\) (\(1.5 \times 10^5\ \text{CFU/mL}\))
Correct Answer: D — 150,000 CFU/mL (1.5 × 10⁵ CFU/mL). A \(0.001\ \text{mL}\) loop samples \(1/1000\) of a milliliter. Therefore, each colony represents \(1000\ \text{CFU/mL}\). Multiplying: \(150\ \text{colonies} \times 1000 = 150,000\ \text{CFU/mL}\) (\(1.5 \times 10^5\ \text{CFU/mL}\)). This exceeds the Kass threshold of \(\ge 10^5\ \text{CFU/mL}\), confirming significant bacteriuria (UTI).
MCQ 381 • Inspissation Temperature for Egg-Based Media
Why is Lowenstein-Jensen (LJ) medium solidified using an inspissator at \(85^\circ\text{C}\) for 45 minutes rather than standard autoclaving at \(121^\circ\text{C}\)?
A Tubercle bacilli are already inoculated into the medium prior to solidification.
B Whole hens' eggs contain heat-coagulable albumin and globulin proteins that solidify into a smooth slant at \(85^\circ\text{C}\), but violently boil, curdle, and form disruptive bubbles at \(121^\circ\text{C}\).
C Malachite green decomposes below \(90^\circ\text{C}\).
D Agar-agar fails to dissolve at autoclave temperatures.
Correct Answer: B — Egg proteins coagulate smoothly at 85°C, but curdle and boil violently at 121°C. LJ medium does not contain agar; it relies entirely on the coagulation of whole egg proteins to form a solid matrix. Controlled fractional heating at 85°C (inspissation) coagulates the egg uniformly without boiling, whereas autoclaving at 121°C causes explosive steam bubbles and protein denaturation.
MCQ 382 • Anaerobic Jar Redox Indicator Quality Control
What chemical transformation occurs to a methylene blue redox indicator strip in a properly functioning anaerobic jar when strict anaerobiosis has been successfully achieved?
A It turns bright blue due to atmospheric oxidation.
B It changes from green to deep yellow.
C It reduces from oxidized blue to completely colorless (leuco-methylene blue).
D It precipitates as black crystals of lead sulfide.
Correct Answer: C — It reduces from oxidized blue to completely colorless (leuco-methylene blue). In the presence of atmospheric oxygen, methylene blue remains blue (oxidized state). When cold palladium catalyst and hydrogen remove all oxygen (\(E_h < -100\ \text{mV}\)), methylene blue is reduced to its colorless form (leuco-methylene blue), confirming total anaerobiosis.
MCQ 383 • CLED Agar & Proteus Swarming Inhibition
Why is Cystine-Lactose-Electrolyte Deficient (CLED) Agar preferred over standard Blood Agar or Nutrient Agar for routine quantitative urine bacteriology?
A The complete deficiency of electrolytes (specifically sodium chloride) prevents the swarming motility of Proteus species across the agar surface, allowing accurate colony counting.
B CLED agar selectively suppresses all Gram-negative coliforms.
C CLED contains vancomycin to eliminate contaminating skin staphylococci.
D CLED converts all non-lactose fermenting bacilli into lactose fermenters.
Correct Answer: A — Deficiency of electrolytes (NaCl) prevents Proteus swarming, allowing accurate colony counts. Proteus species exhibit rapid swarming motility on moist, electrolyte-rich media (like Blood Agar), forming a continuous sheet that covers and obscures all other bacterial colonies. By omitting electrolytes (NaCl), CLED confines Proteus to discrete, non-swarming blue colonies while supporting both Gram-positive and Gram-negative uropathogens.
MCQ 384 • Capnophilic Atmosphere & Candle Extinction Jar
Which group of bacterial pathogens exhibits enhanced or obligatory growth in a Candle Extinction Jar (\(3–5\%\ CO_2\)) compared to standard ambient air?
A Clostridium perfringens, Bacteroides fragilis, and Fusobacterium
B Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae
C Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Burkholderia cepacia
D Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae
Correct Answer: B — N. gonorrhoeae, N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae, and H. influenzae. These are fastidious capnophilic pathogens that require an elevated carbon dioxide concentration (\(3–10\%\ CO_2\)) for metabolic carboxylation reactions during primary isolation. A candle jar provides the ideal low-cost \(3–5\%\ CO_2\) humid micro-environment in district laboratories.

7.5 Biochemical Tests to Identify Bacteria

Standard Operating Procedures for Catalase, Oxidase, Coagulase (Slide & Tube), Bile Solubility, Citrate Utilization, DNA-ase, Indole, Litmus Milk Reduction, Urease & Triple Sugar Iron (TSI/KIA) Sugar Fermentation Reactions.

Monica Cheesbrough Clinical & Laboratory Principle: Biochemical testing reveals the specific metabolic and enzymatic machinery of an organism. Never perform a catalase test with a nichrome wire loop or by gouging red blood cells from blood agar (erythrocytic pseudoperoxidase causes false positives). Never use citrated plasma for coagulase tube tests (citrate-utilizing enterococci clot citrated plasma). Quality control with known positive and negative ATCC control strains must accompany every test run!

High-Yield Core Concept Pulse Cards

Click any highlighted pulse term below to examine high-yield BMLS board exam definitions and clinical applications:

Catalase (3% H2O2) 1% Tetramethyl Oxidase Bound vs Free Coagulase 10% Sodium Deoxycholate Christensen's Urea Medium Indole (Kovac's Reagent) Simmons Citrate Utilization DNA-ase (1M HCl Clearance)
Primary Enzyme Screens High-Impact Differentiation

1. Primary Diagnostic Enzyme Tests: Catalase, Oxidase & Coagulase

Catalase Test (3% \(H_2O_2\))

  • Principle: Catalase enzyme breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and gaseous oxygen: \(2H_2O_2 \xrightarrow{\text{catalase}} 2H_2O + O_2\ \uparrow\).
  • Method & Safety: Place a drop of 3% \(H_2O_2\) on a glass slide inside a closed Petri dish. Emulsify colony with a plastic loop or wooden stick. Rapid vigorous effervescence / bubbling indicates positivity.
  • Differentiates: Staphylococci (Catalase +) from Streptococci (Catalase -); Listeria monocytogenes (+) from Group B Streptococcus (-).
  • Pitfall: Red blood cells contain catalase; taking agar from a blood plate gives a false-positive!

Oxidase Test (1% Reagent)

  • Principle: Cytochrome c oxidase oxidizes 1% tetramethyl-p-phenylenediamine dihydrochloride to indophenol blue (deep blue/purple within 10 seconds).
  • Method: Moisten filter paper with reagent; smear colony using a glass rod or platinum wire. Never use a nichrome wire loop (iron traces catalyze false oxidation).
  • Differentiates: Oxidase + (*Pseudomonas*, *Neisseria*, *Vibrio*, *Campylobacter*) from Oxidase - (all *Enterobacteriaceae*, *Acinetobacter*).

Coagulase Test (Slide vs Tube)

  • Slide Test (Bound Coagulase / Clumping Factor): Emulsify colony in water, add drop of EDTA rabbit plasma. Visible clumping within \(10–15\ \text{seconds}\) = S. aureus. Negative slide tests must always be confirmed by tube test!
  • Tube Test (Free Extracellular Coagulase): Inoculate 0.5 mL diluted rabbit plasma (1:5). Incubate at \(35–37^\circ\text{C}\) for 1–4 hours. Clot formation confirms S. aureus.
  • Rule: Do NOT use citrated plasma (citrate-fermenters cause false clotting).

Plate 7.7: Coagulase Slide Test (Cheesbrough p. 74). Left: Negative smooth suspension; Right: Positive granular agglutination / clumping of S. aureus.

Plate 7.6: Bile Solubility Test (Cheesbrough p. 72). Left: Control tube remains turbid; Right: Complete clearing of S. pneumoniae suspension by sodium deoxycholate.

Confirmatory Panels DNA Hydrolysis

2. Bile Solubility, DNA-ase & Simmons Citrate SOPs

Biochemical Test Substrate & Reagents Used Positive Reaction Hallmark Primary Clinical Differentiation
Bile Solubility Test 10% Sodium Deoxycholate solution added to saline suspension of alpha-hemolytic streptococci. Rapid clearing of optical turbidity within 10–15 minutes at \(37^\circ\text{C}\) (bile salts trigger autolytic amidase enzymes). Differentiates Streptococcus pneumoniae (Bile Soluble / Clears) from Viridans streptococci (Bile Insoluble / Turbid).
DNA-ase Test DNA Agar flooded with 1M Hydrochloric Acid (1M HCl) after overnight incubation. Clear colorless halo around colony (unhydrolyzed DNA precipitates cloudy-white with HCl; hydrolyzed DNA remains clear). Confirms Staphylococcus aureus (DNA-ase +) when coagulase is equivocal; separates Serratia marcescens (+) from *Enterobacter* (-).
Simmons Citrate Utilization Simmons Citrate Agar (Sodium citrate sole carbon source + Ammonium salts nitrogen + Bromothymol Blue indicator). Color shift from Forest Green (\(\text{pH}\ 6.8\)) to Deep Royal Blue (\(\text{pH} > 7.6\)) with visible colony growth. Differentiates Citrate + (*Klebsiella pneumoniae*, *Salmonella*, *Enterobacter*, *Citrobacter*) from Citrate - (*Escherichia coli*, *Shigella*).
Enteric Identification Carbohydrate Fermentation

3. Indole, Christensen Urease & Triple Sugar Iron (TSI/KIA) Protocols

Indole Test (Kovac's Reagent)

Tryptophanase enzyme hydrolyzes tryptophan into indole, pyruvic acid, and ammonia. Addition of Kovac's reagent (p-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde in isoamyl alcohol) produces a bright cherry-red surface ring within 10 minutes.
Indole Positive: Escherichia coli, Proteus vulgaris, Vibrio cholerae.
Indole Negative: Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis, Salmonella.

Christensen's Urease Test

Urease hydrolyzes urea into ammonia and \(CO_2\). Alkaline ammonia raises pH, turning Phenol Red from pale yellow/orange to vivid magenta / hot pink.
Rapid Urease + (within 1–4 h): Proteus mirabilis, Proteus vulgaris, Helicobacter pylori.
Slow Urease + (24 h): Klebsiella pneumoniae, Cryptococcus neoformans.

Litmus Milk Decolorization

Enzyme reductase reduces litmus dye, turning the medium from mauve-purple to white or pale yellow within 4 hours.
Positive Litmus Reduction: Enterococcus faecalis, Clostridium perfringens (stormy fermentation: acid + gas clot).

TSI / KIA Reaction Profile Slant / Butt / Gas / \(H_2S\) Code Fermentation Biochemistry Classic Enteric Organisms
Acid Slant / Acid Butt + Gas (\(H_2S\ - \)) A / A, Gas (+), \(H_2S\) (-) (Yellow / Yellow) Ferments Glucose + Lactose/Sucrose with copious gas production. Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterobacter
Alkaline Slant / Acid Butt + \(H_2S\) K / A, Gas (+/-), \(H_2S\) (+) (Red / Yellow + Black Butt) Ferments Glucose only; produces hydrogen sulfide (\(H_2S\) precipitates with ferrous sulfate). Salmonella enterica (Typhi/Paratyphi), Proteus mirabilis
Alkaline Slant / Acid Butt (No Gas, No \(H_2S\)) K / A, Gas (-), \(H_2S\) (-) (Red / Yellow) Ferments Glucose only without gas or \(H_2S\) production. Shigella dysenteriae / flexneri
Alkaline Slant / Alkaline Butt (Non-Fermenter) K / K, Gas (-), \(H_2S\) (-) (Red / Red) No carbohydrate fermentation; oxidative deamination of peptones. Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii

Section 7.5 Board Review Questions (MCQ 385 – 392)

Test your knowledge of biochemical reactions, enzymatic pathways, and diagnostic decision-making:

MCQ 385 • Catalase Testing Technical Pitfall
Why does accidentally scraping red blood cells from a 5% Sheep Blood Agar plate during a catalase test produce a false-positive result (spurious bubbling)?
A Erythrocytes contain intrinsic catalase and pseudoperoxidase enzymes that actively decompose hydrogen peroxide into oxygen bubbles.
B Sheep blood lowers the pH to acidic levels that boil hydrogen peroxide.
C Defibrinated blood contains live staphylococcal bacteriophages.
D Agar polysaccharides react with hydrogen peroxide to liberate carbon dioxide.
Correct Answer: A — Erythrocytes contain intrinsic catalase that decomposes hydrogen peroxide. Mammalian red blood cells are packed with intracellular catalase. If a technologist gouges the blood agar medium when picking a colony, RBCs are transferred into the 3% \(H_2O_2\), causing immediate false bubbling even with a catalase-negative Streptococcus. Colonies should be picked delicately or subcultured to nutrient agar.
MCQ 386 • Oxidase Reagent & Inoculating Wire Artifacts
Why is the use of a standard nichrome or iron wire loop strictly prohibited when performing the cytochrome oxidase test with 1% tetramethyl-p-phenylenediamine?
A Nichrome permanently bleaches the filter paper white.
B Nichrome loops destroy bacterial cytochrome enzymes on contact.
C Trace iron and nickel oxides on the heated wire surface non-enzymatically oxidize the reagent, producing a false-positive deep purple color.
D Nichrome converts the reagent into volatile cyanide gas.
Correct Answer: C — Trace iron and nickel non-enzymatically oxidize the reagent, causing false positives. Iron and nickel in nichrome loops act as inorganic oxidation catalysts, turning the colorless oxidase reagent deep purple immediately without bacterial enzyme presence. Technologists must always use a glass rod, disposable wooden stick, or platinum loop.
MCQ 387 • Plasma Selection for Coagulase Testing
Why is EDTA-anticoagulated rabbit plasma preferred over human citrated blood bank plasma for the tube coagulase identification of Staphylococcus aureus?
A Citrate kills Staphylococcus aureus within 10 minutes.
B Citrate-utilizing contaminant bacteria (e.g. Enterococcus, Pseudomonas, Serratia) consume citrate, liberating free calcium and causing false-positive fibrin clotting of citrated plasma.
C Human plasma lacks fibrinogen.
D EDTA acts as an enzymatic co-factor for free staphylocoagulase.
Correct Answer: B — Citrate-utilizing bacteria consume citrate, liberating calcium and causing false-positive clotting. When citrated plasma is used, bacteria with citrate-metabolizing enzymes digest the anticoagulant citrate, allowing endogenous calcium to activate the host clotting cascade, producing a false-positive clot. EDTA plasma is immune to this interference.
MCQ 388 • Bile Solubility Biochemical Mechanism
What is the exact enzymatic mechanism that causes Streptococcus pneumoniae suspensions to rapidly clear upon the addition of 10% sodium deoxycholate (bile salt)?
A Bile salts precipitate capsular polysaccharides into an invisible gel.
B Sodium deoxycholate hydrolyzes bacterial ribosomal RNA.
C Bile salts neutralize bacterial teichoic acids to shift the optical refractive index.
D Bile salts lower surface tension and activate the pneumococcal autolytic enzyme (LytA amidase), which rapidly cleaves cell wall peptidoglycan bonds and lyses the bacteria.
Correct Answer: D — Bile salts activate pneumococcal autolytic LytA amidase, rapidly cleaving peptidoglycan bonds. S. pneumoniae produces an endogenous autolysin (N-acetylmuramoyl-L-alanine amidase). Surface-active bile salts like sodium deoxycholate trigger and accelerate this autolytic enzyme, leading to rapid cell wall lysis and complete visual clearing of the cloudy suspension.
MCQ 389 • Simmons Citrate Utilization Color Chemistry
On Simmons Citrate Agar, what metabolic event causes the Bromothymol Blue pH indicator to transition from forest green (pH 6.8) to royal blue (pH > 7.6)?
A Citrate-permease enables citrate uptake as a sole carbon source, while inorganic ammonium phosphate is metabolized to alkaline ammonia and ammonium hydroxide, raising the pH.
B Fermentation of citrate produces lactic and acetic acids.
C Production of hydrogen sulfide gas turns the agar blue.
D Oxidation of bromothymol blue by catalase enzymes.
Correct Answer: A — Citrate uptake and ammonium salt conversion to alkaline ammonia raises the pH. Organisms that possess citrate permease transport citrate into the cell. As they grow, they extract nitrogen from ammonium salts, converting them into alkaline ammonia (\(NH_3\)) and ammonium hydroxide (\(NH_4OH\)). The resulting rise in pH above 7.6 shifts bromothymol blue to deep royal blue.
MCQ 390 • Rapid Urease Hydrolysis Kinetics
A non-lactose fermenting Gram-negative rod isolated from a clean-catch urine specimen turns Christensen's urea slant from yellow to intense magenta-pink within 2 hours of incubation. Which pathogen is responsible?
A Escherichia coli
B Salmonella enterica
C Proteus mirabilis
D Shigella sonnei
Correct Answer: C — Proteus mirabilis. Proteus species are potent, rapid urease producers that split urea into massive amounts of alkaline ammonia within 1–4 hours, rapidly shifting phenol red to bright magenta-pink. This rapid alkalinization predisposes patients to struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate / staghorn) urinary calculi.
MCQ 391 • Triple Sugar Iron (TSI) Salmonella vs Shigella
Which of the following Triple Sugar Iron (TSI) agar reaction patterns definitively distinguishes Salmonella enterica from Shigella dysenteriae?
A Salmonella produces an Acid Slant and Acid Butt (A/A); Shigella produces an Alkaline Slant and Alkaline Butt (K/K).
B Salmonella produces an Alkaline Slant / Acid Butt with Black \(H_2S\) precipitate (K/A, \(H_2S\ +\)); Shigella produces an Alkaline Slant / Acid Butt without \(H_2S\) (K/A, \(H_2S\ -\)).
C Shigella ferments lactose and sucrose, producing a yellow slant.
D Salmonella is non-motile, while Shigella produces gas in the deep butt.
Correct Answer: B — Salmonella produces K/A with black H₂S; Shigella produces K/A without H₂S. Both Salmonella and Shigella are non-lactose fermenters that utilize glucose only in the anaerobic butt (red slant / yellow butt, K/A). However, Salmonella produces thiosulfate reductase, generating hydrogen sulfide (\(H_2S\)) that reacts with ferric ammonium citrate to form a black ferrous sulfide precipitate in the butt; Shigella never produces \(H_2S\).
MCQ 392 • DNA-ase Agar Hydrochloric Acid Flooding
When interpreting a DNA-ase test plate flooded with 1M Hydrochloric Acid (1M HCl), what observation confirms deoxyribonuclease enzyme production by Staphylococcus aureus?
A Evolution of vigorous carbon dioxide gas bubbles across the agar surface.
B Development of a dark blue-purple ring around the colony.
C Formation of an opaque, milky-white precipitate directly surrounding the colony.
D A clear, transparent zone/halo surrounding the bacterial growth against a cloudy, opaque white precipitated background of intact polymerized DNA.
Correct Answer: D — A clear transparent zone surrounding bacterial growth against a cloudy white precipitated background. 1M HCl precipitates intact, polymerized DNA molecules, turning the agar cloudy opaque white. Where S. aureus has grown and secreted extracellular DNA-ase, the DNA is hydrolyzed into soluble nucleotides and oligonucleotides that do not precipitate with acid, leaving a clear transparent zone around the colony.

7.6 Examination of Sputum

Microbiological Investigation of Lower Respiratory Infections, Pneumonia Pathogens, Spot-Morning-Spot Sputum Collection, Bartlett Cytological Grading, Direct ZN Smear vs Sodium Hypochlorite (Bleach) Concentration, Sputum Culture Media & Fungal/Parasitic Identifications.

Monica Cheesbrough Clinical & Laboratory Principle: Sputum examination is the frontline defense against pulmonary tuberculosis and severe community-acquired pneumonia. A true sputum specimen consists of material brought up from the tracheobronchial tree after deep coughing, not superficial oropharyngeal saliva. Microscopic screening using the Bartlett or Murray-Washington criteria (\(<10\) squamous epithelial cells and \(>25\) PMNs per low-power field) prevents misleading culture of normal upper respiratory flora!

2. Collection Protocols & Cytological Quality Assessment

Sputum Collection Protocol & Pediatric Sampling

  • Spot-Morning-Spot Protocol (TB Diagnostic Standard):
    • Sample 1 (On-the-spot): Collected immediately at first clinic visit under outdoor supervision.
    • Sample 2 (Early morning): Brought by patient next morning (deep tracheobronchial secretions accumulated overnight).
    • Sample 3 (Second spot): Collected when patient delivers sample 2.
  • Collection Safety SOP: Instruct patient to rinse mouth with clean water (not antiseptic mouthwash) to clear food particles; cough deeply into a wide-mouthed, leak-proof, screw-capped container in a well-ventilated outdoor booth. Wipe outside with disinfectant.
  • Pediatric Nasopharyngeal Aspirates: Children \(<5\ \text{years}\) swallow sputum. Aseptic catheter aspiration of mucopus from the posterior nasopharynx provides high diagnostic yield for childhood pneumonia.
  • Rejection Standard: 24-hour pooled sputum is strictly rejected (overgrown with saprophytes and autolyzed).

Bartlett & Murray Cytological Screening Criteria

Screen Gram-stained smear under \(10\times\) low-power objective before plating:

Microscopic Element (per \(10\times\) LPF) Bartlett Score Value
Neutrophils (PMNs) \(10–25\) per LPF \(+1\)
Neutrophils (PMNs) \(>25\) per LPF \(+2\)
Presence of Mucus Strands \(+1\)
Squamous Epithelial Cells (SEC) \(10–25\) / LPF \(-1\)
Squamous Epithelial Cells (SEC) \(>25\) / LPF \(-2\) (Rejection)

Interpretation: A total Bartlett score of \(\ge +1\) indicates true lower respiratory purulent sputum suitable for culture. A score of \(\le 0\) or \(>25\ \text{SECs/LPF}\) indicates oropharyngeal saliva: reject specimen and request a repeat deep-cough specimen!

Enhanced Sensitivity Biosafety Enhancement

3. Direct ZN vs Sodium Hypochlorite (Bleach) Concentration Technique

Direct ZN microscopy requires at least \(5,000–10,000\ \text{AFB/mL}\) of sputum for reliable detection. In district laboratories with high HIV coinfection rates (paucibacillary TB), the Sodium Hypochlorite (Bleach) Concentration Method increases diagnostic sensitivity by \(20–30\%\) while simultaneously sterilizing the specimen to eliminate biohazard transmission:

Step-by-Step Bleach Concentration SOP

  1. Digestion: Add an equal volume of 5% commercial sodium hypochlorite (household bleach) to the sputum specimen (e.g. \(1–2\ \text{mL}\) bleach to \(1–2\ \text{mL}\) sputum) in a conical centrifuge tube.
  2. Liquefaction: Mix thoroughly and leave at room temperature for \(10–15\ \text{minutes}\), shaking intermittently until mucus is completely liquefied. Bleach dissolves mucus, pus cells, and background proteins while leaving waxy acid-fast bacilli intact.
  3. Centrifugation: Add \(5–8\ \text{mL}\) of distilled water (to reduce specific gravity); centrifuge at \(3000\ g\) for \(15\ \text{minutes}\).
  4. Smear Preparation: Decant supernatant completely into disinfectant; resuspend the sediment pellet, transfer one loopful to a clean slide, air-dry, heat-fix, and stain by standard Ziehl-Neelsen or Auramine-O.

Clinical & Laboratory Benefits of Bleach Technique

  • Biosafety Sterilization: Bleach rapidly kills vegetative M. tuberculosis within 10 minutes, making subsequent smear handling non-infectious. (Note: Bleach-treated sediment cannot be used for culture!)
  • Crystal-Clear Optical Background: Digestion of cellular debris and mucus eliminates background non-specific artifacts, making red acid-fast bacilli stand out prominently in clean fields.
  • Superior Case Detection in HIV: HIV-positive patients often produce thin watery saliva-like sputum with low bacillary loads; bleach concentration aggregates bacilli into the pellet, dramatically reducing false-negative reads.
Diagnostic Workflow Cheesbrough Chart 7.6

4. Complete Sputum Microbiological Examination Scheme

Diagnostic Stage Standard Operating Procedure Key Findings & Clinical Action
1. Macroscopic Examination Describe visual appearance: Purulent (pus), Mucopurulent, Mucoid, Salivary (watery), Blood-stained (rusty, currant-jelly, frank hemoptysis). Select purulent, blood-streaked, or cheesy flecks for smear preparation and culture inoculation.
2. Direct Gram Stain Stain purulent portion by Gram technique. Evaluate Bartlett score; screen for predominant bacterial morphotypes and PMNs. • Gram-positive diplococci = Presumptive *S. pneumoniae*
• Gram-negative coccobacilli = Presumptive *H. influenzae*
• Large Gram-negative mucoid rods = Presumptive *K. pneumoniae*
3. Acid-Fast Smear (ZN / Auramine-O) Examine 100 oil-immersion fields. Grade according to WHO/IUATLD scale (\(+\) to \(+++\)). Report AFB Positive immediately to initiating DOTS tuberculosis therapy.
4. Primary Culture (When Indicated) Inoculate:
• 5% Sheep Blood Agar (with \(5\ \mu\text{g}\) optochin disc in primary streak, incubated in \(5–10\%\ CO_2\))
• Chocolate Agar (incubated in \(5–10\%\ CO_2\))
• MacConkey Agar (aerobic \(37^\circ\text{C}\))		 Isolate and identify alpha-hemolytic pneumococci (optochin \(\ge 14\ \text{mm}\)), fastidious *H. influenzae*, and coliforms. Perform standardized Kirby-Bauer AST.
5. Additional Special Preparations • Saline Wet Mount: Screen for golden operculated *Paragonimus westermani* eggs.
• 10–20% KOH Mount: Screen for fungal hyphae (*Aspergillus*) and budding yeasts.
• Toluidine Blue-O / Giemsa: Screen for *Pneumocystis jirovecii* cysts in immunocompromised AIDS patients. 		Identifies non-tuberculous causes of chronic cavitary lung disease, pulmonary mycoses, and opportunistic parasitic pneumonias.
Board Examination Section 8 Active Interactive MCQs

Section 7.6 Board Review Questions (MCQ 393 – 400)

Test your knowledge of lower respiratory tract pathogens, cytological criteria, and sputum processing SOPs:

MCQ 393 • Sputum Cytological Rejection (Bartlett Criteria)
A sputum specimen submitted for bacterial culture from a 50-year-old patient with suspected bronchopneumonia demonstrates 35 squamous epithelial cells and 4 polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs) per low-power field (\(10\times\) objective). What is the appropriate laboratory interpretation and standard operating action?
A The Bartlett score is \(+2\); proceed immediately to plate the sample onto blood, chocolate, and MacConkey agar.
B The specimen represents superficial oropharyngeal saliva (Bartlett score \(\le 0\)); reject the specimen for bacterial culture, issue a preliminary microscopy report, and request a fresh early morning deep-cough specimen.
C Treat the specimen with 10% sodium hydroxide to selectively lyse the squamous epithelial cells.
D The presence of squamous cells confirms severe alveolar epithelial necrosis; report as high-grade purulent pneumonia.
Correct Answer: B — The specimen represents superficial saliva (Bartlett score ≤0); reject and request a repeat deep-cough specimen. Microscopic evaluation showing \(>25\) squamous epithelial cells per LPF confirms heavy contamination with upper oropharyngeal saliva. Culturing this specimen would produce misleading results by isolating normal oral flora rather than the true lower respiratory pathogen.
MCQ 394 • Characteristic Sputum Macroscopic Signatures
Which lower respiratory bacterial pathogen is classically associated with the production of thick, highly viscous, dark-red "currant-jelly" mucoid sputum due to its massive polysaccharide capsule and extensive alveolar necrosis?
A Klebsiella pneumoniae
B Streptococcus pneumoniae
C Haemophilus influenzae
D Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Correct Answer: A — Klebsiella pneumoniae. K. pneumoniae produces Friedländer's pneumonia (frequently in alcoholics and diabetics), characterized by severe necrotizing lobar consolidation and copious "currant-jelly" sputum composed of blood, mucus, and thick polysaccharide capsular slime. In contrast, S. pneumoniae produces "rusty-brown" sputum.
MCQ 395 • Sodium Hypochlorite (Bleach) Concentration Mechanism
What is the primary diagnostic mechanism by which the Sodium Hypochlorite (Bleach) Concentration Technique improves the detection of acid-fast bacilli (AFB) in sputum from HIV-infected patients?
A Bleach acts as a mordant that permanently stains non-acid-fast bacteria red.
B Sodium hypochlorite stimulates in vitro bacterial replication during incubation.
C Bleach digests mucus, pus cells, and background proteins, allowing centrifugation to concentrate intact acid-fast bacilli into a dense sediment pellet on a clear optical field.
D Bleach converts carbol fuchsin into a fluorescent compound.
Correct Answer: C — Bleach digests mucus, pus cells, and proteins, concentrating intact AFB into a dense pellet. The waxy, mycolic-acid-rich cell wall of M. tuberculosis resists 5% bleach digestion, while host mucus and cellular debris are completely liquefied. Centrifugation aggregates bacilli into a high-density sediment, increasing smear sensitivity by 20–30% while killing viable bacilli to protect laboratory staff.
MCQ 396 • Diagnostic Limitation of Bleach-Treated Sputum Pellet
Why is a sputum specimen that has been processed using the 5% Sodium Hypochlorite (Bleach) concentration technique completely unsuitable for mycobacterial culture on Lowenstein-Jensen medium?
A Bleach neutralizes the malachite green in LJ medium.
B Sodium hypochlorite digests the agar base of the culture slant.
C Bleach alters the glycerol concentration in LJ medium.
D Sodium hypochlorite is a potent bactericidal disinfectant that kills viable Mycobacterium tuberculosis within 10–15 minutes.
Correct Answer: D — Sodium hypochlorite is bactericidal and kills viable M. tuberculosis within 10–15 minutes. While bleach concentration is outstanding for direct smear microscopy and biosafety, the chemical exposure kills the tubercle bacilli. For mycobacterial culture or drug susceptibility testing, non-lethal decontamination methods (such as the modified Petroff 4% NaOH or NALC-NaOH method) must be used instead.
MCQ 397 • Pediatric Lower Respiratory Tract Specimen Collection
In infants and young children (\(<5\ \text{years}\)) presenting with severe bronchopneumonia who are unable to expectorate sputum, what is the recommended standard district laboratory sampling procedure to isolate bacterial pathogens?
A Aseptic catheter aspiration of mucopus from the posterior nasopharynx.
B Swabbing the buccal mucosa with a dry cotton swab.
C Collection of a 24-hour pooled urine specimen.
D Performing a skin scrape of the anterior chest wall.
Correct Answer: A — Aseptic catheter aspiration of mucopus from the posterior nasopharynx. Young children instinctively swallow respiratory secretions rather than coughing up sputum. Mucopus aspirated from the posterior nasopharynx using a sterile suction catheter provides an excellent diagnostic specimen that correlates closely with the etiological lower respiratory pathogen.
MCQ 398 • Differentiating Paragonimiasis from Pulmonary TB
A 35-year-old patient from an endemic river valley presents with chronic cough, hemoptysis, and cavitary lung lesions on chest radiography. Repeated sputum ZN smears for AFB are negative. Microscopic examination of an unstained wet mount of rusty-brown sputum flecks reveals large, golden-brown operculated eggs (\(80–120 \times 50–60\ \mu\text{m}\)). What is the definitive diagnosis?
A Pulmonary Histoplasmosis
B Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
C Pulmonary Paragonimiasis (Lung Fluke Infection / Paragonimus westermani)
D Hydatid cyst rupture (Echinococcus granulosus)
Correct Answer: C — Pulmonary Paragonimiasis (Paragonimus westermani). Paragonimiasis is a major differential diagnosis of smear-negative tuberculosis in Southeast Asia, Africa, and the Americas. Adult lung flukes encapsulated in cystic lung cavities produce rusty sputum containing classical golden-brown, operculated eggs, acquired by ingesting raw or undercooked freshwater crabs or crayfish.
MCQ 399 • Primary Sputum Plating & Atmospheric Incubation
When processing a purulent sputum specimen for routine bacterial culture, why is 5% Sheep Blood Agar inoculated with an optochin disc placed directly on the primary streak area and incubated in 5–10% \(\text{CO}_2\)?
A To selectively stimulate the growth of Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
B To allow immediate primary presumptive identification of Streptococcus pneumoniae (alpha-hemolytic with \(\ge 14\ \text{mm}\) optochin inhibition zone in capnophilic atmosphere) directly from the primary plate.
C To prevent Staphylococcus aureus from fermenting mannitol.
D To decolorize contaminating Gram-negative rods.
Correct Answer: B — To allow immediate primary identification of S. pneumoniae directly on the primary plate. Placing an optochin disc on the primary streak area on sheep blood agar and incubating in a candle jar (\(5–10\%\ CO_2\)) allows rapid identification of S. pneumoniae (zone \(\ge 14\ \text{mm}\)) on day 1, saving a full 24 hours of subculturing time in critical acute pneumonia cases.
MCQ 400 • Pneumocystis jirovecii Microscopic Demonstration
Which specialized staining technique is utilized on bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) or induced sputum specimens to demonstrate the characteristic cup-shaped or crushed ping-pong ball cysts of Pneumocystis jirovecii in patients with advanced HIV/AIDS?
A Albert's stain with malachite green
B India ink negative wet mount
C Standard Gram stain with neutral red
D Toluidine Blue-O or Gomori Methenamine Silver (GMS) stain
Correct Answer: D — Toluidine Blue-O or Gomori Methenamine Silver (GMS) stain. Pneumocystis jirovecii cannot be cultured in vitro. Microscopic diagnosis relies on staining the thick cyst wall with Toluidine Blue-O (stains cysts blue-lavender) or Gomori Methenamine Silver (GMS, stains cyst walls dark brown/black with characteristic central dark dot / cup shape).

7.7 Examination of Throat and Mouth Specimens

Microbiological Investigation of Acute Pharyngitis, Group A Streptococcus (GAS), Diphtheria Pseudomembrane (*Corynebacterium diphtheriae*), Oral Candidiasis (Thrush), Vincent's Angina (Fusospirochaetosis), Epiglottitis & Elek Toxigenicity Testing.

Monica Cheesbrough Clinical & Laboratory Principle: When swabbing the oropharynx, rub firmly over inflamed tonsils and purulent follicles while strictly avoiding contact with the tongue, uvula, and buccal mucosa to minimize commensal salivary contamination. Never forcefully peel an adherent greyish-black pseudomembrane in suspected diphtheria (causes massive airway bleeding and lethal toxin release); swab the membrane margin gently and inoculate tellurite medium immediately!

Group A Strep (GAS / PYR+) Diphtheria Pseudomembrane Tinsdale / Tellurite Medium Elek Immunoprecipitation Test Vincent's Fusospirochaetosis Oral Thrush (*C. albicans*) Acute Epiglottitis (*Hib*) 0.04 U Bacitracin Disc Test
Clinical Spectrum Tropical Pathologies

1. Major Clinical Conditions & Etiological Pathogens of Throat & Mouth

Clinical Syndrome Major Etiological Pathogens Clinical Manifestations & Lesion Appearance Diagnostic Laboratory Signatures
Acute Streptococcal Pharyngitis / Tonsillitis Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Beta-Hemolytic Streptococcus / GAS) Beefy-red inflamed pharynx, enlarged tonsils studded with punctate yellow-white follicular exudates, anterior cervical lymphadenitis, fever. Beta-hemolytic colonies on sheep blood agar; Bacitracin Sensitive (\(0.04\ \text{U}\)); PYR Test Positive; Catalase Negative.
Pharyngeal Diphtheria Corynebacterium diphtheriae (biotypes gravis, mitis, intermedius, belfanti) Tough, leathery, adherent greyish-yellow to green-black pseudomembrane covering tonsils, uvula, and soft palate; bull-neck cervical edema; myocarditis and neuropathy. Albert's stain shows bluish-black metachromatic volutin granules; black-brown colonies with brown halos on Tinsdale / Tellurite Blood Agar; positive Elek toxigenicity test.
Vincent's Angina (Acute Necrotizing Ulcerative Gingivostomatitis / ANUG) Symbiosis of Treponema vincentii (Borrelia vincentii) + Fusobacterium necrophorum / nucleatum Painful, bleeding, punched-out interdental papillae ulcerations covered by a dirty grey pseudomembrane; severe halitosis (fetid foul breath). Direct Gram smear (counterstained with dilute carbol fuchsin) shows profuse numbers of spirochaetes and long slender spindle-shaped fusiform Gram-negative bacilli.
Oral Candidiasis (Thrush) Candida albicans (frequent AIDS-defining illness) Creamy white curdy patches ("cottage cheese" plaques) on buccal mucosa, tongue, and pharynx that leave raw, bleeding surfaces when scraped. Gram stain shows large Gram-positive budding yeast cells (\(3–6\ \mu\text{m}\)) with pseudohyphae; Germ Tube Test Positive in serum at \(37^\circ\text{C}\) within 2–3 h.
Acute Epiglottitis Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) (medical emergency in children) Cherry-red swollen epiglottis, inspiratory stridor, high fever, drooling, "tripod" sitting position. Caution: Never depress tongue with spatula (triggers fatal laryngospasm!). Fastidious pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacilli; requires Factor X & V; chocolate agar culture; satellite colonies on blood agar around S. aureus.
Viral Pharyngitis & Ulcers Adenovirus, Epstein-Barr Virus (Infectious Mononucleosis), HSV-1, Coxsackie A (Herpangina) Vesicles, shallow ulcers, posterior pharyngeal cobblestoning, heterophile antibodies (Monospot test), atypical Downey lymphocytes. Bacterial throat cultures yield only normal commensal flora (*Viridans* streptococci, *Neisseria* spp., *Diphtheroids*).
Collection SOP Transport Media

2. Standard Swabbing Technique & Normal Flora Differential

Throat Swab Collection Protocol

  1. Patient Positioning: Seat patient facing bright light. Depress the anterior tongue with a sterile wooden tongue spatula.
  2. Targeted Swabbing: Carefully pass a sterile Dacron or cotton swab between the tonsillar pillars. Rub vigorously over inflamed tonsillar crypts, ulcers, or white follicular patches.
  3. Avoid Contamination: Do NOT touch the tongue, buccal mucosa, uvula, or lips (avoids picking up millions of normal oral commensals).
  4. Transport Media: If processing is delayed \(>2\ \text{hours}\), place swab in Amies or Stuart transport medium with charcoal (neutralizes fatty acids toxic to fastidious streptococci and *C. diphtheriae*).

Normal Oropharyngeal Flora Baseline

A normal throat swab culture yields a heavy mixed growth of:

  • Viridans Streptococci: Alpha-hemolytic (*S. mutans*, *S. mitis*, *S. salivarius*).
  • Commensal Neisseria Species: *N. lactamica*, *N. sicca*, *N. subflava*.
  • Non-pathogenic Diphtheroids: *Corynebacterium pseudodiphtheriticum*, *C. xerosis*.
  • Anaerobic Commensals & Spirochaetes: *Peptostreptococcus*, *Veillonella*, non-pathogenic oral treponemes.
  • Clinical Rule: The presence of normal flora is reported as "Normal upper respiratory tract flora isolated; no pathogenic beta-hemolytic streptococci or C. diphtheriae grown."
Diphtheria Protocol Elek Gel Precipitation

3. Laboratory Identification of Corynebacterium diphtheriae & Elek Test

Culture & Staining Identification SOP

  • Primary Media: Inoculate Hoyles Tellurite Medium or Tinsdale Agar and a Loeffler serum slope. Potassium tellurite inhibits normal flora while *C. diphtheriae* reduces tellurite to metal tellurium, producing grey-black colonies with a dark brown/black halo (Tinsdale cystinase reaction).
  • Albert's Staining: Subculture from Loeffler serum; stain with Toluidine Blue-Malachite Green. Reveals slender club-shaped bacilli with bluish-black metachromatic polyphosphate granules (volutin / Babès-Ernst bodies) in V, L, and Chinese-letter angular arrangements.
  • Biochemical Profile: Catalase Positive, Urease Negative, Ferments Glucose and Maltose (fails to ferment Sucrose). (Note: Sucrose fermentation rules out pathogenic C. diphtheriae and identifies commensal C. xerosis).

Elek Immunoprecipitation Toxigenicity Test

Isolation of *C. diphtheriae* is insufficient for clinical diagnosis because non-toxigenic strains exist. Virulence depends on diphtheria exotoxin encoded by the lysogenic corynephage beta gene (tox+):

  • Elek Plate Setup: A sterile filter paper strip soaked in diphtheria antitoxin (1000 IU/mL) is embedded beneath the center of an Elek agar plate.
  • Inoculation: Test strain and known positive/negative control strains are streaked in parallel lines perpendicular to the antitoxin strip.
  • Interpretation: Incubate at \(37^\circ\text{C}\) for 24–48 hours. Toxigenic strains secrete diphtheria toxin that diffuses laterally and meets diffusing antitoxin at optimal proportions, forming distinct white opaque precipitin lines at \(45^\circ\) angles to the streak.
Diagnostic Matrix Differential Diagnosis

4. Diagnostic Differential Matrix for Pharyngeal & Oral Lesions

Diagnostic Feature Streptococcal Pharyngitis Diphtheria Vincent's Angina Oral Candidiasis (Thrush)
Primary Lesion Appearance Red, swollen tonsils with punctate yellow-white follicular exudates. Tough, leathery, adherent grey-black pseudomembrane on tonsils/uvula/pharynx. Punched-out bleeding gingival ulcers covered with grey slough. Curdy, white, wipeable plaques leaving raw erythema.
Membrane Adherence Loose, easily wiped away with swab. Tenacious & tightly adherent; bleeds profusely if forcefully detached. Loose necrotic slough over bleeding ulcers. Plaques easily detached with tongue spatula.
Microscopic Finding Gram-positive cocci in chains + many PMNs. Gram-positive club-shaped rods with volutin granules (Albert stain). Fusiform Gram-negative rods + loose Borrelia spirochaetes. Large Gram-positive budding yeast cells + pseudohyphae.
Definitive Diagnostic Test Culture on Blood agar (Beta-hemolytic, Bacitracin sensitive, PYR+). Black colonies on Tellurite agar + positive Elek toxigenicity test. Direct microscopic smear (anaerobic culture difficult/unnecessary). Positive Germ Tube test in serum at \(37^\circ\text{C}\) (2–3 h).
Primary Chemotherapy Oral Penicillin V or IM Benzathine Penicillin G (or Erythromycin). Equine Diphtheria Antitoxin (DAT) + Penicillin / Erythromycin. Oral Metronidazole + Penicillin + antiseptic mouthwashes. Topical Nystatin oral suspension or oral Fluconazole.

Section 7.7 Board Review Questions (MCQ 401 – 408)

Test your knowledge of oropharyngeal pathogens, differential diagnoses, and specialized laboratory tests:

MCQ 401 • Group A Streptococcus Identification Tests
Which combination of laboratory test results definitively identifies a beta-hemolytic streptococcus isolated from a throat swab as Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus / GAS)?
A Bacitracin resistant (\(0.04\ \text{U}\)) and CAMP test positive.
B Optochin sensitive (\(\ge 14\ \text{mm}\) zone) and bile soluble.
C Susceptible to \(0.04\ \text{U}\) Bacitracin disc and Pyrrolidonyl Arylamidase (PYR) test positive.
D Catalase positive and growth in \(6.5\%\ \text{NaCl}\).
Correct Answer: C — Susceptible to 0.04 U Bacitracin disc and PYR test positive. Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Strep) is uniquely sensitive to low-concentration (\(0.04\ \text{U}\)) bacitracin ("A-disc") and produces the enzyme L-pyrrolidonyl arylamidase (PYR positive, producing a red color with cinnamaldehyde reagent). In contrast, Group B strep is bacitracin-resistant and CAMP positive.
MCQ 402 • Diphtheria Pseudomembrane Clinical & Laboratory Safety
A 6-year-old unimmunized child presents with severe sore throat, fever, hoarseness, cervical lymphadenopathy ("bull-neck"), and an adherent greyish-black pseudomembrane spanning the tonsils and uvula. Why is forceful mechanical removal of the pseudomembrane strictly contraindicated?
A Forceful removal converts the bacteria into spore-forming bacilli.
B The pseudomembrane is tightly anchored into necrotic mucosal capillaries; forceful stripping causes catastrophic pharyngeal hemorrhage and triggers massive systemic absorption of lethal diphtheria exotoxin.
C Stripping the membrane inactivates therapeutic equine antitoxin.
D The pseudomembrane protects the vocal cords from bacterial superinfection.
Correct Answer: B — Forceful stripping causes catastrophic hemorrhage and massive systemic exotoxin absorption. The diphtheria pseudomembrane consists of dense fibrin, necrotic epithelial cells, red blood cells, leukocytes, and proliferating bacilli firmly anchored into vascularized submucosa. Forceful detachment rips open capillaries, causing profuse bleeding and accelerating lethal exotoxin dissemination to cardiac and neural tissue. Swabs must be sampled gently from the membrane edge.
MCQ 403 • Selective Media for Corynebacterium diphtheriae
On Tinsdale or Hoyles Tellurite Blood Agar, what characteristic colonial morphology indicates presumptive isolation of Corynebacterium diphtheriae?
A Bright golden-yellow colonies with yellow zones of mannitol fermentation.
B Luminous yellow-green fluorescent colonies under ultraviolet light.
C Clear mucoid colonies with green alpha-hemolytic rings.
D Greyish-black to black colonies surrounded by a dark brown/black halo.
Correct Answer: D — Greyish-black colonies surrounded by a dark brown/black halo. C. diphtheriae reduces potassium tellurite to metallic tellurium (imparting a grey-black colony color). On Tinsdale medium, the bacterial enzyme cystinase hydrolyzes sodium thiosulfate in the presence of tellurite to form a distinct dark brown-black halo around colonies.
MCQ 404 • Elek Immunoprecipitation Toxigenicity Principle
What is the definitive in vitro immunological principle of the Elek Test used to confirm toxigenicity of Corynebacterium diphtheriae isolates?
A Lateral diffusion of secreted diphtheria toxin from bacterial streaks meets diffusing antitoxin from an embedded paper strip, forming visible white precipitin lines at 45° angles.
B Agglutination of red blood cells sensitized with diphtheria toxoid.
C Lysis of sheep erythrocytes by bacterial hemolysins in an agar well.
D Fluorescent quenching of potassium permanganate by bacterial proteins.
Correct Answer: A — Lateral diffusion of toxin meets diffusing antitoxin, forming white precipitin lines at 45° angles. The Elek test is an in vitro double immunodiffusion (Ouchterlony) gel precipitation assay. Secreted diphtheria exotoxin diffuses perpendicularly from the bacterial streak, while antitoxin diffuses from the embedded filter strip; at the zone of equivalence, opaque insoluble antigen-antibody precipitin lines form at \(45^\circ\) angles.
MCQ 405 • Vincent's Angina Microscopic Diagnosis
A 24-year-old soldier presents with painful, bleeding gingival ulcerations covered by grey necrotic slough, painful chewing, and severe fetid halitosis. A direct Gram-stained smear (counterstained with dilute carbol fuchsin) demonstrates abundant loose, wavy spirochaetes mixed with long, slender spindle-shaped Gram-negative bacilli. What is the diagnosis?
A Oral Thrush (Candida albicans)
B Primary syphilitic chancre of the tongue
C Vincent's Angina (Acute Necrotizing Ulcerative Gingivitis / ANUG / Fusospirochaetosis)
D Pharyngeal Diphtheria
Correct Answer: C — Vincent's Angina (Fusospirochaetosis / ANUG). Vincent's angina is a polymicrobial symbiotic infection caused by anaerobic Fusobacterium species (spindle-shaped Gram-negative bacilli) and Treponema vincentii / Borrelia vincentii (spirochaetes). Diagnosis is strictly made by direct microscopic demonstration of this co-dominant fusospirochaetal complex; anaerobic culture is unnecessary.
MCQ 406 • Rapid Identification of Oral Candida albicans
A swab from white curdy patches on the buccal mucosa of an HIV-infected patient is inoculated into human or horse serum and incubated at \(37^\circ\text{C}\). Microscopic examination at 2.5 hours reveals short, slender tube-like outgrowths without any constriction at the parent yeast junction. What is this definitive diagnostic test?
A Quellung capsular reaction
B Positive Germ Tube Test confirming Candida albicans
C True hyphal sporulation confirming Aspergillus
D Nagler lecithinase precipitation test
Correct Answer: B — Positive Germ Tube Test confirming Candida albicans. The germ tube (Reynolds-Braude) test is the gold-standard rapid screen for Candida albicans. Incubation of yeast cells in serum at \(37^\circ\text{C}\) for 2–3 hours induces true germ tube formation (parallel-sided germ tubes with no constriction/pinch at the mother blastoconidium neck).
MCQ 407 • Susceptibility Testing Policy for Throat Swabs
According to WHO and Monica Cheesbrough guidelines for clinical bacteriology, why is routine antimicrobial disc susceptibility testing on throat swabs generally unnecessary and discouraged in district laboratories?
A Throat bacteria cannot grow on Mueller-Hinton agar.
B Antibiotic discs are inactivated by salivary enzymes.
C All throat pathogens are intrinsically resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics.
D Streptococcus pyogenes remains universally sensitive to Penicillin G / Penicillin V, and testing normal flora commensals leads to inappropriate, misleading broad-spectrum antibiotic prescribing.
Correct Answer: D — S. pyogenes remains universally sensitive to penicillin; testing normal flora causes inappropriate broad-spectrum prescribing. Globally, Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Strep) has never developed penicillin resistance. Performing routine antibiograms on mixed throat cultures frequently results in testing normal flora commensals (*Viridans* streptococci or *Neisseria*), tempting clinicians to prescribe toxic or broad-spectrum reserve drugs for self-limiting viral or simple streptococcal sore throats.
MCQ 408 • Pediatric Acute Epiglottitis Examination Warning
Why must a medical laboratory technologist or clinician NEVER attempt to depress the tongue or insert a throat swab in a young child presenting with acute stridor, high fever, drooling, and suspected Acute Epiglottitis (Haemophilus influenzae type b)?
A Mechanical instrumentation of the inflamed pharynx can trigger catastrophic, complete laryngospasm and acute total airway obstruction.
B Swabbing epiglottis tissue induces permanent vocal cord paralysis.
C H. influenzae dies instantly upon contact with wooden tongue spatulas.
D Saliva permanently neutralizes Factor X and Factor V growth factors.
Correct Answer: A — Mechanical instrumentation can trigger fatal laryngospasm and complete airway obstruction. Acute epiglottitis is a life-threatening pediatric emergency. The severely inflamed, cherry-red epiglottis is hyper-reactive; touching the posterior pharynx with a swab or tongue depressor can stimulate sudden reflexive laryngospasm, causing immediate asphyxiation. Airway must be secured in an operating theatre, and blood cultures should be drawn for microbiological diagnosis.

7.8 Examination of Pus, Ulcer Material and Skin Specimens

Microbiological Investigation of Wound Sepsis, Abscess Aspirates, Burns, Tropical Ulcers (*Fusobacterium* + *Treponema vincentii*), Cutaneous Anthrax (*Bacillus anthracis* & McFadyean's Reaction), Bubonic Plague (*Yersinia pestis* Bubo Aspirates), Gas Gangrene (*Clostridium perfringens*), Mycetoma Grains, Buruli Ulcer (*M. ulcerans*) & Leprosy Slit-Skin Smears.

Monica Cheesbrough Clinical & Laboratory Principle: A syringe-aspirated pus specimen or deep wound biopsy is infinitely superior to a superficial dry surface swab, which predominantly cultures colonizing skin commensals (*S. epidermidis*, *Corynebacterium*). When examining pus from draining sinuses, always wash and crush discharged granules in saline to differentiate treatable bacterial **actinomycetoma** (fine \(1\ \mu\text{m}\) branching filaments) from fungal **eumycetoma** (broad \(2–6\ \mu\text{m}\) true septate hyphae and chlamydospores)!

Aspiration SOP Extreme Biohazards

2. Collection Standard Operating Procedures & High-Risk Biosafety Alerts

Closed Abscess & Wound Aspiration Technique

  1. Skin Decontamination: Disinfect intact skin over abscess with \(70\%\) alcohol followed by \(2\%\) chlorhexidine/iodine; allow to dry completely.
  2. Aspiration: Aseptically aspirate \(1–5\ \text{mL}\) of pus using a sterile syringe and needle. Expel all air bubbles, replace needle with a sterile cap, or inject directly into an anaerobic transport vial / Amies transport medium.
  3. Superiority Over Swabs: Syringe aspirates preserve anaerobic pathogens, prevent drying, and avoid colonizing surface skin commensals.
  4. Sinus Tracts: Do NOT swab open sinus orifices; aspirate deep pus from sinus base using a sterile fine plastic cannula.

Critical Biosafety Precautions for Plague & Anthrax

  • Suspected Cutaneous Anthrax (*B. anthracis*): Unroofing vesicles generates lethal infectious aerosols. Aspirate vesicular fluid with a fine syringe under BSL-3 / Class II cabinet. Never make glass slide smears for transport (send sealed transport swab in double leak-proof container).
  • Suspected Bubonic Plague (*Y. pestis*): Inject \(0.5\ \text{mL}\) sterile saline into bubo and aspirate back. Highly infectious; risk of pneumonic plague transmission from accidental droplet splashes. Handle strictly in safety cabinet; wear FFP3/N95 respirator.
  • Decontamination SOP: Autoclave all contaminated aspirate tubes and needles at \(121^\circ\text{C}\) for \(30\ \text{minutes}\); flood bench spills with \(1.0\%\) sodium hypochlorite (\(10,000\ \text{ppm}\) available chlorine).
Specialized Microscopy Mycetoma Differentiation

3. Specialized Diagnostic Techniques: McFadyean, Granule Washing & Slit-Skin Smears

McFadyean's Reaction (Anthrax)

Rapid presumptive demonstration of the poly-D-glutamic acid capsule of Bacillus anthracis:

  • Fixation: Fix smear by covering with \(4\%\) Potassium Permanganate (\(KMnO_4\)) for \(10\ \text{minutes}\) (kills vegetative bacilli safely).
  • Stain: Polychrome Loeffler Methylene Blue for \(30–60\ \text{seconds}\).
  • Result: Bacilli stain dark blue, surrounded by a distinct reddish-purple / mauve capsular zone (capsule amorphous halo) against a pale background.

Mycetoma Grain Crush SOP

Crucial test to differentiate treatable bacterial actinomycetoma from recalcitrant fungal eumycetoma:

  1. Wash discharge grains in sterile physiological saline.
  2. Place grain on slide; crush firmly under a coverslip.
  3. 10% KOH Mount: Eumycetoma reveals thick (\(2–6\ \mu\text{m}\)) septate fungal hyphae and round chlamydospores.
  4. Gram / Modified ZN: Actinomycetoma reveals delicate (\(0.5–1\ \mu\text{m}\)) branching bacterial filaments (*Actinomadura*, *Nocardia*).

Slit-Skin Smear for Leprosy

Diagnosis and bacteriological index (BI) grading of Mycobacterium leprae:

  • Biopsy Sites: Earlobe margin, nasal mucosa, and active erythematous skin patch border.
  • Pinch & Slit Method: Pinch skin firmly to render it bloodless; make a \(5\ \text{mm}\) scalpel incision; scrape deep dermis tissue juice.
  • Stain: Modified ZN (using 5% \(H_2SO_4\) or 1% acid-alcohol; *M. leprae* is less acid-fast than *M. tb*).
  • Result: Intracellular clumps of AFB ("globi") in lepromatous leprosy.
Culture Protocol Step-by-Step Summary

4. Systematic Microbiological Culture Protocol for Pus & Wounds

Culture Medium Incubation Atmosphere & Duration Target Microorganisms & Action
5% Sheep Blood Agar Aerobic \(35–37^\circ\text{C}\) for \(18–24\ \text{hours}\) Primary isolation of *Staphylococcus aureus* (beta-hemolysis), *Streptococcus pyogenes*, and general aerobes.
MacConkey Agar Aerobic \(35–37^\circ\text{C}\) for \(18–24\ \text{hours}\) Differentiates lactose-fermenting coliforms (*E. coli*, *Klebsiella*) from non-lactose fermenting *Pseudomonas*, *Proteus*, and *Salmonella*.
Neomycin Blood Agar / Anaerobic Blood Agar Anaerobic Jar with Gas-Pak (\(37^\circ\text{C}\) for \(48\ \text{hours}\)) Selective isolation of *Clostridium perfringens*, *Bacteroides fragilis*, and anaerobic streptococci (neomycin inhibits aerobic coliforms).
Robertson's Cooked Meat Medium (RCM) Aerobic \(35–37^\circ\text{C}\) for up to 72 hours Liquid enrichment backup broth for fastidious aerobes and obligate anaerobes. Subcultured onto blood agar if primary plates are negative.

Section 7.8 Board Review Questions (MCQ 409 – 416)

Test your knowledge of wound pathogens, anthrax staining, plague diagnostics, and mycetoma differentiation:

MCQ 409 • McFadyean's Reaction for Bacillus anthracis
In suspected cutaneous anthrax (malignant pustule), what microscopic observation on a smear stained with Polychrome Loeffler Methylene Blue (McFadyean's Reaction) confirms presumptive diagnosis of Bacillus anthracis?
A Red acid-fast beaded bacilli against a blue background.
B Large square-ended blue-stained bacilli in short chains surrounded by an amorphous, distinct reddish-purple (mauve) capsular halo.
C Small Gram-negative coccobacilli demonstrating bipolar safety-pin staining.
D Intracellular Gram-negative diplococci inside degenerated polymorphonuclear leukocytes.
Correct Answer: B — Large blue bacilli in chains surrounded by a mauve/reddish-purple capsular halo. McFadyean's polychrome methylene blue reaction stains the poly-D-glutamic acid capsule of Bacillus anthracis a characteristic pink-mauve color, while the bacillary bacterial body stains dark blue, providing rapid presumptive identification of anthrax.
MCQ 410 • Bubonic Plague Bubo Aspirate Staining
A lymph node aspirate from a patient in an endemic plague focus with acute high fever, prostration, and an exquisitely tender inguinal bubo is stained with Wayson's or Giemsa stain. What classic morphological hallmark identifies Yersinia pestis?
A Gram-positive rods with terminal round drumstick spores.
B Branching filamentous rods with sulfur granules.
C Small pleomorphic bacilli demonstrating intense bipolar "safety-pin" staining (light center with dark-stained poles).
D Slender acid-fast bacilli arranged in intracellular parallel bundles (globi).
Correct Answer: C — Small pleomorphic bacilli with intense bipolar "safety-pin" staining. Yersinia pestis selectively concentrates basic dyes at its cellular poles when stained with Wayson, Giemsa, or methylene blue, producing a pathognomonic "safety-pin" appearance.
MCQ 411 • Mycetoma Grain Crush Prep (Actinomycetoma vs Eumycetoma)
Discharged granules from a chronic draining foot sinus are crushed between a slide and coverslip. Microscopic examination of a 10% KOH preparation reveals wide, thick (\(2–6\ \mu\text{m}\)) septate fungal hyphae with intercalary chlamydospores. How is this mycetoma definitively classified?
A True Fungal Mycetoma (Eumycetoma / e.g. Madurella mycetomatis)
B Bacterial Actinomycetoma (e.g. Actinomadura madurae)
C Cutaneous Leishmaniasis (Oriental Sore)
D Botryomycosis (Staphylococcal pseudomycosis)
Correct Answer: A — True Fungal Mycetoma (Eumycetoma). Crushing mycetoma grains differentiates fungal eumycetoma (broad \(2–6\ \mu\text{m}\) true fungal hyphae and chlamydospores, requiring antifungal therapy like itraconazole or surgery) from bacterial actinomycetoma (fine \(0.5–1\ \mu\text{m}\) branching prokaryotic filaments like Actinomadura, treatable with prolonged co-trimoxazole and amikacin).
MCQ 412 • Gas Gangrene (Clostridium perfringens) Microscopic Hallmarks
A Gram-stained smear of foul-smelling brownish dishwater wound aspirate from a patient with fulminant gas gangrene following a compound fracture reveals large, thick Gram-positive boxcar rods. What additional cytological feature is characteristic of Clostridium perfringens infection?
A Heavy infiltration with thousands of intact polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs).
B Abundant terminal round endospores inside every bacterial rod.
C Presence of intracellular amastigotes.
D A striking absence of intact leukocytes/PMNs (cellular lysis caused by alpha-toxin lecithinase) and lack of spores in active clinical tissue.
Correct Answer: D — Striking absence of intact leukocytes and lack of spores in active tissue. C. perfringens produces massive quantities of necrotizing alpha-toxin (phospholipase C / lecithinase) and theta-toxin (perfringolysin O) that destroy host cell membranes, completely lysing leukocytes so that few or no intact PMNs are seen on the Gram smear despite gross tissue necrosis. Spores are rarely formed in vivo in active tissue.
MCQ 413 • Tropical Phagedenic Ulcer Microbiology
Which polymicrobial synergistic pair of microorganisms is responsible for the etiology of Tropical Phagedenic Ulcer of the lower extremities in malnourished individuals?
A Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa
B Fusobacterium ulcerans (fusiform bacilli) and Treponema vincentii (Borrelia vincentii spirochaetes)
C Mycobacterium ulcerans and Streptococcus pyogenes
D Bacillus anthracis and Clostridium tetani
Correct Answer: B — Fusobacterium ulcerans and Treponema vincentii (Borrelia vincentii). Tropical phagedenic ulcer is a destructive symbiotic fusospirochaetal infection caused by anaerobic fusiform bacilli (F. ulcerans) acting in concert with motile spirochaetes (T. vincentii), commonly seen on the lower legs of children and young adults in hot, humid tropical lowlands.
MCQ 414 • Buruli Ulcer (Mycobacterium ulcerans) Temperature Requirement
Why does Mycobacterium ulcerans, the causative agent of necrotizing Buruli ulcer, exclusively produce lesions in superficial subcutaneous fat and skin of the extremities, and what is its optimal in vitro culture temperature?
A It is a psychrophilic/mesophilic mycobacterium that grows optimally at \(30–32^\circ\text{C}\) and fails to multiply at core body temperature (\(37^\circ\text{C}\)).
B It requires high concentrations of melanin to synthesize mycolactone toxin.
C It is an obligate aerobe that grows only in direct sunlight.
D It requires an optimal culture temperature of \(45^\circ\text{C}\) on MacConkey agar.
Correct Answer: A — Grows optimally at 30–32°C and fails to multiply at 37°C. M. ulcerans possesses temperature sensitivity that restricts its growth to cooler peripheral tissues (\(30–33^\circ\text{C}\)). In the laboratory, culture bottles on Lowenstein-Jensen medium must be incubated at \(30–32^\circ\text{C}\) (incubation at \(37^\circ\text{C}\) yields false-negative results).
MCQ 415 • Leprosy Slit-Skin Smear Technique & Staining
When collecting and staining a slit-skin smear for Mycobacterium leprae from an earlobe, what technical modification is essential during the acid-fast staining procedure?
A Decolorize with concentrated 50% hydrochloric acid for 10 minutes.
B Use boiling water bath for 30 minutes to fix the smear.
C Use a weaker acid decolorizer (e.g. 5% sulfuric acid \(H_2SO_4\) or 1% acid-alcohol) because M. leprae is less acid-fast than M. tuberculosis.
D Counterstain with Kovac's reagent.
Correct Answer: C — Use a weaker acid decolorizer (5% H₂SO₄ or 1% acid-alcohol) because M. leprae is less acid-fast. The mycolic acid content of the M. leprae cell envelope is lower than that of M. tuberculosis. Standard \(20\%\ H_2SO_4\) or \(3\%\) acid-alcohol will completely decolorize leprosy bacilli, causing false-negative readings. Modified ZN or Fite-Faraco staining uses gentle \(5\%\ H_2SO_4\) or \(1\%\) acid-alcohol decolorization.
MCQ 416 • Closed Abscess vs Superficial Swab Sampling
Why is needle and syringe aspiration of pus from a deep, closed wound abscess clinically and microbiologically superior to swabbing the superficial skin surface of the lesion?
A Syringes chemically neutralize beta-lactamase enzymes.
B Superficial swabs kill all Gram-negative organisms on contact.
C Needles convert non-fastidious bacteria into capnophiles.
D Aspiration provides adequate volume, protects oxygen-sensitive anaerobes from drying/atmospheric exposure, and avoids heavy contamination with normal cutaneous commensal flora.
Correct Answer: D — Aspiration provides adequate volume, protects anaerobes, and avoids skin commensals. Superficial swabs dry out rapidly, expose fastidious anaerobes (*Bacteroides*, *Peptostreptococcus*) to toxic atmospheric oxygen, and harvest colonizing cutaneous flora (*S. epidermidis*, *Corynebacterium*), yielding unrepresentative or sterile results. Closed needle aspiration captures true deep pyogenic pathogens in viable condition.

7.9 Examination of Effusions and Sterile Fluids

Microbiological and Cytological Investigation of Synovial, Pleural, Peritoneal (Ascitic), Pericardial and Hydrocele Fluids • Transudate vs. Exudate Differentiation (\(30\ \text{g/L}\) Protein Cutoff) • Aspiration Dispensing Protocols (\(3.8\%\) Tri-Sodium Citrate) • Crystal Analysis (Needle Urate vs Rhomboid Pyrophosphate) • High-Yield Board Diagnostics.

Monica Cheesbrough Diagnostic Principle: When an effusion is collected, always divide the sample immediately into two containers: \(2–3\ \text{mL}\) in a dry plain tube to observe for spontaneous clotting, and \(9\ \text{mL}\) into a tube containing \(1\ \text{mL}\) of sterile \(3.8\%\) tri-sodium citrate for cell count, protein estimation, and culture. If the fluid is a transudate (clear, un-clotted, protein \(<30\ \text{g/L}\), few mononuclear cells), no further microbiological testing is required. If it is an exudate (cloudy, clots, protein \(>30\ \text{g/L}\), elevated leukocytes), proceed immediately to high-speed centrifugation, Gram stain, ZN stain, and culture!
