Critical Decision Rule District SOP

2. District Laboratory Differentiation: Transudates vs. Exudates

The primary clinical obligation of the district laboratory when receiving an effusion is to rapidly categorize it as a transudate (mechanical/hydrostatic) or an exudate (inflammatory/infectious/malignant):

Diagnostic Parameter Transudate (Non-Inflammatory) Exudate (Inflammatory / Infectious / Malignant) Clinical / Diagnostic Significance
Macroscopic Appearance Clear, pale yellow, watery; non-turbid. Cloudy, turbid, purulent, serosanguinous, or frank bloody. Turbidity indicates high cell density or lipid content; purulence denotes acute bacterial infection.
Spontaneous Clot Formation (Plain Tube) Does NOT clot (contains negligible fibrinogen). Often clots (high fibrinogen content from vascular permeability). Observed in the \(2–3\ \text{mL}\) non-citrated tube within \(10–30\ \text{minutes}\).
Total Protein Concentration Less than \(30\ \text{g/L}\) (\(<3.0\ \text{g/dL}\)). Greater than \(30\ \text{g/L}\) (\(>3.0\ \text{g/dL}\)). Effusion diluted \(1:100\) in saline and measured using the CSF protein technique.
Specific Gravity \(< 1.015\) (typically \(1.006–1.015\)) \(> 1.018\) (elevated dissolved solids and protein) Measured via refractometer or hydrometer in hospital laboratories.
Leukocyte Count & Differential Few cells (\(< 1000/\mu\text{L}\)); predominantly mesothelial cells and few lymphocytes. High leukocyte count (\(> 1000/\mu\text{L}\)):
• Neutrophil dominance (\(>50\%\)): Acute pyogenic bacterial infection.
• Lymphocyte dominance (\(>50\%\)): Tuberculosis, viral, or malignancy. 		Determined using improved Neubauer counting chamber; smear stained by Leishman or Gram.
Laboratory Action Required NO FURTHER TESTING REQUIRED. (Report protein, appearance, cell count; discard). PROCEED IMMEDIATELY TO HIGH-SPEED CENTRIFUGATION, GRAM STAIN, ZN STAIN, AND CULTURE. Conserves expensive microbiological media and diagnostic reagents in district labs.
Specimen Protocol Transport Media

3. Specimen Collection, Dispensing Protocols & Laboratory Processing SOP

Hospital Laboratory Dispensing SOP

Aseptically aspirated fluid must be divided immediately at bedside:

  • Container 1 (Plain): \(2–3\ \text{mL}\) into a dry, sterile screw-cap bottle without anticoagulant to observe for spontaneous fibrin clot formation.
  • Container 2 (Citrated): \(9\ \text{mL}\) into a sterile screw-cap container containing \(1\ \text{mL}\) of sterile \(3.8\%\) tri-sodium citrate (prevents in vitro coagulation of exudates; used for cell counting, total protein, microscopy, and culture).
  • Immediate Transport: Deliver to microbiology immediately with clinical history.

Health Centre Dispatch SOP

When effusions are collected at peripheral health centres for transport:

  • Transport Broth: Inoculate \(5\ \text{mL}\) of effusion into a bottle of sterile thioglycollate broth. Keep warm (do not exceed \(37^\circ\text{C}\) or expose to sunlight).
  • Citrated Sample: \(9\ \text{mL}\) into \(1\ \text{mL}\) sterile \(3.8\%\) tri-sodium citrate.
  • Plain Tube: Remaining fluid into dry sterile tube to observe clotting.
  • Dispatch: Transport to reference laboratory within a few hours.

High-Speed Centrifugation & Smear Preparation

  1. Centrifugation: Transfer citrated effusion to a sterile conical centrifuge tube; centrifuge at high speed (\(3000\ g\)) for \(20\ \text{minutes}\) to concentrate bacteria and cells into the sediment.
  2. Supernatant Handling: Aseptically remove and retain supernatant in a sterile tube (do NOT discard; needed for biochemical/protein re-checks). Thoroughly resuspend sediment in remaining drops of fluid.
  3. Gram Stain: Methanol-fix dried smear for \(2\ \text{minutes}\); examine for pus cells, Gram-positive cocci in pairs/clusters (*S. aureus*, *S. pneumoniae*), intracellular Gram-negative diplococci (*N. gonorrhoeae*), and pleomorphic Gram-negative rods (*H. influenzae*).
  4. Ziehl-Neelsen / Auramine Stain: Prepare heavy smear using multiple drops of sediment. Stain by ZN or fluorescent auramine for AFB. Note: AFB are scanty in effusions; negative smear does not exclude tuberculous effusion.
Crystal Examination Malignancy Smear

4. Synovial Crystal Diagnostics (Gout vs. Pseudogout) & Malignancy Cytology

Synovial Wet Preparation for Crystals

Transfer a drop of centrifuged synovial sediment to a glass slide, cover with a coverslip, and examine with iris diaphragm closed to maximize contrast:

  • Monosodium Urate Crystals (Gout):
    • Morphology: Needle-like, sharply pointed crystals measuring \(8–10\ \mu\text{m}\) in length.
    • Location: Free extracellular and intracellular inside phagocytic polymorphs.
    • Clinical: Strongly associated with hyperuricaemia; intense acute podagra / monoarthritis.
  • Calcium Pyrophosphate Dihydrate / CPPD (Pseudogout / Chondrocalcinosis):
    • Morphology: Rod-shaped, rhomboid, or rectangular crystals measuring up to \(25\ \mu\text{m}\) in length; often exhibit a distinct longitudinal line or cleft running through them.
    • Clinical: Serum urate levels are completely normal in pseudogout.

Cytology Smear for Malignant Cells

When pleural or ascitic effusion is suspected to be secondary to malignancy (carcinomatosis, lymphoma, mesothelioma):

  1. Make two thin smears of the freshly concentrated effusion sediment.
  2. Wet Fixation: While smears are still completely wet, immerse immediately in a container of \(95\%\ \text{v/v}\) ethanol for \(20\ \text{minutes}\) (air drying causes cellular distortion and artifact).
  3. Dispatch: Send wet-fixed smears to the Cytology / Histopathology Laboratory for Papanicolaou or Giemsa staining to detect hyperchromatic pleomorphic malignant clusters with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic (N:C) ratios.

Oxidase test positive for *Neisseria*; satellite test / X+V factor requirement for *Haemophilus*.

MCQ 417 • Transudate vs Exudate Protein Cutoff
According to Monica Cheesbrough's District Laboratory SOP, what total protein concentration cutoff strictly differentiates a non-inflammatory transudate from an inflammatory exudate?
A \(10\ \text{g/L}\) (\(1.0\ \text{g/dL}\))
B \(30\ \text{g/L}\) (\(3.0\ \text{g/dL}\)) — Transudates contain \(<30\ \text{g/L}\) while Exudates contain \(>30\ \text{g/L}\)
C \(60\ \text{g/L}\) (\(6.0\ \text{g/dL}\))
D \(100\ \text{g/L}\) (\(10.0\ \text{g/dL}\))
Correct Answer: B — 30 g/L (3.0 g/dL). A total protein concentration of \(30\ \text{g/L}\) is the definitive cutoff. Transudates (due to hydrostatic/osmotic disturbances such as heart failure or cirrhosis) contain \(<30\ \text{g/L}\) protein and require no further microbiological investigation. Exudates (due to increased vascular permeability from infection or malignancy) contain \(>30\ \text{g/L}\) protein and mandate microscopic and culture workup.
MCQ 418 • Anticoagulant Dispensing Protocol for Effusions
When collecting an effusion for comprehensive cell count, protein estimation, microscopy, and microbiological culture, what anticoagulant formulation and volume ratio is prescribed by Monica Cheesbrough?
A \(5\ \text{mL}\) fluid into \(5\ \text{mL}\) of \(10\%\) EDTA.
B \(10\ \text{mL}\) fluid into \(2\ \text{mL}\) of heparinized formalin.
C \(9\ \text{mL}\) of aspirated fluid into a sterile container containing \(1\ \text{mL}\) of sterile \(3.8\%\) tri-sodium citrate.
D \(1\ \text{mL}\) of fluid into \(9\ \text{mL}\) of potassium oxalate.
Correct Answer: C — 9 mL of fluid into 1 mL of sterile 3.8% tri-sodium citrate. Tri-sodium citrate (\(3.8\%\)) prevents spontaneous clotting (which traps bacteria and leukocytes in fibrin clots) while preserving bacterial viability for culture and maintaining cell morphology for cytological and biochemical evaluation.
MCQ 419 • Gout (Monosodium Urate) Crystal Morphology
A wet preparation of centrifuged synovial fluid sediment from an intensely painful, inflamed first metatarsophalangeal joint reveals intracellular and extracellular needle-like crystals measuring \(8–10\ \mu\text{m}\) in length. What condition is diagnosed?
A Acute Gout (Monosodium Urate crystals)
B Pseudogout (Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate)
C Cholesterol crystal effusion
D Hydroxyapatite crystal disease
Correct Answer: A — Acute Gout (Monosodium Urate crystals). Monosodium urate crystals are characteristically sharp, needle-like crystals measuring \(8–10\ \mu\text{m}\) found in effusions from patients with gout (accompanied by elevated serum urate). Calcium pyrophosphate crystals in pseudogout are rod-shaped or rhomboid and measure up to \(25\ \mu\text{m}\).
MCQ 420 • Pseudogout (CPPD) Crystal Characteristics
Which microscopic and biochemical profile is pathognomonic for Pseudogout (Chondrocalcinosis) during synovial fluid analysis?
A Needle-shaped crystals with marked hyperuricaemia.
B Star-shaped calcium oxalate crystals with acid urine.
C Clumps of intracellular Gram-negative diplococci with low protein.
D Rod-shaped or rectangular/rhomboid crystals (up to \(25\ \mu\text{m}\)) often with a central line/cleft, accompanied by normal serum urate levels.
Correct Answer: D — Rod-shaped/rhomboid crystals (up to 25 µm) with normal serum urate. Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals in pseudogout are larger (up to \(25\ \mu\text{m}\)), rod-shaped or rectangular/rhomboid, often displaying a longitudinal central fissure, and occur in patients with normal serum urate levels.
MCQ 421 • Pericardial Effusion in Developing Countries
What is recognized by Monica Cheesbrough as the single most common infectious cause of large pericardial effusions in developing countries, particularly in association with HIV co-infection?
A Staphylococcus aureus purulent pericarditis
B Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Pericardial Tuberculosis / PCTB)
C Entamoeba histolytica pericardial abscess
D Brugia malayi filarial pericarditis
Correct Answer: B — Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Pericardial Tuberculosis / PCTB). Pericardial tuberculosis is the commonest cause of pericardial effusion and constrictive pericarditis in tropical and developing countries, heavily exacerbated by the HIV pandemic. The fluid is typically an exudate with high lymphocyte counts.
MCQ 422 • Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP) Etiology
In a patient with cirrhotic ascites presenting with fever and abdominal pain, what is the most frequently isolated aerobic Gram-negative bacterial pathogen in Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP)?
A Escherichia coli
B Vibrio cholerae
C Shigella dysenteriae
D Campylobacter jejuni
Correct Answer: A — Escherichia coli. Enteric Gram-negative bacilli that translocate across the intestinal mucosal barrier (primarily Escherichia coli followed by Klebsiella pneumoniae) account for the vast majority of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis cases in cirrhotic ascites.
MCQ 423 • Fixation Method for Cytology Effusion Smears
When preparing smears of concentrated effusion sediment to examine for malignant cells (cytodiagnosis of metastatic carcinoma or lymphoma), how must the smears be fixed?
A Heat-fixed over a roaring Bunsen burner flame until scorched.
B Air-dried at room temperature for 24 hours without chemical fixative.
C Immersed while still wet into \(95\%\ \text{v/v}\) ethanol for \(20\ \text{minutes}\) (Wet Fixation).
D Flooded with \(10\%\) sodium hydroxide for 1 hour.
Correct Answer: C — Immersed while still wet into 95% v/v ethanol for 20 minutes (Wet Fixation). Cytological examination of malignant cells requires immediate wet fixation in \(95\%\) ethanol before the smear dries. Air-drying produces severe cell flattening, swelling, and nuclear chromatin distortion, preventing accurate assessment of malignant nuclear architecture.
MCQ 424 • Culture Media Battery for Effusion Sediment
Which triad of solid culture media is routinely inoculated with the concentrated sediment of an exudative effusion, and under what incubation atmosphere is the Chocolate agar incubated?
A Lowenstein-Jensen, Sabouraud dextrose, and TCBS in pure oxygen.
B XLD, DCA, and SS agar in anaerobic jar.
C Nutrient agar, CLED agar, and Blood agar at \(45^\circ\text{C}\).
D Blood agar (aerobic), MacConkey agar (aerobic), and Chocolate agar incubated in a \(5–10\%\ \text{CO}_2\) enriched atmosphere (candle jar) at \(35–37^\circ\text{C}\).
Correct Answer: D — Blood agar (aerobic), MacConkey (aerobic), and Chocolate agar in CO₂ (candle jar). The routine district protocol for effusion sediment requires: Blood agar for general pyogenic organisms (*S. aureus*, *Streptococcus*), MacConkey agar for coliforms (*E. coli*, *Klebsiella*, *Pseudomonas*), and Chocolate agar in \(5–10\%\ \text{CO}_2\) for fastidious organisms (*N. gonorrhoeae*, *H. influenzae*, *S. pneumoniae*).

You have mastered Examination of Effusions and Sterile Fluids (Cheesbrough Part 2 pp. 92–97).

7.10 Examination of Urogenital Specimens

Laboratory Diagnosis of Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) & Puerperal Sepsis • Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Intracellular Gram-negative Diplococci & MNYC/Thayer-Martin Culture) • Chlamydia trachomatis • Trichomonas vaginalis (Wet Prep Motility) • Candida albicans (Vaginal Thrush) • Gardnerella vaginalis & Bacterial Vaginosis (Clue Cells & Whiff Test) • Treponema pallidum (Dark-Field Microscopy) • Haemophilus ducreyi (Chancroid) • Klebsiella granulomatis (Donovan Bodies).

Monica Cheesbrough Diagnostic Principle: In symptomatic men with urethral discharge, the finding of intracellular Gram-negative kidney bean diplococci inside pus cells has \(>95\%\) sensitivity and specificity for gonorrhoea. However, in women, endocervical Gram smear sensitivity drops to \(40–60\%\); thus, selective culture on MNYC or Thayer-Martin medium incubated in moist \(5–10\%\ \text{CO}_2\) is mandatory. Always distinguish inflammatory vaginitis (T. vaginalis with copious PMNs and pH \(>5\); Candida with budding yeast/pseudohyphae and acid pH \(<4.5\)) from non-inflammatory bacterial vaginosis (epithelial clue cells studded with polymorphic bacteria, absence of lactobacilli and PMNs, fishy amine odor on \(10\%\ \text{KOH}\), and pH \(>5\))!

• Chlamydia trachomatis (Serovars D–K: Non-Gonococcal Urethritis / NGU)
• Ureaplasma urealyticum, Mycoplasma genitalium
• Trichomonas vaginalis (rare) 		Profuse creamy yellow purulent discharge with severe dysuria (gonorrhoea) vs watery/mucoid scanty morning discharge (chlamydia). Complications: Epididymitis, urethral stricture, prostatitis, reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome). Gram Smear: Pus cells containing intracellular Gram-negative diplococci (presumptive gonorrhoea). \(\ge 5\) pus cells per high power field without diplococci = NGU.
Endocervicitis & Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) • Neisseria gonorrhoeae
• Chlamydia trachomatis (D–K)
• Streptococcus pyogenes (GAS)
• Herpes simplex virus (HSV-2) 		Mucopurulent cervical discharge, cervical friability/erythema; \(>60\%\) of cases are asymptomatic in women. Ascending infection leads to salpingitis, pelvic abscess, ectopic pregnancy, and tubal factor infertility. Endocervical swab inoculated onto MNYC or Thayer-Martin medium in \(5–10\%\ \text{CO}_2\); rapid Chlamydia antigen test / PCR; Oxidase+ and Superoxol+ colonies.
Vaginitis & Bacterial Vaginosis (Vaginal Discharge) • Trichomonas vaginalis (Trichomoniasis)
• Candida albicans (Candidiasis / Vaginal Thrush)
• Gardnerella vaginalis + Anaerobes (Bacteroides, Mobiluncus, Peptostreptococcus) 		• Trichomoniasis: Copious greenish-yellow frothy discharge, vulvar itching, "strawberry cervix", pH \(>5\).
• Candidiasis: Thick white "curd-like" / cottage cheese odourless discharge, intense pruritus, pH \(<4.5\).
• Bacterial Vaginosis: Thin, homogeneous greyish-white discharge with foul fishy amine odour, pH \(>5\). 		• Saline wet mount: Jerky, motile flagellated *Trichomonas* trophozoites.
• Gram smear: Gram-positive budding yeast with pseudohyphae (*Candida*).
• Clue cells: Vaginal squamous epithelial cells covered with coccobacilli; positive \(10\%\ \text{KOH}\) Whiff test.
Genital Ulcer Disease (GUD) • Treponema pallidum (Primary Syphilis / Chancre)

• Klebsiella granulomatis (Granuloma Inguinale / Donovanosis)
• Chlamydia trachomatis L1–L3 (Lymphogranuloma Venereum / LGV)

• Chancroid: Multiple, extremely painful, soft ragged ulcers + tender suppurative bubo.
• Donovanosis: Beefy red, painless, progressive granulomatous ulceration without lymphadenopathy.
• LGV: Transient small ulcer followed by massive painful inguinal buboes (groove sign). 		• Dark-Field: Tightly coiled motile spirochaetes (*T. pallidum*).
• Giemsa Smear: Intracellular bipolar "closed safety-pin" Donovan bodies (*K. granulomatis*).

Puerperal Sepsis & Septic Abortion • Streptococcus pyogenes (GAS) & Group B Strep (GBS)
• Clostridium perfringens (Fulminant uterine gas gangrene)
• Staphylococcus aureus, Bacteroides fragilis, Enterococcus, E. coli, Listeria 		Postpartum/post-abortion fever, foul purulent lochia, lower abdominal pain, uterine tenderness, toxic shock, and septic thrombophlebitis. Blood agar (aerobic + anaerobic), MacConkey, Cooked Meat Broth subcultures; Gram smear showing boxcar rods without spores (*C. perfringens*) or Gram-positive chains (GAS).
Collection SOP Charcoal Amies

2. Urogenital Specimen Collection SOPs & Transport Standards

Male Urethral Discharge SOP

  1. Timing: Ensure the patient has not urinated for at least \(2–4\ \text{hours}\) (urination flushes pus cells and gonococci from the urethra).
  2. Cleaning: Cleanse the glans penis and urethral meatus with sterile physiological saline.
  3. Milking: Gently "milk" or massage the urethra from above downwards.
  4. Smear Prep: Collect discharge on a sterile swab; gently roll the swab onto a clean glass slide (rubbing or spreading ruptures fragile pus cells, releasing intracellular gonococci into the extracellular space).
  5. Inoculation: Inoculate MNYC / Thayer-Martin plate directly or place swab in Charcoal Amies transport medium.

Endocervical Specimen SOP

  1. Speculum Insertion: Moisten a sterile bivalve vaginal speculum with sterile warm water ONLY. (Caution: Never use antiseptic gels, KY-jelly, or bactericidal lubricants).
  2. Expose Cervix: Visualize the external os; gently swab away excess cervical mucus with a sterile cotton swab and discard.
  3. Endocervical Swab: Insert a sterile cotton-wool/dacron swab \(20–30\ \text{mm}\) into the endocervical canal; rotate firmly against the endocervical wall for \(10–15\ \text{seconds}\) to collect columnar epithelial cells and exudate.
  4. Direct Plating: Inoculate MNYC plate immediately and incubate in candle jar within \(30\ \text{minutes}\).

Charcoal Amies Transport SOP

  • Formulation: Amies Transport Medium with Charcoal neutralizes toxic fatty acids and metabolic peroxides that kill fastidious *N. gonorrhoeae*.
  • Holding Time: Preserves viability of gonococci and commensals for up to \(24\ \text{hours}\) during transport from peripheral clinics.
  • Temperature: Transport swabs in a cool box (\(4–8^\circ\text{C}\) or ambient tropical shade); do not expose to direct heat or sunlight.
  • Inoculation Speed: If plated at bedside, transfer plates to a \(35–37^\circ\text{C}\) moist \(\text{CO}_2\) incubator within \(30\ \text{minutes}\).
Vaginitis Differential Amsel Criteria

3. Clinical & Laboratory Differentiation of Vaginal Infections

Monica Cheesbrough details the systematic differentiation of the three classic causes of vaginal discharge:

Feature / Parameter Trichomonas vaginalis (Trichomoniasis) Candida albicans (Vaginal Thrush) Gardnerella vaginalis (Bacterial Vaginosis)
Discharge Character Profuse, yellow-green, frothy/bubbly, purulent. Thick, white, curdy / "cottage-cheese" like, adherent plaques. Thin, homogeneous, greyish-white, smoothly coating vaginal walls.
Vaginal pH Elevated (\(> 5.0\)) Acidic (\(< 4.5\)) (Typically \(4.0–4.5\)) Elevated (\(> 5.0\)) (Typically \(5.0–6.0\))
Amine "Whiff" Test (\(10\%\ \text{KOH}\)) Negative or faint Negative (No fishy odor) Strongly Positive: Intense pungent "fishy / ammoniacal" odor on adding \(10\%\ \text{KOH}\).
Direct Microscopy (Saline Wet Mount) Motile flagellated trophozoites (\(10–20\ \mu\text{m}\)) with jerky, non-directional undulating motility; numerous polymorphonuclear pus cells (PMNs). Budding yeast cells (blastoconidia) and branching pseudohyphae; moderate to numerous PMNs. Clue Cells: Vaginal squamous epithelial cells completely encrusted with polymorphic coccobacilli; borders obscured; absence of lactobacilli and absent PMNs.
Gram Smear Findings Pus cells with mixed flora; trichomonads poorly stained (pale pink). Large Gram-positive oval budding yeast cells (\(3–6\ \mu\text{m}\)) with Gram-positive pseudohyphae. Clue cells studded with Gram-variable coccobacilli (*Gardnerella*), curved Gram-negative rods (*Mobiluncus*), loss of large Gram-positive *Lactobacillus* rods.
Diagnostic Culture Indication Feinberg or Diamond medium (only when microscopy is negative). Sabouraud dextrose agar (not routinely indicated; small numbers are commensals). Culture not recommended (low specificity; diagnosis is purely clinical/microscopical via Amsel/Nugent).
Dark-Field Donovan Bodies

4. Genital Ulcer Diagnostics: Dark-Field, Donovan Bodies & Chancroid

Dark-Field Microscopy (*T. pallidum*)

Direct demonstration of living Treponema pallidum from primary chancre or condylomata lata:

  • Sampling: Cleanse chancre with saline; abrade gently to express clear serous fluid (avoid red blood cells). Place drop on clean slide, coverslip immediately.
  • Microscopy: Examine under \(40\times\) objective using a dark-field stop in the condenser filter holder.
  • Morphology: Brightly glowing, slender, delicate spirochaetes (\(6–15\ \mu\text{m}\) long) with \(8–14\) regular, tightly wound coils.
  • Motility: Characteristic slow rotational spinning, bending in the middle, and lengthening/shortening accordion motion (differentiated from coarse, irregular saprophytic spirochaetes).

Donovan Bodies (*K. granulomatis*)

Diagnosis of Granuloma Inguinale (Donovanosis) caused by Klebsiella granulomatis:

  • Tissue Crush Technique: Pinch off a small piece of clean granulation tissue from ulcer edge; crush firmly between two glass slides.
  • Staining: Fix with methanol for \(2\ \text{minutes}\); stain with Giemsa or RapiDiff for \(20\ \text{minutes}\).
  • Microscopical Hallmark: Large mononuclear histiocytes/macrophages packed with intracellular pleomorphic coccobacilli demonstrating intense bipolar "closed safety-pin" staining (Donovan bodies).

Chancroid (*Haemophilus ducreyi*)

Diagnosis of Soft Sore / Chancroid with painful suppurative inguinal bubo:

  • Smear Morphology: Gram-negative tiny, slender coccobacilli arranged in parallel chains or clusters resembling a "school of fish" or "railroad tracks".
  • Culture: Fastidious; requires Mueller-Hinton chocolate agar supplemented with \(1–2\%\) IsoVitaleX, \(3\ \mu\text{g/mL}\) vancomycin, incubated in \(5–10\%\ \text{CO}_2\) at \(33–35^\circ\text{C}\) with high humidity for up to \(7\ \text{days}\).
Culture Media Laboratory Identification

5. Selective Media, Incubation & Identification of Neisseria gonorrhoeae

Culture Medium Key Selective Agents & Inhibitors Colony Appearance & Growth Requirements Confirmatory Biochemical Reactions
Modified New York City (MNYC) Medium • Vancomycin: Inhibits Gram-positive bacteria.
• Colistin: Inhibits Gram-negative commensals.
• Trimethoprim: Inhibits *Proteus* swarming.
• Amphotericin B / Nystatin: Inhibits yeasts. 		Small, raised, grey, translucent, shiny mucoid colonies after 24–48 h in moist \(5–10\%\ \text{CO}_2\) at \(35–37^\circ\text{C}\). Advantage: Colonies can be tested directly for beta-lactamase and sugars without subculture. • Oxidase Test: Rapidly positive (deep purple within 10 sec).
• Carbohydrate Utilization: Ferments Glucose ONLY (Acid positive, Gas negative); Maltose negative, Sucrose negative, Lactose negative.
• Superoxol (\(30\%\ H_2O_2\)): Immediate explosive bubbling.
Thayer-Martin / Modified Thayer-Martin (MTM) Chocolate agar base supplemented with Vancomycin, Colistin, Nystatin, and Trimethoprim (VCNT inhibitor cocktail). Small grey-white convex colonies. Note: Colonies require subculturing to non-selective chocolate agar before carbohydrate utilization testing. Oxidase positive; Gram stain reveals Gram-negative kidney-bean diplococci; Beta-lactamase (Nitrocefin test) positive in PPNG strains.
Blood Agar (Aerobic + Anaerobic) & Cooked Meat Broth Unsupplemented sheep blood agar and Robertson's Cooked Meat Broth (RCM). Inoculated for suspected puerperal sepsis and septic abortion to isolate Streptococcus pyogenes, Clostridium perfringens, S. aureus, and Bacteroides. Subculture cooked meat broth at 24 h, 48 h, and 72 h if primary blood agar plates show no growth despite pus cells on direct Gram smear.
Board Examination Section 8 Active Interactive MCQs

Section 7.10 Board Review Questions (MCQ 425 – 432)

Test your mastery of STI diagnostics, gonococcal smear interpretations, clue cell criteria, dark-field microscopy, and selective media:

MCQ 425 • Male Urethral Gram Smear for Gonorrhoea
Why does a Gram-stained smear of male urethral discharge have a diagnostic accuracy of \(>95\%\) for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, whereas an endocervical smear in women has a sensitivity of only \(40–60\%\)?
A Women do not mount a polymorphonuclear leukocyte response to gonococcal infection.
B Estrogen chemically converts Gram-negative diplococci into Gram-positive rods.
C The male urethra is normally sterile with few commensals, while the female cervix contains normal commensal vaginal flora and non-pathogenic morphologically similar coccobacilli that obscure low numbers of gonococci.
D N. gonorrhoeae loses its cell wall inside the endocervical canal.
Correct Answer: C — The male urethra is normally sterile with few commensals, whereas the female cervix contains abundant commensal flora. In symptomatic males, urethral discharge contains millions of PMNs packed with intracellular Gram-negative diplococci with virtually no competing flora. In women, complex resident flora (*Veillonella*, *Acinetobacter*, *Gardnerella*), mucus barriers, and lower bacterial burdens reduce smear sensitivity, requiring selective culture (MNYC/Thayer-Martin) for definitive diagnosis.
MCQ 426 • Bacterial Vaginosis "Clue Cell" Definition
During microscopic examination of a vaginal wet preparation and Gram smear from a patient with a thin, homogenous greyish discharge, what microscopic finding definitively defines a "Clue Cell"?
A A neutrophil containing phagocytosed budding yeast cells.
B A vaginal squamous epithelial cell whose entire surface and outer borders are heavily studded and obscured by small Gram-variable coccobacilli (*Gardnerella* and anaerobes).
C A columnar cell with a multinucleated giant inclusion body.
D A large macrophage packed with acid-fast bacilli in parallel globi.
Correct Answer: B — A vaginal squamous epithelial cell heavily studded and obscured by coccobacilli. Clue cells are the pathognomonic hallmark of bacterial vaginosis (Amsel criterion). Adherent *Gardnerella vaginalis* and anaerobic rods coat the epithelial cell surface, giving it a stippled, granular appearance and completely blurring its sharp cellular margins, accompanied by an absence of protective *Lactobacillus* and lack of PMNs.
MCQ 427 • Vaginal Infection Differentiation & pH
A female patient presents with intense vulvar pruritus, severe dyspareunia, and a thick, white, odourless "curd-like" vaginal discharge. Measurement of vaginal secretions reveals a pH of 4.2 (acidic) and a negative 10% KOH Whiff test. What is the diagnosis?
A Vaginal Candidiasis (Vaginal Thrush / Candida albicans)
B Trichomonas vaginalis vaginitis
C Bacterial Vaginosis (*Gardnerella*)
D Mucopurulent Endocervicitis (*C. trachomatis*)
Correct Answer: A — Vaginal Candidiasis (Candida albicans). *Candida* vulvovaginitis uniquely presents with a normal to low acidic pH (\(<4.5\)), thick white curd-like discharge, intense erythema/pruritus, and a negative amine test. In contrast, both *Trichomonas* vaginitis and bacterial vaginosis consistently produce an elevated pH (\(>5.0\)).
MCQ 428 • Dark-Field Microscopy for Treponema pallidum
When performing dark-field microscopy on serous fluid from a suspected primary syphilitic chancre, how is Treponema pallidum reliably differentiated from non-pathogenic saprophytic genital spirochaetes?
A *T. pallidum* is three times thicker and possesses broad, loose, irregular waves.
B *T. pallidum* fluoresces bright green under blue light without any stains.
C *T. pallidum* forms rigid non-motile straight rods.
D *T. pallidum* is extremely thin, delicate (\(6–15\ \mu\text{m}\) long), with 8–14 tightly regular coils, demonstrating slow rotation, midpoint flexion, and accordion lengthening/shortening.
Correct Answer: D — Thin, delicate spirochaete with 8–14 regular coils and slow rotation/flexion motility. *T. pallidum* exhibits uniform, tightly wound helical coils (resembling a fine corkscrew) with deliberate, graceful motility. Commensal genital treponemes (e.g. *T. refringens*) are thicker, coarser, with few irregular undulating waves and rapid, thrashing motility.
MCQ 429 • Donovan Bodies in Granuloma Inguinale
In a patient from an endemic tropical region presenting with extensive, painless, beefy-red ulcerating genital granulomas without regional lymphadenopathy, a Giemsa-stained tissue crush smear reveals large macrophages packed with intracellular pleomorphic coccobacilli demonstrating bipolar "safety-pin" staining (Donovan bodies). What is the etiological organism?
A Haemophilus ducreyi
B Klebsiella granulomatis (formerly Calymmatobacterium granulomatis)
C Chlamydia trachomatis serovar L2
D Yersinia enterocolitica
Correct Answer: B — Klebsiella granulomatis (Donovanosis). Granuloma inguinale is characterized by intracellular Donovan bodies (encapsulated Gram-negative bacilli with prominent polar chromatin condensation resembling closed safety pins) inside large histiocytes on Giemsa or Leishman stain.
MCQ 430 • Neisseria gonorrhoeae Carbohydrate Fermentation
An oxidase-positive, Gram-negative diplococcus isolated on Modified New York City (MNYC) medium from an endocervical swab is tested for carbohydrate utilization in cystine trypticase agar (CTA) sugars. What specific fermentation profile confirms Neisseria gonorrhoeae?
A Glucose Positive (+), Maltose Negative (-), Sucrose Negative (-), Lactose Negative (-)
B Glucose Positive (+), Maltose Positive (+), Sucrose Negative (-), Lactose Negative (-)
C Glucose Negative (-), Maltose Negative (-), Sucrose Negative (-), Lactose Negative (-)
D Glucose Positive (+), Maltose Positive (+), Sucrose Positive (+), Lactose Positive (+)
Correct Answer: A — Glucose (+), Maltose (-), Sucrose (-), Lactose (-). Neisseria gonorrhoeae ferments Glucose ONLY (acid without gas). In contrast, N. meningitidis ferments both Glucose AND Maltose, N. lactamica ferments Glucose, Maltose, and Lactose, and Moraxella catarrhalis is asaccharolytic (all negative).
MCQ 431 • Non-Gonococcal Urethritis (NGU) Microscopic Criteria
According to Cheesbrough, what microscopic finding on a male urethral smear establishes a presumptive diagnosis of Non-Gonococcal Urethritis (NGU) (most commonly caused by Chlamydia trachomatis)?
A Complete absence of all white blood cells and epithelial cells.
B Abundant intracellular Gram-negative diplococci with zero pus cells.
C \(\ge 5\) pus cells (polymorphonuclear neutrophils) per high power field (\(100\times\)) with NO intracellular Gram-negative diplococci seen.
D Presence of branching Gram-positive sulfur granules.
Correct Answer: C — ≥ 5 pus cells per HPF with NO intracellular diplococci. A urethral smear showing \(\ge 5\) PMNs/HPF (or \(>15\) PMNs/HPF in centrifuged first-voided urine sediment) in the absence of Gram-negative diplococci fulfills the diagnostic criteria for NGU, indicating infection with Chlamydia trachomatis (up to \(40\%\)), Mycoplasma genitalium, or Ureaplasma.
MCQ 432 • Specimen Collection Precautions for Gonorrhoea & Trichomonas
Why must vaginal speculums be lubricated with sterile warm water ONLY (and never surgical antiseptic jellies), and why must patients not urinate for 2–4 hours prior to male urethral swab collection?
A Water stimulates spirochaetes to produce endospores.
B Lubricant gels permanently stain slides purple during Gram staining.
C Urination converts aerobic bacteria into strict anaerobes.
D Commercial lubricating gels contain bactericidal agents that kill fragile *N. gonorrhoeae*, while urination washes away diagnostic purulent exudate and intracellular diplococci from the anterior urethra.
Correct Answer: D — Lubricating gels contain bactericidal preservatives that kill gonococci, and urination flushes out diagnostic pus cells. Antiseptic gels, chlorhexidine, and methylparaben preservatives in standard lubricants are lethal to fastidious *N. gonorrhoeae* and immobilize *T. vaginalis*. Waiting 2–4 hours after micturition allows adequate pooling of pus cells and bacterial burden inside the urethral lumen for diagnostic sampling.

You have mastered Examination of Urogenital Specimens (Cheesbrough Part 2 pp. 97–104).

7.11 Examination of Faecal Specimens

Microbiological Investigation of Acute Gastroenteritis, Bacillary Dysentery, Epidemic Cholera & Diarrhoeal Outbreaks • Shigella dysenteriae (Sd1 Shiga Toxin) • Salmonella enterica Serovars • Vibrio cholerae (O1 El Tor & O139 Bengal on TCBS/APW) • Campylobacter jejuni (Gull-Wing Fuchsin Smears & \(42^\circ\text{C}\) Microaerophilic Isolation) • Enteropathogenic E. coli Pathotypes (ETEC, EPEC, EIEC, EHEC/VTEC O157:H7 on SMAC) • Cary-Blair Transport • Comprehensive Biochemical Identification Algorithms (KIA, LDC, Indole, Urease).

Monica Cheesbrough Diagnostic Principle: When screening non-lactose fermenting colonies from stool cultures, always perform a 2–4 hour urease test first! A positive urease test eliminates harmless *Proteus* immediately, conserving expensive media and antisera. On XLD agar, *Shigella* produces translucent pink-red colonies (no xylose fermentation), while *Salmonella* produces pink-red colonies with black centers (lysine decarboxylation + \(H_2S\) production). For suspected cholera, never perform an oxidase test directly on yellow TCBS colonies (acid inhibits the enzyme); subculture first onto nutrient agar for \(4–6\ \text{hours}\)!

Collection & Transport Direct Microscopy

2. Stool Collection SOPs, Cary-Blair Transport & Microscopic Examination

Cary-Blair Stool Transport SOP

  • Acute Stage: Collect stool during the acute diarrhoeal phase before antimicrobial therapy.
  • Container: Clean, dry, leakproof container (disinfectant-free; avoid urine contamination). Select portions with blood and mucus.
  • Cary-Blair Medium: Semisolid transport medium with low nutrient content and high pH (\(8.4\)); preserves Salmonella, Shigella, Vibrio, and Yersinia for up to \(48\ \text{hours}\) (and Campylobacter for \(6\ \text{hours}\)).
  • Alkaline Peptone Water (APW): When cholera is suspected, inoculate \(1\ \text{mL}\) of stool into \(10\ \text{mL}\) of sterile APW (pH \(8.6\)); transport to lab within \(8\ \text{hours}\).

Faecal Leukocytes (Methylene Blue Prep)

Rapid bedside differentiation of invasive bacterial vs non-invasive toxigenic diarrhoea:

  • Mix one drop of fresh stool with one drop of Loeffler's Methylene Blue on a glass slide.
  • Invasive Pathogens: Abundant polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs / pus cells) with lobed nuclei (*Shigella*, *Campylobacter*, *EIEC*, *Salmonella*).
  • Mononuclear Leukocytes: Predominantly seen in typhoid fever (*Salmonella Typhi*).
  • Non-Invasive Pathogens: Zero or negligible pus cells (*V. cholerae*, *ETEC*, *Rotavirus*, *EHEC O157*).

Basic Fuchsin Smear (*Campylobacter*)

Rapid presumptive diagnosis of Campylobacter jejuni enteritis in children \(<2\ \text{years}\):

  • Prepare thin faecal smear; heat-fix gently.
  • Stain with \(1\%\) Basic Fuchsin for \(10–20\ \text{seconds}\); rinse with tap water.
  • Microscopical Hallmark: Abundant small, slender, curved, spiral Gram-negative bacilli demonstrating classic "gull-wing" pairs, S-shapes, and comma forms under \(100\times\) oil immersion.
Selective Media Biochemical Differentiation

• Salmonella spp.: Red colonies with black centers (\(H_2S\) production).

MacConkey Agar Bile salts, Lactose, Neutral red. • Non-Lactose Fermenters (*Shigella*, *Salmonella*, *Proteus*): Pale, colorless colonies.

Serological Testing & Vi Antigen Heat Inactivation SOP

  • Autoagglutination Control: Always emulsify growth in saline first. If clumping occurs without antiserum (autoagglutination), the strain is rough and un-typable.
  • Vi Antigen Masking in *Salmonella Typhi*: The capsular **Vi (virulence) polysaccharide antigen** physically covers somatic **O (lipopolysaccharide) antigen** epitopes, causing false-negative O-agglutination.
  • Heat Inactivation Protocol: Heat a dense saline bacterial suspension in a boiling water bath (\(100^\circ\text{C}\)) for \(15–30\ \text{minutes}\). This destroys heat-labile Vi antigen, exposing underlying heat-stable somatic O9 and O12 antigens for definitive slide agglutination!
Board Examination Section 8 Active Interactive MCQs

Section 7.11 Board Review Questions (MCQ 433 – 440)

Test your mastery of enteric pathogen isolation, XLD chemistry, TCBS oxidase rules, SMAC differentiation, and biochemical algorithms:

MCQ 433 • XLD Agar Differentiation Chemistry
On Xylose Lysine Deoxycholate (XLD) agar, why do Salmonella species form red colonies with black centers, whereas Shigella species form plain translucent pink-red colonies without blackening?
A *Shigella* ferments lactose and produces hydrogen sulfide, but lacks phenol red.
B *Salmonella* decarboxylates lysine to alkaline cadaverine and reduces sodium thiosulfate to black iron sulfide (\(H_2S\)), whereas *Shigella* cannot decarboxylate lysine or produce \(H_2S\) and ferments no carbohydrates.
C *Shigella* produces gelatinase which dissolves iron salts.
D *Salmonella* absorbs neutral red dye directly into its capsule.
Correct Answer: B — Salmonella decarboxylates lysine and produces H₂S; Shigella produces neither. *Salmonella* initially ferments xylose (acid/yellow), but subsequently decarboxylates lysine to revert the pH back to alkaline (red) and reduces thiosulfate to produce black ferrous sulfide centers. *Shigella* cannot ferment xylose, lactose, or sucrose, and is LDC negative and \(H_2S\) negative, thus appearing as plain pink-red colonies.
MCQ 434 • TCBS Agar & Oxidase Testing Rule
Why must an oxidase test NEVER be performed directly from yellow colonies growing on Thiosulfate Citrate Bile-Salts Sucrose (TCBS) agar when screening for Vibrio cholerae?
A Bile salts convert the oxidase reagent into toxic cyanide gas.
B Bromothymol blue permanently oxidizes the platinum loop.
C The acidic pH generated by vigorous sucrose fermentation on TCBS inhibits the intracellular cytochrome oxidase enzyme, causing false-negative reactions.
D *V. cholerae* is naturally oxidase negative on all culture media.
Correct Answer: C — Acid produced by sucrose fermentation inhibits the oxidase enzyme. Fermentation of sucrose creates localized acidity (pH \(<6.0\)) around colonies on TCBS, which inactivates the bacterial cytochrome oxidase system and produces false-negative oxidase results. Isolates must be subcultured to nutrient agar for \(4–6\ \text{hours}\) to test oxidase activity accurately.
MCQ 435 • Rapid Exclusion of Proteus with Urease
In a district laboratory examining non-lactose fermenting colonies from stool cultures, why does Monica Cheesbrough recommend performing an immediate 2–4 hour urease test before setting up complex sugars or KIA?
A A positive urease test rapidly identifies non-pathogenic commensal Proteus and excludes it immediately, avoiding unnecessary expensive biochemical and serological testing.
B Shigella dysenteriae produces urease faster than any other enteric pathogen.
C Urease hydrolyzes lactose into sorbitol.
D Urease testing kills contaminating bacteriophages.
Correct Answer: A — Rapidly identifies Proteus and excludes it immediately. *Proteus* species mimic *Salmonella* on XLD (producing red colonies with black centers) and MacConkey (colorless non-lactose fermenters). Because *Proteus* produces potent urease within 2–4 hours while *Salmonella* and *Shigella* are urease negative, this single test eliminates *Proteus* early and saves resources.
MCQ 436 • Sorbitol MacConkey (SMAC) for EHEC O157:H7
During an outbreak of acute bloody diarrhoea without faecal leukocytes (haemorrhagic colitis) complicated by acute renal failure (HUS), what characteristic colonial morphology differentiates Enterohaemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC O157:H7) on Sorbitol MacConkey (SMAC) agar?
A Bright pink-red colonies with bile precipitation rings.
B Jet-black colonies with metallic green sheen.
C Mucoid yellow colonies surrounded by a clearing zone.
D Colorless / pale translucent colonies because EHEC O157 strains are non-sorbitol fermenting (whereas \(>95\%\) of commensal E. coli ferment sorbitol to produce pink colonies).
Correct Answer: D — Colorless/pale colonies due to lack of sorbitol fermentation. Verotoxigenic *E. coli* O157:H7 lacks the enzyme to ferment D-sorbitol within 24 hours, forming colorless colonies on SMAC, whereas normal fecal *E. coli* flora rapidly ferments sorbitol, producing bright pink colonies.
MCQ 437 • Campylobacter jejuni Microscopic & Culture Requirements
Which laboratory combination of staining morphology, atmospheric requirement, and incubation temperature confirms the isolation of Campylobacter jejuni from a diarrhoeic infant?
A Thick Gram-positive boxcar rods, strict anaerobiosis, \(25^\circ\text{C}\).
B Slender "gull-wing" curved Gram-negative bacilli on basic fuchsin, incubated under microaerophilic conditions (\(5\%\ \text{O}_2, 10\%\ \text{CO}_2, 85\%\ \text{N}_2\)) at \(42–43^\circ\text{C}\).
C Large pleomorphic coccobacilli, pure oxygen atmosphere, \(30^\circ\text{C}\).
D Acid-fast branching filaments, aerobic atmosphere, \(37^\circ\text{C}\).
Correct Answer: B — "Gull-wing" curved rods, microaerophilic conditions at 42–43°C. *Campylobacter jejuni* is a thermophilic microaerophile that grows optimally at \(42–43^\circ\text{C}\) (which suppresses competing normal coliform fecal flora) in a reduced oxygen (\(5\%\ \text{O}_2\)) atmosphere and shows classic "gull-wing" morphology on basic fuchsin/Gram stain.
MCQ 438 • Salmonella Typhi Vi Antigen Masking & Boiling SOP
A suspect Salmonella isolate from blood/stool culture agglutinates strongly with Vi antiserum but fails to agglutinate with Salmonella O Group 1 (O9, O12) factor antisera. How must this isolate be processed to confirm Salmonella Typhi?
A Heat a dense saline suspension in a boiling water bath (\(100^\circ\text{C}\)) for \(15–30\ \text{minutes}\) to destroy heat-labile Vi capsular antigen, then retest with O antisera.
B Treat with concentrated hydrochloric acid to destroy flagella.
C Incubate on MacConkey agar at \(4^\circ\text{C}\) for 7 days.
D Discard the isolate as a harmless contaminant.
Correct Answer: A — Heat in a boiling water bath for 15–30 minutes to inactivate Vi antigen. The capsular Vi polysaccharide antigen in virulent *S. Typhi* strains physically shields somatic O antigen receptors from agglutinating antibodies. Boiling the bacterial suspension for 15–30 minutes strips away the heat-labile Vi capsule while preserving heat-stable somatic O lipopolysaccharide epitopes.
MCQ 439 • KIA Profile of Salmonella Typhi vs S. Typhimurium
How is Salmonella Typhi distinguished from non-typhoidal Salmonella Typhimurium on Kligler Iron Agar (KIA)?
A *S. Typhi* ferments lactose producing a yellow slope.
B *S. Typhimurium* produces neither acid nor gas in the butt.
C *S. Typhi* produces a trace/weak ring of \(H_2S\) blackening and NO gas (anaerogenic), whereas *S. Typhimurium* produces heavy \(H_2S\) blackening and abundant gas cracks in the yellow butt.
D *S. Typhi* liquefies KIA within 1 hour.
Correct Answer: C — S. Typhi produces trace H₂S and NO gas; S. Typhimurium produces heavy H₂S and abundant gas. In KIA, *S. Typhi* characteristically ferments glucose without gas production (anaerogenic) and forms a delicate narrow mustache of \(H_2S\) at the slope-butt junction. *S. Typhimurium* ferments glucose with copious gas bubbles/cracks and intense blackening throughout the entire tube.
MCQ 440 • Cary-Blair Stool Transport Medium Features
Why is Cary-Blair medium the WHO-recommended standard transport medium for faecal specimens in tropical and district laboratories?
A It contains high concentrations of penicillin to kill non-enteric commensals.
B It actively multiplies rotaviruses during transport.
C It stains all Gram-negative bacilli fluorescent yellow.
D It has a low nutrient content, high pH (\(8.4\)), and lacks carbohydrate, preventing bacterial overgrowth and acid production that would kill fragile *Shigella* and *Vibrio*.
Correct Answer: D — Low nutrient, high alkaline pH (8.4), prevents overgrowth and acid destruction. Cary-Blair transport medium maintains viability without promoting cellular proliferation. Its alkaline pH (\(8.4\)) prevents acidification from normal fermentative coliform metabolism, which is rapidly lethal to delicate pathogens like *Shigella dysenteriae* and *Vibrio cholerae*.

7.12 Examination of Urine

Microbiological and Microscopical Investigation of Urinary Tract Infections (UTI), Cystitis & Pyelonephritis • Clean-Catch Midstream Urine (MSU) SOP & Boric Acid Preservative (\(1\%\ \text{w/v}\)) • Significant Pyuria (\(>10\ \text{WBCs}/\mu\text{L}\)) • Semi-Quantitative Calibrated Loop Inoculation (\(1/500\ \text{mL}\)) • Kass Criterion for Significant Bacteriuria (\(\ge 10^5\ \text{CFU/mL}\)) • CLED Agar Differentiation & Proteus Swarming Prevention • Biochemical Triad (Protein, Greiss Nitrite, Leukocyte Esterase) • Urinary Parasitology (*S. haematobium*, *T. vaginalis*, *W. bancrofti*).

Monica Cheesbrough Diagnostic Principle: An unpreserved clean-catch midstream urine left standing at room temperature undergoes rapid bacterial proliferation and urea hydrolysis by Proteus, raising pH and lysing diagnostic pus cells and urinary casts! When a delay of \(>2\ \text{hours}\) is expected, immediately add \(1\%\ \text{w/v}\) boric acid (\(0.1\ \text{g}/10\ \text{mL}\)), which arrests bacterial multiplication without killing pathogens. On CLED agar (electrolyte-deficient to prevent Proteus swarming), uropathogenic E. coli produces opaque yellow colonies (lactose-positive), while Proteus produces translucent blue-grey colonies. Under Kass criteria, a pure growth of \(\ge 10^5\ \text{CFU/mL}\) (\(\ge 200\ \text{colonies}\) on a \(1/500\ \text{mL}\) loop) confirms significant bacteriuria!

Collection Standards Boric Acid SOP

2. Midstream Urine (MSU) Collection & Boric Acid Preservation SOP

Clean-Catch Midstream Urine SOP

  1. First Morning Urine: Best specimen; overnight bladder incubation allows bacterial multiplication and nitrate reduction.
  2. Female Patients: Wash hands; cleanse urethral peri-meatal area with clean water (no disinfectants); part labia; void initial \(20\ \text{mL}\) into toilet; catch middle \(10–20\ \text{mL}\) into sterile wide-mouthed container.
  3. Male Patients: Wash hands; retract foreskin; cleanse meatus; void initial stream; collect midstream portion.
  4. Prompt Delivery: Deliver to laboratory within \(1\ \text{hour}\).

1% Boric Acid Preservative SOP

  • Indication: Required whenever delivery/processing delay will exceed \(2\ \text{hours}\).
  • Concentration: Add \(0.1\ \text{g}\) of boric acid powder per \(10\ \text{mL}\) of urine (\(1.0\%\ \text{w/v}\) / \(10\ \text{g/L}\)).
  • Mechanism: Bacteriostatic; maintains constant bacterial count for up to \(48\ \text{hours}\) without killing organisms.
  • Cytological Integrity: Preserves WBCs, RBCs, and casts from lysis; does not interfere with protein or glucose measurements.

Standing Urine Deterioration

  • Bacterial Multiplication: Commensal urethral contaminants double every 20 min, causing false-positive Kass counts.
  • Urea Splitting & Cell Lysis: Proteus produces ammonia, raising pH (\(>8.0\)), which rapidly lyses pus cells, RBCs, and renal casts.
  • Glucose & Bilirubin Oxidation: Bacteria consume glucose; bilirubin is oxidized to biliverdin (false-negative strips).
  • Amorphous Precipitation: Urates precipitate in acid urine; phosphates/carbonates in alkaline urine, obscuring cells.
Sediment Microscopy Casts & Crystals

3. Microscopic Examination of Urine Sediment (Cells, Casts, Crystals & Parasites)

Pyuria & Microscopic Cell Grading

  • Significant Pyuria Definition: \(>10\ \text{WBCs}/\mu\text{L}\) of uncentrifuged urine (corresponds to \(>10^6\ \text{WBCs/L}\) or moderate/many pus cells on sediment).
  • Sediment Reporting Scale (\(40\times\) HPF):
    • Few: \(0–10\ \text{WBCs/HPF}\) (normal physiological excretion).
    • Moderate: \(11–40\ \text{WBCs/HPF}\) (indicates infection/inflammation).
    • Many / Clumps: \(>40\ \text{WBCs/HPF}\) or sheet of pus cells (acute UTI).
  • Red Blood Cells: Disc-shaped, ringed (\(7\ \mu\text{m}\)); crenated in concentrated hypertonic urine; dysmorphic in glomerulonephritis.
  • Yeast vs RBC Differentiation: Run a drop of dilute acetic acid under coverslip; RBCs lyse immediately, whereas yeast cells remain intact with single budding.

Urinary Casts & High-Yield Crystals

  • Renal Casts (Tamm-Horsfall Mucoprotein Cylinders):
    • Hyaline Casts: Pale, transparent; damage to glomerular filter; seen after strenuous exercise.
    • White Cell (WBC) Casts: Packed with leukocytes; diagnostic of acute pyelonephritis.
    • Red Cell (RBC) Casts: Orange-red; diagnostic of acute glomerulonephritis.
    • Waxy Casts: Dense, yellowish, notched/clefted cylinders; pathognomonic of chronic renal failure / tubular atrophy.
  • Diagnostic Urinary Crystals:
    • Triple Phosphate: "Coffin-lid" prisms in alkaline urine (*Proteus* infection).
    • Calcium Oxalate: "Envelope" octahedra or dumbbells in acid urine (calculi).
    • Cystine Crystals: Pathognomonic flat hexagonal plates in congenital cystinuria.
CLED Agar Kass Bacteriuria

4. Calibrated Loop Inoculation, CLED Differentiation & Kass Criteria

Bacterial Uropathogen Colony Appearance on CLED Agar Lactose Reaction & Biochemical Chemistry Confirmatory Tests
Escherichia coli Opaque, deep yellow colonies with a deeper yellow central zone. Lactose Fermenter (+); bromothymol blue indicator turns bright yellow. Indole positive (+), Beta-glucuronidase positive (+), Citrate negative (-), Markedly acid urine.
Klebsiella pneumoniae Large, highly mucoid, dome-shaped yellow to yellow-white colonies. Lactose Fermenter (+); viscous capsular polysaccharide. Indole negative (-), Citrate positive (+), Non-motile (-), Urease slow positive.
Proteus mirabilis / vulgaris Translucent, pale blue-grey colonies; NO SWARMING. Non-Lactose Fermenter (-); medium remains blue/green. Swarming is inhibited by electrolyte deficiency (low electrolyte formulation). Urease rapidly positive (++ within 2–4 h), Phenylalanine deaminase (PPA) positive (+), Highly alkaline urine (ammonia smell).
Pseudomonas aeruginosa Greenish-blue rough colonies with serrated margins and sweet grape-like odor. Non-Lactose Fermenter (-); produces green pyocyanin and fluorescein pigments. Oxidase positive (+), Catalase positive (+), Motile, Non-fermenter.
Enterococcus faecalis Small, compact, deep yellow colonies (\(1–1.5\ \text{mm}\)). Lactose Fermenter (+); Gram-positive diplococci / short chains. Catalase negative (-), Bile-esculin hydrolysis positive (+), Grows in \(6.5\%\ \text{NaCl}\).
Staphylococcus saprophyticus Uniform, opaque, pale yellow to white colonies (\(1–2\ \text{mm}\)). Lactose variable; Gram-positive clusters. Catalase positive (+), Coagulase negative (-), Novobiocin Resistant (\(5\ \mu\text{g}\) disc) (differentiates from sensitive *S. epidermidis*).

Quantitative Culture & Kass Criterion Interpretation

Inoculate a quarter or half plate of CLED agar with a calibrated wire loop holding \(1/500\ \text{mL}\) (\(0.002\ \text{mL}\)) of uncentrifuged urine. Incubate aerobically at \(35–37^\circ\text{C}\) overnight:

  • Calculation Formula: \(\text{CFU/mL} = \text{Colony Count} \times 500\). (Example: \(200\ \text{colonies} \times 500 = 100,000\ \text{CFU/mL}\)).
  • \(\ge 10^5\ \text{CFU/mL}\) (\(\ge 100,000\ \text{CFU/mL}\) / \(\ge 200\ \text{colonies}\)): Significant Bacteriuria (Kass Criterion) — Confirms active urinary tract infection in pure culture. Proceed to antibiotic susceptibility testing.
  • \(10^4–10^5\ \text{CFU/mL}\) (\(20–200\ \text{colonies}\)): Doubtful Significance — Request a repeat clean-catch specimen (unless patient is symptomatic, catheterized, or on prior antibiotics).
  • \(< 10^4\ \text{CFU/mL}\) (\(< 20\ \text{colonies}\)): Not Significant — Represents normal commensal urethral / perineal contamination.
Board Examination Section 8 Active Interactive MCQs

Section 7.12 Board Review Questions (MCQ 441 – 448)

Test your mastery of urine microbiology, Kass criteria, CLED swarming prevention, boric acid preservation, and renal cast diagnostics:

MCQ 441 • Kass Criterion for Significant Bacteriuria
Using a calibrated \(1/500\ \text{mL}\) (\(0.002\ \text{mL}\)) wire loop on CLED agar, how many colonies must grow from a pure culture of clean-catch midstream urine to fulfill the Kass criterion for significant bacteriuria (\(\ge 10^5\ \text{CFU/mL}\))?
A \(\ge 10\ \text{colonies}\)
B \(\ge 50\ \text{colonies}\)
C \(\ge 200\ \text{colonies}\) (since \(200 \times 500 = 100,000\ \text{CFU/mL} = 10^5\ \text{CFU/mL}\))
D \(\ge 1000\ \text{colonies}\)
Correct Answer: C — ≥ 200 colonies (200 × 500 = 100,000 CFU/mL). A calibrated loop delivering \(1/500\ \text{mL}\) (\(0.002\ \text{mL}\)) has a multiplication factor of \(500\). Therefore, \(200\ \text{colonies}\) corresponds exactly to \(200 \times 500 = 100,000\ \text{organisms/mL}\) (\(10^5\ \text{CFU/mL}\)), which is the established Kass threshold for significant bacteriuria in acute uncomplicated UTI.
MCQ 442 • CLED Agar Mechanism & Proteus Swarming
Why is Cystine Lactose Electrolyte-Deficient (CLED) agar preferred over standard Blood or MacConkey agar for routine primary quantitative urine culture in district laboratories?
A It completely sterilizes all commensal vaginal bacteria on contact.
B It supports the growth of both Gram-negative and Gram-positive uropathogens while its electrolyte deficiency prevents the swarming of Proteus species across the plate.
C It selectively isolates Mycobacterium tuberculosis within 24 hours.
D It turns bright red in the presence of viral particles.
Correct Answer: B — Supports both Gram-negatives and Gram-positives while electrolyte deficiency prevents Proteus swarming. CLED agar contains lactose with bromothymol blue indicator and cystine to support dwarf-colony coliforms. Omission of electrolytes (sodium chloride) restricts the hyper-flagellated swarming motility of *Proteus*, allowing discrete, countable colonies of all co-existing pathogens (*E. coli*, *Enterococcus*, *Staphylococcus*) to be isolated.
MCQ 443 • Boric Acid Preservative Formulation
When a urine specimen collected at a peripheral health centre cannot reach the microbiology laboratory within 2 hours, what chemical preservative and concentration is prescribed by Monica Cheesbrough?
A Boric acid powder at \(1.0\%\ \text{w/v}\) (\(0.1\ \text{g}\) per \(10\ \text{mL}\) of urine / \(10\ \text{g/L}\))
B Formalin solution at \(10\%\ \text{v/v}\)
C Concentrated hydrochloric acid (\(5\ \text{mL}\))
D Sodium hypochlorite bleach (\(0.5\%\))
Correct Answer: A — Boric acid powder at 1.0% w/v (0.1 g per 10 mL urine). Boric acid at \(1\%\ \text{w/v}\) acts as a bacteriostatic preservative, holding bacterial numbers constant for up to 48 hours without killing them, preserving leukocytes and casts from lysis, and causing no interference with protein or glucose measurements. Bactericidal agents (formalin, bleach, acid) must never be used for culture specimens.
MCQ 444 • Pathognomonic Cast for Acute Pyelonephritis
A patient presents with high fever, rigors, and severe right loin pain. Microscopic examination of the centrifuged urine sediment reveals cylindrical structures composed of protein matrices densely packed with polymorphonuclear leukocytes. What is this cast and what does it diagnose?
A Hyaline cast indicative of severe dehydration.
B Waxy cast diagnostic of end-stage renal failure.
C Fatty cast diagnostic of nephrotic syndrome.
D White Blood Cell (WBC / Leukocyte) Cast, pathognomonic of Acute Pyelonephritis (upper urinary tract infection).
Correct Answer: D — White Blood Cell Cast, pathognomonic of Acute Pyelonephritis. Because casts are formed exclusively within renal tubular lumens from Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein, the inclusion of leukocytes inside a cast definitively proves that the inflammatory/infectious process originates in the kidney parenchyma (pyelonephritis), distinguishing it from lower UTI (cystitis/urethritis).
MCQ 445 • Greiss Nitrite Test Principle & Limitations
Why does the Greiss Nitrite reagent strip test produce a positive pink-red reaction in urinary tract infections caused by E. coli and Proteus, but yields a negative result in infections caused by Enterococcus faecalis or Staphylococcus saprophyticus?
A *E. faecalis* hydrolyzes sulfanilic acid into ammonia.
B E. coli and Proteus possess nitrate reductase enzymes that reduce dietary urinary nitrate to nitrite, whereas E. faecalis and staphylococci lack nitrate reductase.
C Gram-positive cocci ferment alpha-naphthylamine into glucose.
D Staphylococci destroy all leukocyte esterase enzymes.
Correct Answer: B — E. coli and Proteus reduce nitrate to nitrite, whereas E. faecalis and staphylococci lack nitrate reductase. Gram-negative enteric bacilli contain nitrate reductase, converting dietary urinary nitrate into nitrite during bladder incubation (\(>4\ \text{hours}\)), reacting with Greiss reagent to form a pink-red diazonium dye. Non-nitrate-reducing pathogens (*Enterococcus*, *Pseudomonas*, *S. saprophyticus*, *Candida*) yield a negative nitrite test despite active infection.
MCQ 446 • Staphylococcus saprophyticus Identification
A sexually active 20-year-old female presents with acute dysuria and frequency. Urine culture yields a pure growth of \(\ge 10^5\ \text{CFU/mL}\) of catalase-positive, coagulase-negative Gram-positive cocci in clusters forming white/pale yellow colonies on CLED. What disc test confirms Staphylococcus saprophyticus?
A Resistance to Novobiocin (\(5\ \mu\text{g}\) disc) (zone diameter \(< 16\ \text{mm}\))
B Sensitivity to Bacitracin (\(0.04\ \text{units}\))
C Sensitivity to Optochin (\(5\ \mu\text{g}\))
D Resistance to Metronidazole (\(5\ \mu\text{g}\))
Correct Answer: A — Resistance to Novobiocin (5 µg disc). Staphylococcus saprophyticus (a leading cause of young adult female uncomplicated UTI) is inherently resistant to novobiocin, distinguishing it from *Staphylococcus epidermidis* and other coagulase-negative staphylococci, which are novobiocin susceptible (zone \(\ge 16\ \text{mm}\)).
MCQ 447 • Yeast vs Red Blood Cell Differentiation
When examining an unstained urine sediment wet mount, how can oval Candida yeast cells be rapidly and conclusively differentiated from non-nucleated red blood cells?
A Adding concentrated sulfuric acid to boil the slide.
B Heating the slide over a Bunsen burner for 5 minutes.
C Running a drop of dilute (\(2–5\%\)) acetic acid under the coverslip — RBCs lyse immediately, whereas yeast cells remain intact and show single budding/pseudohyphae.
D Adding potassium ferricyanide to form blue granules.
Correct Answer: C — Dilute acetic acid lyses RBCs immediately while yeast cells remain intact. Dilute acetic acid rapidly dissolves red blood cell lipid bilayers, leaving them invisible. *Candida* yeast cells possess rigid glucan/chitin fungal cell walls resistant to weak acid, preserving their oval morphology and single buds. Glove powder starch granules turn blue-black with Lugol's iodine.
MCQ 448 • Schistosoma haematobium Egg Morphology
Centrifugation of terminal urine from a school-aged child with painless terminal haematuria in an endemic river basin reveals large yellowish-brown eggs measuring \(145 \times 55\ \mu\text{m}\). What morphological landmark identifies Schistosoma haematobium?
A A prominent lateral spine near the posterior pole.
B A small inconspicuous lateral knob and rounded shape.
C An operculum with thickened abopercular knob.
D A distinct, sharp terminal spine at one end of the elongated oval shell containing a fully developed ciliated miracidium.
Correct Answer: D — Distinct, sharp terminal spine at one end of the shell. *Schistosoma haematobium* eggs are characteristically elongated, measuring \(110–170 \times 40–70\ \mu\text{m}\), with a prominent terminal spine. In contrast, *Schistosoma mansoni* eggs possess a large lateral spine, and *S. japonicum* eggs have a small lateral knob.

7.13 Examination of Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF)

Emergency Microbiological, Cytological & Biochemical Investigation of Acute Bacterial, Tuberculous, Cryptococcal & Viral Meningitis • Lumbar Puncture 2-Tube Protocol • Fuchs-Rosenthal / Improved Neubauer Cell Counts (\(0.1\%\) Toluidine Blue) • Urgent Direct Gram Smear • India Ink Wet Mount for Cryptococcus neoformans • Direct Latex Antigen Testing • Pandy Globulin Test • CSF Glucose / Blood Ratio • African Trypanosomiasis Morula (Mott) Cells • Naegleria fowleri Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis.

Monica Cheesbrough Critical Emergency Principle: Cerebrospinal fluid is a critical, irreplaceable STAT specimen. Never refrigerate CSF intended for bacterial culture, as *Neisseria meningitidis* and *Haemophilus influenzae* are extremely cold-sensitive and die rapidly at \(4^\circ\text{C}\)! In pyogenic meningitis, CSF appears purulent/cloudy with marked neutrophilia (\(>1000\ \text{pus cells}/\mu\text{L}\)), protein \(>1.0\ \text{g/L}\) (Pandy positive), and glucose undetectable or \(<1.0\ \text{mmol/L}\). In tuberculous meningitis, the fluid is clear/turbid with lymphocyte dominance, marked hyperproteinuria (\(1.0–5.0\ \text{g/L}\)), low glucose, and "cobweb" clot formation. In cryptococcal meningitis, India ink reveals wide, clear, unstained mucopolysaccharide capsules against a jet-black background!

1. Monica Cheesbrough Master CSF Differential Matrix (Chart 7.9)

The cornerstone reference table for clinical laboratory differentiation of central nervous system infections:

Condition / Etiology Macroscopic Appearance Leukocytes (WBCs / \(\mu\text{L}\)) & Differential Total Protein & Pandy Glucose (\(\text{mmol/L}\) & Ratio) Microscopy & Confirmatory Tests
Normal Healthy Adult Clear, colorless, "crystal clear" water-like; no clots. \(0–5\ \text{cells}/\mu\text{L}\) (\(100\%\ \text{lymphocytes}\)); no PMNs. Neonates: Up to \(30/\mu\text{L}\). \(0.15–0.40\ \text{g/L}\) (\(15–40\ \text{mg/dL}\)); Pandy Negative (-). \(2.5–4.0\ \text{mmol/L}\) (\(45–72\ \text{mg/dL}\)) (\(60–70\%\) of plasma glucose). Sterile; no bacteria, yeasts, or parasites seen.
Acute Pyogenic Bacterial Meningitis Turbid, cloudy, or frankly purulent (pus-like); spontaneous fibrin clot. Markedly Elevated (\(100–10,000+/\mu\text{L}\)); \(>80–90\%\) Polymorphonuclear Neutrophils (PMNs). Markedly Raised (\(1.0–5.0+\ \text{g/L}\)); Pandy Strongly Positive (+++). Markedly Reduced to Zero (\(<1.0\ \text{mmol/L}\) or \(<0.3\) CSF:Blood ratio). Direct Gram Smear:
• *N. meningitidis*: Gram-negative intracellular diplococci.
• *S. pneumoniae*: Gram-positive lancet diplococci.
• *H. influenzae*: Pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacilli.
Tuberculous Meningitis (TBM) Clear or slightly opalescent; forms delicate "spider-web / cobweb" clot on standing. Moderately elevated (\(50–500/\mu\text{L}\)); Predominantly Lymphocytes (\(>80\%\)). Markedly Raised (\(1.0–6.0\ \text{g/L}\)); Pandy Positive (++). Significantly Reduced (\(<2.0\ \text{mmol/L}\) or \(<0.3\) ratio). High-speed centrifuged sediment stained by Ziehl-Neelsen / Auramine (AFB scanty; requires examination of entire smear).
Cryptococcal Meningitis (*C. neoformans*) Clear, slightly turbid, or opalescent. Mild to moderate increase (\(20–500/\mu\text{L}\)); Predominantly Lymphocytes (scanty in severe AIDS). Moderately raised (\(0.5–2.0\ \text{g/L}\)); Pandy Positive (+). Normal to moderately reduced (\(1.5–3.0\ \text{mmol/L}\)). India Ink Wet Mount: Round/oval budding yeast cells (\(2–10\ \mu\text{m}\)) surrounded by wide, prominent unstained clear capsules; Latex cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) positive.
Aseptic / Viral Meningoencephalitis Clear or slightly hazy; no clots. Mild to moderate increase (\(10–500/\mu\text{L}\)); Predominantly Lymphocytes / Mononuclears. Normal or slightly elevated (\(0.4–1.0\ \text{g/L}\)); Pandy Negative / Trace. COMPLETELY NORMAL (\(2.5–4.0\ \text{mmol/L}\); CSF:Blood ratio \(>0.6\)). Gram smear negative; sterile bacterial cultures; RT-PCR / serology for enteroviruses, arboviruses, HSV.
Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM) Cloudy, purulent, or reddish-brown (haemorrhagic). Markedly elevated; Predominantly Pus Cells (PMNs) + numerous RBCs. Significantly raised; Pandy Positive (++). Markedly reduced to low. Direct Wet Mount (\(40\times\)): Motile, sluggishly active amoebic trophozoites of Naegleria fowleri with granular cytoplasm and vacuoles; Gram smear shows pus cells without bacteria.
African Trypanosomiasis (Late Stage CNS) Clear or slightly hazy; elevated opening pressure. Elevated (\(>5\ \text{cells}/\mu\text{L}\)); Lymphocytic pleocytosis. Significantly raised (\(>0.4\ \text{g/L}\)); Extremely High IgM in CSF; Pandy Positive. Normal to slightly reduced. Wet Mount / Double Centrifugation: Actively motile Trypanosoma brucei flagellates. Giemsa Smear: Morula (Mott) cells (IgM-packed plasma cells).
Lumbar Puncture SOP Strict Temperature Rule

2. Lumbar Puncture Two-Container Protocol & Specimen Handling SOP

Two-Container Dispensing SOP

  • Container No. 1 (First \(1\ \text{mL}\)): Used strictly for Microbiological Culture. (Any transient skin commensal picked up during needle passage is confined to tube 1).
  • Container No. 2 (\(2–3\ \text{mL}\)): Used for Cell Count, Differential, Gram/India ink Smears, Protein, and Glucose.
  • Traumatic vs Pathological Bleed: In a traumatic tap, tube 1 has heavy blood and tube 2 is clearer (supernatant clear after centrifugation). In subarachnoid haemorrhage, both tubes are equally bloody and supernatant is xanthochromic (yellow-orange).

NEVER REFRIGERATE CSF!

  • Extreme Cold Sensitivity: Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae are killed rapidly at refrigerator temperatures (\(2–6^\circ\text{C}\)).
  • Holding Temperature: If an immediate culture cannot be performed, hold CSF in a \(35–37^\circ\text{C}\) incubator or water bath.
  • Rapid Glycolysis: Glucose in unseparated CSF drops significantly within \(20\ \text{minutes}\) due to leukocyte and bacterial glycolysis; measure glucose immediately.

Immediate STAT Action & Call

  • Direct Gram Smear: Prepare immediately on uncentrifuged purulent CSF (or sediment of clear CSF).
  • Critical Telephone Alert: Immediately notify the attending clinician if the Gram smear shows intracellular diplococci, Gram-positive pairs, Gram-negative rods, or if India ink shows encapsulated yeasts!
  • Empiric Therapy: Early notification allows instant administration of parenteral ceftriaxone / penicillin / amphotericin B before irreversible neurological damage occurs.
Cell Counting SOP Pandy & India Ink

3. Quantitative Cell Counting, Pandy Globulin Test & Specialized Smears

Fuchs-Rosenthal Cell Count SOP

  1. Dilution: Mix 1 drop of uncentrifuged CSF with 1 drop of \(0.1\%\) Toluidine Blue diluting fluid (stains leukocyte nuclei deep blue, leaving RBCs unstained). Dilution factor = \(2\).
  2. Chamber: Charge a clean Fuchs-Rosenthal chamber (depth \(0.2\ \text{mm}\)). Allow cells to settle for \(2\ \text{min}\).
  3. Counting Rule: Count white cells in 5 large squares (\(W_1\) to \(W_5\)).
  4. Calculation: \(\text{Cells}/\mu\text{L} = \text{Count} \times 2\). (Normal: \(\le 5/\mu\text{L}\)). If using Improved Neubauer, count 4 large corner squares and multiply by \(5\).

Pandy's Test for CSF Globulin

  • Reagent: Saturated aqueous phenol solution (\(100\ \text{g/L}\) phenol crystals in distilled water).
  • Procedure: Add \(1\ \text{mL}\) of Pandy's reagent to a small tube; add 1 drop of clear CSF supernatant.
  • Positive Test: Immediate development of a cloudy white precipitate / smoky haze indicates elevated globulin/protein (meningitis, neurosyphilis, trypanosomiasis).
  • Negative Test: Fluid remains crystal clear (normal CSF contains negligible globulin).

India Ink Mount (*C. neoformans*)

  • Technique: Place 1 drop of centrifuged CSF sediment on a slide; add 1 drop of Pelikan India ink (or \(20\%\) nigrosin); mix and coverslip thinly.
  • Principle: Large colloidal carbon particles cannot penetrate the thick glucuronoxylomannan (GXM) polysaccharide capsule.
  • Diagnostic Landmark: Round budding yeasts surrounded by a conspicuous, wide, bright, halo-like unstained capsule against a dark background.
Culture Protocols Pathogen Identification

Section 7.13 Board Review Questions (MCQ 449 – 456)

Test your mastery of CSF diagnostics, meningitis differentiation matrices, cell counting, India ink preparations, and specimen handling:

MCQ 449 • Master Meningitis Matrix: Bacterial vs Viral vs TB
A lumbar puncture is performed on a patient with severe headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia. The CSF analysis reveals: Turbid appearance, WBC count \(3,500/\mu\text{L}\) (\(92\%\) PMNs), Total protein \(3.8\ \text{g/L}\) (Pandy positive), and Glucose \(0.4\ \text{mmol/L}\) (CSF:blood glucose ratio \(<0.2\)). What is the diagnosis?
A Aseptic Viral Meningitis
B Tuberculous Meningitis
C Acute Pyogenic Bacterial Meningitis (e.g. *N. meningitidis* or *S. pneumoniae*)
D Cryptococcal Meningitis
Correct Answer: C — Acute Pyogenic Bacterial Meningitis. The triad of marked neutrophil pleocytosis (\(>1000\ \text{PMNs}/\mu\text{L}\)), severe hyperproteinuria (\(>1.0\ \text{g/L}\)), and profound hypoglycorrhachia (glucose \(<1.0\ \text{mmol/L}\) or ratio \(<0.3\)) is classic for acute pyogenic bacterial meningitis. In viral meningitis, lymphocytes predominate and glucose is normal; in tuberculous meningitis, lymphocytes predominate with cobweb clot.
MCQ 450 • Strict CSF Temperature Preservation Rule
Why must a cerebrospinal fluid specimen collected for microbiological culture NEVER be refrigerated at 2–6°C, and how must it be maintained if an unavoidable delay occurs before plating?
A Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae are fastidious, extremely cold-sensitive pathogens that die rapidly at \(4^\circ\text{C}\); uninoculated CSF must be held at \(35–37^\circ\text{C}\).
B Cold temperatures permanently polymerize glucose into glycogen.
C Refrigeration causes bacteria to produce excessive beta-lactamases.
D Cold shock transforms Gram-negative diplococci into Gram-positive rods.
Correct Answer: A — N. meningitidis and H. influenzae are extremely cold-sensitive; hold at 35–37°C. Cold exposure causes rapid autolysis of fragile *N. meningitidis* and *H. influenzae*. CSF must never be placed in a refrigerator. If culture cannot be performed immediately, maintain the specimen in an incubator or water bath at \(35–37^\circ\text{C}\).
MCQ 451 • India Ink Preparation for Cryptococcus neoformans
In an HIV-seropositive patient presenting with subacute headache and lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis, an India ink wet mount of centrifuged sediment reveals round budding yeast cells measuring \(2–10\ \mu\text{m}\) surrounded by a wide, unstained, clear halo-like capsule. What is the diagnosis?
A Candida albicans systemic thrush
B Histoplasma capsulatum
C Blastomyces dermatitidis
D Cryptococcus neoformans Cryptococcal Meningitis (Cryptococcosis)
Correct Answer: D — Cryptococcus neoformans (Cryptococcal Meningitis). *Cryptococcus neoformans* is a major opportunistic pathogen in advanced AIDS. Its thick polysaccharide (glucuronoxylomannan) capsule repels India ink carbon particles, creating a wide, prominent, clear halo around the budding yeast body against the jet-black background.
MCQ 452 • Tuberculous Meningitis & Cobweb Clot Formation
Why does cerebrospinal fluid from a patient with Tuberculous Meningitis characteristically form a delicate "cobweb / spider-web" (pellicle) clot upon standing undisturbed at room temperature for several hours?
A *M. tuberculosis* secretes high concentrations of collagenase.
B Severe meningeal vascular inflammation allows large molecular weight fibrinogen to cross the blood-brain barrier alongside massive total protein elevation (\(1.0–6.0\ \text{g/L}\)).
C The presence of motile trypanosomes spins fibrin into web-like threads.
D High glucose content crystallizes into fibrillar meshes.
Correct Answer: B — Elevated fibrinogen crossing the inflamed blood-brain barrier alongside high total protein. Chronic granulomatous inflammation in TBM causes severe vascular permeability, leading to massive CSF protein elevation (\(>1.0–6.0\ \text{g/L}\)) and leakage of fibrinogen, which slowly polymerizes upon standing into a delicate, dangling "cobweb" or pellicle clot (which traps tubercle bacilli for ZN staining).
MCQ 453 • Fuchs-Rosenthal Chamber Calculation
When performing a CSF cell count diluted \(1:2\) in \(0.1\%\) Toluidine Blue using a Fuchs-Rosenthal counting chamber (depth \(0.2\ \text{mm}\)), a total of 160 leukocytes are counted across 5 large squares. What is the calculated CSF white cell count?
A \(320\ \text{cells}/\mu\text{L}\) (\(320 \times 10^6\ \text{cells/L}\)) — Formula: \(\text{Count} \times 2\)
B \(800\ \text{cells}/\mu\text{L}\)
C \(160\ \text{cells}/\mu\text{L}\)
D \(1,600\ \text{cells}/\mu\text{L}\)
Correct Answer: A — 320 cells/µL (Count × 2). In a Fuchs-Rosenthal chamber with a \(1:2\) dilution, counting 5 large squares (each of \(0.2\ \text{mm}^3\) volume, total volume \(1.0\ \text{mm}^3 = 1\ \mu\text{L}\)) yields a direct multiplication factor of \(2\) (for the \(1:2\) dilution). Therefore, \(160 \times 2 = 320\ \text{cells}/\mu\text{L}\).
MCQ 454 • Mott Morula Cells in African Trypanosomiasis
In a patient suspected of late-stage sleeping sickness (African Trypanosomiasis with CNS involvement), a Giemsa-stained CSF smear reveals large, abnormal plasma cells containing multiple vesicular, droplet-like cytoplasmic vacuoles packed with IgM antibodies. What are these cells called?
A Reed-Sternberg cells
B LE cells
C Donovan bodies
D Morula Cells of Mott (Mott cells)
Correct Answer: D — Morula Cells of Mott. Mott cells (morula cells) are altered plasma cells containing spherical cytoplasmic inclusions of immunoglobulin M (Russell bodies), pathognomonic of stage 2 meningoencephalitic African trypanosomiasis (*Trypanosoma brucei gambiense / rhodesiense*).
MCQ 455 • Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis (Naegleria fowleri)
A teenager presents with fulminant meningitis 5 days after swimming in a warm freshwater lake. The CSF is purulent and contains thousands of PMNs and RBCs with high protein and low glucose, but direct Gram and ZN stains show NO bacteria. Examination of a fresh unstained wet mount under \(40\times\) reveals small, clear, motile amoebae with vacuoles. What is the etiological organism?
A Entamoeba histolytica
B Naegleria fowleri (Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis / PAM)
C Acanthamoeba castellanii
D Balamuthia mandrillaris
Correct Answer: B — Naegleria fowleri (Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis). *Naegleria fowleri* is a free-living thermophilic amoeba found in warm freshwater. It enters the cribriform plate via the nasal mucosa, producing fulminant necrotizing meningoencephalitis with neutrophilic pleocytosis and motile amoebic trophozoites on warm saline wet mounts.
MCQ 456 • Traumatic Tap vs Subarachnoid Haemorrhage
How does a medical laboratory scientist conclusively differentiate a traumatic (bloody) lumbar puncture from a true pathological subarachnoid haemorrhage?
A Traumatic CSF turns bright green with Pandy's reagent.
B Subarachnoid haemorrhage produces colonies of *Proteus* on CLED.
C In a traumatic tap, sequential tubes show clearing of blood (Tube 1 is bloodier than Tube 2) and the centrifuged supernatant is water-clear; in subarachnoid haemorrhage, all tubes are uniformly bloody and the supernatant is xanthochromic (yellow/orange).
D Traumatic CSF has zero glucose and normal protein.
Correct Answer: C — Traumatic tap shows clearing in serial tubes and clear supernatant; subarachnoid bleed shows uniform blood and xanthochromic supernatant. In traumatic lumbar puncture, puncture of the epidural venous plexus causes blood that clears across containers No. 1 and No. 2, and immediate centrifugation leaves a colorless supernatant. In subarachnoid haemorrhage, blood is evenly mixed throughout all tubes and in vivo erythrocyte breakdown produces yellow-orange bilirubin/oxyhaemoglobin (xanthochromia) in the centrifuged supernatant.

7.14 Culturing Blood & Investigation of Bacteremia

Microbiological Investigation of Bacteremia, Septicemia & Infective Endocarditis • Venepuncture Skin Asepsis (\(70\%\) Ethanol + \(2\%\) Iodine) • Blood-to-Broth Volume Dilution Ratios • Diphasic (Castaneda) Columbia Media • Sodium Polyanethol Sulfonate (SPS / Liquoid) Multi-Action Chemistry • Thioglycollate Anaerobic Broth • Buffy Coat Smears (Gram, ZN, Giemsa) • Blind Subculturing Protocols • Transfusion Reaction Bacteriology.

Monica Cheesbrough Blood Culture Principle: Blood culture is the gold-standard diagnostic modality for systemic septicemia and infective endocarditis. The single most vital additive in blood culture media is Sodium Polyanethol Sulfonate (SPS / Liquoid) at \(0.025–0.05\%\ \text{w/v}\). SPS serves four indispensable functions: (1) prevents in vitro coagulation which traps bacteria in fibrin meshes, (2) inactivates serum complement, (3) inhibits leukocyte phagocytosis, and (4) neutralizes aminoglycoside and polypeptide antibiotics (gentamicin, streptomycin, polymyxin B). Because SPS is inhibitory to Peptostreptococcus, backup thioglycollate broth without SPS at a \(1:10\) dilution is essential for strict anaerobes!
