1. Major Etiological Agents of Bacteremia, Septicemia & Endocarditis

Clinical Syndrome Primary Pathogens Isolated Underlying Sources / Pathophysiology Diagnostic Signatures & Notes
Enteric Fever (Typhoid & Paratyphoid) • Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi
• Salmonella Paratyphi A, B, C 		Invasion of Peyer's patches; primary bacteremia in **Week 1–2** (\(75–90\%\) culture positive). Excreted in stool/urine in Week 3. Culture in Ox-gall broth or diphasic Columbia medium; Motile, LDC+, \(H_2S\) trace, anaerogenic (no gas in KIA); Vi-serotyping.
Infective Endocarditis (Subacute & Acute) • Viridans streptococci (*S. mutans*, *S. mitis*, *S. sanguinis*) — Subacute (SBE)
• Staphylococcus aureus — Acute IE (IV drug users, prosthetic valves)
• Enterococcus faecalis, Streptococcus bovis (associated with colon cancer) 		Colonization of damaged heart valves following dental procedures or bacteremic seeding. Continuous, low-grade bacteremia. Requires **at least 3 sets of blood cultures** drawn at separate venepuncture sites over 24 h; extended incubation (\(14–21\ \text{days}\)).
Neonatal Sepsis & Meningitis • Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Strep / GBS)
• Escherichia coli (K1 capsular strain)
• Listeria monocytogenes, Klebsiella pneumoniae 		Vertical transmission from maternal genital tract during delivery; immature neonatal immune defenses. High mortality. Inoculate \(1–2\ \text{mL}\) peripheral blood into diphasic bottle; CAMP test positive (GBS); tumbling motility at \(25^\circ\text{C}\) (*Listeria*).
Brucellosis (Undulant Fever) Brucella melitensis, B. abortus, B. suis Ingestion of unpasteurized goat/cow milk or direct contact with livestock placenta. Intracellular survival in reticuloendothelial system. Tryptic soy diphasic bottle; loosen cap for **\(5–10\%\ \text{CO}_2\)**; incubate for **up to 4 weeks**; extreme BSL-3 laboratory biohazard.
HIV-Associated Opportunistic Bacteremia • Non-typhoid Salmonella (NTS: *S. Typhimurium*, *S. Enteritidis*)
• Streptococcus pneumoniae (recurrent bacteremia)
• Mycobacterium tuberculosis / M. avium complex (MAC)
• Cryptococcus neoformans 		Severe CD4 T-cell depletion allows mucosal translocation of NTS and disseminated mycobacterial/fungal proliferation. Lysis-centrifugation blood culture; ZN staining of peripheral blood buffy coat smears (reveals intracellular AFB).
Collection SOP Asepsis & Dilution

2. Blood Collection Protocols, Skin Antisepsis & Broth Dilution

2-Step Skin Antisepsis SOP

  1. Step 1: Apply tourniquet, locate vein; release cuff. Cleanse skin over a \(50\ \text{mm}\) area with \(70\%\) ethanol; allow to air-dry completely.
  2. Step 2: Swab with \(2\%\) Tincture of Iodine in centrifugal concentric circles from the center outwards. Allow iodine to dry for at least 1 full minute (iodine requires contact time to kill skin flora).
  3. Never Palpate Vein Again: Do NOT touch the disinfected venepuncture site with unsterile fingers before needle insertion!

Blood Volume & Dilution Ratio

  • Adults: Draw \(10–20\ \text{mL}\) of blood total. Dispense \(10–12\ \text{mL}\) into \(25\ \text{mL}\) Columbia diphasic bottle (with SPS) and \(5\ \text{mL}\) into \(50\ \text{mL}\) thioglycollate broth.
  • Children / Neonates: Draw \(1–2\ \text{mL}\) (bacterial densities are much higher in infants, \(>1000\ \text{CFU/mL}\)).
  • Dilution Ratio: Without SPS, blood must be diluted at least \(1:5\) to \(1:10\) in broth to neutralize natural serum bactericidal antibodies, complement, and lysozyme.

SPS (Liquoid) Multi-Action

Sodium Polyanethol Sulfonate (\(0.025–0.05\%\ \text{w/v}\)) performs 4 crucial functions:

  • Anticoagulation: Prevents clotting which traps pathogens.
  • Anticomplementary: Rapidly destroys serum complement.
  • Antiphagocytic: Paralyzes host leukocytes.
  • Antibiotic Inactivation: Neutralizes aminoglycosides (gentamicin, streptomycin) and polymyxin B.
Diphasic Culture Anaerobic Broth

3. Diphasic Castaneda System, Inspection Signs & Subculturing SOP

Diphasic (Castaneda) Bottle Principle

Combines a solid Columbia agar slope on one side with liquid Columbia broth at the bottom (with SPS):

  • Tilt & Wash Inoculation: Invert or tilt the bottle daily so the blood-broth mixture flows over the agar slope without wetting the neck.
  • Self-Subculturing: Colonies grow directly on the agar slope (originating at the broth-agar interface), allowing immediate visual detection without opening the bottle!
  • Biosafety & Contamination: Eliminates aerosol risks and reduces laboratory contamination during repeated subcultures (ideal for dangerous *Brucella*).

Thioglycollate Broth for Anaerobes

Nutrient broth supplemented with sodium thioglycollate (\(0.5\ \text{g/L}\)) and resazurin / methylene blue indicator:

  • No SPS Added: SPS is toxic to Peptostreptococcus anaerobes; therefore, a \(1:10\) volume dilution (\(5\ \text{mL}\) blood into \(50\ \text{mL}\) broth) is used instead.
  • Oxidation Check: Discard or boil/steam bottle if upper \(>1/3\) turns pink (resazurin oxidation) before inoculation.
  • Growth Signs: Turbidity above the settled red cell layer, gas bubbles, hemolysis, or floating "cotton-ball / puff-ball" colonies on the RBC surface.

Blind Subculturing & Incubation Schedule

  1. Day 1 (Overnight): Perform Blind Subculture onto Chocolate Agar (in \(\text{CO}_2\)), Blood Agar, and MacConkey Agar even if broth appears clear (*N. meningitidis* and *S. pneumoniae* often grow without macroscopic turbidity). Prepare a **\(0.5\%\) Toluidine Blue smear**.
  2. Day 2–7: Inspect twice daily for colonial growth on agar slope; subculture immediately upon turbidity.
  3. Final Day 7: Subculture broth before issuing final negative report ("No bacterial growth after 7 days incubation").
  4. Special Cases: Hold bottles for **4 weeks** in \(5–10\%\ \text{CO}_2\) if Brucella is suspected; hold for **\(14–21\ \text{days}\)** if infective endocarditis (*Viridans*, *HACEK*) is suspected.
QA & Contamination Transfusion Reactions

4. Differentiating Contaminants from True Pathogens & Transfusion Reaction Sepsis

Recognizing Blood Culture Contaminants

  • Common Skin Flora Contaminants: Coagulase-negative staphylococci (*S. epidermidis*), *Corynebacterium* (diphtheroids), *Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes*, *Micrococcus*, *Bacillus* species.
  • Hallmarks of Contamination:
    • Growth in only 1 bottle out of multiple sets collected simultaneously.
    • Mixed polymicrobial growth of skin commensals.
    • Delayed growth appearing after \(>4–5\ \text{days}\).
  • Hallmarks of True Bacteremia:
    • Isolation of *S. aureus*, *S. pneumoniae*, *E. coli*, *S. Typhi*, *Pseudomonas*, or *Candida*.
    • Identical organism recovered from 2 or more separate venepuncture blood culture bottles within \(24–48\ \text{hours}\).

Transfusion Reaction Sepsis SOP

  • Pathophysiology: Transfusion of bank blood contaminated with cold-tolerant (psychrophilic) Gram-negative bacilli (*Pseudomonas fluorescens*, *Yersinia enterocolitica*, *Achromobacter*, *Serratia*) causing immediate endotoxic shock and DIC.
  • Laboratory Investigation:
    • Inspect donor bag: Dark discolored blood, clots, purple/red hemolyzed plasma.
    • Direct Gram smear & motility test of donor plasma.
    • Inoculate 3 bottles of thioglycollate broth: Incubate at \(35–37^\circ\text{C}\), room temp (\(20–25^\circ\text{C}\)), and \(4^\circ\text{C}\) for 7 days.

Section 7.14 Board Review Questions (MCQ 457 – 464)

Test your mastery of blood culturing protocols, SPS mechanisms, Castaneda bottles, venepuncture asepsis, and contamination criteria:

MCQ 457 • SPS (Liquoid) 4-Fold Action in Blood Culture
What four distinct physiological and biochemical functions are performed by Sodium Polyanethol Sulfonate (SPS / Liquoid) when incorporated into blood culture media?
A Lyses red blood cells, ferments lactose, stimulates spore formation, and stains capsules.
B Prevents blood coagulation, destroys serum complement, inhibits leukocyte phagocytosis, and neutralizes aminoglycosides (gentamicin, streptomycin) and polymyxins.
C Converts Gram-negative bacilli into spheroplasts and kills anaerobes.
D Enhances anaerobic sporulation and acts as a pH indicator.
Correct Answer: B — Anticoagulant, anticomplementary, antiphagocytic, and aminoglycoside-neutralizing. SPS is the universal anticoagulant of choice for blood culture. It prevents clot formation (trapping bacteria), inactivates serum bactericidal complement, inhibits ongoing phagocytosis by polymorphonuclear neutrophils, and binds/inactivates therapeutic aminoglycoside and polypeptide antibiotics present in the patient's bloodstream.
MCQ 458 • Castaneda Diphasic Bottle Mechanism
Why is a diphasic (Castaneda) medium (combining an agar slope and broth in a single bottle) particularly recommended for the isolation of fastidious organisms and Brucella species?
A The agar slope chemically converts CO₂ into oxygen.
B It changes color from red to yellow when viruses replicate.
C Tilting the bottle washes the broth over the agar slope, allowing colonies to grow directly on the solid medium without opening the bottle, minimizing contamination and biohazard exposure.
D It allows aerobic bacteria to multiply only in total darkness.
Correct Answer: C — Allows colonies to grow on the agar slope without opening the bottle. By periodically tilting the Castaneda bottle, broth is washed over the agar slant. Colonies appear directly on the slope (starting at the broth-agar interface). This eliminates the need for daily invasive needle subculturing, vastly reducing accidental external contamination and protecting laboratory staff from laboratory-acquired Brucella aerosol infections.
MCQ 459 • Skin Disinfection Protocol for Blood Culture
According to Monica Cheesbrough, what is the mandatory two-step skin antisepsis protocol prior to venepuncture for blood culture, and why must 2% tincture of iodine be left on the skin for 1 minute?
A Cleanse with 70% ethanol, apply 2% tincture of iodine in expanding concentric circles, and allow 1 full minute to dry (iodine requires contact time to penetrate pores and kill resident skin commensals).
B Wash with tap water and immediately insert the needle through wet skin.
C Apply sterile petroleum jelly and palpate vigorously.
D Wipe with hydrogen peroxide and rinse with saline within 5 seconds.
Correct Answer: A — 70% ethanol followed by 2% tincture of iodine allowed to dry for 1 full minute. Ethanol removes surface grease and dirt, while tincture of iodine penetrates hair follicles and sebaceous glands to sterilize resident commensal flora (*S. epidermidis*, *Corynebacterium*). Iodine must remain in contact with skin for at least 60 seconds to exert its bactericidal effect.
MCQ 460 • Blood-to-Broth Dilution Ratio Principle
Why must blood collected in conventional culture media without SPS be diluted at least 1:5 to 1:10 with culture broth (e.g., \(5\ \text{mL}\) blood into \(50\ \text{mL}\) broth)?
A To provide enough water for bacteria to swim across the bottle.
B To prevent the broth from turning acidic.
C To stimulate rapid lysis of all white blood cells into urea.
D To dilute out and neutralize natural host bactericidal substances in fresh blood (complement, specific antibacterial antibodies, and lysozyme) and prevent in vitro clotting.
Correct Answer: D — Dilutes natural host bactericidal substances (complement, antibodies, lysozyme). Whole blood contains powerful humoral and cellular antimicrobial mechanisms. Diluting blood at least \(1:10\) in nutrient broth lowers the concentration of active complement, natural antibodies, and lysozyme below bactericidal thresholds, permitting low numbers of circulating pathogens (\(1–10\ \text{CFU/mL}\)) to multiply.
MCQ 461 • Brucella Blood Culture Incubation Protocol
When brucellosis (undulant fever) is clinically suspected, what specific atmosphere and prolonged incubation time must be maintained for blood culture bottles?
A Pure anaerobic jar at \(45^\circ\text{C}\) for 24 hours.
B \(5–10\%\ \text{CO}_2\) enriched atmosphere at \(35–37^\circ\text{C}\) with incubation extended for up to 4 weeks (28 days).
C Aerobic refrigerator at \(4^\circ\text{C}\) for 14 days.
D Direct sunlight at room temperature for 3 days.
Correct Answer: B — 5–10% CO₂ atmosphere at 35–37°C for up to 4 weeks. Fastidious Brucella species (especially B. abortus) are capnophilic and exceptionally slow-growing. Blood cultures must be maintained in a \(\text{CO}_2\)-enriched incubator (with bottle caps loosened or punctured with a sterile needle) and examined twice weekly for up to 28 days before discarding as negative.
MCQ 462 • Differentiating Blood Culture Contaminants
Which laboratory scenario strongly indicates that an isolate of Staphylococcus epidermidis recovered from a blood culture bottle is a skin contaminant rather than a true pathogen?
A The organism is recovered from only 1 bottle out of 3 sets drawn from separate venepuncture sites, appearing after 5 days of incubation.
B The organism grows in all 3 blood culture sets within 18 hours in a patient with a prosthetic heart valve.
C The organism produces beta-lactamase and ferments mannitol.
D The isolate is recovered from both blood culture and synovial fluid.
Correct Answer: A — Isolated from only 1 bottle out of 3 sets with delayed growth. Common skin commensals (*S. epidermidis*, *Corynebacterium*, *Bacillus*) recovered from a single bottle among multiple sets with delayed growth reflect venepuncture contamination. True bacteremia (e.g. prosthetic valve endocarditis) is confirmed when identical strains grow rapidly across 2 or more independent venepuncture sets.
MCQ 463 • Rapid Diagnosis via Buffy Coat Smears in Infants
Why is microscopic examination of a centrifuged EDTA plasma buffy coat layer smear clinically valuable in suspected neonatal septicaemia or advanced HIV disease?
A It converts non-motile bacteria into motile vibrios.
B It is used exclusively to measure blood urea nitrogen.
C Centrifugation concentrates circulating leukocytes and phagocytosed/extracellular bacteria or acid-fast bacilli, allowing rapid presumptive diagnosis within 30 minutes before culture results become available.
D It neutralizes all antibiotics in the infant's bloodstream.
Correct Answer: C — Concentrates leukocytes and bacteria for rapid presumptive diagnosis within 30 minutes. In high-grade neonatal bacteremia and disseminated mycobacterial infections in AIDS, circulating bacterial loads are concentrated in the leukocyte buffy coat. Staining buffy coat smears with Gram, ZN, or Giemsa yields rapid same-day identification hours to days before culture growth.
MCQ 464 • Transfusion Reaction Sepsis Bacteriology
When investigating a fatal septic transfusion reaction from a contaminated unit of donor blood, what incubation temperature triad must be used for culturing the suspect donor blood?
A \(50^\circ\text{C}\), \(60^\circ\text{C}\), and \(70^\circ\text{C}\) for 1 hour.
B \(-20^\circ\text{C}\) only for 30 days.
C \(100^\circ\text{C}\) boiling water bath.
D Three bottles of thioglycollate broth incubated at \(35–37^\circ\text{C}\), room temperature (\(20–25^\circ\text{C}\)), and refrigerator temperature (\(4^\circ\text{C}\)) for up to 7 days.
Correct Answer: D — 35–37°C, room temperature (20–25°C), and 4°C for up to 7 days. Transfusion sepsis is commonly caused by psychrophilic (cold-tolerant) bacteria (*Pseudomonas fluorescens*, *Yersinia enterocolitica*, *Achromobacter*, *Serratia*) that multiply during blood bank refrigeration (\(4^\circ\text{C}\)) or at room temperature. Testing across all three temperature ranges ensures recovery of both mesophilic and psychrophilic contaminants.

7.15 Examination of Semen (Seminal Fluid Analysis)

Clinical Investigation of Male Infertility • Specimen Collection SOP (3–7 Days Abstinence, 1-Hour Delivery) • Macroscopic Evaluation (Liquefaction, Viscosity, Volume \(\ge 2.0\ \text{mL}\), Alkaline \(\text{pH}\ 7.2–7.8\)) • Microscopic Motility Grading (Categories a, b, c, d • \(\ge 50\%\) Progressive) • Eosin-Nigrosin Supravital Vitality Testing • Neubauer Hemocytometer Sperm Concentration (\(1:20\) Dilution, Normal \(\ge 20 \times 10^6/\text{mL}\)) • Carbol Fuchsin-Methylene Blue Morphology • Biochemical Markers (Seminal Fructose & Prostatic Acid Phosphatase).

Monica Cheesbrough Semen Analysis Principle: Semen analysis is a cornerstone investigation in reproductive biology and male infertility. Freshly ejaculated semen is a coagulum that undergoes enzymatic liquefaction within 30–60 minutes at room temperature via prostatic fibrinolysin. Crucial collection rules: (1) 3–7 days of sexual abstinence, (2) specimen delivered to the laboratory within 1 hour maintained warm (\(20–37^\circ\text{C}\)), (3) condoms and coitus interruptus are strictly unacceptable (condom powder/spermicide kills spermatozoa; coitus interruptus loses the first sperm-rich fraction and introduces vaginal acid/flora).

Click any highlighted pulse term below to examine high-yield BMLS board exam definitions and clinical applications:

3–7 Days Abstinence SOP 30–60 Min Liquefaction WHO Motility (a, b, c, d) Eosin-Nigrosin Vitality (Live White vs Dead Red) Neubauer Count (1:20 Dilution) Oligo / Astheno / Terato / Azoospermia Sperm Anatomy & Abnormalities Resorcinol Seminal Fructose Test
Pre-Analytical Phase Macroscopic Evaluation

1. Semen Collection Protocol & Physical / Macroscopic Parameters

Specimen Collection & Transport SOP

  • Sexual Abstinence: Strictly 3 to 7 days. Shorter periods cause falsely low sperm counts; longer periods cause decreased motility and increased abnormal/dead forms.
  • Container: Clean, dry, leak-proof wide-mouthed plastic/glass container.
  • Transport Window: Must be delivered to the laboratory within 1 hour of collection, kept warm (\(20–37^\circ\text{C}\), inside an inner coat/pocket).
  • Prohibited Collection Methods:
    • Standard Condoms: Rubber powder, spermicides, and latex toxins immobilize and kill spermatozoa.
    • Coitus Interruptus: First portion of ejaculate (which contains the highest sperm concentration) is frequently lost; acidic vaginal fluid destroys motility.

Macroscopic Physical Examination

  • Liquefaction Time: Normal semen liquefies within 30–60 minutes at room temperature. If complete liquefaction does not occur within 60 min, report abnormal viscosity.
  • Appearance / Color: Normally grayish-white, opalescent/translucent. Red/brown = hematospermia (blood/trauma); deep yellow = leukospermia (pus/infection) or severe jaundice.
  • Normal Volume: \(\ge 2.0\ \text{mL}\) (typically \(2.0–5.0\ \text{mL}\)). \(<2.0\ \text{mL}\) indicates retrograde ejaculation, androgen deficiency, or ejaculatory duct obstruction.
  • Normal pH: \(7.2–7.8\) (Alkaline). \(\text{pH} < 7.0\) in azoospermic specimens suggests congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens (CBAVD) or seminal vesicle agenesis (seminal vesicle secretes alkaline fluid).
Motility Kinetics Vitality Staining

2. Motility Grading, Vitality (Eosin-Nigrosin) & Agglutination

WHO Motility Classification (a, b, c, d)

Place \(10\ \mu\text{L}\) liquefied semen on a slide, cover with \(22 \times 22\ \text{mm}\) coverslip, and examine under \(40\times\) objective within 60 min:

Grade Motility Description Kinetic Velocity
Grade a Rapid progressive linear motility \(\ge 25\ \mu\text{m/s}\) (5 head lengths/s)
Grade b Slow or sluggish progressive motility Meandering / non-linear
Grade c Non-progressive motility Flagellar beating in place
Grade d Immotile spermatozoa No movement observed

WHO Reference Threshold: \(\ge 50\%\) progressive motility (Grade a + b) OR \(\ge 25\%\) rapid progressive (Grade a) within 60 min.

Supravital Eosin-Nigrosin Vitality SOP

Performed whenever motility is \(<50\%\) to differentiate immotile live spermatozoa (asthenozoospermia) from dead spermatozoa (necrozoospermia):

  • Reagent: \(1\%\) aqueous Eosin Y + \(10\%\) Nigrosin background stain.
  • Exclusion Principle: Intact cell membranes of living sperm exclude eosin (remain unstained / white). Damaged cell membranes of dead sperm allow dye penetration (stain pink / red). Nigrosin provides dark background contrast.
  • Reference Value: \(\ge 50–75\%\) viable (white) spermatozoa.
  • Agglutination & WBCs: Head-to-head or tail-to-tail clumpings indicate antisperm antibodies. Leukocytes \(>1 \times 10^6/\text{mL}\) indicates leukocytospermia (pyospermia).
Hemocytometer Math Andrology Terminology

3. Neubauer Sperm Counting SOP & WHO Diagnostic Criteria

Neubauer Chamber Dilution & Calculation

  1. Dilution Fluid: Mix \(50\ \mu\text{L}\) well-mixed semen with \(950\ \mu\text{L}\) of sperm diluent (\(1:20\) dilution). Diluent contains \(5\%\ \text{NaHCO}_3\) (dissolves mucus), \(1\%\) formalin (kills/straightens sperm), and gentian violet (stains heads).
  2. Chamber Loading: Fill both sides of Improved Neubauer hemocytometer; allow to settle in a moist chamber for 5 minutes.
  3. Counting Rule: Count all sperm heads in the 5 large squares of the central grid (total area \(0.2\ \text{mm}^2\), depth \(0.1\ \text{mm}\), volume \(0.02\ \mu\text{L}\)).
  4. Formula:
    \(\text{Sperm/mL} = N \times 10,000 \times 20\ (\text{dilution}) = N \times 200,000\)

Andrology Diagnostic Nomenclature Matrix

Diagnostic Term Standard Diagnostic Definition
Normozoospermia Normal sperm concentration, motility, and morphology.
Oligozoospermia Sperm concentration \(<20 \times 10^6/\text{mL}\).
Asthenozoospermia Progressive motility \(<50\%\) (or Grade a \(<25\%\)).
Teratozoospermia Normal morphological forms \(<50\%\).
Oligoasthenoteratozoospermia (OAT) All three variables (count, motility, morphology) abnormal.
Azoospermia Total absence of spermatozoa in ejaculate (post-centrifuge).
Aspermia Complete lack of semen volume / absence of ejaculate.
Necrozoospermia All spermatozoa non-viable / dead (\(>50–75\%\) take up eosin).
Leukocytospermia (Pyospermia) WBC count \(>1 \times 10^6/\text{mL}\) (\(>5\ \text{per HPF}\)).
Morphology Staining Seminal Biochemistry

4. Spermatozoal Morphology Staining & Seminal Fructose Testing

Sperm Morphology Staining & Normal Dimensions

  • Staining Method: Dilute Carbol Fuchsin (\(1:20\)) for 3 min, counterstain with Loeffler's Methylene Blue (\(1:20\)) for 2 min. (Alternative: Papanicolaou / Giemsa).
  • Staining Colors: Nucleus of head = dark blue; Acrosome/cytoplasm = pale blue; Midpiece and tail = pink-red.
  • Normal Sperm Dimensions: Total length \(50–70\ \mu\text{m}\); Oval head \(3–5 \times 2–3\ \mu\text{m}\) with acrosome covering \(40–70\%\) of head; slender midpiece (\(7–8\ \mu\text{m}\)); thin uncoiled tail (\(\ge 45\ \mu\text{m}\)).
  • Morphological Abnormalities: Pyriform/tapering heads, pin-heads (microcephalic), giant heads, double heads, absent acrosome (globozoospermia), cytoplasmic droplets, coiled/double tails.
  • Reference Value: \(\ge 50\%\) normal forms (WHO 1999) / most specimens contain \(<20\%\) abnormal forms.

Seminal Fructose & Prostatic Markers

  • Seminal Fructose (Resorcinol Test):
    • Secreted by the seminal vesicles under androgen control to provide energy for sperm motility.
    • Procedure: Add \(0.1\ \text{mL}\) semen to \(5\ \text{mL}\) resorcinol reagent (\(50\ \text{mg}\) resorcinol in \(33\ \text{mL}\) concentrated HCl diluted to \(100\ \text{mL}\)). Boil in water bath for 5 minutes.
    • Positive Result: Forms a distinct red / orange precipitate.
    • Clinical Significance: Absence of fructose in an azoospermic male indicates bilateral ejaculatory duct obstruction or congenital absence of the seminal vesicles.
  • Prostatic Acid Phosphatase: Secreted by the prostate gland. Used to evaluate prostatic secretory function and in forensic medicine to confirm the presence of semen in rape/sexual assault cases.

Section 7.15 Board Review Questions (MCQ 465 – 472)

Test your mastery of semen collection protocols, WHO motility grading, eosin-nigrosin vitality, Neubauer hemocytometer counts, morphology, and seminal biochemistry:

MCQ 465 • Semen Specimen Collection Guidelines
According to WHO and Monica Cheesbrough guidelines, what are the mandatory pre-analytical conditions for collecting a semen specimen for infertility analysis?
A Collect after 1 day of abstinence into a commercial condom and freeze at \(-20^\circ\text{C}\).
B Collect after 3–7 days of sexual abstinence into a clean, dry, leak-proof container, avoid condoms and coitus interruptus, and deliver to the laboratory within 1 hour maintained warm (\(20–37^\circ\text{C}\)).
C Collect by coitus interruptus after 14 days of abstinence and dilute with tap water.
D Collect immediately after strenuous exercise using sterile soapy water.
Correct Answer: B — 3–7 days abstinence, clean container, deliver within 1 hour kept warm. Sexual abstinence of 3–7 days ensures standardized sperm concentration and motility. Standard condoms contain spermicidal and toxic chemicals, while coitus interruptus misses the initial sperm-rich portion of the ejaculate. Samples must be delivered within 60 minutes kept at body/room temperature to preserve motility.
MCQ 466 • Semen Liquefaction and Physical Characteristics
What is the normal physiological liquefaction time of fresh semen, and what are the standard reference values for normal semen volume and pH?
A Liquefaction in \(>4\ \text{hours}\); volume \(0.5\ \text{mL}\); \(\text{pH}\ 5.0–6.0\).
B Liquefaction does not occur normally; volume \(\ge 10\ \text{mL}\); \(\text{pH}\ 8.5–9.0\).
C Liquefaction occurs within 30–60 minutes at room temperature; normal volume is \(\ge 2.0\ \text{mL}\); normal pH is alkaline (\(7.2–7.8\)).
D Liquefaction occurs instantly within 5 seconds; volume \(1.0\ \text{mL}\); \(\text{pH}\ 6.5–6.8\).
Correct Answer: C — Liquefaction in 30–60 min; volume \(\ge 2.0\ \text{mL}\); alkaline pH \(7.2–7.8\). Fresh semen is coagulated and liquefies within 30–60 minutes via proteolytic enzymes (fibrinolysin/PSA) from the prostate gland. The normal volume is \(\ge 2.0\ \text{mL}\) and the pH is slightly alkaline (\(7.2–7.8\)) to neutralize acidic vaginal secretions.
MCQ 467 • WHO Motility Grading System
Under the WHO semen analysis classification, how are spermatozoa categorized into Grades a, b, c, and d, and what is the minimum threshold for normal progressive motility?
A Grade a = rapid progressive; Grade b = slow/sluggish progressive; Grade c = non-progressive; Grade d = immotile; Normal threshold is \(\ge 50\%\) progressive (a + b) or \(\ge 25\%\) Grade a.
B Grade a = immotile; Grade b = non-progressive; Grade c = slow; Grade d = fast; Normal is \(\ge 90\%\) Grade d.
C Grade a = circular motility only; Normal threshold is \(\ge 10\%\) Grade c.
D Motility is measured only after 24 hours of refrigeration; Normal threshold is \(\ge 5\%\).
Correct Answer: A — Grade a (rapid linear), b (slow progressive), c (non-progressive), d (immotile); \(\ge 50\%\) a+b or \(\ge 25\%\) a. The WHO system grades forward velocity. At least \(50\%\) of spermatozoa must demonstrate progressive motility (Category \(a + b\)) within 60 minutes of ejaculation, or at least \(25\%\) must exhibit rapid linear forward velocity (\(\ge 25\ \mu\text{m/s}\), Category \(a\)).
MCQ 468 • Supravital Eosin-Nigrosin Vitality Testing Principle
Why is supravital Eosin-Nigrosin staining performed during semen analysis, and how are live versus dead spermatozoa differentiated under the microscope?
A To stain bacterial flagella; live sperm stain purple and dead sperm stain green.
B To measure DNA fragmentation; live sperm turn completely black.
C To count white blood cells; live sperm dissolve completely within 10 seconds.
D To differentiate live immotile sperm from dead sperm; intact membranes of live sperm exclude eosin (remain white/unstained), whereas dead sperm absorb eosin (stain pink/red) against the dark nigrosin background.
Correct Answer: D — Live sperm remain white/unstained; dead sperm stain pink/red against dark nigrosin. When sperm motility is \(<50\%\), vitality testing differentiates necrozoospermia (dead sperm) from asthenozoospermia (immotile but living sperm, e.g. ciliary dyskinesia / Kartagener syndrome). Live spermatozoa with intact cell membranes exclude eosin, appearing white/unstained, while dead cells with leaky membranes stain pink-red. Normal vitality is \(\ge 50–75\%\).
MCQ 469 • Neubauer Hemocytometer Sperm Count Calculation
A semen sample is diluted 1:20 in formalin-bicarbonate diluent and loaded onto an Improved Neubauer hemocytometer. A total of 150 sperm are counted across the 5 large secondary squares (\(0.2\ \text{mm}^2\)). What is the sperm concentration per mL, and does this meet the WHO normal reference threshold?
A \(1.5 \times 10^6/\text{mL}\) (Severely oligozoospermic).
B \(30 \times 10^6/\text{mL}\) (\(30\ \text{million/mL}\)), which meets the normal reference threshold (\(\ge 20 \times 10^6/\text{mL}\)).
C \(150 \times 10^6/\text{mL}\) (Polyzoospermic).
D \(300,000/\text{mL}\) (Azoospermic).
Correct Answer: B — \(30 \times 10^6/\text{mL}\), which is normal (\(\ge 20 \times 10^6/\text{mL}\)). Calculation: \(\text{Sperm/mL} = N \times 10,000 \times 20\ (\text{dilution}) = 150 \times 200,000 = 30,000,000/\text{mL} = 30 \times 10^6/\text{mL}\). This exceeds the WHO normal cut-off of \(\ge 20 \times 10^6/\text{mL}\) (or \(\ge 40 \times 10^6/\text{ejaculate}\)).
MCQ 470 • Andrology Diagnostic Nomenclature
Match the correct andrology diagnostic term to its definition: complete absence of spermatozoa in ejaculate even after centrifugation, and sperm count below \(20 \times 10^6/\text{mL}\):
A Azoospermia (total absence of spermatozoa) and Oligozoospermia (sperm concentration \(<20 \times 10^6/\text{mL}\)).
B Asthenozoospermia and Aspermia.
C Teratozoospermia and Necrozoospermia.
D Pyospermia and Hemospermia.
Correct Answer: A — Azoospermia (zero sperm) and Oligozoospermia (\(<20 \times 10^6/\text{mL}\)). Standard terms: Azoospermia = zero spermatozoa recovered after centrifugation at \(3000 \times g\); Oligozoospermia = concentration \(<20 \times 10^6/\text{mL}\); Asthenozoospermia = progressive motility \(<50\%\); Teratozoospermia = normal morphology \(<50\%\); Aspermia = complete lack of semen fluid.
MCQ 471 • Sperm Morphology & Anatomy
What are the anatomical dimensions and staining reactions of a morphologically normal spermatozoon stained with dilute Carbol Fuchsin and Methylene Blue?
A Spherical head \(10\ \mu\text{m}\) wide, bright yellow nucleus, completely unstained tail.
B Triangular head \(1–2\ \mu\text{m}\), green nucleus, pink acrosome.
C Total length \(50–70\ \mu\text{m}\); oval head (\(3–5 \times 2–3\ \mu\text{m}\)) with dark blue nucleus and pale blue acrosomal cap (covering \(40–70\%\) of anterior head); pink-red middle piece and long thin tail (\(\ge 45\ \mu\text{m}\)).
D Bifurcated head with three separate coiled tails measuring \(15\ \mu\text{m}\).
Correct Answer: C — 50–70 μm length, oval head (3–5 × 2–3 μm), dark blue nucleus, pale blue acrosome, pink-red tail. A normal spermatozoon consists of an oval head (\(3–5 \times 2–3\ \mu\text{m}\)) with an acrosomal cap covering \(40–70\%\) of the anterior head, a slender midpiece (\(7–8\ \mu\text{m}\)), and an uncoiled tail (\(\ge 45\ \mu\text{m}\)). At least \(50\%\) of spermatozoa in normal semen should exhibit normal morphology.
MCQ 472 • Seminal Fructose & Resorcinol Testing
Which accessory sex gland produces seminal fructose, and what is the clinical significance of a negative Resorcinol test in an azoospermic patient?
A Prostate gland; negative test indicates benign prostatic hyperplasia.
B Bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands; negative test indicates urinary tract infection.
C Testicular Leydig cells; negative test indicates testosterone excess.
D Seminal vesicles; a negative Resorcinol test (failure to form red/orange color upon boiling) in an azoospermic male indicates congenital absence of the seminal vesicles or bilateral ejaculatory duct obstruction.
Correct Answer: D — Seminal vesicles; negative Resorcinol test indicates seminal vesicle agenesis or ejaculatory duct obstruction. Fructose is synthesized exclusively by the seminal vesicles under androgen control. When semen from an azoospermic patient is tested with Resorcinol in concentrated HCl and fails to yield a red/orange precipitate upon boiling, it confirms obstructive azoospermia due to seminal vesicle agenesis or bilateral ejaculatory duct obstruction.

You have mastered Examination of Semen (Seminal Fluid Analysis) (Cheesbrough Part 2 pp. 137–140).

7.16 Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (AST)

Principles of Selective Toxicity & Modes of Antimicrobial Action • Mueller-Hinton Agar (MHA) \(4\ \text{mm}\) Depth & Cation / Thymidine Controls • Inoculum Standardization (0.5 McFarland = \(1.5 \times 10^8\ \text{CFU/mL}\)) • CLSI / NCCLS Modified Kirby-Bauer Disc Diffusion • Stokes Comparative Disc Diffusion • Etest Quantitative MIC Gradients • Beta-Lactamase Rapid Assays (Nitrocefin, Acidimetric, Iodometric) • Special Resistance Mechanisms (MRSA / Cefoxitin, High-Level Aminoglycoside Resistance, Heaped-Up Cliff-Edge Effect) • Quality Control Reference Strains (*E. coli* ATCC 25922, *S. aureus* ATCC 25923, *P. aeruginosa* ATCC 27853, *E. faecalis* ATCC 29212).

Monica Cheesbrough AST Golden Standard: Standardized disk diffusion depends strictly on physical and biological parameters. Mueller-Hinton agar must be poured to a precise depth of \(4\ \text{mm}\) (\(\approx 25\ \text{mL}\) per \(90\ \text{mm}\) plate): if \(<4\ \text{mm}\), antibiotics diffuse further laterally yielding falsely large zones (false susceptibility); if \(>4\ \text{mm}\), downward diffusion predominates yielding falsely small zones (false resistance). Inoculate with 0.5 McFarland standard within 15 minutes, apply max 6 discs (\(\ge 25\ \text{mm}\) apart), and incubate at \(35^\circ\text{C}\) (never \(>35^\circ\text{C}\) for MRSA detection)!

Pharmacodynamics Resistance Mechanisms

1. Major Classes of Antimicrobial Agents & Mechanisms of Resistance

Antimicrobial Class Representative Drug Agents Target & Biochemical Mode of Action Principal Bacterial Resistance Mechanisms
Penicillins (Beta-Lactams) Benzylpenicillin (Pen G), Phenoxymethylpenicillin (Pen V), Ampicillin, Amoxicillin, Cloxacillin, Piperacillin Inhibit transpeptidase cross-linking of peptidoglycan cell wall; bactericidal; bacteriolysis triggered by autolysins. • Beta-lactamase (penicillinase) destruction of beta-lactam ring.
• Altered Penicillin-Binding Proteins (PBPs), e.g. PBP2a in MRSA (*mecA* gene).
• Reduced outer membrane porin permeability in Gram-negatives.
Cephalosporins (Beta-Lactams) 1st Gen: Cephradine, Cefalexin
2nd Gen: Cefuroxime
3rd Gen: Ceftriaxone, Cefotaxime, Ceftazidime 		Inhibit bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan synthesis; stable against standard staphylococcal penicillinase; broad-spectrum. • Extended-Spectrum Beta-Lactamases (ESBLs): Hydrolyze 3rd gen cephalosporins & aztreonam; inhibited by clavulanic acid.
• AmpC beta-lactamases & carbapenemases (KPC, NDM-1, OXA).
Glycopeptides Vancomycin, Teicoplanin Binds to D-Alanyl-D-Alanine terminus of cell wall peptidoglycan precursors, blocking polymer elongation; strictly Gram-positive. • VanA / VanB operon in Enterococcus (VRE): modifies target to D-Alanyl-D-Lactate.
• VISA (thickened cell wall) / VRSA (*vanA* acquisition).
Aminoglycosides Gentamicin, Streptomycin, Amikacin, Tobramycin, Kanamycin, Netilmicin Irreversibly bind to **30S ribosomal subunit**, causing mRNA misreading and premature termination of protein synthesis; bactericidal. • Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes (AMEs): Acetyltransferases (AAC), Phosphotransferases (APH), Adenyltransferases (ANT).
• Active efflux pumps; ribosomal 16S rRNA methylation.
Macrolides & Lincosamides Erythromycin, Azithromycin, Clarithromycin; Clindamycin Reversibly bind to **50S ribosomal subunit**, inhibiting peptide chain elongation / translocation; bacteriostatic. • *erm* gene mediated 23S rRNA methylation (inducible/constitutive MLS_B resistance).
• *msr* gene active efflux pumps.
Tetracyclines & Chloramphenicol Tetracycline, Doxycycline; Chloramphenicol Tetracyclines bind 30S (blocks aminoacyl-tRNA binding); Chloramphenicol binds 50S (inhibits peptidyl transferase). • Tetracyclines: *tet* efflux pumps and ribosomal protection proteins.
• Chloramphenicol: Chloramphenicol acetyltransferase (CAT).
Quinolones & Fluoroquinolones Nalidixic acid, Ciprofloxacin, Norfloxacin, Ofloxacin, Levofloxacin Inhibit bacterial **DNA gyrase (Topoisomerase II)** and **Topoisomerase IV**, blocking DNA replication and transcription; bactericidal. • Point mutations in Quinolone Resistance-Determining Regions (QRDR) of *gyrA* and *parC* genes.
• Plasmid-mediated quinolone resistance (PMQR / *qnr* proteins).
Folate Pathway Inhibitors Co-trimoxazole (Sulfamethoxazole + Trimethoprim, 5:1 ratio) Sequential dual blockade of folic acid biosynthesis: Sulfonamides inhibit dihydropteroate synthase; Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase. • Mutation or plasmid acquisition of resistant *sul* and *dfr* enzymes resistant to drug binding.
• Thymidine scavenging from rich medium / pus.
CLSI / Kirby-Bauer MHA Standards

2. Modified Kirby-Bauer Disc Diffusion SOP & MHA Media Control

MHA Preparation & Depth Rule

  • Mueller-Hinton Agar (MHA): Low in sulfonamide, trimethoprim, and tetracycline inhibitors; provides batch-to-batch reproducibility.
  • Precise 4 mm Depth Rule: Pour precisely **\(4\ \text{mm}\)** agar depth (\(\approx 25\ \text{mL}\) for \(90\ \text{mm}\) plate).
    • If \(<4\ \text{mm}\): Lateral diffusion is too fast \(\to\) falsely large zones (false susceptibility).
    • If \(>4\ \text{mm}\): Downward diffusion \(\to\) falsely small zones (false resistance).
  • pH & Cation Control: \(\text{pH}\ 7.2–7.4\). \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\) and \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) levels must be controlled; excessive cations falsely reduce aminoglycoside zones against *P. aeruginosa*.

0.5 McFarland Inoculum Standardization

  • McFarland 0.5 Formula: \(0.5\ \text{mL}\) of \(1.175\%\ \text{w/v}\ \text{BaCl}_2\cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + 99.5\ \text{mL}\) of \(1\%\ \text{v/v}\ \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) (forms fine barium sulfate precipitate = **\(1.5 \times 10^8\ \text{CFU/mL}\)**).
  • Direct Colony Suspension: Touch 3–5 identical colonies from an 18–24 h plate, emulsify in sterile peptone water/saline, match turbidity against McFarland card with black lines under good light.
  • Lawn Swabbing: Dip sterile cotton swab, express excess liquid against tube wall, streak across entire agar in **3 directions at \(60^\circ\) angles**, and finish with a circular rim swipe.

Disc Placement & Incubation

  • Timing: Apply paper discs within **15 minutes** of swab inoculation; press firmly onto agar.
  • Disc Spacing: Discs must be \(\ge 25\ \text{mm}\) apart (center to center) and \(\ge 15\ \text{mm}\) from edge. Maximum 6 discs per \(90\ \text{mm}\) plate (max 12 per \(150\ \text{mm}\) plate).
  • Incubation Conditions: Invert plates within 30 min and incubate at **\(35^\circ\text{C}\)** in ambient air for **\(16–18\ \text{hours}\)**.
  • Strict Temperature Limit: Never incubate above \(35^\circ\text{C}\) (temperatures \(>35^\circ\text{C}\) mask heteroresistant MRSA expression!).
Stokes Technique Etest Quantitation

3. Stokes Comparative Method vs Etest Gradient Technology

Stokes Comparative Technique Principle

Used in laboratories where standard Kirby-Bauer conditions cannot be strictly maintained:

  • Plate Layout: Test organism is inoculated across the upper and lower thirds of an MHA plate, while a known ATCC control strain is inoculated in the center horizontal band (or vice versa).
  • Disc Placement: Discs are placed precisely along the interface between test and control lawns.
  • Interpretation (Zone Radius Difference):
    • Sensitive: Zone radius is equal to, larger than, or not more than \(3\ \text{mm}\) smaller than control.
    • Intermediate: Zone radius is \(>12\ \text{mm}\) but smaller than control by \(>3\ \text{mm}\).
    • Resistant: Zone radius is \(\le 12\ \text{mm}\) or no zone.

Etest (Epsilometer) Quantitative Strip SOP

Plastic carrier strip with a continuous, predefined exponential gradient of 15 two-fold dilutions of antimicrobial:

  • Principle: Upon application to an MHA lawn, antimicrobial immediately diffuses into agar, creating a continuous concentration gradient.
  • Elliptical Zone of Inhibition: Produces a symmetrical inhibition ellipse.
  • Reading MIC: Read the Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC in \(\mu\text{g/mL}\)) directly off the calibrated upper scale at the point where the edge of the inhibition ellipse intersects the strip.
  • Clinical Utility: Crucial for fastidious organisms (*S. pneumoniae*, *H. influenzae*, *N. gonorrhoeae*) and determining precise MICs for vancomycin / penicillin.
Rapid Beta-Lactamase MRSA & QC Strains

4. Rapid Beta-Lactamase Assays, MRSA Detection & ATCC Quality Control

Rapid Beta-Lactamase Diagnostic Tests

  • 1. Chromogenic Cephalosporin (Nitrocefin) Test: Most sensitive and rapid. Touch Nitrocefin paper stick/disc with colony. Hydrolysis of beta-lactam ring produces an immediate color shift from Yellow \(\to\) Red / Pink within 1–5 minutes.
  • 2. Acidimetric Penicillin Test: Penicillin G + Bromocresol Purple pH indicator. Beta-lactamase cleavage produces penicilloic acid, dropping pH and turning color from Purple \(\to\) Yellow.
  • 3. Iodometric Penicillin Test: Penicillin G + Starch-Iodine complex. Hydrolysis to penicilloic acid reduces iodine to colorless iodide, turning color from Blue / Black \(\to\) Colorless within 10 minutes.

MRSA Detection & Heaped-Up Zone Edge

  • MRSA Screening (Cefoxitin \(30\ \mu\text{g}\) / Oxacillin \(1\ \mu\text{g}\)): Cefoxitin is the preferred surrogate inducer of *mecA* gene. Inoculate MHA (with \(2–4\%\ \text{NaCl}\) for oxacillin) and incubate at **\(35^\circ\text{C}\) for 24 hours**. Resistance implies resistance to ALL penicillins, cephalosporins, and carbapenems!
  • Staphylococcal "Cliff-Edge" Rule:
    • Sensitive non-producers: Show a thin, hazy, tapering zone edge.
    • Beta-lactamase producers: Show a sharp, elevated, heaped-up "cliff-like" zone margin around penicillin G discs (report as RESISTANT regardless of zone diameter).

Standard ATCC Quality Control Reference Strains

*E. coli* ATCC 25922

Gram-negative control for coliforms, aminoglycosides, and broad-spectrum beta-lactams.

*S. aureus* ATCC 25923

Gram-positive control for staphylococci, macrolides, and beta-lactamase-negative baseline.

*P. aeruginosa* ATCC 27853

Control for antipseudomonal agents (ceftazidime, carbapenems) and agar cation (\(\text{Ca}^{2+}/\text{Mg}^{2+}\)) levels.

*E. faecalis* ATCC 29212

Control for sulfonamide/trimethoprim (zone must be \(\ge 20\ \text{mm}\) to confirm low thymidine in MHA).

Board Examination Section 8 Active Interactive MCQs

Section 7.16 Board Review Questions (MCQ 473 – 480)

Test your mastery of Mueller-Hinton depth rules, 0.5 McFarland standardization, Kirby-Bauer vs Stokes, Etest, beta-lactamase assays, and MRSA screening:

MCQ 473 • Mueller-Hinton Agar 4 mm Depth Rule
Why must Mueller-Hinton Agar (MHA) plates used for disc diffusion susceptibility testing be poured to a precise depth of exactly \(4\ \text{mm}\) (\(\approx 25\ \text{mL}\) per \(90\ \text{mm}\) plate), and what technical errors occur if the agar is too thin or too thick?
A Too thin causes the plate to crack; too thick causes bacteria to grow anaerobically.
B If agar depth is \(<4\ \text{mm}\), lateral diffusion of antibiotic is increased yielding falsely large inhibition zones (false susceptibility); if \(>4\ \text{mm}\), downward diffusion predominates yielding falsely small zones (false resistance).
C Agar depth only alters the color of the pH indicator.
D Agar depth has no effect on zone diameter as long as discs contain full antibiotic potency.
Correct Answer: B — \(<4\ \text{mm}\) gives falsely large zones (false susceptibility); \(>4\ \text{mm}\) gives falsely small zones (false resistance). Antimicrobial disc diffusion is three-dimensional. In thin agar (\(<4\ \text{mm}\)), less antibiotic diffuses vertically into the depth of the medium, forcing excessive radial/lateral diffusion that artificially enlarges the zone of inhibition. In thick agar (\(>4\ \text{mm}\)), vertical diffusion drains the drug, producing falsely constricted zones.
MCQ 474 • 0.5 McFarland Standard Inoculum Preparation
What chemical formulation constitutes the 0.5 McFarland turbidity standard, what approximate bacterial density does it represent, and how should it be used to streak the Mueller-Hinton agar plate?
A \(0.5\ \text{mL}\) of \(1.175\%\ \text{BaCl}_2 + 99.5\ \text{mL}\) of \(1\%\ \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) (\(\approx 1.5 \times 10^8\ \text{CFU/mL}\)); swab is streaked in 3 directions at \(60^\circ\) angles with a final circular rim swipe to produce a confluent lawn.
B \(10\ \text{mL}\) pure hydrochloric acid + \(1\ \text{mL}\) copper sulfate (\(10^4\ \text{CFU/mL}\)); inoculated as a single streak down the center.
C Pure barium sulfide powder diluted in olive oil (\(10^{12}\ \text{CFU/mL}\)); poured over the entire plate.
D \(5\%\) saline solution boiled for 20 minutes (\(10^2\ \text{CFU/mL}\)); sprayed with an atomizer.
Correct Answer: A — \(0.5\ \text{mL}\) \(1.175\%\ \text{BaCl}_2 + 99.5\ \text{mL}\) \(1\%\ \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) (\(1.5 \times 10^8\ \text{CFU/mL}\)); 3-direction \(60^\circ\) lawn streaking. Mixing barium chloride with sulfuric acid forms a finely dispersed barium sulfate precipitate. A density matching the 0.5 McFarland standard provides an inoculum of \(\approx 1.5 \times 10^8\ \text{CFU/mL}\), which yields an even, confluent, non-overlapping bacterial lawn when streaked across the agar in 3 directions at \(60^\circ\) angles.
MCQ 475 • Disc Application Rules & Incubation Temperature
According to CLSI and Monica Cheesbrough standards, what are the mandatory rules regarding disc spacing, disc application timing, and incubation temperature for modified Kirby-Bauer testing?
A Place 15 discs per plate touching each other; incubate at \(42^\circ\text{C}\) for 48 hours.
B Apply discs after 6 hours of drying; incubate at \(25^\circ\text{C}\) in total darkness.
C Apply discs within 15 minutes of inoculation; space discs \(\ge 25\ \text{mm}\) apart with max 6 discs per \(90\ \text{mm}\) plate; incubate at \(35^\circ\text{C}\) (never \(>35^\circ\text{C}\) for MRSA) for \(16–18\ \text{hours}\).
D Discs must be heated to \(100^\circ\text{C}\) before placement; incubate at \(37^\circ\text{C}\) with \(20\%\ \text{CO}_2\).
Correct Answer: C — Within 15 min, \(\ge 25\ \text{mm}\) apart, max 6 discs/\(90\ \text{mm}\) plate, \(35^\circ\text{C}\) for \(16–18\ \text{h}\). Applying discs within 15 minutes ensures bacteria do not enter log-phase growth before drug diffusion starts. Discs must be \(\ge 25\ \text{mm}\) apart to prevent zone overlap. The incubation temperature must strictly be maintained at \(35^\circ\text{C}\) (never \(>35^\circ\text{C}\)) because temperatures above \(35^\circ\text{C}\) suppress phenotypic expression of heteroresistant MRSA.
MCQ 476 • Stokes Comparative Disc Diffusion Method
How does the Stokes comparative disc diffusion method differ fundamentally from the Kirby-Bauer method, and how are results interpreted?
A Stokes uses liquid broth in test tubes instead of agar plates.
B Stokes tests antiviral drugs rather than antibacterial agents.
C Stokes measures colony height rather than zone diameter.
D Both the test organism and a known control ATCC strain are inoculated on the same agar plate, with discs placed along their interface; the zone radius of the test organism is directly compared to that of the control strain.
Correct Answer: D — Test and control strains inoculated on same plate with direct zone radius comparison. In the Stokes technique, an internal control strain is cultured side-by-side with the patient isolate on the very same plate. This internal control automatically compensates for minor laboratory variations in agar depth, incubation temperature, or disc potency, making it exceptionally reliable in resource-limited district laboratories.
MCQ 477 • Etest Quantitative Technology & MIC Determination
What is the operating principle of the Etest (Epsilometer test), and where is the Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) read?
A It measures turbidity change in a spectrophotometer cuvette after 1 hour.
B A plastic strip impregnated with a continuous exponential antimicrobial gradient is applied to an agar lawn; the MIC (\(\mu\text{g/mL}\)) is read directly where the edge of the symmetrical inhibition ellipse intersects the calibrated scale.
C It produces circular colored rings that turn purple when bacteria are killed.
D It measures the electrical resistance across an inoculated agar block.
Correct Answer: B — Plastic strip with predefined gradient; MIC read at the intersection of the inhibition ellipse. The Etest strip carries a continuous, stable concentration gradient covering 15 two-fold dilutions. As the drug diffuses radially and downward, a symmetrical teardrop/ellipse of inhibition forms. The exact MIC (\(\mu\text{g/mL}\)) corresponds precisely to the number on the strip scale where the bacterial growth margin touches the strip.
MCQ 478 • Rapid Beta-Lactamase Testing Principles
What is the color change observed in a positive Nitrocefin (chromogenic cephalosporin) test and a positive Acidimetric penicillin test for rapid beta-lactamase detection?
A Nitrocefin: Yellow to Red/Pink within 1–5 minutes; Acidimetric: Purple to Yellow (due to penicilloic acid formation lowering pH).
B Nitrocefin: Blue to Colorless; Acidimetric: Green to Black.
C Nitrocefin: Red to Bright Yellow; Acidimetric: Colorless to Navy Blue.
D Both tests remain completely colorless in positive reactions.
Correct Answer: A — Nitrocefin: Yellow to Red/Pink; Acidimetric: Purple to Yellow. Nitrocefin is a chromogenic cephalosporin whose beta-lactam ring cleavage shifts electron resonance, producing an immediate red/pink color. In the acidimetric assay, hydrolysis of penicillin G yields penicilloic acid, which drops the pH and causes the bromocresol purple indicator to change from purple to yellow.
MCQ 479 • Quality Control ATCC Reference Strains
Which standard ATCC reference strain is specifically utilized during quality assurance testing of Mueller-Hinton agar batches to exclude excessive levels of thymidine / thymine (which cause false resistance to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole)?
A *Staphylococcus aureus* ATCC 25923
B *Escherichia coli* ATCC 25922
C *Enterococcus faecalis* ATCC 29212 (zone of inhibition around co-trimoxazole disc must be \(\ge 20\ \text{mm}\) with clear zone edge)
D *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* ATCC 27853
Correct Answer: C — *Enterococcus faecalis* ATCC 29212 (\(\ge 20\ \text{mm}\) zone around co-trimoxazole). Enterococci can utilize exogenous thymidine to bypass the metabolic block imposed by sulfonamides and trimethoprim. If an MHA batch contains excessive thymidine, *E. faecalis* ATCC 29212 will show a constricted or hazy zone (\(<20\ \text{mm}\)), alerting the laboratory to reject the medium batch for folate antagonist testing.
MCQ 480 • MRSA Resistance Biology & The "Cliff-Edge" Phenomenon
What is the therapeutic implication of detecting methicillin / oxacillin / cefoxitin resistance in *Staphylococcus aureus* (MRSA), and how does the zone margin appearance of a penicillinase producer differ from a penicillin-susceptible strain?
A MRSA is susceptible to all 3rd generation cephalosporins; zone edges are always completely fuzzy.
B MRSA can only be treated with oral ampicillin; zone edges show red discoloration.
C MRSA is resistant only to oxacillin but sensitive to penicillin G; zone edges are inverted.
D MRSA produces altered PBP2a (encoded by *mecA*), conferring clinical resistance to ALL beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems); beta-lactamase producers exhibit a sharp, elevated, heaped-up "cliff-like" zone edge around penicillin discs.
Correct Answer: D — MRSA confers cross-resistance to all beta-lactams; beta-lactamase producers show a sharp "cliff-edge" zone margin. The *mecA* gene encodes penicillin-binding protein 2a (PBP2a), which possesses low affinity for all beta-lactam antibiotics, making penicillins, cephalosporins, and carbapenems clinically ineffective. Furthermore, staphylococci producing penicillinase produce a distinctive sharp, heaped-up "cliff-like" colony edge around penicillin discs, which mandates reporting resistance regardless of zone size.

Section 7.16 Complete!

You have mastered Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (AST) (Cheesbrough Part 2 pp. 139–151).

7.17 Water-Related Diseases & Testing of Water Supplies

Bradley Classification of Water-Related Diseases • Thermotolerant (Faecal) Coliforms & *Escherichia coli* Indicator Biology (\(44.0^\circ\text{C}\) Lactose Fermentation) • WHO Drinking Water Guidelines (0 CFU / \(100\ \text{mL}\)) • Sanitary Survey Risk Scoring • Water Sampling Protocol & Sodium Thiosulfate Neutralization (\(18\ \text{mg/L}\)) • Membrane Filtration SOP (\(0.45\ \mu\text{m}\) Grid Filter, MLSB Broth) • Multiple Tube Fermentation / Most Probable Number (MPN) McCrady Probability Matrix • Free Residual Chlorine DPD No. 1 Lovibond Comparator Assay.

Monica Cheesbrough Water Quality Principle: The greatest public health threat from drinking water is contamination by human and animal excreta. Rather than testing for individual elusive pathogens, laboratories monitor Thermotolerant (Faecal) Coliforms / *E. coli*, which ferment lactose with gas and acid at \(44.0^\circ\text{C} \pm 0.5^\circ\text{C}\) within 24 hours. In treated piped supplies, WHO mandates 0 Faecal Coliforms / 0 *E. coli* per \(100\ \text{mL}\). Water with \(\ge 0.2–0.5\ \text{mg/L}\) free residual chlorine (measured via DPD No. 1) and turbidity \(<5\ \text{NTU}\) is safe from bacterial pathogens.

Epidemiology Bradley Classification

1. Bradley Epidemiological Classification of Water-Related Diseases

Disease Category Transmission Mechanism Representative Pathogens & Diseases Primary Preventive Interventions
1. Water-Borne Diseases Ingestion of drinking water contaminated by human or animal faeces. • Bacterial: *Vibrio cholerae*, *Salmonella* Typhi/Paratyphi, *Campylobacter*, *Shigella*, ETEC.
• Viral: Hepatitis A & E viruses, Rotavirus, Norovirus, Poliovirus.
• Protozoal: *Cryptosporidium parvum*, *Giardia lamblia*, *Entamoeba histolytica*. 		Improve drinking water microbiological quality, protect water catchments, boiling, water filtration, and chlorination.
2. Water-Washed (Water-Scarce) Infections spread person-to-person due to inadequate volume of water available for personal hygiene and washing. • Skin & Eye: Trachoma (*Chlamydia trachomatis*), Scabies (*Sarcoptes scabiei*), bacterial conjunctivitis.
• Faecal-Oral / Ectoparasitic: Bacillary dysentery, relapsing fever & epidemic typhus (body lice). 		Increase water quantity and accessibility (providing \(\ge 20–50\ \text{L/capita/day}\)), promote handwashing with soap.
3. Water-Based Diseases Infections transmitted through aquatic intermediate invertebrate hosts living in water. • Schistosomiasis (Bilharzia): *Schistosoma mansoni*, *S. haematobium* (cercariae from freshwater snails penetrate skin).
• Dracunculiasis (Guinea Worm): *Dracunculus medinensis* (ingestion of water containing infected *Cyclops* copepods). 		Avoid skin contact with infested water, aquatic snail control (niclosamide), filter drinking water through monofilament cloth (\(100\ \mu\text{m}\)).
4. Water-Related Insect Vectors Pathogens transmitted by insects that breed in or bite near freshwater habitats. • Mosquitoes: Malaria (*Anopheles* in pools/marshes), Dengue/Yellow fever (*Aedes* in domestic containers), Filariasis (*Culex* in polluted drains).
• Flies: Onchocerciasis (*Simulium* blackflies breeding in fast-flowing rapids), African trypanosomiasis (*Glossina* tsetse flies near rivers). 		Source reduction, eliminate artificial water containers, larviciding, insecticide-treated bed nets (ITNs), clearance of riverine vegetation.
5. Water-Dispersed (Aerosol) Inhalation of aerosolized droplets from artificial water distribution/cooling systems. • Legionnaires' Disease & Pontiac Fever: *Legionella pneumophila* multiplying in warm water cooling towers and shower heads. Thermal disinfection (\(>60^\circ\text{C}\)), hyperchlorination of cooling towers and hospital water distribution circuits.
Indicator Biology WHO Thresholds

2. Microbial Indicators of Faecal Pollution & WHO Standards

Thermotolerant Coliforms & *E. coli* Biology

  • Why Use Indicator Organisms? Directly testing for pathogens (*S.* Typhi, *V.* cholerae) is impracticable because they are excreted intermittently, in low numbers, and require complex, costly media.
  • Thermotolerant (Faecal) Coliforms: Gram-negative, non-sporing rods capable of fermenting lactose with gas and acid production at \(44.0^\circ\text{C} \pm 0.5^\circ\text{C}\) within 24 hours.
  • *Escherichia coli* (Definitive Faecal Indicator): Thermotolerant, produces **Indole from tryptophan at \(44^\circ\text{C}\)**, \(\beta\)-glucuronidase positive (MUG assay), and oxidase-negative. Exclusively of human/warm-blooded animal intestinal origin.
  • Faecal Streptococci (Enterococci): *E. faecalis*, *E. faecium*; survive longer than coliforms; confirm faecal pollution in doubtful samples and saline waters.
  • *Clostridium perfringens* Spores: Survive for years; indicate remote or intermittent faecal pollution and breach of filtration.

WHO Drinking Water Guidelines & Risk Classification

Treated / Disinfected Piped Water: Must contain 0 Faecal Coliforms / 0 *E. coli* per \(100\ \text{mL}\).

Faecal Coliform Count / 100 mL Risk Classification Category Required Public Health Action
0 CFU / 100 mL Conformity / Excellent Safe for drinking; maintain routine monitoring.
1 – 10 CFU / 100 mL Low Health Risk Investigate sanitary defects; chlorinate.
10 – 100 CFU / 100 mL Intermediate Risk Urgent sanitary repair; boil/chlorinate water.
100 – 1000 CFU / 100 mL High Health Risk Alternative water source needed; emergency disinfection.
> 1000 CFU / 100 mL Very High (Gross) Risk Immediate ban on consumption; severe faecal sewage influx.
Sampling SOP Membrane Filtration

3. Sampling Protocols, Chlorine Neutralization & Membrane Filtration SOP

Water Sampling SOP & Thiosulfate Treatment

  • Sampling Bottle: Clean, sterile glass or polypropylene container (\(250–500\ \text{mL}\)).
  • Chlorine Neutralization: For chlorinated supplies, add \(0.1\ \text{mL}\) of \(3\%\ \text{w/v}\) sodium thiosulfate per \(100\ \text{mL}\) of bottle capacity (\(\approx 18\ \text{mg/L}\)) before autoclaving to halt disinfectant action immediately.
  • Tap Sampling: Clean orifice, sterilize by flaming with a spirit lamp until hot, turn on tap at medium flow for 1–2 minutes to clear service line, and fill bottle leaving air space.
  • Open Source Sampling: Hold bottle base, submerge downward \(20–30\ \text{cm}\) below surface, turn mouth upstream against current.
  • Transport: Transport on melting ice in an insulated container; process within 6 hours (max 24 h).

Membrane Filtration Technique SOP

  1. Apparatus & Filter: Sterile filtration assembly fitted with a \(0.45\ \mu\text{m}\) pore size, \(47\ \text{mm}\) grid membrane filter (grid-side uppermost).
  2. Filtration: Filter precisely **\(100\ \text{mL}\)** of well-mixed water under gentle manual/vacuum suction.
  3. Broth Pad Placement: Transfer membrane aseptically onto an absorbent pad saturated with **Membrane Lauryl Sulfate Broth (MLSB)** or MacConkey membrane broth in an aluminum Petri dish (ensure zero air bubbles).
  4. Resuscitation & Incubation: Resuscitate at \(30–35^\circ\text{C}\) for 4 h (or \(25–30^\circ\text{C}\) for 2 h) to recover stressed coliforms; then incubate in water bath at **\(44.0^\circ\text{C} \pm 0.5^\circ\text{C}\)** for **\(14–18\ \text{hours}\)**.
  5. Colony Reading: Count all **yellow lactose-fermenting colonies** (acid turns phenol red indicator yellow). Number of yellow colonies = **Faecal coliforms / \(100\ \text{mL}\)**.
MPN Method DPD Chlorine

4. Multiple Tube Fermentation (MPN) & Free Residual Chlorine DPD Assay

Multiple Tube Fermentation / MPN Matrix

Indispensable for turbid waters that clog \(0.45\ \mu\text{m}\) membranes:

  • Presumptive Phase (MacConkey / Lauryl Tryptose Broth):
    • 1 bottle (\(50\ \text{mL}\) double-strength broth) + \(50\ \text{mL}\) water.
    • 5 bottles (\(10\ \text{mL}\) double-strength broth) + \(10\ \text{mL}\) water each.
    • 5 bottles (\(5\ \text{mL}\) single-strength broth) + \(1\ \text{mL}\) water each.
    • (Total volume tested = \(105\ \text{mL}\)).
  • Incubation & Positive Reaction: Incubate at **\(44.0^\circ\text{C} \pm 0.5^\circ\text{C}\)** for \(24–48\ \text{hours}\). Positive = Color change (purple \(\to\) yellow acid) + **gas filling \(\ge 1/10\) of inverted Durham tube**.
  • MPN Statistical Table: Count number of positive tubes in each volume group (e.g. 1-4-2) and read **Most Probable Number (MPN) of faecal coliforms / \(100\ \text{mL}\)** from McCrady probability tables.
  • Confirmatory Test: Subculture positive tubes to **Brilliant Green Lactose Bile (BGLB)** broth at \(44^\circ\text{C}\) (gas) and **Tryptone water** at \(44^\circ\text{C}\) (add Kovacs reagent \(\to\) red ring confirms indole-positive *E. coli*).

DPD No. 1 Free Residual Chlorine SOP

Measures active disinfectant power in chlorinated piped water supplies:

  • Reagent: DPD No. 1 tablet (\(N,N\)-diethyl-\(p\)-phenylenediamine).
  • Chemical Principle: Free available chlorine (\(\text{HOCl} + \text{OCl}^-\)) immediately oxidizes DPD to form a **red-violet semiquinoid dye** in proportion to chlorine concentration.
  • Comparator Reading: Place cell in Lovibond visual comparator, rotate disc against blank cell, match color within 1 minute, and record free chlorine in **\(\text{mg/L}\) (ppm)**.
  • Target Standard: \(0.2–0.5\ \text{mg/L}\) free residual chlorine at point of delivery (and \(\ge 0.5\ \text{mg/L}\) during cholera/typhoid epidemics).
  • Safety Rule: Water containing \(\ge 0.2\ \text{mg/L}\) free chlorine with turbidity \(<5\ \text{NTU}\) is safe; bacterial culture is not needed.
Board Examination Section 8 Active Interactive MCQs

Section 7.17 Board Review Questions (MCQ 481 – 488)

Test your mastery of Bradley water-disease classifications, faecal coliform 44°C biology, membrane filtration SOPs, MPN tables, and DPD chlorine assays:

MCQ 481 • Bradley Classification of Water-Related Diseases
Under the Bradley classification of water-related diseases, what defines a water-washed (water-scarce) infection (such as Trachoma or Scabies), and what is the primary public health intervention required to control it?
A Ingestion of pathogenic bacteria in water; controlled solely by boiling drinking water.
B Infections caused by insufficient volume of water available for personal hygiene and washing; controlled by increasing the quantity and accessibility of water regardless of microbiological purity.
C Infection caused by cercariae penetrating human skin during swimming in snail-infested rivers.
D Diseases transmitted exclusively by mosquitoes breeding in fast-flowing river rapids.
Correct Answer: B — Infections caused by lack of water for washing; controlled by increasing water quantity and accessibility. Water-washed diseases (trachoma, scabies, conjunctivitis, louse-borne typhus) thrive when water supplies are scarce or distant, preventing regular bathing and facial cleansing. The remedy is providing copious quantities of easily accessible water for domestic hygiene, rather than focusing purely on drinking water purification.
MCQ 482 • Faecal Coliform & *E. coli* Microbiological Definition
What physiological and biochemical criteria define Thermotolerant (Faecal) Coliforms / *Escherichia coli* as the premier indicators of recent faecal contamination in drinking water?
A Gram-negative, non-sporing rods capable of fermenting lactose with gas and acid production at \(44.0^\circ\text{C} \pm 0.5^\circ\text{C}\) within 24 hours, and producing indole from tryptophan at \(44^\circ\text{C}\).
B Spore-forming anaerobic rods that reduce sulfite at \(20^\circ\text{C}\).
C Gram-positive cocci in chains that grow in \(10\%\ \text{NaCl}\) at \(55^\circ\text{C}\).
D Strictly aerobic micrococci that ferment glucose without gas.
Correct Answer: A — Lactose fermentation with gas/acid at \(44.0^\circ\text{C}\) and indole production at \(44^\circ\text{C}\). Total coliforms ferment lactose at \(35–37^\circ\text{C}\), but include environmental non-faecal species. Incubation at the elevated thermotolerant temperature of \(44.0^\circ\text{C} \pm 0.5^\circ\text{C}\) restricts growth specifically to enteric coliforms of human and warm-blooded animal intestinal origin (*E. coli*), which additionally produce indole from tryptophan.
MCQ 483 • WHO Microbiological Drinking Water Standard
According to the World Health Organization (WHO) Guidelines for Drinking-Water Quality, what is the mandatory bacteriological limit for Faecal Coliforms / *E. coli* in treated piped drinking water supplies?
A \(\le 50\ \text{CFU} / 100\ \text{mL}\)
B \(\le 10\ \text{CFU} / 100\ \text{mL}\)
C Zero (0) Faecal Coliforms / 0 *E. coli* per \(100\ \text{mL}\) of water sample
D \(\le 100\ \text{CFU} / 100\ \text{mL}\) as long as chlorine is absent
Correct Answer: C — Zero (0) Faecal Coliforms / 0 *E. coli* per 100 mL. For all treated or piped drinking water entering the distribution system, WHO guidelines mandate complete absence of faecal coliforms (0 per \(100\ \text{mL}\)). Any detection of *E. coli* indicates treatment breakdown, distribution pipe breach, or sewage cross-contamination requiring immediate investigation and corrective re-chlorination.
MCQ 484 • Sodium Thiosulfate Chlorine Neutralization in Sampling
Why must sodium thiosulfate (\(0.1\ \text{mL}\) of \(3\%\ \text{w/v}\) per \(100\ \text{mL}\) bottle\)) be added to sterile sample bottles before collecting chlorinated water for bacteriological testing?
A To provide a sulfur carbon energy source for coliform multiplication.
B To prevent the water sample from freezing during ice transport.
C To stain bacterial flagella yellow for rapid darkfield microscopy.
D To instantly neutralize free residual chlorine and chloramines upon sample collection, preventing the ongoing killing of bacteria during transport to the laboratory.
Correct Answer: D — Neutralizes free residual chlorine, preventing ongoing bactericidal action during transit. If chlorinated water is bottled without sodium thiosulfate, residual chlorine will continue to disinfect the sample in transit, killing any surviving indicator bacteria and yielding a falsely sterile laboratory report. Sodium thiosulfate instantly reduces free chlorine to harmless chloride ions.
MCQ 485 • Membrane Filtration Technique Parameters
In the standard membrane filtration method for water bacteriology, what are the specifications of the membrane filter, the culture medium, and the incubation temperature used to enumerate faecal coliforms?
A \(5.0\ \mu\text{m}\) paper filter; Nutrient agar; \(25^\circ\text{C}\) for 72 hours.
B Sterile \(0.45\ \mu\text{m}\) pore size, \(47\ \text{mm}\) grid membrane; Membrane Lauryl Sulfate Broth (MLSB); incubated at \(44.0^\circ\text{C} \pm 0.5^\circ\text{C}\) for \(14–18\ \text{hours}\) (counting yellow lactose-fermenting colonies).
C \(0.1\ \mu\text{m}\) glass fiber filter; Blood agar; \(37^\circ\text{C}\) with \(10\%\ \text{CO}_2\).
D \(10\ \mu\text{m}\) nylon mesh; Peptone water; \(100^\circ\text{C}\) boiling water.
Correct Answer: B — 0.45 μm pore size, 47 mm grid membrane; MLSB medium; 44.0°C incubation for yellow colonies. The \(0.45\ \mu\text{m}\) cellulose ester membrane retains all bacterial cells on its upper grid surface. Placed on an absorbent pad soaked in Membrane Lauryl Sulfate Broth (which contains phenol red indicator and sodium lauryl sulfate to suppress non-coliforms) and incubated at \(44.0^\circ\text{C}\), faecal coliforms form distinct, easily countable yellow colonies.
MCQ 486 • Multiple Tube Fermentation / MPN Principle
Why is the Multiple Tube / Most Probable Number (MPN) technique preferred over membrane filtration for highly turbid water samples, and what constitutes a positive presumptive tube?
A Turbid water clogs \(0.45\ \mu\text{m}\) membrane pores; a positive presumptive reaction consists of acid production (purple MacConkey broth turning yellow) plus gas occupying \(\ge 1/10\) of the inverted Durham tube within 24–48 h at \(44^\circ\text{C}\).
B MPN is used because membranes cannot filter viruses; positive reaction is blackening of iron agar.
C MPN requires zero incubation; positive reaction is immediate precipitation of calcium.
D Turbidity destroys culture broth; positive reaction is complete evaporation of water.
Correct Answer: A — Suspended solids clog 0.45 μm membranes; positive tube shows acid (yellow) + gas in Durham tube. Particulate matter in river/pond water rapidly blocks membrane filters before \(100\ \text{mL}\) can pass through. The multiple tube method inoculates water directly into tubes of double- and single-strength MacConkey broth. Lactose fermentation generates acid (yellow color) and gas trapped in the inner Durham tube, allowing statistical estimation of the MPN via McCrady tables.
MCQ 487 • Confirmatory Tests for *E. coli* in Water Testing
Which two media and biochemical reactions are used in the confirmatory and completed phases of water testing to verify that gas-positive MPN broth tubes contain genuine thermotolerant *Escherichia coli*?
A TCBS agar (yellow colonies) and Urea broth (pink color).
B Lowenstein-Jensen slope (rough buff colonies) and Ziehl-Neelsen stain.
C Brilliant Green Lactose Bile (BGLB) broth at \(44.0^\circ\text{C}\) (gas production) and Tryptone water at \(44.0^\circ\text{C}\) (indole production confirmed by red surface ring upon adding Kovacs reagent).
D Cetrimide agar (pyocyanin pigment) and Oxidase strip (purple color).
Correct Answer: C — BGLB broth (gas at 44°C) and Tryptone water (indole red ring with Kovacs at 44°C). Brilliant Green and bile salts in BGLB inhibit non-coliforms while confirming thermotolerant lactose fermentation with gas. Tryptone water contains rich tryptophan; *E. coli* possesses tryptophanase, cleaving tryptophan to indole at \(44.0^\circ\text{C}\), which reacts with *p*-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde in Kovacs reagent to form a characteristic cherry-red surface ring.
MCQ 488 • DPD Free Residual Chlorine Assay
What is the target concentration range for free residual chlorine in municipal drinking water, and what color reaction occurs when a DPD No. 1 tablet is dissolved in water containing active hypochlorous acid (\(\text{HOCl}\))?
A \(10–20\ \text{mg/L}\); turns bright green.
B \(0.01\ \text{mg/L}\); turns deep navy blue.
C \(5.0–10.0\ \text{mg/L}\); forms a black precipitate.
D \(0.2–0.5\ \text{mg/L}\) (and \(\ge 0.5\ \text{mg/L}\) during epidemics); DPD No. 1 is instantly oxidized by free chlorine to form a red-violet color whose intensity is measured in a Lovibond comparator.
Correct Answer: D — 0.2–0.5 mg/L; DPD No. 1 forms a red-violet color in Lovibond comparator. Maintaining \(0.2–0.5\ \text{mg/L}\) (\(\text{ppm}\)) of free residual chlorine ensures that any pathogens introduced downstream in the pipe network are inactivated within 30 minutes of contact. DPD (\(N,N\)-diethyl-\(p\)-phenylenediamine) reacts specifically with free chlorine to form a proportional red-violet semiquinoid meriquinone dye measured visually against calibrated comparator discs.

7.18 Diagnostic Compendium of Bacterial, Fungal & Viral Pathogens

The Comprehensive Monica Cheesbrough Diagnostic Compendium • Systematic Master Identification Matrices: Gram-Positive Cocci (*S. aureus*, *S. pyogenes*, *S. agalactiae*, *S. pneumoniae*, *Enterococcus*) • Spore-Forming & Toxigenic Bacilli (*B. anthracis*, *C. perfringens*, *C. tetani*, *C. diphtheriae*, *Listeria*) • Fastidious Cocci & Bacilli (*Neisseria*, *Haemophilus*, *Bordetella*, *Brucella*) • Enterobacteriaceae Differential Diagnostic Battery (*Salmonella*, *Shigella*, *E. coli*, *Klebsiella*, *Proteus*, *Yersinia*) • Non-Fermenters & Vibrios (*P. aeruginosa*, *V. cholerae*, *Campylobacter*) • Mycobacteriology (*M. tuberculosis*, *M. leprae*, *M. ulcerans*) • Spirochaetales (*Treponema*, *Borrelia*, *Leptospira*) • Medical Mycology & Virological Markers.

Monica Cheesbrough Diagnostic Golden Rule: Precise microbiological identification combines morphological grouping, selective cultural characteristics, and definitive biochemical markers. Core differential dichotomies: (1) Staphylococcus vs Streptococcus (Catalase \(+ / -\)), (2) *S. pneumoniae* vs *Viridans* (Optochin Sensitive • Bile Soluble vs Resistant/Insoluble), (3) Enterobacteriaceae vs *Pseudomonas*/*Vibrio* (Oxidase Negative vs Positive), (4) *Salmonella* vs *Shigella* (Motile, \(H_2S+\), LDC+ vs Non-motile, \(H_2S-\), LDC-), (5) *M. tuberculosis* vs NTM (Niacin+, Nitrate+, cord factor, slow buff growth).
