Gram-Positive Cocci Catalase & Hemolysis

1. Systematic Identification of Medically Important Gram-Positive Cocci

Pathogen Organism Cell Morphology & Gram Stain Colonial Features & Hemolysis Key Diagnostic Reactions & Virulence Markers Major Clinical Diseases
Staphylococcus aureus Gram-positive cocci in grape-like irregular clusters (\(0.8–1.0\ \mu\text{m}\)). Golden-yellow (staphyloxanthin) colonies; **Beta-hemolytic** on blood agar. • Catalase Positive, Coagulase Positive (tube & slide).
• Ferments Mannitol (yellow on MSA), DNAse+, Protein A+.
• Toxins: Enterotoxins A–E (food poisoning), TSST-1, Exfoliatin (SSSS). 		Boils, carbuncles, osteomyelitis, acute endocarditis, scalded skin syndrome, toxic shock syndrome.
Coagulase-Negative Staphylococci (CoNS) Gram-positive cocci in clusters. White/porcelain colonies; usually non-hemolytic. • Catalase Positive, Coagulase Negative.
• S. epidermidis: Novobiocin Sensitive (\(\ge 16\ \text{mm}\)); biofilm/slime.
• S. saprophyticus: Novobiocin Resistant (\(<16\ \text{mm}\)). 		*S. epidermidis*: Prosthetic valve & catheter sepsis.
*S. saprophyticus*: Primary UTI in sexually active young women.
Streptococcus pyogenes (GAS / Group A) Gram-positive cocci in pairs and long chains. Small pin-point colonies with a wide, clear zone of **Beta-hemolysis**. • Catalase Negative, Bacitracin Sensitive (\(0.04\ \text{U}\) disc).
• PYR Test Positive; Lancefield Group A serogrouping.
• Antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer \(>200\ \text{IU/mL}\). 		Streptococcal pharyngitis, scarlet fever, erysipelas, impetigo, necrotizing fasciitis, Rheumatic Fever, Post-streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN).
Streptococcus agalactiae (GBS / Group B) Gram-positive cocci in short to medium chains. Slightly larger grayish-white colonies; narrow zone of **Beta-hemolysis**. • Catalase Negative, CAMP Test Positive (arrowhead hemolysis with *S. aureus* beta-lysin).
• Hippurate Hydrolysis Positive (deep purple with ninhydrin).
• Bacitracin resistant; PYR negative. 		Neonatal sepsis, neonatal meningitis, postpartum endometritis, diabetic foot infections.
Streptococcus pneumoniae (Pneumococcus) Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci (in pairs, pointed outer ends). Small flattened, indented / **"draughtsman" colonies** surrounded by greenish **Alpha-hemolysis** (autolysis). • Catalase Negative, Optochin Sensitive (\(5\ \mu\text{g}\) disc zone \(\ge 14\ \text{mm}\)).
• Bile Soluble (lysed within 15 min by \(10\%\) sodium deoxycholate).
• Quellung capsular swelling reaction with specific anticapsular sera. 		Lobar pneumonia, bacterial meningitis, otitis media, acute sinusitis, occult bacteremia in infants.
Viridans Streptococci (*S. mutans*, *S. mitis*) Gram-positive cocci in chains. Small colonies with **Alpha-hemolysis** (greenish discoloration). • Catalase Negative, Optochin Resistant (zone \(<14\ \text{mm}\)).
• Bile Insoluble (does not lyse in sodium deoxycholate).
• Dextran synthesis from sucrose (dental plaque adhesion). 		Subacute bacterial endocarditis (SBE) on damaged valves, dental caries.
Enterococcus faecalis & E. faecium (Group D) Gram-positive cocci in pairs and short chains (ovoid). Non-hemolytic (gamma) or alpha-hemolytic. • Bile Esculin Positive (hydrolyzes esculin forming black iron complex).
• Grows in **\(6.5\%\ \text{NaCl}\) broth** and at **\(45^\circ\text{C}\)**.
• PYR Positive; intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins; VRE (*vanA/vanB*). 		Nosocomial UTIs, bacteremia, intra-abdominal sepsis, endocarditis.
Toxigenic Bacilli Spores & Toxins

2. Aerobic & Anaerobic Spore-Forming and Non-Spore-Forming Bacilli

Pathogen Morphology & Staining Culture & Biochemical Signatures Pathogenicity & Diagnostic Hallmarks
Bacillus anthracis Large square-ended Gram-positive rods in long chains ("bamboo stick"); central/subterminal spores (in soil, never in living tissue); non-motile. • **Non-hemolytic**, rough grey-white **"Medusa-head" colonies** (curled hair edges).
• String-of-pearls reaction: Rounded balloon cells on nutrient agar with \(0.05–0.5\ \text{U/mL}\) penicillin.
• Inverted fir-tree liquefaction in gelatin stab; poly-D-glutamic acid capsule. 		• Cutaneous Anthrax: Malignant pustule with painless central black necrotic eschar.
• Inhalation (Woolsorter's) & GI Anthrax: Severe hemorrhagic mediastinitis; McFadyean capsule reaction.
Corynebacterium diphtheriae Gram-positive pleomorphic slender rods with swollen clubbed ends; arranged in **palisades / Chinese letters / V & L shapes**. • **Albert / Neisser Staining:** Blue-black volutin (metachromatic / polyphosphate) granules against green/yellow cytoplasm.
• **Loeffler Serum Slope:** Rapid 12–18 h growth.
• **Hoyle / Tellurite Agar:** Black/grey colonies (potassium tellurite reduction).
• **Elek Immunodiffusion Test:** Filter paper soaked in diphtheria antitoxin precipitates with exotoxin (white precipitin lines at \(45^\circ\)). 		• Diphtheria: Tough, leathery, adherent grey-white **pseudomembrane** over tonsils/pharynx (bleeds upon scraping).
• Diphtheria toxin (AB toxin inhibits EF-2 / protein synthesis), causing myocarditis, bull-neck lymphadenopathy, and peripheral neuropathy.
Listeria monocytogenes Small Gram-positive coccobacilli in pairs/short chains (resembles diphtheroids). • Narrow zone of beta-hemolysis on blood agar; **CAMP Test Positive** with *S. aureus*.
• **Tumbling Motility** in wet mounts and umbrella motility in semi-solid agar at **\(25^\circ\text{C}\)** (non-motile at \(37^\circ\text{C}\)).
• **Cold enrichment at \(4^\circ\text{C}\)**; catalase positive, bile esculin positive. 		Neonatal granulomatosis infantiseptica, neonatal meningitis, sepsis in pregnancy, foodborne infection from unpasteurized dairy/delicatessen meats.
Clostridium perfringens Large, blunt-ended, encapsulated Gram-positive rod; subterminal spores rarely seen in clinical specimens; strictly anaerobic; non-motile. • **Double Zone of Beta-Hemolysis** (inner theta-toxin, outer alpha-toxin).
• Nagler Reaction (Egg Yolk Agar): Alpha-toxin (lecithinase C) causes opalescence around growth, completely inhibited on the side containing *C. perfringens* anti-alpha-toxin.
• **Stormy Fermentation** in litmus milk (acid + clot ripped by violent gas). 		Gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis), clostridial food poisoning (enterotoxin), enteritis necroticans (pigbel caused by Type C beta-toxin).
Clostridium tetani Slender Gram-positive anaerobic rod; developing round **terminal spores** giving a classic **"drumstick / tennis racquet"** appearance; highly motile. • Delicate, translucent swarming film over anaerobic blood agar.
• Gelatin liquefaction positive; indole positive. 		• **Tetanus:** Tetanospasmin neurotoxin retrograde axonal transport blocks inhibitory neurotransmitter (GABA / Glycine) release from Renshaw cells.
• Spastic paralysis, trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus, opisthotonos.
Clostridium botulinum Gram-positive anaerobic rod with oval subterminal spores. Lipase positive on egg yolk agar (pearly iridescent film); anaerobic culture. • **Botulism:** Botulinum neurotoxin blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction \(\to\) symmetrical descending **flaccid paralysis**.
• Foodborne (canned foods), infant botulism (honey spores), wound botulism.

Bacterial Genus / Species MacConkey Agar XLD / EMB Agar Motility Biochemical Signatures (TSI / IMViC / Urease / Oxidase) Key Clinical Pathology
Escherichia coli Lactose Fermenter (LF: Smooth pink-red colonies with precipitated bile). Metallic green sheen on EMB; Yellow on XLD. Motile (peritrichous). • Oxidase Negative, Catalase Positive.
• **IMViC:** \(++--\) (Indole+, MR+, VP-, Citrate-).
• **TSI:** \(A/A\) + Gas, \(H_2S\) negative; LDC positive. 		UTIs, neonatal meningitis (K1 capsule), gastroenteritis (ETEC, EPEC, EIEC, EAEC, EHEC O157:H7 / HUS).

• **TSI (NTS):** \(K/A\) + Gas + \(H_2S\) (blackening).
• **TSI (*S.* Typhi):** \(K/A\), **no gas**, trace \(H_2S\) ring; Vi antigen+. 		Enteric (typhoid/paratyphoid) fever, invasive NTS gastroenteritis, osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease.
Shigella (*S. dysenteriae*, *S. flexneri*, *S. boydii*, *S. sonnei*) NLF (Pale, colorless); *S. sonnei* is a late LF. **XLD:** Pure red/pink colonies (no blackening, \(H_2S\) negative). Non-Motile. • **Oxidase Negative**; Urease Negative; **LDC Negative**.
• **TSI:** \(K/A\), **no gas (anaerogenic)**, **\(H_2S\) negative**.
• Extremely low infectious dose (\(10–100\) bacilli). 		Bacillary dysentery (mucus, pus, and blood in stool, severe tenesmus), Shiga toxin hemolytic uremic syndrome.
Klebsiella pneumoniae LF: Large, mucoid, dome-shaped, stringy pink colonies. Mucoid pink-purple on EMB (no metallic sheen). Non-Motile. • **Oxidase Negative**; **IMViC:** \(--++\) (Indole-, MR-, VP+, Citrate+).
• **TSI:** \(A/A\) + Profuse Gas; **Urease Positive (slow)**.
• Large polysaccharide capsule (string test positive \(\ge 5\ \text{mm}\)). 		Friedländer's pneumonia with thick, blood-tinged **"currant-jelly sputum"**, lung cavitation, hospital-acquired UTIs and bacteremia.
Proteus (*P. mirabilis*, *P. vulgaris*) NLF (Pale colonies; swarming inhibited on MacConkey by bile). Swarming in concentric waves on blood agar (prevented by CLED). Hyper-Motile (Swarming). • Rapid Urease Positive (splits urea to ammonia in minutes, turning Christensen urea bright pink).
• **PAD Positive** (Phenylalanine deaminase \(\to\) green with \(10\%\ \text{FeCl}_3\)).
• \(H_2S\) Positive; *P. mirabilis* Indole-, *P. vulgaris* Indole+. 		Complicated UTIs, formation of alkaline **struvite (staghorn) calculi** (\(\text{MgNH}_4\text{PO}_4\)), wound infections.
Vibrio cholerae (O1 & O139) NLF (Pale on MacConkey). **TCBS Agar:** Large, smooth, glistening **yellow colonies** (sucrose fermentation). Darting "Shooting-Star" Motility (single polar flagellum). • Oxidase Positive; Catalase Positive.
• Grows in Alkaline Peptone Water (\(\text{pH}\ 8.6\)).
• **String Test Positive** in \(0.5\%\) sodium deoxycholate. 		Epidemic Cholera: Profuse watery **"rice-water stools"**, fatal dehydration within hours (Cholera toxin activates Gs \(\to\) cAMP \(\to\) massive \(\text{Cl}^-\) secretion).
Pseudomonas aeruginosa NLF (Pale, irregular, flat colonies with serrated margins). Cetrimide agar: Blue-green pigmented colonies. Motile (polar flagella). • Oxidase Positive, Catalase Positive, Strict Aerobe (non-fermenter).
• **Pigments:** **Pyocyanin (blue-green)** & **Pyoverdine (fluorescent yellow-green)**.
• Sweet, fruity, **grape-like / corn-tortilla odor** (aminoacetophenone). 		Burn wound sepsis, ventilator-associated pneumonia in CF, ecthyma gangrenosum, malignant otitis externa, hot tub folliculitis.
Yersinia pestis NLF (Pinpoint colonies at 24 h). CIN agar: "Bull's-eye" colonies (deep red center with translucent border). Non-Motile at all temperatures. • **Safety-pin Bipolar Staining** with Wayson / Giemsa stain.
• "Stalactite" growth in broth hanging from oil droplet layer. 		Bubonic plague (painful inguinal/axillary buboes), pneumonic plague, septicemic plague (black death DIC).
Mycobacteria & Fastidious Spirochaetes & Fungi

4. Fastidious Pathogens, Mycobacteria, Spirochaetes & Medical Mycology

Fastidious & Zoonotic Pathogens

  • Haemophilus influenzae: Pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacilli; requires **Factor X (hemin)** and **Factor V (NAD)** for growth; demonstrates **Satellitism** (grows as larger satellite colonies around *S. aureus* streak on blood agar); capsular type b (Hib) causes infant epiglottitis and meningitis.
  • Haemophilus ducreyi: Causes **Chancroid** (painful genital ulcer with ragged undermined edges and fluctuant bubo); Gram smear reveals tiny rods in parallel chains (**"school of fish" / "railroad tracks"**).
  • Bordetella pertussis: Whooping cough; requires **Regan-Lowe or Bordet-Gengou medium**; colonies appear as tiny, shiny, domed **"drops of mercury / bisected pearls"** surrounded by a hazy hemolytic zone.
  • Brucella species (*B. melitensis*, *B. abortus*): Undulant fever; intracellular; oxidase+, catalase+, rapid urease+; requires 4-week Castaneda diphasic incubation in \(5–10\%\ \text{CO}_2\); severe BSL-3 laboratory biohazard.

Mycobacteriology & Spirochaetales

  • Mycobacterium tuberculosis: Slender, curved, beaded acid-fast bacilli (ZN / Auramine-O); **Cord Factor** (trehalose dimycolate causes serpentine cording); slow growth (\(3–6\ \text{weeks}\) at \(37^\circ\text{C}\)) on **Lowenstein-Jensen (LJ) medium** producing rough, dry, crumbly, cream/buff **"cauliflower" colonies**; **Niacin Positive**, **Nitrate Reduction Positive**, Catalase negative at \(68^\circ\text{C}\).
  • Mycobacterium leprae: Leprosy (Hansen's disease); obligate intracellular; non-culturable on cell-free media; infects Schwann cells and macrophages; modified ZN / Fite-Faraco stain reveals intracellular **globi ("cigar-packet" bundles)** in Virchow foamy lepra cells.
  • Treponema pallidum subsp. pallidum: Syphilis; delicate slender spirochaete with regular tight coils; actively motile with **corkscrew rotation and flexion** on Dark-field microscopy; diagnosed serologically by non-treponemal (VDRL, RPR) and treponemal (TPHA, FTA-ABS) tests.
  • Borrelia recurrentis: Epidemic louse-borne relapsing fever; loose, irregular coils easily visible on **Giemsa- or Wright-stained peripheral blood thick/thin films**.
  • Leptospira interrogans: Leptospirosis (Weil disease); very tightly coiled spirochaete with **hooked / question-mark ends**; active spinning motility on darkfield; cultured in EMJH / Fletcher medium.

Key Medical Mycology Diagnostic Markers

  • Candida albicans: Oval budding yeast (\(3–5\ \mu\text{m}\)); produces **Germ Tubes** within 2–3 h in human serum at \(37^\circ\text{C}\); forms thick-walled **Chlamydospores** on cornmeal-Tween 80 agar.
  • Cryptococcus neoformans: Round encapsulated budding yeast; highlighted by **India Ink negative staining** (clear halo of wide mucopolysaccharide capsule against dark background); **Urease Positive**; produces brown-black melanin on Niger seed (birdseed) agar.
  • Histoplasma capsulatum: Thermal dimorphic fungus; yeast phase at \(37^\circ\text{C}\) (small intracellular yeasts inside histiocytes/macrophages); mould phase at \(25^\circ\text{C}\) with **large, tuberculate (knobby) macroconidia**.
  • Dermatophytes: *Trichophyton* (pencil-shaped micro/macroconidia), *Microsporum* (spindle-shaped, rough, thick-walled macroconidia), *Epidermophyton* (club-shaped/beaver-tail smooth macroconidia, no microconidia).

Atypical Bacteria & Viral Diagnostics

  • Chlamydia trachomatis: Obligate intracellular; biphasic lifecycle (small infectious extracellular **Elementary Body [EB]** vs larger intracellular metabolically active **Reticulate Body [RB]**); inclusion bodies stain brown with Lugol's iodine (glycogen matrix).
  • Mycoplasma pneumoniae: Completely **lacks a peptidoglycan cell wall** (unaffected by penicillins/cephalosporins; bounded by sterol-containing membrane); tiny colonies with a **"fried-egg" appearance**; cold agglutinins (\(\text{IgM}\) autoantibodies).
  • Hepatitis Viruses: HAV/HEV (faecal-oral RNA); HBV (DNA hepadnavirus, HBsAg marker, HBeAg active replication, anti-HBc \(\text{IgM}\) window period); HCV (parenteral/sexual, anti-HCV screening + viral RNA PCR).
  • HIV Diagnostics: Dual rapid antibody/antigen tests (screening + confirmatory algorithm), p24 core antigen detection in early acute seroconversion, CD4 T-cell enumeration (FACS/Dynabeads) for staging.

Section 7.18 Board Review Questions (MCQ 489 – 496)

Test your comprehensive mastery of the Monica Cheesbrough Diagnostic Pathogen Compendium:

MCQ 489 • Gram-Positive Cocci Identification Battery
An alpha-hemolytic, Gram-positive diplococcus is isolated from the sputum of a patient with lobar pneumonia. Which two diagnostic tests definitively differentiate Streptococcus pneumoniae from commensal Viridans streptococci?
A Catalase test and Coagulase test.
B Optochin susceptibility disc test (\(5\ \mu\text{g}\) disc zone \(\ge 14\ \text{mm}\)) and Bile Solubility test (complete lysis by \(10\%\) sodium deoxycholate).
C Bacitracin sensitivity and CAMP test.
D Growth in \(6.5\%\ \text{NaCl}\) and PYR test.
Correct Answer: B — Optochin sensitive (\(\ge 14\ \text{mm}\)) and bile soluble. Both *S. pneumoniae* and *Viridans streptococci* produce alpha-hemolysis on blood agar. *Streptococcus pneumoniae* is selectively inhibited by ethylhydrocupreine hydrochloride (Optochin zone \(\ge 14\ \text{mm}\)) and undergoes rapid autolysis in the presence of bile salts (sodium deoxycholate), whereas *Viridans* streptococci are optochin resistant (zone \(<14\ \text{mm}\)) and bile insoluble.
MCQ 490 • *Bacillus anthracis* Diagnostic Triad
Which triad of cultural, physiological, and microscopic characteristics definitively identifies Bacillus anthracis and distinguishes it from saprophytic Bacillus cereus?
A Non-motile, non-hemolytic on blood agar, rough grey-white "Medusa-head" colonies, positive "string-of-pearls" reaction on penicillin agar, and poly-D-glutamic acid capsule.
B Highly motile with peritrichous flagella, strongly beta-hemolytic, smooth yellow colonies.
C Obligate anaerobe, terminal drumstick spores, swarming growth across the entire plate.
D Catalase negative, oxidase positive, acid-fast rods that ferment lactose within 2 hours.
Correct Answer: A — Non-motile, non-hemolytic, Medusa-head colonies, string-of-pearls positive. *Bacillus anthracis* is distinguished from common motile, beta-hemolytic environmental bacilli (*B. cereus*) by its lack of motility, absence of hemolysis on sheep blood agar, characteristic tangled hair ("Medusa-head") colony edges, susceptibility to low-dose penicillin forming rounded spheroplasts resembling a string of pearls, and distinctive polypeptide (poly-D-glutamic acid) capsule.
MCQ 491 • *Neisseria* Carbohydrate Utilization Matrix
How are pathogenic Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae differentiated biochemically in Cystine Trypticase Agar (CTA) carbohydrate utilization tests?
A *N. meningitidis* ferments lactose only; *N. gonorrhoeae* ferments sucrose only.
B Both species ferment glucose, maltose, lactose, and sucrose with abundant gas.
C *N. meningitidis* oxidizes both Glucose and Maltose (Mnemonic: Meningitidis = Maltose + Men); *N. gonorrhoeae* oxidizes Glucose ONLY (Mnemonic: Gonorrhoeae = Glucose only).
D *N. gonorrhoeae* is asaccharolytic (oxidizes no sugars); *N. meningitidis* ferments mannitol.
Correct Answer: C — *N. meningitidis* oxidizes Glucose and Maltose; *N. gonorrhoeae* oxidizes Glucose only. Both organisms are Gram-negative diplococci, catalase positive, and oxidase positive. In CTA sugar media, *N. meningitidis* produces acid from Glucose and Maltose (neither utilizes lactose or sucrose), while *N. gonorrhoeae* produces acid from Glucose alone.
MCQ 492 • Enterobacteriaceae Differential Diagnostic Battery
Which laboratory profile correctly differentiates Salmonella from Shigella on Xylose Lysine Deoxycholate (XLD) agar and in motility/biochemical tests?
A *Salmonella* is non-motile and forms yellow colonies; *Shigella* is motile and black.
B Both are rapid lactose fermenters that turn Christensen urea agar magenta.
C *Salmonella* is oxidase positive and LDC negative; *Shigella* is oxidase negative and LDC positive.
D *Salmonella* is motile, Lysine Decarboxylase (LDC) positive, produces \(H_2S\) (red colonies with black centers on XLD); *Shigella* is non-motile, LDC negative, \(H_2S\) negative (plain red/translucent colonies on XLD).
Correct Answer: D — *Salmonella* is motile, LDC+, \(H_2S+\) (black centers); *Shigella* is non-motile, LDC-, \(H_2S-\). On XLD agar, both organisms are non-lactose fermenters. *Salmonella* ferments xylose, decarboxylates lysine (reverting the medium to red/purple), and produces \(H_2S\) (black iron sulfide precipitate). *Shigella* does not decarboxylate lysine, does not produce \(H_2S\), and lacks flagellar motility.
MCQ 493 • *Vibrio cholerae* vs *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* Non-Enteric Gram-Negatives
What key cultural features identify Vibrio cholerae on Thiosulfate-Citrate-Bile Salts-Sucrose (TCBS) agar and Pseudomonas aeruginosa on nutrient agar?
A *V. cholerae* produces blue-green colonies; *P. aeruginosa* ferments lactose on MacConkey with gas.
B *V. cholerae* forms large, glistening yellow colonies on TCBS (sucrose fermentation) and is string test positive; *P. aeruginosa* produces pyocyanin (blue-green pigment), pyoverdine, and a sweet grape-like / tortilla odor.
C *V. cholerae* is strictly anaerobic; *P. aeruginosa* is a Gram-positive spore-former.
D Both organisms are oxidase-negative coliforms that grow only in milk.
Correct Answer: B — *V. cholerae* forms yellow colonies on TCBS; *P. aeruginosa* produces pyocyanin and grape-like odor. *Vibrio cholerae* is an oxidase-positive, comma-shaped rod that ferments sucrose on selective TCBS agar, turning bromothymol blue indicator yellow, and lyses in sodium deoxycholate to form a viscous string. *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* is an oxidase-positive non-fermenter characterized by blue-green pyocyanin pigment and a distinctive grape-like / corn-tortilla aroma.
MCQ 494 • *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* Cultural & Biochemical Hallmarks
Which combination of growth rate, colonial morphology on Lowenstein-Jensen (LJ) medium, and biochemical markers confirms the identification of Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
A Slow growth (3–6 weeks at \(37^\circ\text{C}\)), rough, dry, crumbly, buff/cream "cauliflower-like" colonies, Niacin test Positive, Nitrate reduction Positive, and Catalase heat-labile (\(68^\circ\text{C}\) negative).
B Rapid growth in 24 hours, smooth bright orange colonies in the dark, Niacin negative.
C Completely unculturable on LJ medium; forms intracellular globi in Schwann cells only.
D Growth at \(45^\circ\text{C}\) on MacConkey agar; urease negative and oxidase positive.
Correct Answer: A — Slow growth (3–6 weeks), rough buff colonies, Niacin+, Nitrate+, heat-labile catalase. *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* is a slow-growing eugonic mycobacterium. Its rough, non-pigmented (buff-colored) "breadcrumb / cauliflower" colonies on egg-based LJ medium are distinctively positive for niacin accumulation (lacks the enzyme to convert niacin to niacin ribonucleotide) and strongly reduce nitrate to nitrite, confirming speciation within the *M. tuberculosis* complex.
MCQ 495 • Spirochaetal Motility & Staining Characteristics
Match the three major pathogenic spirochaete genera (Treponema, Borrelia, Leptospira) to their distinctive morphological and microscopical diagnostic signatures:
A *Treponema* = straight rods with spores; *Borrelia* = branching filaments; *Leptospira* = diplococci.
B *Treponema* = thick chains in Giemsa; *Borrelia* = unculturable on blood; *Leptospira* = acid-fast beads.
C *Treponema* = regular tight coils with active corkscrew motility on dark-field; *Borrelia* = loose irregular waves visible on Giemsa-stained blood smears; *Leptospira* = very fine tight coils with characteristic hooked/question-mark ends.
D All three spirochaetes are easily Gram-stained and form large yellow colonies on nutrient agar.
Correct Answer: C — *Treponema* (tight coils, darkfield corkscrew), *Borrelia* (loose waves, Giemsa blood smear), *Leptospira* (tight coils, hooked ends). Spirochaetes are too thin for standard brightfield Gram staining. *Treponema pallidum* is visualized via dark-field illumination showing deliberate corkscrew rotation. *Borrelia* species (*B. recurrentis*) are wider and take up Giemsa/Wright stains in blood films. *Leptospira interrogans* features rapid flexion with classic semicircular hooked ends.
MCQ 496 • Medical Mycology Diagnostic Hallmarks
Which diagnostic feature definitively identifies Cryptococcus neoformans in CSF and differentiates it from Candida albicans and other yeast pathogens?
A Forms rapid germ tubes in serum within 2 hours and produces pseudohyphae.
B Acid-fast staining with Ziehl-Neelsen and production of gas from sucrose.
C Highly motile with polar flagella and string test positive.
D Spherical budding yeast surrounded by a wide, gelatinous polysaccharide capsule visible as a prominent clear halo in India ink negative staining; Urease Positive; produces brown-black melanin on birdseed (Niger seed) agar.
Correct Answer: D — Wide polysaccharide capsule in India ink, Urease positive, melanin on birdseed agar. *Cryptococcus neoformans* is an encapsulated opportunistic basidiomycetous yeast. India ink particles are excluded by its thick glucuronoxylomannan capsule, creating a striking wide luminous halo around the spherical yeast cell. It is urease positive (unlike *C. albicans* which is urease negative and germ-tube positive) and synthesizes melanin via phenoloxidase on caffeic acid / Niger seed medium.

8.1 Haematology in District Laboratories & Quality Assurance

Essential Haematological Priorities in Tropical Public Health • Investigation of Anaemias, Malarial Sepsis, Haemoglobinopathies & ART Monitoring • Pre-Analytical Phlebotomy Variables (Tourniquet Stasis, Anticoagulant Ratios, "Milking" Artifacts) • Analytical Controls (Stabilized Whole Blood, Sahli Pipetting, Water-Free Methanol Fixation, Buffer \(\text{pH}\ 6.8\)) • Levey-Jennings Charts & Westgard Quality Control Rules • Post-Analytical Reporting & Critical / Panic Value Alerts.

Monica Cheesbrough Haematology QA Principle: Diagnostic haematology in district laboratories provides critical guidance for managing nutritional anaemias, hemoglobinopathies, severe malaria, and antiretroviral toxicities (e.g. zidovudine-induced severe anaemia). Strict pre-analytical control is paramount: never apply a tourniquet for \(>1\ \text{minute}\) (causes hemoconcentration \(\to\) falsely elevated Hb/PCV), never squeeze or "milk" skin puncture sites (dilutes blood with interstitial fluid \(\to\) falsely low counts), and maintain exact \(1:9\) or \(1:50\) anticoagulant-to-blood ratios to prevent cell shrinkage or microclot formation.

Clinical Scope Pre-Analytical QA

1. District Haematology Spectrum & Pre-Analytical Error Control

Primary Indications in District Health Care

  • Investigation of Anaemias: Nutritional (iron deficiency, folate/B12 megaloblastic), hemolytic (malaria, G6PD deficiency, sickle cell), and anaemia of chronic disease (tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS).
  • Infections & Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO): Leukocytosis, shift to left, toxic granulation, eosinophilia in helminthiasis, atypical lymphocytosis.
  • Haemoglobinopathies: Sickle cell disease (HbSS), sickle trait (HbAS), thalassaemia major/minor.
  • Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) Monitoring: Baseline and routine monitoring of zidovudine (AZT)-induced bone marrow suppression and severe macrocytic anaemia.
  • Early Leukaemia / Myeloma Detection: Recognizing blasts, immature myeloid forms, or rouleaux formation for timely referral to specialist oncology centers.

Pre-Analytical Phlebotomy Pitfalls

  • Tourniquet Hemoconcentration: Applying tourniquet for \(>1\ \text{minute}\) causes fluid transudation into tissue spaces, yielding falsely elevated Hb, PCV, RBC, and total protein.
  • Skin Puncture "Milking": Vigorously squeezing an infant's heel or patient's finger forces interstitial tissue fluid into the sample, causing falsely reduced Hb and cell counts.
  • Anticoagulant Ratio Errors (EDTA \(1.5–2.0\ \text{mg/mL}\)):
    • Underfilling Tube: Excess EDTA exerts hypertonic osmotic pressure, shrinking red cells (falsely lowering PCV and MCV).
    • Overfilling Tube: Insufficient EDTA allows microclots to form, trapping platelets and white cells.
  • Mechanical Hemolysis: Forcing blood through a narrow needle into a tube without removing the needle lyses fragile erythrocytes.
Analytical Stage Statistical QC

2. Analytical Quality Control, Levey-Jennings Charts & SOP Execution

Blood Mixing & Pipetting

  • Sample Re-mixing: Invert anticoagulated blood 10–20 times manually or mix on a mechanical roller mixer for 2–5 minutes before sampling (settled RBCs cause catastrophic counting errors).
  • Outer Tip Wiping: Carefully wipe blood from the outside of pipette tips using clean lint-free tissue without touching the orifice (touching the opening draws fluid out by capillary action).
  • Chipped Pipettes: Discard chipped or etched volumetric pipettes immediately.

Film Fixation & Buffer Control

  • Water-Free Methanol: Thin blood films must be fixed in **pure water-free methanol** within 1–2 hours. Traces of water in methanol cause red cell crenation, water-ring artifacts, and autolysis.
  • Buffer \(\text{pH}\ 6.8\) Standardization: Romanowsky stains (Leishman, Giemsa, Wright) require buffered water at **\(\text{pH}\ 6.8\)**.
    • If \(\text{pH} < 6.8\): Overly acidic \(\to\) cells stain too red/pink.
    • If \(\text{pH} > 6.8\): Overly alkaline \(\to\) cells stain too blue/dark.

Levey-Jennings Control Charts

  • Stabilized Control Blood: Run stabilized whole blood control (2–3 year stability) and hemolysate daily with every batch.
  • Statistical Limits:
    • Mean (\(\bar{X}\)): Centerline.
    • \(\pm 2\text{SD}\) (Warning Limit): \(95.5\%\) of values must fall within \(\pm 2\text{SD}\).
    • \(\pm 3\text{SD}\) (Action Limit): Any single value outside \(\pm 3\text{SD}\) or 2 consecutive values outside \(\pm 2\text{SD}\) requires immediate halt, investigation, and rejection of the analytical run!
Panic Values Reporting SOP

3. Post-Analytical Stage, Reference Ranges & Critical Emergency Alerts

Critical / Panic Value Notification Thresholds

Results indicating an immediate life-threatening physiological emergency requiring immediate telephonic notification to the clinician:

Haematological Parameter Critical / Panic Alert Threshold Immediate Clinical Hazard
Haemoglobin (Hb) \(< 5.0\ \text{g/dL}\) (\(< 50\ \text{g/L}\)) OR \(> 20.0\ \text{g/dL}\) High-output cardiac failure; hyperviscosity stroke.
Platelet Count \(< 20 \times 10^9/\text{L}\) Spontaneous fatal intracranial / internal hemorrhage.
Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC) \(< 0.5 \times 10^9/\text{L}\) (Agranulocytosis) Fulminant septicemia; opportunistic bacteremia.
Total White Blood Cells (WBC) \(> 50 \times 10^9/\text{L}\) OR Presence of Blasts Hyperleukocytosis leukostasis; acute leukaemia.
Prothrombin Time (INR) \(\text{INR} > 5.0\) Major lethal hemorrhagic risk.

Local Reference Ranges & Altitude Adjustments

  • Altitude Effect: Populations living at high altitudes (\(>1500\ \text{meters}\) above sea level) experience physiological hypoxia, triggering increased erythropoietin secretion \(\to\) higher baseline Hb and PCV reference ranges.
  • Age & Gender Variations: Neonates exhibit high physiological Hb (\(15–20\ \text{g/dL}\)); adult males have higher Hb than females due to androgens; pregnancy causes dilutional "pseudoanaemia" (expanded plasma volume).
  • Standard SI Units: Report clearly in SI units (\(\text{g/dL}\) or \(\text{g/L}\) for Hb, \(\text{L/L}\) for PCV, \(\times 10^9/\text{L}\) for WBC and platelets).
  • Audit Trail: Retain duplicate carbon copies of work sheets and patient report books for at least 3 years for clinical quality auditing.

Section 8.1 Board Review Questions (MCQ 497 – 504)

Test your mastery of district haematology priorities, phlebotomy pre-analytical variables, blood film buffer controls, and Levey-Jennings QC:

MCQ 497 • Pre-Analytical Tourniquet Stasis Pitfall
Why must a tourniquet never be left tightly applied to a patient's arm for longer than 1 minute during venepuncture for haematological testing?
A It converts arterial blood into pure cerebrospinal fluid.
B Prolonged venous stasis causes local hypoxia and fluid transudation into tissue spaces, producing localized hemoconcentration that falsely elevates haemoglobin, PCV, red cell count, and total protein.
C It causes rapid destruction of all blood grouping antigens within 30 seconds.
D It neutralizes EDTA anticoagulant inside the vacutainer tube.
Correct Answer: B — Prolonged venous stasis causes hemoconcentration, falsely elevating Hb, PCV, RBCs, and protein. When venous outflow is obstructed for \(>1\ \text{minute}\), hydrostatic pressure forces plasma water and low-molecular-weight electrolytes out of the capillary bed into interstitial tissues. Large non-diffusible cellular elements and protein-bound constituents are concentrated, creating artificially high hematocrit and hemoglobin values.
MCQ 498 • Capillary Blood Collection & "Milking" Error
During capillary blood collection from an infant's heel or an adult's finger, why is vigorous squeezing or "milking" of the puncture site strictly contraindicated?
A Excessive squeezing forces interstitial tissue fluid into the puncture site, diluting the blood sample and causing falsely low haemoglobin, PCV, and cell counts.
B It transforms lymphocytes into sickle cells.
C It converts fetal haemoglobin into adult haemoglobin A.
D It increases blood viscosity to the level of bone marrow.
Correct Answer: A — Excessive squeezing dilutes blood with interstitial tissue fluid, producing falsely low counts. A proper skin puncture must be sufficiently deep to allow spontaneous, free-flowing blood drops. Vigorous manual pressure ("milking") extracts clear tissue juices that mix with the capillary blood, severely diluting cellular constituents and leading to false diagnoses of anaemia.
MCQ 499 • EDTA Anticoagulant Ratio & Tube Underfilling
What physical and morphological artifact occurs when a blood sample container with dipotassium EDTA is severely underfilled with blood (excessive EDTA-to-blood ratio)?
A Red cells burst immediately and turn bright green.
B White blood cells multiply rapidly inside the tube.
C Excessive EDTA creates a hypertonic environment, drawing water out of erythrocytes and causing red cell shrinkage (crenation), which falsely reduces Packed Cell Volume (PCV) and Mean Cell Volume (MCV).
D Platelets aggregate into macroscopic fibrin ropes.
Correct Answer: C — Hypertonic red cell shrinkage falsely reducing PCV and MCV. Dipotassium EDTA is calibrated at \(1.5–2.0\ \text{mg}\) per mL of blood. When significantly less blood is added, the high hyperosmolar concentration of dry EDTA salt draws intracellular water out of red blood cells. The resulting shrunken, crenated erythrocytes pack tighter upon centrifugation, falsely lowering hematocrit (PCV) and calculated MCV.
MCQ 500 • Thin Blood Film Methanol Fixation Rule
Why must methanol used for fixing thin blood films be strictly 100% water-free (anhydrous), and what artifact appears on the blood film if water-contaminated methanol is used?
A Water in methanol turns all white cells into eosinophils.
B Water causes the glass slide to dissolve during staining.
C Water creates permanent yellow fluorescent staining of platelets.
D Water in methanol prevents proper protein coagulation, causing red cell crenation, partial hemolysis, and circular "water-ring / target-like" refractive artifacts inside erythrocytes.
Correct Answer: D — Water causes red cell crenation, partial lysis, and refractive water-ring artifacts. Pure absolute methanol instantly precipitates cell proteins without damaging red cell architecture. If methanol absorbs atmospheric moisture or contains water, the osmotic balance is disrupted during fixation, creating characteristic pale, punched-out central optical halos ("water rings") that mimic hypochromasia or target cells.
MCQ 501 • Romanowsky Staining Buffer pH Standardization
What is the standard pH required for the buffered water used to dilute Romanowsky stains (Leishman / Giemsa), and how does improper buffer pH alter the microscopic coloration of a blood film?
A \(\text{pH}\ 4.0\); causes all cells to stain pure black.
B \(\text{pH}\ 6.8\); if the buffer is too acidic (\(\text{pH} < 6.8\)), the film stains excessively red/pink with pale nuclei; if too alkaline (\(\text{pH} > 6.8\)), the film stains intensely blue/dark with obscured chromatin.
C \(\text{pH}\ 9.5\); causes red cells to stain golden yellow.
D \(\text{pH}\ 1.0\); completely bleaches out all Romanowsky dyes.
Correct Answer: B — \(\text{pH}\ 6.8\); too acidic = overly red/pink; too alkaline = overly blue/dark. Romanowsky staining depends on the precise ionization balance between basic methylene blue (and azure dyes) and acidic eosin. At the optimal \(\text{pH}\ 6.8\), eosin stains basic hemoglobin pink-red while azure stains acidic nucleic acids purple-violet. Deviations below \(6.8\) favor eosin (excessive red), while deviations above \(6.8\) favor azure/methylene blue (excessive blue).
MCQ 502 • Levey-Jennings Quality Control Chart Action Rule
When monitoring the daily performance of an automated cell counter or haemoglobinometer on a Levey-Jennings quality control chart, which statistical occurrence constitutes an immediate **Action Limit violation** requiring rejection of the analytical run?
A A single control value falling outside the \(\pm 3\text{SD}\) action limit (\(1_{3s}\) rule), or two consecutive control values exceeding the \(\pm 2\text{SD}\) warning limit on the same side (\(2_{2s}\) rule).
B A control value that lands exactly on the calculated mean line.
C Three consecutive values falling within \(\pm 0.5\text{SD}\) of the mean.
D A single value falling between \(+1\text{SD}\) and \(+2\text{SD}\).
Correct Answer: A — Value outside \(\pm 3\text{SD}\) (\(1_{3s}\)) or 2 consecutive values outside \(\pm 2\text{SD}\) (\(2_{2s}\)). In Gaussian distribution statistics, \(99.7\%\) of valid measurements fall within \(\pm 3\text{SD}\). Any single point exceeding \(\pm 3\text{SD}\) represents a serious random or systematic error (\(p < 0.003\)), mandating immediate cessation of patient testing, recalibration, and investigation before any patient results are released.
MCQ 503 • Critical Panic Value Alert Protocol
Which laboratory haematology test result represents an immediate life-threatening **Critical / Panic Value** requiring urgent telephonic communication to the attending clinician?
A Haemoglobin of \(13.5\ \text{g/dL}\) in an adult male.
B Total WBC count of \(7.5 \times 10^9/\text{L}\) with \(60\%\) neutrophils.
C Platelet count \(< 20 \times 10^9/\text{L}\) (\(20,000/\mu\text{L}\)) or Haemoglobin \(< 5.0\ \text{g/dL}\) (\(50\ \text{g/L}\)).
D ESR of \(8\ \text{mm/1st hour}\) in an elderly female.
Correct Answer: C — Platelet count \(<20 \times 10^9/\text{L}\) or \(\text{Hb} < 5.0\ \text{g/dL}\). Severe thrombocytopenia (\(<20 \times 10^9/\text{L}\)) places the patient at imminent risk of spontaneous, fatal intracranial and gastrointestinal hemorrhage. A haemoglobin \(<5.0\ \text{g/dL}\) carries extreme risk of anoxic heart failure. Both are internationally defined panic values requiring direct verbal reporting.
MCQ 504 • High Altitude Physiological Haematological Adaptation
Why do healthy individuals living in permanent high-altitude settlements (\(>1500–2500\ \text{meters}\) above sea level) have **significantly higher baseline haemoglobin and PCV reference ranges** than sea-level populations?
A High atmospheric ultraviolet light turns white blood cells into red blood cells.
B They have a complete genetic absence of blood plasma.
C Reduced gravity allows red cells to float in the lungs.
D Lower atmospheric partial pressure of oxygen (\(\text{pO}_2\)) causes chronic tissue hypoxia, stimulating renal production of erythropoietin, which enhances bone marrow erythropoiesis.
Correct Answer: D — Hypoxia stimulates renal erythropoietin secretion, increasing red cell mass. At elevated altitudes, the reduced barometric pressure lowers alveolar oxygen tension, producing arterial hypoxemia. Renal peritubular interstitial cells sense this hypoxia and upregulate erythropoietin (EPO) synthesis, driving erythroid hyperplasia in the bone marrow to expand total red cell mass and restore tissue oxygen delivery.

8.2 Functions of Blood, Haematopoiesis & Blood Cell Disorders

Physiological Roles of Blood • Ontogeny of Haematopoiesis (Yolk Sac \(\to\) Hepatosplenic \(\to\) Medullary) • Erythropoiesis Stages & Iron Metabolism (Ferritin vs Transferrin) • Master Morphological & Etiological Classification of Anaemias (Chart 8.2) • Haemoglobinopathies: Sickle Cell Disease (HbSS / HbAS) • Thalassaemia Syndromes (\(\alpha\) & \(\beta\) Thalassaemias, Chart 8.3) • Reactive Leukocyte Patterns • Leukaemias Diagnostic Battery (ALL, AML / Auer Rods, CML / Philadelphia, CLL / Smudge Cells, Chart 8.4) • Burkitt's Lymphoma "Starry-Sky" Pathology.

Monica Cheesbrough Haematology Principle: Differentiating microcytic hypochromic anaemias is a vital laboratory skill. Iron Deficiency Anaemia (IDA) features \(\downarrow\) Serum Ferritin, \(\downarrow\) Serum Iron, \(\uparrow\) TIBC, and \(\downarrow\) Transferrin Saturation (\(<15\%\)). In contrast, \(\beta\)-Thalassaemia Minor (Trait) displays a disproportionately high RBC count (\(>5.0 \times 10^{12}/\text{L}\)), Mentzer Index \((\text{MCV}/\text{RBC}) < 13\), normal/high ferritin, and elevated \(\text{HbA}_2 > 3.5\%\). In Anaemia of Chronic Disease (ACD), inflammatory hepcidin blocks iron release from macrophages, resulting in low serum iron, low TIBC, and normal or elevated serum ferritin.

Stem Cells Erythropoiesis

1. Ontogeny of Haematopoiesis, Stem Cells & Erythropoietic Kinetics

Anatomical Sites of Haematopoiesis

  • Mesoblastic (Yolk Sac) Stage (0–2 months): Primitive nucleated erythroblasts synthesizing embryonic hemoglobins (Gower 1, Gower 2, Portland).
  • Hepatic & Splenic Stage (2–7 months): Fetal liver (and spleen) is the predominant site synthesizing **Fetal Haemoglobin (\(\text{HbF} = \alpha_2\gamma_2\))**.
  • Myeloid / Medullary Stage (5 months \(\to\) Adult): Bone marrow cavities become primary.
    • Infancy & Childhood: All bones contain active hematopoietic **red marrow**.
    • Adulthood (post-puberty): Red marrow is restricted to the **axial skeleton** (vertebrae, sternum, ribs, skull, pelvis, proximal humerus/femur). Long bone shafts contain fatty **yellow marrow** (which can revert during severe hemolysis).

Erythroid Maturation Sequence

  1. Pronormoblast (Proerythroblast, \(14–20\ \mu\text{m}\)): Large nucleus, fine chromatin, prominent nucleoli, deep royal blue cytoplasm.
  2. Basophilic Normoblast (Early, \(12–17\ \mu\text{m}\)): Condensing chromatin, no nucleoli, intense basophilia (rich in RNA ribosomes).
  3. Polychromatic Normoblast (Intermediate, \(10–14\ \mu\text{m}\)): First stage where hemoglobin synthesis becomes visible (muddy grey/purple hue).
  4. Orthochromatic Normoblast (Late, \(8–10\ \mu\text{m}\)): Dense, pyknotic, structureless nucleus; pink cytoplasm; nucleus extruded at end of this stage.
  5. Reticulocyte (\(8–9\ \mu\text{m}\)): Anucleate immature RBC with residual RNA reticulum (stained by new methylene blue / brilliant cresyl blue); circulates 1–2 days in marrow and 1 day in blood.
  6. Mature Erythrocyte (\(7.2\ \mu\text{m}\)): Biconcave disc, \(120\ \text{day}\) lifespan.
Anaemia Matrix Iron Kinetics

2. Morphological Classification of Anaemias & Microcytic Differential Matrix

Diagnostic Parameter Iron Deficiency Anaemia (IDA) \(\beta\)-Thalassaemia Minor (Trait) Anaemia of Chronic Disease (ACD) Sideroblastic Anaemia
Pathophysiology Depleted total body iron stores (dietary, hookworm, blood loss). Impaired \(\beta\)-globin synthesis with relative \(\alpha\)-chain excess. Hepcidin excess blocks iron egress from macrophages/enterocytes. Defective protoporphyrin/heme ring synthesis in mitochondria.
Red Cell Indices \(\text{MCV} \downarrow\), \(\text{MCH} \downarrow\), \(\text{RDW} \uparrow\) (Marked anisocytosis). \(\text{MCV} \downarrow\downarrow\) (\(60–75\ \text{fl}\)), **\(\text{RBC} \uparrow\) (\(>5.0 \times 10^{12}/\text{L}\))**, normal RDW. \(\text{MCV}\) Normal or mildly \(\downarrow\), \(\text{MCH}\) Normal/\(\downarrow\), RDW Normal. \(\text{MCV} \downarrow\) or dimorphic (dual population), \(\text{RDW} \uparrow\).
Mentzer Index \((\frac{\text{MCV}}{\text{RBC}})\) \(> 13\) \(< 13\) Variable (\(>13\)) Variable
Serum Iron Markedly Decreased (\(\downarrow\downarrow\)) Normal or Elevated Decreased (\(\downarrow\)) Markedly Elevated (\(\uparrow\uparrow\))
Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC) Elevated (\(\uparrow\uparrow\)) Normal Decreased (\(\downarrow\)) Normal or Decreased
Serum Ferritin Markedly Decreased (\(< 15\ \mu\text{g/L}\)) Normal or Elevated Normal or Elevated (\(\uparrow\)) (Acute phase reactant) Markedly Elevated (\(\uparrow\uparrow\))
Blood Film Hallmarks Microcytic, hypochromic, pencil / cigar cells, elliptocytes. Microcytic, hypochromic, prominent **Target cells**, basophilic stippling. Mild normocytic or microcytic hypochromic; rouleaux formation. Dimorphic population; coarse basophilic stippling; Pappenheimer bodies.
Diagnostic Test of Choice Serum Ferritin \(<15\ \mu\text{g/L}\); response to oral iron. \(\text{HbA}_2 > 3.5\%\) on electrophoresis/HPLC. Elevated Ferritin + Low Serum Iron + Low TIBC. Ring Sideroblasts on bone marrow Perls Prussian blue stain.
Sickle Cell & Thal Genetics

3. Sickle Cell Disorders & Thalassaemia Syndromes (Chart 8.3 Matrix)

Sickle Cell Anaemia (HbSS) vs Trait (HbAS)

  • Molecular Defect: Point mutation in \(\beta\)-globin gene (codon 6: **Glutamic acid \(\to\) Valine**). Deoxygenated HbS polymerizes into insoluble rigid tactical crystals, deforming RBCs into crescent **sickle cells (drepanocytes)**.
  • Sickle Cell Anaemia (HbSS): Severe chronic hemolytic anaemia (\(\text{Hb}\ 6.0–9.0\ \text{g/dL}\)); blood film reveals classic sickle cells, target cells, polychromasia, and Howell-Jolly bodies (functional **autosplenectomy** by childhood due to repeated splenic infarcts). Vaso-occlusive painful crises, dactylitis, acute chest syndrome, stroke, aplastic crises (Parvovirus B19).
  • Sickle Cell Trait (HbAS): Heterozygous (\(\approx 60\%\ \text{HbA}, 40\%\ \text{HbS}\)); clinically asymptomatic with normal baseline blood film; protected against severe *P. falciparum* malaria; sickle solubility/slide tests are positive.

Thalassaemia Syndromes (Chart 8.3)

  • \(\beta\)-Thalassaemia Major (Cooley's Anaemia, \(\beta^0/\beta^0\)): Complete absence of \(\beta\)-chain synthesis; severe microcytic hypochromic anaemia apparent at \(3–6\ \text{months}\) of life (as HbF switches to HbA); blood film shows extreme poikilocytosis, target cells, teardrops, abundant **nucleated RBCs (normoblasts)**; massive hepatosplenomegaly, "chipmunk" facies, hair-on-end skull X-ray; **\(\text{HbF} > 70–90\%\)**; life-long transfusion dependent (requires iron chelation with desferrioxamine).
  • \(\beta\)-Thalassaemia Minor (\(\beta/\beta^0\)): Asymptomatic microcytic anaemia (\(\text{MCV}\ 60–75\ \text{fl}\)), high RBC count, **\(\text{HbA}_2 > 3.5\%\)**.
  • \(\alpha\)-Thalassaemias: Deletion of 1 to 4 \(\alpha\)-genes:
    • *HbH Disease (3 genes deleted):* Excess \(\beta\)-chains form unstable \(\beta_4\) tetramers (**HbH**); brilliant cresyl blue produces "golf-ball / pitted" inclusion bodies.
    • *Hb Barts Hydrops Fetalis (4 genes deleted):* \(\gamma_4\) tetramers cannot release oxygen; fatal in utero.
Oncology Burkitt's Lymphoma

4. Diagnostic Spectrum of Leukaemias & Burkitt's Lymphoma (Chart 8.4)

Neoplastic Disorder Typical Demographics Blood Film & Cytochemical Hallmarks Bone Marrow & Molecular Markers
Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia (ALL) Peak age **2–5 years** (commonest childhood cancer). Pancytopenia; circulating lymphoblasts with high N:C ratio, non-granular cytoplasm; **PAS Positive** (block/chunk pattern), Sudan Black B negative, MPO negative. \(\ge 20\%\) lymphoblasts in bone marrow; **TdT Positive**; CD10 (CALLA) positive in common B-ALL.
Acute Myeloid Leukaemia (AML) Adults (\(>50\ \text{years}\)); can occur at any age. Anaemia, thrombocytopenia, circulating myeloblasts with delicate chromatin, prominent nucleoli; **Auer Rods** (red needle-like cytoplasmic inclusions of fused lysosomal granules); **Myeloperoxidase (MPO) Positive**, **Sudan Black B Positive**. \(\ge 20\%\) myeloblasts in marrow; Acute Promyelocytic Leukaemia (APL, M3) associated with \(t(15;17)\) *PML-RARA* and severe life-threatening DIC.
Chronic Myeloid Leukaemia (CML) Adults (\(30–60\ \text{years}\)); massive splenomegaly. Marked leukocytosis (**\(50–500 \times 10^9/\text{L}\)**) showing the **entire spectrum of myeloid maturation** (myeloblasts \(<10\%\), promyelocytes, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, bands, neutrophils); absolute **basophilia and eosinophilia**. **Philadelphia Chromosome \(t(9;22)(q34;q11)\)** creating the *BCR-ABL1* fusion tyrosine kinase gene; **Leukocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) score markedly reduced / zero**.
Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia (CLL) Elderly adults (\(>60\ \text{years}\), Male predominance). Marked, sustained absolute lymphocytosis (\(20–200 \times 10^9/\text{L}\)) composed of small, mature, monomorphic round lymphocytes with condensed clumped "soccer-ball" chromatin; abundant fragile **"Smudge / Basket cells"** (ruptured during spreading). Clonal B-cell expansion co-expressing **CD5, CD19, CD20, and CD23**; associated with autoimmune hemolytic anaemia (positive DAT).
Burkitt's Lymphoma (Endemic BL) Children in equatorial tropical belts (**jaw / orbital tumor** or abdominal mass). Imprint smears from biopsy / FNA stained with Leishman/Giemsa show classic **"Starry-Sky Pattern"**: sheets of uniform, deeply basophilic, medium-sized B-lymphoblasts containing lipid vacuoles interspersed with pale, "tingible-body" macrophages. **EBV DNA association** (\(>95\%\)) in malaria-endemic zones; reciprocal translocation **\(t(8;14)(q24;q32)\)** translocating the *c-MYC* proto-oncogene to the Ig heavy chain enhancer.
Board Examination Section 8 Active Interactive MCQs

Section 8.2 Board Review Questions (MCQ 505 – 512)

Test your mastery of haematopoiesis ontogeny, microcytic differential matrices, sickle cell mutations, thalassaemias, leukaemias, and Burkitt's lymphoma:

MCQ 505 • Developmental Ontogeny of Haematopoiesis
What is the chronological sequence of anatomical organs responsible for haematopoiesis from early embryonic life through adulthood?
A Brain \(\to\) Heart \(\to\) Lungs \(\to\) Kidney.
B Yolk Sac (0–2 months) \(\to\) Liver & Spleen (2–7 months) \(\to\) Bone Marrow (from 5th month onward; restricted to the axial skeleton in healthy adults).
C Spleen exclusively for the first 20 years of life, then switching to the pancreas.
D Long bone shafts in adults only, with zero activity in the pelvic bones.
Correct Answer: B — Yolk sac (0–2m) \(\to\) Liver/spleen (2–7m) \(\to\) Bone marrow (5m+ \(\to\) adult axial skeleton). Mesoblastic blood formation starts in the embryonic yolk sac. By the second month, the fetal liver (and secondarily spleen) takes over, synthesizing \(\text{HbF}\). From the fifth gestational month, medullary bone marrow becomes the primary site. In adults, active hematopoietic red marrow is concentrated in the axial skeleton (vertebrae, ribs, sternum, pelvis, skull).
MCQ 506 • Microcytic Anaemia Differential Laboratory Battery
A patient presents with severe microcytic hypochromic anaemia (\(\text{MCV}\ 64\ \text{fl}\)). Which laboratory profile definitively differentiates Iron Deficiency Anaemia (IDA) from \(\beta\)-Thalassaemia Minor (Trait) and Anaemia of Chronic Disease (ACD)?
A IDA: Low Ferritin (\(<15\ \mu\text{g/L}\)), High TIBC, Low Serum Iron, Mentzer Index \(>13\); \(\beta\)-Thal Minor: Normal/High Ferritin, Normal TIBC, High RBC Count (\(>5.0 \times 10^{12}/\text{L}\)), Mentzer Index \(<13\), \(\text{HbA}_2 > 3.5\%\); ACD: Normal/High Ferritin, Low TIBC, Low Serum Iron.
B IDA has elevated ferritin; Thalassaemia has zero white blood cells; ACD has massive hemoglobinuria.
C All three conditions have identical ferritin and are differentiated only by blood typing.
D IDA is macrocytic with hypersegmented neutrophils; Thalassaemia is normocytic.
Correct Answer: A — IDA: Low ferritin, High TIBC; \(\beta\)-Thal Minor: \(\text{HbA}_2 > 3.5\%\), \(\text{RBC} > 5.0\), Mentzer \(<13\); ACD: High ferritin, Low TIBC. Serum ferritin is the single most sensitive indicator of total body iron depletion (\(<15\ \mu\text{g/L}\) in IDA). In \(\beta\)-thalassaemia trait, ineffective erythropoiesis drives high microcytic RBC output (\(\text{Mentzer} < 13\)) with characteristic elevation of \(\text{HbA}_2 > 3.5\%\). In ACD, inflammatory IL-6 upregulates hepcidin, trapping iron inside macrophages (yielding high ferritin but low circulating serum iron and low TIBC).
MCQ 507 • Sickle Cell Anaemia Molecular Genetics & Pathology
What is the precise genetic and molecular defect responsible for Sickle Cell Anaemia (HbSS), and why do adult patients with homozygous HbSS exhibit functional asplenia (autosplenectomy)?
A Deletion of all four alpha-globin genes; spleen is destroyed by viral infection.
B Single base mutation replacing lysine with glycine at codon 26 of alpha-chain.
C Point mutation at codon 6 of the \(\beta\)-globin gene substituting Glutamic Acid with Valine (\(\text{GAG} \to \text{GTG}\)); deoxygenation causes HbS polymerization and red cell sickling, producing recurrent microvascular vaso-occlusions and repeated splenic infarctions that fibrose the spleen by early childhood.
D Complete failure of bone marrow stem cells caused by autoantibodies against spectrin.
Correct Answer: C — \(\beta^6\) Glutamic Acid \(\to\) Valine; recurrent splenic infarction leading to autosplenectomy. The non-polar hydrophobic valine residue creates a "sticky patch" on deoxygenated HbS molecules, causing them to assemble into rigid helical polymers that distort erythrocytes into rigid, sickle-shaped forms. In the hypoxic, acidic splenic red pulp, sickled cells lodge in microvessels, producing repeated ischemic infarcts that progressively shrink and fibrose the spleen into a small calcified remnant (autosplenectomy).
MCQ 508 • \(\beta\)-Thalassaemia Major (Cooley's Anaemia) Diagnostic Profile
What are the classic clinical, peripheral blood film, and electrophoretic findings in an infant with homozygous \(\beta\)-Thalassaemia Major (Cooley's Anaemia) presenting at 6 months of age?
A Mild normocytic anaemia, zero reticulocytes, normal skull X-ray, \(\text{HbA} = 100\%\).
B Macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils and absent HbF.
C Polycythemia with \(\text{Hb} > 22\ \text{g/dL}\) and elevated platelets.
D Severe transfusion-dependent microcytic hypochromic anaemia, extreme poikilocytosis, target cells, abundant nucleated RBCs (normoblasts), marked hepatosplenomegaly, and \(\text{HbF} > 70–90\%\) with absent/minimal HbA.
Correct Answer: D — Severe microcytic anaemia, target cells, abundant normoblasts, \(\text{HbF} > 70–90\%\). In \(\beta\)-thalassaemia major, failure of \(\beta\)-globin synthesis leads to precipitating \(\alpha\)-chain tetramers that destroy erythroid precursors in the bone marrow (severe ineffective erythropoiesis) and in the spleen. Severe anemia appears at 3–6 months as fetal \(\gamma\)-chains switch down. Electrophoresis shows almost pure Fetal Haemoglobin (\(\text{HbF} = \alpha_2\gamma_2\)) with absent or trace HbA.
MCQ 509 • Reactive Leukocyte Morphological Patterns
Which morphological changes in peripheral blood neutrophils signify an active, severe bacterial infection or septicemia (leukemoid / shift-to-the-left reaction)?
A Increased band neutrophils (\(>10\%\)), coarse dark Toxic Granulation, cytoplasmic Vacuolation, and light-blue cytoplasmic Döhle Bodies (aggregates of rough endoplasmic reticulum).
B Hypersegmentation of neutrophils into 6–8 lobes with absent granules.
C Complete loss of all cytoplasmic granules and conversion into eosinophils.
D Auer rods inside mature segmented neutrophils.
Correct Answer: A — Band forms \(>10\%\), toxic granulation, cytoplasmic vacuolation, and Döhle bodies. Severe acute bacterial infections accelerate marrow granulopoiesis, releasing immature band forms ("shift to left"). Toxic granules represent persisting primary azurophilic granules with high enzyme content, Döhle bodies represent ribosomes/rER remnants, and vacuolation reflects active in vivo phagocytosis and autophagocytosis.
MCQ 510 • Acute Myeloid Leukaemia (AML) & Auer Rods
What are Auer rods, in which haematological malignancy are they pathognomonic, and what cytochemical stain confirms their presence?
A Nuclear DNA loops pathognomonic of chronic lymphocytic leukemia; PAS positive.
B Pink/red needle-shaped cytoplasmic inclusions composed of fused azurophilic lysosomal granules, pathognomonic of Acute Myeloid Leukaemia (AML / Myeloblasts), and confirmed by positive Myeloperoxidase (MPO) and Sudan Black B staining.
C Parasitic inclusions found only in severe *Plasmodium falciparum* malaria.
D Iron granules in mature red cells confirmed by Prussian blue.
Correct Answer: B — Fused azurophilic granules pathognomonic of AML; MPO and Sudan Black B positive. Auer rods are crystalline aggregates of abnormal primary granules containing lysosomal enzymes. Finding even a single Auer rod in a blast cell conclusively establishes a myeloid lineage (AML), ruling out ALL. They stain strongly with Myeloperoxidase (MPO) and Sudan Black B.
MCQ 511 • Chronic Myeloid Leukaemia (CML) vs Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia (CLL)
Match the distinct laboratory and chromosomal signatures of Chronic Myeloid Leukaemia (CML) and Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia (CLL):
A CML has smudge cells and elevated LAP; CLL has Philadelphia chromosome and Auer rods.
B CML occurs exclusively in neonates; CLL occurs only in pregnant females.
C CML: Massive leukocytosis (\(50–500 \times 10^9/\text{L}\)) with the entire spectrum of myeloid precursors, absolute basophilia, Philadelphia chromosome \(t(9;22)\) (*BCR-ABL1*), and very low LAP score; CLL: Monomorphic small mature lymphocytes, abundant fragile Smudge/Basket cells, and clonal B-cell markers (CD5/CD19/CD23).
D Both conditions feature severe pancytopenia with zero white cells in peripheral blood.
Correct Answer: C — CML: Full myeloid maturation, basophilia, \(t(9;22)\) BCR-ABL, low LAP; CLL: Small mature lymphocytes, smudge cells, CD5/CD19+. In CML, unregulated ABL tyrosine kinase drives massive granulocyte proliferation showing all developmental stages (myelocytes, metamyelocytes, bands, neutrophils) with characteristic low Leukocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP). In CLL, neoplastic non-functional B-cells accumulate, appearing as small round lymphocytes that easily rupture during slide spreading to form pathognomonic "smudge" or "basket" cells.
MCQ 512 • Burkitt's Lymphoma Etiology & "Starry-Sky" Pathology
In tropical Africa, a 6-year-old child presents with a rapidly expanding jaw tumour. A fine needle aspiration imprint smear reveals a classic "Starry-Sky" pattern. What infectious co-factors and chromosomal translocation drive this B-cell lymphoma?
A Hepatitis B virus and Schistosoma mansoni; \(t(15;17)\) translocation.
B Tuberculosis and Hookworm; Trisomy 21.
C HIV-2 and Yellow fever virus; \(t(9;22)\) BCR-ABL translocation.
D Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) and chronic Plasmodium falciparum malaria; reciprocal chromosomal translocation \(t(8;14)\) juxtaposing the c-MYC proto-oncogene next to the immunoglobulin heavy chain (IgH) enhancer.
Correct Answer: D — EBV + malaria co-factors; \(t(8;14)\) translocating c-MYC to IgH enhancer. Endemic Burkitt's lymphoma is tightly linked geographically to holoendemic *P. falciparum* malaria, which causes chronic B-cell polyclonal activation and T-cell immunosuppression, facilitating latent Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) oncogenesis. The hallmark \(t(8;14)(q24;q32)\) translocation drives constitutive over-expression of the *c-MYC* transcription factor. The "starry sky" histology represents intensely basophilic B-lymphoblasts (the dark "sky") peppered with pale, tingible-body macrophages engulfing apoptotic debris (the "stars").

8.3 Collection of Blood (Capillary & Venous Phlebotomy)

SOPs for Safe Blood Sampling • Capillary Skin Puncture: Infant Plantar Heel Safety Boundaries (\(\le 2.0\ \text{mm}\) Depth) & Adult Fingerstick Protocols • Venous Phlebotomy: Antecubital Fossa Anatomy (Median Cubital, Cephalic, Basilic) • Anticoagulant Chemistry: \(\text{K}_2\text{EDTA}\) (\(1.5–2.0\ \text{mg/mL}\)), Sodium Citrate (\(1:9\) Coagulation vs \(1:4\) Westergren ESR), Heparin & Sodium Fluoride • CLSI Standard Order of Draw • EDTA-Induced Pseudothrombocytopenia.

Monica Cheesbrough Phlebotomy Golden Rule: Capillary blood collection from neonates and infants must strictly be confined to the most medial or lateral plantar borders of the heel using a lancet with a maximum puncture depth of \(\le 2.0\ \text{mm}\). Puncturing the posterior curve or central plantar arch risks piercing the calcaneus bone, causing crippling osteomyelitis. In all capillary sticks, always wipe away the first drop of blood to eliminate excess tissue thromboplastin and interstitial fluid!

Pediatric Phlebotomy Calcaneal Safety

1. Capillary Blood Sampling, Infant Heel Safety & Fingerstick SOP

Infant Heel Stick SOP (\(<1\ \text{Year}\))

  • Anatomical Boundaries: Strictly within the medial or lateral plantar borders of the heel (lateral to a line drawn from the middle of the great toe to the heel, or medial to a line from between the 4th and 5th toes to the heel).
  • Strict Prohibition: Never puncture the posterior curvature of the heel or central plantar arch (the calcaneus bone is only \(2.0–2.4\ \text{mm}\) beneath the skin surface in premature infants; risk of osteomyelitis and cartilage necrosis).
  • Puncture Depth: Maximum depth strictly \(\le 2.0\ \text{mm}\) (or \(\le 0.85\ \text{mm}\) in premature neonates).
  • Pre-Warming: Warm the heel with a warm moist towel (\(40–42^\circ\text{C}\) for 3–5 min) to increase arterialized blood flow 7-fold.

Adult & Older Child Fingerstick SOP

  • Selected Site: Palmar surface of the distal phalanx of the **3rd (middle) or 4th (ring) finger** of the non-dominant hand.
  • Prohibited Sites:
    • Thumb: Has an active pulse and thicker calloused skin.
    • Index Finger: Highly sensitive with frequent calluses.
    • 5th (Little) Finger: Tissue volume is too thin over the bone.
  • Puncture Technique: Make puncture **perpendicular (across) the fingerprint ridges**, not parallel (parallel punctures cause blood to run down grooves rather than forming round standing drops).
  • Wipe First Drop: Always discard the first drop with sterile gauze (contains excess interstitial tissue fluid and tissue factor, causing clotting and dilutional errors).
Venous Sampling Vascular Anatomy

2. Venous Blood Collection & Antecubital Fossa Vascular Anatomy

Antecubital Vein Selection

  1. 1st Choice: Median Cubital Vein: Center of antecubital fossa; large, well-anchored, least tendency to roll, lowest pain sensation.
  2. 2nd Choice: Cephalic Vein: Lateral (outer) aspect of upper forearm; well-anchored, ideal for obese patients.
  3. 3rd Choice: Basilic Vein: Medial (inner) aspect; close proximity to the brachial artery and median nerve (risk of accidental arterial puncture and nerve injury; highly painful).

Phlebotomy Technical Rules

  • Tourniquet Limit: Apply \(7.5–10\ \text{cm}\) above site; release strictly within **1 minute** once blood starts flowing.
  • Needle Angle & Gauge: Insert needle bevel-up at a **\(15^\circ–30^\circ\) angle** to the skin. Standard adult gauge is **21G (green)**; pediatric/fragile veins use **22G/23G butterfly**.
  • Fist Clenching: Patient should form a gentle fist without vigorous pumping (pumping causes transient hyperkalemia).

Preventing Mechanical Hemolysis

  • Alcohol Drying: Allow \(70\%\) alcohol to air-dry completely (wet alcohol lyses RBCs).
  • Syringe Dispensing: If using a syringe, **remove the needle** before gently dispensing blood down the inside wall of the tube (forcing blood through a narrow needle causes severe shear hemolysis).
  • Gentle Mixing: Invert tubes gently 5–10 times; never shake vigorously.
Anticoagulant Chemistry Ratios & Mechanisms

3. Anticoagulant Formulations, Calcium Chelation & Ratios

Anticoagulant Agent Standard Concentration / Ratio Mode of Action & Biochemistry Recommended Diagnostic Uses & Limitations
Dipotassium EDTA (\(\text{K}_2\text{EDTA}\)) \(1.5–2.0\ \text{mg/mL}\) of blood (Lavender / Purple Top) Irreversibly binds and chelates ionized **Calcium (\(\text{Ca}^{2+}\))**, blocking coagulation cascade initiation. \(\text{K}_2\text{EDTA}\) spray-dried salt dissolves rapidly. • **CBC / FBC**, differential WBC, platelet count, reticulocytes, HbA1c.
• Blood films must be prepared within **1–2 hours**.
• Causes in vitro **EDTA-dependent pseudothrombocytopenia** in \(0.1\%\) of patients.
Trisodium Citrate (\(3.2\%\) / \(0.109\ \text{M}\)) \(1:9\) Ratio (1 part citrate + 9 parts blood) (Light Blue Top) Loosely binds/chelates Calcium ions; completely reversible upon addition of \(\text{CaCl}_2\) during coagulation testing. • Coagulation Screening: Prothrombin Time (PT/INR), APTT, Thrombin Time (TT), Fibrinogen, Factor Assays.
• Confirming true platelet count in EDTA pseudothrombocytopenia.
Trisodium Citrate (\(3.8\%\) / \(0.129\ \text{M}\)) \(1:4\) Ratio (1 part citrate + 4 parts blood) (Black Top) Chelates Calcium; provides specific viscosity and dilution for standard sedimentation. • Westergren Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) exclusively.
Lithium / Sodium Heparin \(10–20\ \text{IU/mL}\) of blood (Green Top) Accelerates and potentiates **Antithrombin III (AT-III)**, inactivating Thrombin (IIa), Factor Xa, and IXa. • Osmotic fragility test, blood gases, clinical chemistry plasma.
• STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED FOR BLOOD FILMS: Produces intense dark blue-violet background with Romanowsky stains and causes leukocyte/platelet clumping.
Sodium Fluoride / Potassium Oxalate \(1.0\ \text{mg}\) NaF + \(3.0\ \text{mg}\) Oxalate/mL (Grey Top) Fluoride inhibits **enolase** in the glycolytic pathway (preventing in vitro glycolysis); Oxalate chelates calcium. • Blood glucose and lactate testing (prevents RBCs from consuming glucose at \(5–7\%\ \text{per hour}\)).
Order of Draw Platelet Artifacts

4. CLSI Evacuated Tube Order of Draw & EDTA Pseudothrombocytopenia

Standard Evacuated Tube Order of Draw

Strict sequence prevents cross-contamination of tube additives (e.g. EDTA chelating calcium in coagulation tubes):

  1. 1. Blood Culture Bottles (Yellow / Castaneda): Must be drawn first to maintain strict sterility.
  2. 2. Sodium Citrate Tube (Light Blue): Drawn before serum/heparin to prevent tissue factor / clot activator contamination.
  3. 3. Serum Tubes (Red / Gold SST): With or without clot activator / gel separator.
  4. 4. Heparin Tube (Green): Lithium or sodium heparin.
  5. 5. EDTA Tube (Lavender / Purple): \(\text{K}_2\text{EDTA}\) for haematology.
  6. 6. Sodium Fluoride / Oxalate Tube (Grey): Glycolytic inhibitor drawn last.

EDTA-Induced Pseudothrombocytopenia

  • Mechanism: Naturally occurring anti-platelet autoantibodies (\(\text{IgG/IgM}\)) recognize cryptic epitopes on platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa exposed only when EDTA chelates calcium.
  • Laboratory Phenomenon: Causes in vitro **platelet agglutination (large clumps)** or platelet satellitism around neutrophils. Automated cell counters count large clumps as single leukocytes, reporting severe spurious **thrombocytopenia (\(<20–50 \times 10^9/\text{L}\))** in a completely asymptomatic patient with no bleeding!
  • Corrective SOP:
    • Inspect peripheral blood film under \(100\times\) oil immersion for platelet clumps at the feather edge.
    • Collect a fresh blood sample in a **Sodium Citrate tube (Light Blue)**, repeat count, and multiply the result by **\(1.1\)** to correct for the \(10\%\) liquid volume dilution.
Board Examination Section 8 Active Interactive MCQs

Section 8.3 Board Review Questions (MCQ 513 – 520)

Test your mastery of infant heel safety boundaries, phlebotomy anatomy, anticoagulant chemistry, order of draw, and EDTA artifacts:

MCQ 513 • Infant Heel Stick Safety Boundaries
According to Monica Cheesbrough and international pediatric phlebotomy standards, what are the mandatory anatomical boundaries and maximum puncture depth for a capillary heel stick in an infant?
A Posterior curvature of the heel; depth \(5.0\ \text{mm}\).
B Medial or lateral plantar surfaces of the heel with a maximum puncture depth of \(\le 2.0\ \text{mm}\) (avoiding the posterior curve and central arch to prevent calcaneal osteomyelitis).
C Central plantar arch directly over the plantar nerve; depth \(4.0\ \text{mm}\).
D Dorsum of the foot between the toes; depth \(3.0\ \text{mm}\).
Correct Answer: B — Medial/lateral plantar borders of the heel; depth \(\le 2.0\ \text{mm}\). In infants, the calcaneus bone lies within \(2.0–2.4\ \text{mm}\) of the skin surface at the posterior curvature. Punctures must be restricted to the safe medial or lateral plantar margins and must never exceed a depth of \(2.0\ \text{mm}\) (\(\le 0.85\ \text{mm}\) in premature infants) to prevent puncturing the periosteum and introducing osteomyelitis.
MCQ 514 • Capillary Puncture Protocol & First Drop Elimination
Why must the first drop of blood always be wiped away with sterile gauze following a skin puncture before collecting blood for haematological counts?
A The first drop contains tissue fluids and intracellular thromboplastin released from damaged epidermis, which dilutes cellular elements and initiates rapid microclotting.
B The first drop contains only pure alcohol from skin preparation.
C The first drop has no white blood cells.
D The first drop is always contaminated with bone marrow cells.
Correct Answer: A — First drop contains excess tissue fluid and thromboplastin causing dilution and microclots. The mechanical trauma of lancet penetration releases tissue fluids and cellular thromboplastin into the initial droplet. Discarding this first drop ensures that subsequent free-flowing blood represents genuine circulating capillary blood without dilutional error or pre-analytical microaggregates.
MCQ 515 • Antecubital Fossa Phlebotomy Anatomy
Why is the Median Cubital vein the primary vessel of choice for venepuncture, and why is the Basilic vein considered the last choice in the antecubital fossa?
A Median cubital vein has no red blood cells; basilic vein contains only arterial blood.
B Median cubital vein is deep inside the elbow joint; basilic vein is always thrombosed.
C Median cubital vein is large, superficial, well-anchored, and has the lowest pain; the Basilic vein is situated in close proximity to the brachial artery and median nerve, carrying high risk of accidental arterial puncture and debilitating nerve damage.
D Both veins are avoided in adults and used only in neonates.
Correct Answer: C — Median cubital is well-anchored with low pain; basilic vein is close to brachial artery and median nerve. The median cubital vein lies superficially over the bicipital aponeurosis, providing excellent stability and minimal rolling. In contrast, the basilic vein on the medial aspect of the antecubital fossa lies directly adjacent to the brachial artery and median nerve trunk, where deep needle exploration risks catastrophic arterial pseudoaneurysm or permanent median nerve neuropraxia.
MCQ 516 • EDTA Anticoagulant Mechanism & Blood Film Stability
What is the biochemical mechanism of action of Dipotassium EDTA (\(\text{K}_2\text{EDTA}\)) at \(1.5–2.0\ \text{mg/mL}\), and within what timeframe must thin blood films be prepared to prevent morphological artifacts?
A Destroys platelets; films must be made after 48 hours of refrigeration.
B Activates protein C; films must be made within 10 seconds.
C Precipitates fibrinogen; films can be made at any time up to 1 month.
D Irreversibly chelates ionized Calcium (\(\text{Ca}^{2+}\)); blood films must be prepared within 1–2 hours of collection (beyond which neutrophils undergo nuclear pyknosis/lobulation and monocytes develop vacuoles).
Correct Answer: D — Chelates Calcium (\(\text{Ca}^{2+}\)); blood films made within 1–2 hours. EDTA removes free ionized calcium necessary for coagulation factor complexes. While cell counts and hemoglobin remain stable for \(24\ \text{hours}\) at \(4^\circ\text{C}\), morphological degradation of white cells begins within 2–3 hours at room temperature, producing pyknotic neutrophil nuclei, monocyte vacuolation, red cell crenation, and platelet disintegration.
MCQ 517 • Trisodium Citrate Concentration & Volume Ratios
What are the precise anticoagulant-to-blood dilution ratios for trisodium citrate when performing (1) Coagulation screening tests (PT/INR, APTT) and (2) Westergren Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)?
A 1:1 for coagulation; 1:10 for ESR.
B 1:9 ratio (1 part \(3.2\%\) citrate to 9 parts blood) for Coagulation tests; 1:4 ratio (1 part \(3.8\%\) citrate to 4 parts blood) for Westergren ESR.
C 1:4 for coagulation; 1:9 for ESR.
D Coagulation requires pure undiluted dry powder with zero liquid citrate.
Correct Answer: B — 1:9 ratio for Coagulation (3.2%); 1:4 ratio for Westergren ESR (3.8%). Coagulation testing requires \(3.2\%\) (\(0.109\ \text{M}\)) sodium citrate in an exact \(1:9\) proportion (\(0.5\ \text{mL}\) citrate + \(4.5\ \text{mL}\) blood) to avoid excess free citrate prolonging clotting times. Westergren ESR requires a \(1:4\) proportion (\(0.4\ \text{mL}\) citrate + \(1.6\ \text{mL}\) blood) to establish standard red cell sedimentation kinetics.
MCQ 518 • Heparin Mechanism & Blood Film Contraindication
Why is heparinized blood strictly contraindicated for preparing and staining routine diagnostic blood films?
A Heparin reacts with Romanowsky stains to produce an intense, unsightly dark blue-violet background coloration and induces in vitro clumping of leukocytes and platelets.
B Heparin converts all hemoglobin into carboxyhemoglobin instantly.
C Heparin dissolves red cell membranes, leaving zero cells on the slide.
D Heparin bleaches out all Romanowsky dyes, rendering the film completely invisible.
Correct Answer: A — Produces dark blue-violet background staining and induces cell clumping. Heparin is a highly sulfated, negatively charged glycosaminoglycan that strongly binds basic dyes (methylene blue and azure), creating a dense, opaque blue haze across the entire slide that obscures cell morphology. It also causes artificial aggregation of white blood cells and platelets.
MCQ 519 • CLSI Standard Evacuated Tube Order of Draw
What is the correct CLSI order of draw when collecting multiple blood tubes during a single venepuncture procedure?
A EDTA \(\to\) Fluoride \(\to\) Heparin \(\to\) Serum \(\to\) Citrate \(\to\) Blood Cultures.
B Fluoride \(\to\) EDTA \(\to\) Serum \(\to\) Heparin \(\to\) Citrate.
C Blood Culture Bottles \(\to\) Sodium Citrate (Light Blue) \(\to\) Serum (Red/Gold) \(\to\) Heparin (Green) \(\to\) EDTA (Lavender) \(\to\) Sodium Fluoride / Oxalate (Grey).
D Heparin \(\to\) EDTA \(\to\) Citrate \(\to\) Blood Cultures \(\to\) Serum.
Correct Answer: C — Blood cultures \(\to\) Citrate \(\to\) Serum \(\to\) Heparin \(\to\) EDTA \(\to\) Fluoride. Drawing sterile blood culture bottles first prevents microbial contamination. Citrate is drawn before serum tubes containing silica clot activators to avoid thromboplastin carryover. EDTA is drawn after heparin and serum to prevent potassium/EDTA carryover into electrolyte and coagulation assays. Fluoride is drawn last.
MCQ 520 • EDTA-Induced Pseudothrombocytopenia Resolution
An automated cell counter reports a severe platelet count of \(18 \times 10^9/\text{L}\) in an EDTA blood sample from an asymptomatic outpatient with no history of bleeding. A peripheral blood film reveals numerous large platelet clumps. What is the standard laboratory procedure to confirm and report the patient's genuine platelet count?
A Order an urgent platelet transfusion immediately.
B Heat the EDTA tube to \(56^\circ\text{C}\) for 30 minutes and re-run.
C Report the result as immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).
D Recognize EDTA-induced pseudothrombocytopenia; redraw a fresh blood specimen in a Sodium Citrate tube (Light Blue), run the platelet count, and multiply the result by \(1.1\) to correct for citrate liquid dilution.
Correct Answer: D — Redraw in Sodium Citrate tube and multiply result by 1.1. EDTA-dependent agglutinins (autoantibodies) cause in vitro platelet clumping that automated impedance counters misclassify as white blood cells or debris. Re-collecting blood in sodium citrate prevents this antibody-induced clumping. Because \(3.2\%\) citrate is a liquid solution adding \(10\%\) volume, multiplying the measured platelet count by \(1.1\) yields the patient's true circulating platelet concentration.

Section 8.3 Complete!

You have mastered Collection of Blood (Capillary & Venous Phlebotomy) (Cheesbrough Part 2 pp. 295–299).
