8.4 Measurement of Haemoglobin (HiCN, Photometry & Colour Scale)

Standardization of Haemoglobinometry • ICSH International Reference Cyanmethemoglobin (HiCN / Hemiglobincyanide) Method at \(540\ \text{nm}\) • Neutral Drabkin's Chemistry & Detergents • Sources of Turbidity, Lipemia & Monoclonal Paraprotein Interference • Direct-Reading Battery Photometers (DHT 523 & AHD Method) • Non-Dilution Microcuvette Technology (HemoCue 201+ Dual-Wavelength \(570/880\ \text{nm}\)) • WHO Haemoglobin Colour Scale for Primary Care (\(4–14\ \text{g/dL}\)) • Sahli & Lovibond Inaccuracies • Age/Sex Reference Ranges • Preliminary Diagnostic Algorithms for Tropical Anaemias.

Monica Cheesbrough Haemoglobinometry Principle: The ICSH Cyanmethemoglobin (HiCN) method is the definitive international gold standard, converting all physiologically active forms of hemoglobin (oxyHb, deoxyHb, carboxyHb, and metHb) into stable hemiglobincyanide read at \(540\ \text{nm}\). Note that sulfhemoglobin (\(\text{SHb}\)) cannot be converted to HiCN. In district laboratories, false elevations in HiCN are almost universally caused by turbidity (severe leukocytosis \(>30 \times 10^9/\text{L}\), lipemia, or paraproteinemia in multiple myeloma), which must be corrected by centrifugation or alkali buffering before reporting!

ICSH Cyanmethemoglobin (Hemiglobincyanide / HiCN) Reference Method

The International Council for Standardization in Haematology (ICSH) and WHO recommend the Cyanmethemoglobin (HiCN) method as the universal reference standard for blood hemoglobin estimation. Its paramount advantages are the availability of internationally certified, stable reference standards and the quantitative conversion of virtually all functional human hemoglobin variants.

Two-Step Chemical Reaction Mechanism

Step 1: Oxidation
Potassium ferricyanide (\(\text{K}_3[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]\)) oxidizes the divalent ferrous iron (\(\text{Fe}^{2+}\)) of hemoglobin, oxyhemoglobin, and carboxyhemoglobin to trivalent ferric iron (\(\text{Fe}^{3+}\)), producing methaemoglobin (hemiglobin, \(\text{Hi}\)): \[\text{HbFe}^{2+} + \text{K}_3[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6] \longrightarrow \text{MetHbFe}^{3+} (\text{Hi})\]

Step 2: Cyanide Complexation
Potassium cyanide (\(\text{KCN}\)) reacts with methaemoglobin to form stable, red-colored cyanmethaemoglobin (hemiglobincyanide, \(\text{HiCN}\)): \[\text{MetHbFe}^{3+} (\text{Hi}) + \text{KCN} \longrightarrow \text{HiCN}\]

Spectral Property: HiCN demonstrates an intense, broad optical absorbance peak with a maximum at \(\lambda = 540\ \text{nm}\) (measured using a green filter, e.g., Ilford 604 or equivalent narrow bandpass filter). At \(540\ \text{nm}\), light absorbance follows the Beer-Lambert Law directly proportional to concentration over a wide clinical range (\(0–200\ \text{g/L}\)).

Neutral Drabkin's Reagent Formulation (pH 7.0–7.4)

Chemical Component Quantity / 1 Liter Functional Role
Potassium ferricyanide (\(\text{K}_3[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]\)) \(200\ \text{mg}\) (\(0.20\ \text{g}\)) Oxidizing agent (\(\text{Fe}^{2+} \to \text{Fe}^{3+}\))
Potassium cyanide (\(\text{KCN}\)) \(50\ \text{mg}\) (\(0.05\ \text{g}\)) Cyanide ligand provider for HiCN complex
Potassium dihydrogen phosphate (\(\text{KH}_2\text{PO}_4\)) \(140\ \text{mg}\) (\(0.14\ \text{g}\)) Buffers reagent to neutral \(\text{pH}\ 7.0–7.4\)
Non-ionic Detergent (Triton X-100 / Tergitol) \(1.0\ \text{mL}\) Accelerates RBC stromal lysis & prevents turbidity
Deionized / Distilled Water to \(1000\ \text{mL}\) (\(1.0\ \text{L}\)) Solvent matrix (\(\text{pH}\) must read \(7.0–7.4\))
Reagent Storage & Safety: Drabkin's reagent is clear and pale yellow. Store in a tightly closed, chemically resistant amber brown borosilicate glass bottle at room temperature in the dark. Discard if it turns cloudy or loses its yellow tint. Drabkin's contains toxic cyanide; never mouth-pipette!

Standard Dilution & Spectrophotometric Test Method

1 Pipetting Blood

Accurately measure \(20\ \mu\text{L}\) (\(0.02\ \text{mL}\)) of well-mixed EDTA venous or capillary blood with a calibrated positive-displacement or precision micropipette. Carefully wipe the outside of the pipette tip without drawing blood from the bore.

2 Dispensing & Mixing

Dispense blood into \(5.0\ \text{mL}\) of Drabkin's neutral reagent (giving a standard \(1:251\) dilution). Rinse pipette \(3\times\) in the reagent. Stopper the tube, invert gently \(5\times\), and allow to stand for 3 to 5 minutes at room temperature (\(18–25^\circ\text{C}\)).

3 Photometric Measurement

Zero the colorimeter/spectrophotometer at \(540\ \text{nm}\) using Drabkin's reagent as the reagent blank. Transfer solution to a \(10\ \text{mm}\) optical path cuvette. Read absorbance (\(A_{540}\)) and derive Hb from the pre-calibrated HiCN standard curve.

Matrix of Turbidity, Interferences & Corrective Troubleshooting

Because colorimetry measures optical attenuation (light scattering plus absorbance), sample turbidity falsely elevates absorbance readings, resulting in spurious overestimation of hemoglobin concentration:

Clinical Interfering Factor Pathophysiological Mechanism Spurious Effect Mandatory Corrective Action
Marked Leukocytosis (\(\text{WBC} > 30 \times 10^9/\text{L}\)) Massive leukocyte membrane fragments and unlysed nuclei scatter incident light at \(540\ \text{nm}\). False Elevation of \(\text{Hb}\) (\(+\,10–30\ \text{g/L}\)) Centrifuge the diluted HiCN solution at \(1500\ \text{g}\) for \(5\ \text{min}\) or filter supernatant through a \(0.45\ \mu\text{m}\) filter before reading.
Severe Lipemia / Hypertriglyceridemia High concentrations of chylomicrons and VLDL form a milky emulsion causing light scattering. False Elevation of \(\text{Hb}\) Add an equal volume of diethyl ether or chloroform, shake vigorously, centrifuge, and measure the clear lower aqueous layer; or prepare a patient plasma blank.
Paraproteinemia / Multiple Myeloma Monoclonal immunoglobulins precipitate in the acidic/neutral ionic environment of Drabkin's reagent. False Elevation of \(\text{Hb}\) Add \(0.1\ \text{g}\) of potassium carbonate (\(\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3\)) to the Drabkin's reagent or use alkaline hematin detergent (AHD) method.
Hemoglobins S and C (\(\text{HbS}, \text{HbC}\)) Insoluble mutant hemoglobin crystals resist rapid lysis in standard Drabkin's reagent. Turbidity & False High \(\text{Hb}\) Dilute the hemolysate \(1:1\) with distilled water, multiply final reading by 2, and allow \(10\ \text{minutes}\) complete lysis time.
Sulfhemoglobin (\(\text{SHb}\)) Sulfur irreversibly bound to heme ring cannot be oxidized by ferricyanide or bind cyanide. Underestimation of Total \(\text{Hb}\) HiCN cannot measure SHb. Total pigments must be measured by isobestic spectral scanning or gas chromatography.

Direct Photometers & Non-Dilution Microcuvette Technology

District health facilities and rural peripheral laboratories require robust, temperature-stable, and battery-operable instruments that eliminate manual reagent preparation and hazardous cyanide handling.

Developing Health Technology (DHT) 523 Haemoglobinometer

A specialized, direct-reading battery-operated field photometer engineered specifically for tropical district laboratories:

  • Diluting Fluid: Utilizes weak \(0.4\ \text{mL/L}\) (\(0.04\%\)) ammonia water (stable for 6 weeks, non-toxic, inexpensive, no refrigeration required).
  • Dilution Ratio: \(20\ \mu\text{L}\) capillary or EDTA venous blood in \(2.0\ \text{mL}\) ammonia fluid (\(1:101\) dilution).
  • Optical System: High-efficiency Green LED emitter with an interference bandpass filter peaking at \(523\ \text{nm}\) matched to a silicon photodiode.
  • Operational Precision: Photometric precision \(\text{CV} \le 1.5\%\), method accuracy within \(\pm 2\%\). Operational range \(10–35^\circ\text{C}\) up to \(80\%\) relative humidity.
  • Quality Control Standard: Calibrated with a supplied optical Glass Control Standard inserted before each testing batch (\(\text{target} \pm 5\ \text{g/L}\)).

Alkaline Hematin Detergent (AHD575) Method

A non-toxic, environmentally safe, cyanide-free international candidate reference method:

  • Principle: Blood is diluted in an alkaline solution containing \(0.1\ \text{M}\ \text{NaOH}\) and Triton X-100. Hemoglobin is converted within 2 minutes into stable alkaline hematin (monodispersed micellar complex).
  • Wavelength: Measured spectrophotometrically at \(540–575\ \text{nm}\).
  • Standard: Calibrated against a remarkably stable, synthetic chlorhaemin (hemin chloride) standard solution.
  • Advantages: Eliminates toxic cyanide waste; converts carboxyhemoglobin, sulfhemoglobin, and fetal hemoglobin with uniform kinetics.

HemoCue 201+ Automated Microcuvette System

The HemoCue 201+ is a portable, non-dilution, direct-reading hemoglobinometer widely utilized in global clinical trials, antenatal clinics, and blood transfusion donor screening:

  • Internal Microcuvette Chemistry: Dry reagent coating in a disposable plastic microcuvette (\(\sim 10\ \mu\text{L}\) sample capacity):
    • Sodium Deoxycholate: Immediately hemolyzes erythrocytes and disperses membranes.
    • Sodium Nitrite: Converts hemoglobin \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) to methaemoglobin (\(\text{Fe}^{3+}\)).
    • Sodium Azide: Complexes with methemoglobin to form stable azidemethaemoglobin.
  • Measuring Range & Speed: \(0–256\ \text{g/L}\) (\(0–25.6\ \text{g/dL}\)); result displayed within \(15–60\ \text{seconds}\).
  • Accuracy: Correlates within \(\pm 1.5\%\) of the ICSH HiCN reference method without interference from bilirubin.
Dual-Wavelength Turbidity Compensation:
The HemoCue optical engine takes absorbance measurements at two distinct wavelengths:
  • \(570\ \text{nm}\): Primary absorption peak of azidemethemoglobin.
  • \(880\ \text{nm}\): Background infrared wavelength to measure and mathematically subtract background light scattering caused by lipemia or extreme leukocytosis.
Tropical Microcuvette Humidity Alert:
HemoCue microcuvette dry reagents are highly hygroscopic. In tropical climates, store microcuvettes in tightly capped containers with desiccant in pack sizes of 25. Once opened, containers must be used rapidly and never exposed to open ambient humidity, or reagent degeneration will cause severe testing errors!

WHO Haemoglobin Colour Scale & Obsolete Visual Methods

In remote primary healthcare facilities and community mobile clinics lacking electricity, battery photometers, or centrifuges, point-of-care visual screening devices guide immediate clinical triage.

WHO Haemoglobin Colour Scale (Plate 95)

Developed under WHO guidance by Stott and Lewis as an inexpensive, robust, quality-controlled clinical screening tool:

Standard Operational Procedure (SOP):
  1. Place a standardized drop of fresh capillary blood (approx. \(20\ \mu\text{L}\)) onto the test chromatography paper strip.
  2. Wait exactly \(30–60\ \text{seconds}\) for the blood to fully absorb and interact with atmospheric oxygen (forming bright oxyHb). Do not read after 2 minutes (drying causes darkening).
  3. Compare the blood spot against the 6 calibrated reference color shades viewed in direct daylight or under a white light lamp.
Colour Shade (g/dL) Equivalent (g/L) Clinical Classification & Action
\(14\ \text{g/dL}\) & \(12\ \text{g/dL}\) \(140\ \text{g/L}\) & \(120\ \text{g/L}\) Normal (Non-anaemic)
\(10\ \text{g/dL}\) \(100\ \text{g/L}\) Mild Anaemia (Oral iron + folic acid supplementation)
\(8\ \text{g/dL}\) & \(6\ \text{g/dL}\) \(80\ \text{g/L}\) & \(60\ \text{g/L}\) Moderate Anaemia (Investigate malaria, hookworm; therapeutic iron)
\(4\ \text{g/dL}\) \(40\ \text{g/L}\) Severe Life-Threatening Anaemia (Urgent hospital admission & transfusion triage)

Obsolete & Unreliable Visual Techniques

Sahli Acid Hematin Method (Not Recommended):
  • Principle: \(20\ \mu\text{L}\) blood mixed with \(0.1\ \text{M}\ \text{HCl}\) converting Hb to brown acid hematin. Diluted dropwise with water until color matches a tinted glass prism.
  • Severe Analytical Errors (\(\pm 15–30\%\)):
    • Acid hematin is unstable and color darkens progressively over hours.
    • Fetal Hemoglobin (\(\text{HbF}\)) is totally resistant to conversion into acid hematin; completely useless for neonates and infants \(<3\ \text{months}\).
    • Severe subjective visual variation, light source discrepancies, and comparator glass fading.
Lovibond & Tallqvist Blotting Paper Methods:

Lovibond disc comparator in multicenter trials yielded unacceptable quality in \(>63\%\) of tests. Tallqvist paper estimation has excessive random error and is completely condemned by WHO.

Reference Ranges & Preliminary Diagnostic Matrix

Interpretation of blood hemoglobin concentrations must always account for biological variables including age, sex, gestational state, and physiological altitude adaptation:

Normal Haemoglobin Reference Ranges (Sea Level)

Patient Demographic SI Units (\(\text{g/L}\)) Conventional Units (\(\text{g/dL}\))
Newborns (Cord / Capillary at Birth) \(135–195\ \text{g/L}\) \(13.5–19.5\ \text{g/dL}\)
Infants (1–12 Months) \(100–140\ \text{g/L}\) \(10.0–14.0\ \text{g/dL}\)
Children (2–5 Years) \(110–140\ \text{g/L}\) \(11.0–14.0\ \text{g/dL}\)
Children (6–12 Years) \(115–155\ \text{g/L}\) \(11.5–15.5\ \text{g/dL}\)
Adult Males \(130–180\ \text{g/L}\) \(13.0–18.0\ \text{g/dL}\)
Adult Non-Pregnant Females \(120–150\ \text{g/L}\) \(12.0–15.0\ \text{g/dL}\)
Pregnant Females (2nd & 3rd Trimesters) \(110–140\ \text{g/L}\) \(11.0–14.0\ \text{g/dL}\)
High Altitude Physiological Compensation: At altitudes \(>1000\ \text{meters}\) above sea level, atmospheric oxygen tension (\(\text{pO}_2\)) decreases, stimulating renal erythropoietin secretion. Basal normal hemoglobin ranges increase by \(+5–20\ \text{g/L}\).

Chart 8.5: Differential Diagnosis Matrix of Tropical Anaemias

Anaemia Etiology Peripheral Film Morphology Key Laboratory Indices & Confirmatory Tests
Iron Deficiency (IDA) Microcytic, hypochromic RBCs, pencil/cigar cells, marked anisopoikilocytosis. \(\text{MCV} < 78\ \text{fL}\), \(\text{MCHC} < 320\ \text{g/L}\), Serum ferritin \(\downarrow\), Stool hookworm ova / occult blood positive.
Megaloblastic (Folate / \(\text{B}_{12}\)) Macro-ovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils (\(\ge 5\) lobes), pancytopenia in late stages. \(\text{MCV} > 100\ \text{fL}\), \(\text{MCHC}\) normal, Reticulocytes \(\downarrow\), Megaloblasts in bone marrow smears.
Sickle Cell Disease (HbSS, HbSC) Sickle/drepanocytes, target cells, nucleated RBCs, basophilic stippling, Howell-Jolly bodies. Positive Sodium Metabisulfite Sickling Test, Reticulocytosis (\(>5\%\)), \(\text{HbS}\) band on Alkaline Electrophoresis (\(\text{pH}\ 8.6\)).
Falciparum Malaria Normocytic normochromic RBCs, intraerythrocytic delicate ring trophozoites, Maurer's dots. Thick & Thin blood film Giemsa stain; hemozoin malaria pigment phagocytosed inside monocytes/neutrophils.
G6PD Deficiency Crisis Bite/degmacytes, blister cells, spherocytes, irregularly contracted cells, polychromasia. Heinz bodies visualized on Supravital Methyl Violet stain; G6PD screening assay (performed after crisis resolves).
Clostridial Sepsis (\(C. \text{perfringens}\)) Microspherocytes, extreme polychromasia, ghost RBCs, severe toxic neutrophil granulations. Massive intravascular hemolysis, blood cultures, positive anaerobic Clostridium identification.

8.5 Packed Cell Volume (PCV / Haematocrit) & Red Cell Indices

Microhaematocrit Centrifugation SOP (\(11,800–12,000\ \text{rpm}\) / \(12,000–15,000\times g\) for \(5\ \text{minutes}\)) • Capillary Tube Specifications (Plain Blue vs Heparinized Red Band) • Sealing Protocols & Rotary Reader Alignment • Trapped Plasma Errors in Sickle Cell Disease (\(+20\%\)) & Spherocytosis (\(+6\%\)) • Plasma Inspection (Icterus, Hemolysis, Lipemia) • Mathematical Formulations & Unit Derivations: \(\text{MCHC}\) (\(\text{g/L}\) & \(\text{g/dL}\)), \(\text{MCV}\) (\(\text{fL}\)), \(\text{MCH}\) (\(\text{pg}\)), \(\text{RDW}\) • Diagnostic Cutoffs for Tropical Anaemias.

Monica Cheesbrough Microhaematocrit Golden Rule: When reading a centrifuged PCV tube, the baseline of the packed red cell column (above the clay sealant) must align on the \(0\) line and the top of the plasma meniscus on the \(100\) line. The reading MUST be taken strictly at the junction between the red cell column and the buffy coat. Never include the buffy coat (consisting of leukocytes and platelets) in the PCV measurement! In Sickle Cell Disease, rigid sickled cells trap up to \(20\%\) excess interstitial plasma, causing substantial overestimation of the true PCV.

Packed Cell Volume (PCV / Haematocrit) Micro Method

The Packed Cell Volume (PCV), or haematocrit, represents the proportion of whole blood volume occupied by red blood cells, expressed as a decimal fraction (\(\text{L/L}\)) in SI units or as a percentage (\(\%\)). It provides a rapid, accurate screen for anaemia and hemoconcentration.

Capillary Tube Selection & Filling SOP

Standardized capillary tubes are precision bore glass tubes (\(75\ \text{mm}\) length, internal diameter \(1.1–1.2\ \text{mm}\)):

  • Heparinized Capillaries (Red Ring / Band): Internally coated with \(1–2\ \text{IU}\) ammonium or lithium heparin. Mandatory for direct skin puncture (capillary blood).
  • Plain Non-Heparinized Capillaries (Blue Ring / Band): Uncoated glass. Mandatory when sampling from well-mixed EDTA anticoagulated venous blood.
  • Filling Volume: Allow blood to enter the capillary by capillary action until it fills \(2/3\ \text{to}\ 3/4\) of the tube length (approx. \(50–60\ \text{mm}\)). Leave \(15–20\ \text{mm}\) unfilled.
  • Tube Sealing: Seal the dry, unfilled end with non-absorbent clay / plasticine sealant (e.g., Cristaseal) at an angle of \(90^\circ\) by rotating into the sealant tray. The sealant plug must be \(4–6\ \text{mm}\) deep with a flat internal surface.

Centrifugation Mechanics & Safety Protocol

Centrifuge Parameter Standard Specification Rationale & Safety Rule
Centrifugal Force (RCF) \(12,000–15,000 \times g\) Ensures maximum erythrocyte packing
Rotational Speed \(11,800–12,000\ \text{rpm}\) High speed required for micro-rotor geometry
Spinning Time Exactly 5 Minutes Optimal packing; undercentrifugation leaves excess trapped plasma
Rotor Placement Rule Sealed end facing outward against rubber gasket Centrifugal force presses clay into glass; inverted placement causes complete blood expulsion!
Inner Rotor Safety Lid Firmly screwed down before closing main outer lid Prevents tube fly-out, glass breakage, and aerosol biohazards in motor housing

Microhaematocrit Reading SOP & Ruler Calculation

Using a Graphic Microhaematocrit Reader (Spiral / Card Reader):

  1. Place the capillary tube in the grooved channel of the reader.
  2. Align the bottom junction of the red cell column and sealant plug precisely on the \(0\%\) / \(0.00\) baseline.
  3. Adjust the movable rule or rotary scale until the line intersects the top meniscus of the plasma column at the \(100\%\) / \(1.00\) line.
  4. Read the PCV value directly from the scale at the apex of the packed red cell column (immediately below the grayish-white buffy coat layer).

Calculation When No Graphic Reader is Available (Millimeter Ruler Method):

\[\text{PCV (L/L)} = \frac{\text{Length of Red Cell Column (mm)}}{\text{Total Length of Column [Red Cells + Plasma] (mm)}}\]

Example: If the red cell column measures \(18\ \text{mm}\) and the total column (from clay interface to plasma meniscus) measures \(50\ \text{mm}\): \[\text{PCV} = \frac{18\ \text{mm}}{50\ \text{mm}} = 0.36\ \text{L/L}\quad (36\%)\]

Wintrobe Red Cell Indices: Mathematical Formulations & Unit Derivations

Red cell indices define the physical dimensions, volume, and hemoglobin concentration of average circulating erythrocytes. They are indispensable for morphological classification of anaemias.

MCHC (Mean Cell Hb Concentration)

Concentration of hemoglobin in \(1\ \text{L}\) of packed erythrocytes.

\[\text{MCHC (g/L)} = \frac{\text{Hb (g/L)}}{\text{PCV (L/L)}}\] \[\text{MCHC (g/dL)} = \frac{\text{Hb (g/dL)} \times 100}{\text{PCV (\%)}}\]
  • Reference Range: \(315–360\ \text{g/L}\) (\(31.5–36.0\ \text{g/dL}\)).
  • District Feasibility: Calculable in any basic district laboratory possessing a photometer and microhaematocrit centrifuge without needing an electronic RBC count!
  • Clinical Sensitivity: \(\downarrow <315\ \text{g/L}\) in severe Iron Deficiency Anaemia & advanced hypochromia.

MCV (Mean Cell Volume)

Average volume / size of a single red blood cell.

\[\text{MCV (fL)} = \frac{\text{PCV (L/L)} \times 1000}{\text{RBC Count } (10^{12}/\text{L})}\] (\(1\ \text{femtolitre [fL]} = 10^{-15}\ \text{L}\))
  • Reference Range: \(80–98\ \text{fL}\).
  • Microcytosis (\(<80\ \text{fL}\)): Iron deficiency, Thalassaemia trait, Sideroblastic anaemia, ACD.
  • Macrocytosis (\(>98\ \text{fL}\)): Megaloblastic anaemia (\(\text{B}_{12}\)/Folate deficiency \(>100–120\ \text{fL}\)), reticulocytosis, severe liver disease.
  • Requirement: Requires automated electronic cell counter for accurate RBC enumeration.

MCH (Mean Cell Haemoglobin)

Average mass / weight of hemoglobin in a single red cell.

\[\text{MCH (pg)} = \frac{\text{Hb (g/L)}}{\text{RBC Count } (10^{12}/\text{L})}\] (\(1\ \text{picogram [pg]} = 10^{-12}\ \text{g}\))
  • Reference Range: \(27–32\ \text{pg}\).
  • Hypochromia (\(<27\ \text{pg}\)): Microcytic hypochromic anaemias. In \(\beta\)-Thalassaemia minor, MCH is markedly reduced even when anaemia is very mild (MCHC may remain normal).
  • Hyperchromia (\(>32\ \text{pg}\)): True hyperchromia does not occur, but MCH increases in macrocytes due to their enlarged cellular volume.

Summary Matrix of Red Cell Indices across Morphological Classes

Morphological Classification MCV (\(80–98\ \text{fL}\)) MCH (\(27–32\ \text{pg}\)) MCHC (\(315–360\ \text{g/L}\)) Prototypic Tropical Etiologies
Normocytic Normochromic Normal Normal Normal Acute blood loss, Plasmodium falciparum malaria, aplastic anaemia, anaemia of chronic kidney disease.
Microcytic Hypochromic \(\downarrow\) Reduced (\(<78\ \text{fL}\)) \(\downarrow\) Reduced (\(<27\ \text{pg}\)) \(\downarrow\) Reduced (\(<315\ \text{g/L}\)) Iron deficiency anaemia (hookworm/schistosomiasis/dietary), severe untreated thalassaemia major.
Microcytic Normochromic / Borderline \(\downarrow\) Reduced \(\downarrow\) Reduced Normal \(\beta\)-Thalassaemia trait / minor, early Anaemia of Chronic Disease (ACD), lead poisoning.
Macrocytic Normochromic \(\uparrow\) Elevated (\(>100\ \text{fL}\)) \(\uparrow\) Elevated (\(>32\ \text{pg}\)) Normal Folate deficiency (malnutrition/pregnancy), Vitamin \(\text{B}_{12}\) deficiency, severe reticulocytosis, chronic alcoholism.

Trapped Plasma Dynamics & Analytical Quality Control

When red blood cells are packed under high centrifugal force, a small volume of plasma remains trapped within the intercellular spaces between adjacent RBC membranes. In healthy individuals, this trapped plasma represents approximately \(1–3\%\) of the packed column.

Pathological Trapped Plasma Hyper-Elevation

Any alteration in erythrocyte flexibility, deformability, or abnormal geometric contour significantly impairs tight physical packing:

Sickle Cell Disease (HbSS / HbSC):

Rigid, non-deformable irreversibly sickled cells (drepanocytes) cannot align or compress tightly in the micro-centrifuge field. Trapped plasma increases up to \(+20\%\) of the measured PCV value. A measured PCV of \(0.24\ \text{L/L}\) may represent a true cellular PCV of only \(\approx 0.19–0.20\ \text{L/L}\)!

Hereditary Spherocytosis & Marked Anisopoikilocytosis:

Spherical erythrocytes lack the normal biconcave disc deformability, increasing trapped plasma by \(+4–6\%\). Similar trapping occurs in severe microcytosis and macrocytic target cell states.

Systematic Sources of Error & Quality Control SOP

Error Mechanism Analytical Consequence Corrective Prevention Rule
Centrifugation \(<12,000\times g\) or \(<5\ \text{min}\) Falsely Elevated PCV Ensure fixed speed (\(11,800–12,000\ \text{rpm}\)) and strict 5-minute timer control.
Excess EDTA (Underfilled Tube) Falsely Reduced PCV High anticoagulant hypertonicity draws water out of RBCs causing cellular shrinkage (\(\downarrow \text{PCV}\)). Fill tubes to line!
Delayed Reading (\(>6\ \text{hours}\) old blood) Falsely Elevated PCV In vitro storage causes red cells to swell due to ATP depletion and sodium influx. Test within \(4–6\ \text{hours}\).
Microclots in Anticoagulated Blood Falsely Reduced PCV Fibrin entrapment removes red cells from suspension; always inspect blood for microclots before filling capillary.
Inadequate Venous Mixing Erratic / Spurious PCV Invert EDTA tube gently \(8–10\times\) immediately before sampling.
Reading Delay Post-Centrifugation Plasma evaporation / Cell relaxation Read capillary within \(10\ \text{minutes}\) of centrifuge stopping.
Duplicate Testing Rule: Routine QC requires running duplicate capillary tubes for each patient batch. Duplicate values must agree within \(\pm 5\%\) (or within \(0.01\ \text{L/L}\)).

Reference Ranges, Clinical Correlations & Supernatant Plasma Inspection

The microhaematocrit tube yields crucial ancillary clinical diagnostic clues beyond the packed red cell volume alone, including the physical appearance of the supernatant plasma column and the thickness of the buffy coat.

PCV Reference Ranges (Sea Level)

Demographic Group SI Units (\(\text{L/L}\)) Conventional Units (\(\%\))
Newborn Infants (at Birth) \(0.44–0.54\ \text{L/L}\) \(44–54\%\)
Children (2–5 Years) \(0.34–0.40\ \text{L/L}\) \(34–40\%\)
Children (6–12 Years) \(0.35–0.45\ \text{L/L}\) \(35–45\%\)
Adult Males \(0.40–0.54\ \text{L/L}\) \(40–54\%\)
Adult Females (Non-Pregnant) \(0.36–0.46\ \text{L/L}\) \(36–46\%\)
Pathological Elevations: Increased PCV occurs in Polycythaemia vera, secondary erythrocytosis (chronic hypoxia / cyanotic congenital heart disease), and acute plasma loss causing relative hemoconcentration (severe cholera dehydration, extensive thermal burns, and Dengue Haemorrhagic Fever capillary plasma leakage syndrome).

Visual Inspection of Supernatant Plasma Column

Always inspect the color and clarity of the supernatant plasma layer in the microhaematocrit tube before discarding:

Plasma Appearance Underlying Pathology Differential Diagnosis
Clear Pale Straw Normal Physiological State Healthy baseline.
Deep Golden-Yellow / Orange Marked Hyperbilirubinaemia (\(\text{Icterus}\)) Hemolytic crisis, viral hepatitis, biliary obstruction, severe neonatal jaundice.
Pink to Deep Red (Clear) Free Plasma Hemoglobin (\(\text{Haemoglobinaemia}\)) Intravascular hemolysis (Blackwater fever, G6PD crisis, ABO mismatch transfusion reaction) or traumatic phlebotomy lysis.
Milky / Opalescent White Hypertriglyceridemia / Chylomicrons (\(\text{Lipaemia}\)) Postprandial blood draw, familial hyperlipidemia, pancreatitis. Causes false HiCN elevation!
Exaggerated White Buffy Coat (\(>1.5\ \text{mm}\)) Marked Leukocytosis / Thrombocytosis Leukemias (CML/AML), severe pyogenic infections, leukemoid reactions.

8.6 White Blood Cell & Platelet Counting (Manual & Automated)

Manual Hemocytometry SOPs • Turk's Diluting Fluid Chemistry (2% Glacial Acetic Acid + Gentian Violet) • Improved Neubauer Bright-Line Grid Geometry (\(9\ \text{mm}^2\) Total Area, \(0.1\ \text{mm}\) Depth, \(4\ \text{mm}^2\) Corner Squares \(W_1–W_4\)) • Newton's Interference Rings • Mathematical Formulations: WBC Factor \(\frac{\text{Count}}{20}\times 10^9/\text{L}\) • Nucleated RBC (NRBC) Correction Algorithm • High/Low Count Dilution Adjustments • Manual Platelet Enumeration (\(1\%\) Ammonium Oxalate Reagent No. 70 in Central Small Squares \(P\)) • Humidified Petri Dish Incubation (\(20\ \text{min}\)) • Onyalai Acute Bleeding Syndrome • Electronic Impedance Aperture Physics (Coulter Principle & Sysmex Thresholding).

Monica Cheesbrough Hemocytometry Golden Rules: (1) When counting in an Improved Neubauer chamber, observe the inclusion boundary rule: count all cells inside the square plus those touching the top and left boundary lines, ignoring cells touching the bottom and right lines to avoid double-counting. (2) When a stained thin blood film reveals \(>10\ \text{nucleated red blood cells (NRBCs) per 100 WBCs}\), the manual or impedance WBC count is spuriously elevated because erythroblast nuclei resist acid lysis; you MUST apply the mandatory NRBC correction formula before reporting!

Improved Neubauer Counting Chamber (Haemocytometer) Architecture

The Improved Neubauer ruled hemocytometer is the international reference manual counting chamber. For optimum visibility and optical contrast in tropical district laboratories, a metallized surface ('Bright-Line') double-cell chamber is strongly recommended over plain glass chambers.

Grid Dimensions & Geometric Volumes

  • Total Grid Surface Area: \(3.0\ \text{mm} \times 3.0\ \text{mm} = \mathbf{9.0\ \text{mm}^2}\).
  • Chamber Depth (\(d\)): Precisely \(0.1\ \text{mm}\) (\(1/10\ \text{mm}\)) between the ruled grid floor and the underside of the heavy optical coverslip.
  • Total Chamber Volume: \(9.0\ \text{mm}^2 \times 0.1\ \text{mm} = \mathbf{0.9\ \text{mm}^3}\) (\(0.9\ \mu\text{L}\)).
  • Four Large Corner Squares (\(W_1, W_2, W_3, W_4\)):
    • Each corner square = \(1.0\ \text{mm} \times 1.0\ \text{mm} = \mathbf{1.0\ \text{mm}^2}\).
    • Each is subdivided into \(16\) smaller squares of \(0.25\ \text{mm} \times 0.25\ \text{mm}\).
    • Combined area used for WBC counting = \(4 \times 1.0\ \text{mm}^2 = \mathbf{4.0\ \text{mm}^2}\) (Volume = \(0.4\ \text{mm}^3\)).
  • Central Large Square (RBC & Platelet Grid):
    • Dimensions = \(1.0\ \text{mm} \times 1.0\ \text{mm} = \mathbf{1.0\ \text{mm}^2}\).
    • Subdivided into \(25\) group squares by triple boundary lines, each group containing \(16\) tiny squares (\(400\) mini-squares total).
    • Five group squares marked \(P\) (4 corners + 1 center) = \(5 \times 0.04\ \text{mm}^2 = \mathbf{0.2\ \text{mm}^2}\) (Volume = \(0.02\ \text{mm}^3\)), used for platelet counting.

Chamber Assembly & Newton's Rings

Accurate cell counting requires precise assembly with specialized optical glass coverslips:

Newton's Interference Rings Verification:

Standard microscope coverslips are too flexible and bow under capillary surface tension, altering chamber depth. You must use a special thick, optically plane hemocytometer cover glass (\(0.4–0.5\ \text{mm}\) thickness). Moisten the polished glass supports, slide the cover glass horizontally over the central grids, and apply firm downward thumb pressure until brilliant rainbow-colored concentric interference fringes (Newton's rings) appear on both sides, confirming exact \(0.1\ \text{mm}\) chamber depth.

Bulb Pipettes Warning: Historical Thoma white/red cell glass bulb pipettes are prone to inadequate mixing, difficult to clean, and cause biohazard mouth-pipetting risks. Always use precision micropipettes (\(20\ \mu\text{L}\)) or calibrated glass capillaries with safe bulb fillers.

Manual Total White Blood Cell (WBC) Count Protocol

The total white blood cell count enumerates all circulating leukocytes per liter of blood, guiding diagnosis in acute bacterial infections, leukemias, appendicitis, and HIV-related leukopenia.

Turk's Diluting Fluid (Reagent No. 88) & Dilution SOP

Component Concentration Functional Action
Glacial Acetic Acid \(2.0\ \text{mL}\) in \(100\ \text{mL}\) (\(2\%\)) Rapidly lyses non-nucleated erythrocytes; leaves leukocytes and nucleated RBCs intact
Gentian / Crystal Violet (1% aq) \(1.0\ \text{mL}\) in \(100\ \text{mL}\) Stains leukocyte nuclei deep violet-black for crisp microscopical visualization
Distilled Water to \(100\ \text{mL}\) Solvent matrix (filter before use to remove dye crystals)
Standard 1:20 Dilution Procedure:
  1. Dispense \(0.38\ \text{mL}\) (\(380\ \mu\text{L}\)) of Turk's diluting fluid into a small tube.
  2. Add \(20\ \mu\text{L}\) (\(0.02\ \text{mL}\)) of well-mixed EDTA blood (or capillary blood), wiping the pipette exterior. This gives an exact \(1:20\) dilution.
  3. Mix thoroughly and charge the hemocytometer using a capillary or pastette held at \(45^\circ\). Allow cells to settle for 2 minutes in a humidified petri dish.

Mathematical Formula & Simplified Shortcut

Using the \(10\times\) objective, count all leukocytes in the 4 large corner squares (\(W_1, W_2, W_3, W_4\), total area = \(4.0\ \text{mm}^2\)):

\[\text{Total WBC Count (per Liter)} = \frac{N \times \text{Dilution (20)} \times 10^6}{\text{Area } (4.0\ \text{mm}^2) \times \text{Depth } (0.1\ \text{mm})}\] \[\text{Total WBC Count} = \frac{N \times 20 \times 10^6}{0.4} = N \times 50 \times 10^6 = \mathbf{\frac{N}{20} \times 10^9/\text{L}}\]

Monica's Quick Mental Shortcut:
1. Divide total cells counted (\(N\)) by \(2\).
2. Divide the result by \(10\).
3. The resulting number is your WBC count in \(\times 10^9/\text{L}\).
Example: If \(84\) cells are counted in 4 squares: \(84 \div 2 = 42\); \(42 \div 10 = \mathbf{4.2 \times 10^9/\text{L}}\).

Nucleated RBC (NRBC) Correction Algorithm

In conditions with high erythropoietic drive (severe hemolytic anaemias, Sickle Cell crisis, \(\beta\)-Thalassaemia major, erythroblastosis fetalis), nucleated red cells are released into peripheral blood. Because acetic acid lyses the red cell cytoplasm but leaves the nucleus intact, NRBCs are indistinguishable from small lymphocytes on the hemocytometer and falsely elevate the raw WBC count.

Mandatory Correction Formula (when \(\text{NRBC} > 10 / 100\ \text{WBC}\)): \[\text{Corrected WBC Count } (10^9/\text{L}) = \text{Uncorrected WBC Count} \times \frac{100}{100 + \text{NRBC Count}}\]

Example: If the uncorrected WBC count is \(24.0 \times 10^9/\text{L}\) and the stained blood film shows \(25\ \text{NRBCs per } 100\ \text{WBCs}\): \[\text{Corrected WBC} = 24.0 \times \frac{100}{100 + 25} = 24.0 \times \frac{100}{125} = \mathbf{19.2 \times 10^9/\text{L}}\]

Dilution Adjustments for Extreme WBC Counts

Clinical Situation Modified Dilution Technique Calculation Factor
Counts \(> 50.0 \times 10^9/\text{L}\) (Severe Leukaemia / Leukemoid) Dispense \(0.76\ \text{mL}\) diluent + \(20\ \mu\text{L}\) blood (\(1:39\) approx \(1:40\) dilution). Calculate standard WBC count and multiply by 2.
Counts \(< 2.0 \times 10^9/\text{L}\) (Profound Leukopenia / Aplastic) Dispense \(0.38\ \text{mL}\) diluent + \(40\ \mu\text{L}\) blood (\(1:10.5\) approx \(1:10\) dilution). Calculate standard WBC count and divide by 2.
Reference Ranges: Adults \(4.0–10.0 \times 10^9/\text{L}\) (Adults of African origin \(2.6–8.3 \times 10^9/\text{L}\) due to benign ethnic neutropenia); Children 1 yr \(6.0–18.0 \times 10^9/\text{L}\); Pregnancy up to \(15.0 \times 10^9/\text{L}\).

Manual Platelet Enumeration & Tropical Thrombocytopenias

Platelets (thrombocytes) are delicate, non-nucleated fragments (\(2–4\ \mu\text{m}\)) prone to aggregation and lysis. Manual platelet counting requires precision dilution and phase-contrast or low-illumination brightfield microscopy.

1% Ammonium Oxalate Reagent (No. 70) SOP

Principle: \(1\%\ \text{w/v}\) Ammonium oxalate (\((\text{NH}_4)_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4\)) completely hemolyzes erythrocytes while preserving platelet structure and preventing adhesion.

  • Dilution: Add \(20\ \mu\text{L}\) of EDTA venous blood to \(0.38\ \text{mL}\) of \(1\%\) ammonium oxalate (\(1:20\) dilution). Mix gently for 2 minutes.
  • Charging Chamber: Fill the Improved Neubauer chamber.
  • Humidified Incubation (Crucial Step): Place chamber in a closed Petri dish lined with water-dampened filter paper for exactly 20 minutes to allow platelets to settle onto the grid floor without evaporation.
  • Microscopical Reading: Using the \(40\times\) objective with the condenser lowered/aperture stopped down, count refractile oval/round platelet bodies in the 5 small squares marked \(P\) of the central square (\(0.2\ \text{mm}^2\) total area).
\[\text{Platelet Count (per Liter)} = \frac{N \times 20 \times 10^6}{0.2 \times 0.1} = \frac{N \times 20 \times 10^6}{0.02} = \mathbf{N \times 10^9/\text{L}}\] Direct Rule: The total platelets counted in the 5 group squares (\(N\)) directly equals the platelet count in \(\times 10^9/\text{L}\) (e.g., \(150\ \text{platelets counted} = \mathbf{150 \times 10^9/\text{L}}\)).

Tropical Thrombocytopenias & Onyalai Syndrome

Normal Platelet Range: \(150–400 \times 10^9/\text{L}\). Platelet counts \(\le 20 \times 10^9/\text{L}\) constitute critical panic values for spontaneous intracranial/mucosal hemorrhage.

Onyalai (Acute Tropical Thrombocytopenic Purpura):
  • Geographic Endemicity: Southern Africa (Southern Angola, Northern Namibia, Kavango, Ovamboland). Primarily affects children and young adults.
  • Hallmark Presentation: Sudden appearance of massive blood-filled haemorrhagic bullae on the buccal mucosa and palate, epistaxis, hematuria, and severe thrombocytopenia (\(\le 20 \times 10^9/\text{L}\)).
  • Etiology & Mortality: Presumed immune-mediated destruction triggered by mycotoxins in moldy grain/sorghum; mortality reaches \(10\%\) from acute hemorrhagic shock without blood/platelet support.
Other Key Causes of Severe Thrombocytopenia: Severe falciparum malaria (sequestration/consumption), Dengue Haemorrhagic Fever, Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC), Visceral Leishmaniasis, and ITP.

Automated Electronic Impedance Blood Cell Counting

Modern automated haematology analyzers (e.g., Beckman Coulter, Sysmex, Mindray) utilize the Coulter principle of electrical impedance to enumerate cells and measure volumetric distributions.

The Coulter Principle of Electrical Impedance

Blood cells are suspended in an isotonic conductive electrolyte diluent and drawn by constant vacuum through a micro-aperture (\(70–100\ \mu\text{m}\) diameter) across which a constant electrical direct current flows between internal and external platinum electrodes:

  • Non-Conductivity: Blood cells act as near-perfect electrical insulators. As a cell passes through the aperture, it displaces its own volume of electrolyte, momentarily increasing electrical resistance (impedance).
  • Pulse Height (Amplitude): The voltage pulse amplitude produced is directly proportional to the cell's physical volume (\(\text{Pulse Height} \propto \text{Cell Volume in fL}\)).
  • Pulse Count (Frequency): The total number of pulses generated per unit volume of blood corresponds to the absolute cell count.
  • Electronic Thresholding: Lower and upper discriminators filter electronic noise and separate platelets (\(2–20\ \text{fL}\)), red blood cells (\(36–360\ \text{fL}\)), and white blood cells (after reagent lysis of RBCs).

Operational Prerequisites for District Laboratories

Cheesbrough outlines strict criteria before deploying automated electronic analyzers in tropical resource-limited settings:

Critical Requirement Specification & Risk Mitigation
Workload & Cost Sufficiently high daily test volume to justify expensive consumable reagents, calibrants, and commercial controls.
Environmental Control Mains voltage stabilizer / UPS battery backup; operating temperature \(15–30^\circ\text{C}\); dust-free air-conditioned environment.
Reagent Supply Chain Guaranteed local availability of isotonic diluent, lysing agent, enzymatic cleaner, and fresh calibrators with valid expiry dates.
Technical Maintenance Biannual servicing by factory-trained biomedical engineers; routine background count checks and aperture de-clogging.

8.7 Blood Films, Romanowsky Staining & Morphological Identification

Thin Blood Smear Spreading Dynamics (\(30–45^\circ\) Spreader Angle, Monolayer Feathered Edge) • Water-Free Absolute Methanol Fixation Protocol (\(<2\ \text{minutes}\)) • Romanowsky Dye Chemistry: Methylene Blue / Azure Azurophilic Oxidation & Eosin Y Acidophilic Binding • Buffer pH 6.8 Tight Tolerance • Staining Formulations: Leishman, Giemsa, Field Stain, Wright's • Battlement Tracking Count Technique (\(100–200\ \text{WBCs}\)) • Leukocyte Morphology: Toxic Granulations, Döhle Bodies, Neutrophil Hypersegmentation (\(\ge 5\) Lobes), Reactive / Atypical Lymphocytes • Erythrocyte Morphology Atlas: Microcytes, Macrocytes, Pencil Cells, Target Cells (Leptocytes), Sickle Cells (Drepanocytes), Spherocytes, Schistocytes, Burr Cells (Echinocytes), Acanthocytes, Tear Drop Cells (Dacryocytes), Half-Ghost Blister Cells • Intraerythrocytic Inclusions: Howell-Jolly Bodies, Basophilic Stippling, Cabot Rings, Pappenheimer Bodies & Auer Rods.

Monica Cheesbrough Blood Film Golden Rules: (1) Methanol containing even trace moisture produces severe water-fixation artifacts (refractile vacuoles and notched RBC margins). Always use pure, water-free absolute methanol dispensed from a tightly capped TK dropping bottle. (2) When washing off Leishman or Giemsa stain, flood the slide with clean water before tilting; never tip off the stain directly, or an insoluble metallic surface scum will permanently precipitate across the blood film. (3) Differential WBC counts must be conducted using the battlement track technique exclusively within the optimal monolayer behind the feathered edge.

Thin Blood Film Preparation & Water-Free Methanol Fixation

A well-made, properly fixed thin blood film is the cornerstone of diagnostic haematology in tropical medicine, allowing high-resolution microscopical appraisal of leukocyte lineage, erythrocyte architecture, and blood parasites.

Thin Film Spreading Standard Operating Procedure (SOP)

  • Slide Selection: Use clean, grease-free glass slides with ground-glass polished edges. Wipe with 70% ethanol and dry before use.
  • Blood Drop Placement: Place a small drop of blood (approx. \(5–10\ \mu\text{L}\) / \(2–3\ \text{mm}\) diameter) about \(1\ \text{cm}\) from the frosted end of the slide.
  • Spreader Angle: Place a smooth-edged glass spreader at an angle of \(30^\circ\ \text{to}\ 45^\circ\) in front of the blood drop. Draw the spreader back until it touches the drop, allowing blood to spread along the line of contact.
  • Spreading Motion: With a single, smooth, continuous, rapid motion, push the spreader forward along the slide surface.
  • Anatomy of a Perfect Smear:
    • Should occupy \(2/3\) the length of the slide (\(\approx 30–40\ \text{mm}\)).
    • Smooth, lateral margins narrower than the slide width.
    • Gradual transition from thick body to a translucent monolayer with a feathered, tongue-shaped tail without streaks, ridges, or holes.

Water-Free Absolute Methanol Fixation

Thin smears must be completely air-dried before fixation. Fixing wet blood causes osmotic lysis and artifactual cell rupture:

Fixation SOP & Chemical Storage:
  • Fixative: 100% water-free absolute methanol (acetone-free). Technical grade methanol is strictly prohibited.
  • Fixation Time: Immerse or flood slide for \(1–2\ \text{minutes}\) (or \(2–3\ \text{minutes}\) in humid climates).
  • Dispensing Container: Use a tightly stoppered amber glass drop bottle (e.g., TK bottle). Methanol is highly hygroscopic; exposure to humid air causes absorption of atmospheric water.
Water-Contamination Artifacts (Plate 8.4):

When methanol contains as little as \(1–2\%\) water, erythrocytes exhibit marked crenation, central unstained punched-out holes, refractile rings, and distorted nuclear chromatin, masquerading as hypochromia, malaria rings, or target cells.

Romanowsky Dye Chemistry & Staining Formulations

All Romanowsky-type stains consist of a mixture of polychromed (oxidized) basic dyes (Methylene Blue and Azures A, B, C) and an acidic dye (Eosin Y / Eosin B), producing the characteristic polychromatic Romanowsky effect.

Romanowsky Chemical Principles & Buffer pH 6.8

  • Basic Components (Methylene Blue & Azures): Cationic dyes that bind to acidic, negatively charged cell components (DNA, RNA, basophilic granules, nucleoli), imparting deep purple-blue to violet staining.
  • Acidic Component (Eosin Y): Anionic dye that binds to basic, positively charged proteins (hemoglobin, eosinophilic cationic granules), imparting bright orange-pink to red staining.
  • Crucial Role of Buffer pH 6.8:
    • The optimum pH for Romanowsky staining of blood cells is strictly \(\text{pH}\ 6.8\) (using Sörensen's or buffered water Reagent No. 15).
    • If Buffer \(\text{pH} < 6.4\) (Acidic): Red cells stain bright red/orange; leukocyte nuclei stain pale pink; granules fail to stain (understaining).
    • If Buffer \(\text{pH} > 7.2\) (Alkaline): Red cells stain slate blue/gray; leukocyte nuclei and cytoplasm stain dark blue-black; toxic granulations are falsely exaggerated (overstaining).

Comparative Matrix of Romanowsky Staining Protocols

Staining Protocol Fixation Step Staining Method & Time Key District Laboratory Utility
Leishman Stain (Reagent No. 43) Self-fixing (undiluted stain contains pure methanol) Flood smear with neat stain for \(2\ \text{min}\) (fixes), add \(2\times\) volume buffered water (\(\text{pH}\ 6.8\)), mix, stain for \(8–10\ \text{min}\). Standard routine haematology stain for differential WBC counts and general morphology.
Giemsa Stain (Reagent No. 34) Pre-fix with methanol for \(2\ \text{min}\) Dilute stock \(1:10\) in buffered water (\(\text{pH}\ 6.8–7.2\)); stain for \(20–30\ \text{min}\). Gold standard for blood parasites (malaria, trypanosomes, borrelia) and bone marrow aspirates.
Field Stain (Reagents No. 27 & 28) Pre-fix with methanol for \(1\ \text{min}\) Dip in Field Stain A (Azure) for \(5\ \text{sec}\), rinse, dip in Field Stain B (Eosin) for \(5\ \text{sec}\), wash. Rapid 30-second stat staining in emergency rooms and peripheral mobile clinics.
Wright's Stain Self-fixing in methanol Neat stain \(1–2\ \text{min}\), add equal volume buffer, stain \(4–6\ \text{min}\). Common in North American practice; rapid differentiation.
Washing Off Rule: Always wash off stain with running tap/buffered water while the slide is horizontal. Never tip off stain before flooding, or the oxidized dye scum on the surface will stick to the film as insoluble metallic debris.

Differential WBC Counting & Leukocyte Morphological Anomalies

The differential leukocyte count enumerates the percentage and absolute concentration of each mature and immature white blood cell lineage in peripheral blood.

Battlement (Meander) Scanning Technique

Heavier white cells (neutrophils and monocytes) are pushed toward the lateral edges and tail of a blood film, while lighter lymphocytes remain concentrated in the body. To obtain an unbiased representation, use the battlement tracking pattern:

  • Scan across 3 fields along the edge of the monolayer.
  • Move 3 fields in toward the central body of the film.
  • Move 3 fields parallel to the edge, then 3 fields back to the edge.
  • Count a minimum of \(100\ \text{WBCs}\) (or \(200\ \text{WBCs}\) if total WBC is elevated).

Adult Leukocyte Reference Ranges (Relative & Absolute)

Leukocyte Lineage Relative Percentage (%) Absolute Count (\(\times 10^9/\text{L}\))
Neutrophils (Segmented + Bands) \(40–75\%\) \(2.0–7.5 \times 10^9/\text{L}\)
Lymphocytes \(20–45\%\) \(1.0–4.0 \times 10^9/\text{L}\)
Monocytes \(2–10\%\) \(0.2–0.8 \times 10^9/\text{L}\)
Eosinophils \(1–6\%\) \(0.04–0.4 \times 10^9/\text{L}\)
Basophils \(0–1\%\) \(0.01–0.1 \times 10^9/\text{L}\)
Benign Ethnic Neutropenia: Healthy individuals of African descent frequently exhibit baseline absolute neutrophil counts of \(1.0–1.5 \times 10^9/\text{L}\) with total WBC \(2.6–8.3 \times 10^9/\text{L}\).

High-Yield Leukocyte Morphological Abnormalities

Toxic Granulations & Döhle Bodies

Description: Coarse dark purple-violet primary azurophilic granules in neutrophil cytoplasm; paired with light-blue peripheral cytoplasmic inclusion patches (Döhle bodies / rough ER).
Significance: Severe bacterial sepsis, lobar pneumonia, deep abscesses, and septic shock.

Hypersegmented Neutrophils

Description: Neutrophils showing \(\ge 5\) distinct nuclear lobes in \(>5\%\) of cells (or a single 6-lobed neutrophil).
Significance: Highly specific hallmark of Megaloblastic Anaemia (Folic Acid or Vitamin \(\text{B}_{12}\) deficiency) due to impaired nuclear DNA synthesis.

Reactive (Atypical) Lymphocytes

Description: Large, pleomorphic lymphocytes with abundant deep-blue basophilic cytoplasm skirting and indenting around neighboring erythrocytes ('skirt effect').
Significance: Acute viral infections (EBV Infectious Mononucleosis, CMV, HIV seroconversion) and acute falciparum malaria.

Comprehensive Erythrocyte Morphology & Inclusions Atlas

Evaluation of red cell size, staining characteristics, geometric shapes (poikilocytes), and intracellular inclusions provides essential differential diagnostic clues in tropical haematology.

Diagnostic Atlas of Erythrocyte Morphologies (Plates 96–112)

Poikilocyte / Abnormality Microscopical Morphology Pathophysiological Mechanism & Key Etiologies
Pencil / Cigar Cells (Plate 98) Elongated, narrow, thin red cells with central pallor. Severe Iron Deficiency Anaemia (IDA) due to chronic hookworm, schistosomiasis, or active blood loss.
Target Cells / Leptocytes (Plate 103) 'Bull's-eye' appearance: central hemoglobin spot surrounded by a clear ring and outer pigmented rim. Excess membrane surface area relative to intracellular volume. Found in \(\beta\)-Thalassaemia syndromes, Sickle Cell Disease (HbSC/HbSS), HbC disease, obstructive liver disease, and post-splenectomy.
Sickle Cells / Drepanocytes (Plate 99) Crescentic, boat-shaped, or holly-leaf erythrocytes with pointed polar ends. Polymerization of insoluble \(\text{HbS}\) polymers under deoxygenated conditions. Found in Sickle Cell Anaemia (HbSS), HbS/\(\beta\)-thalassaemia, and HbSC disease.
Spherocytes (Plate 109) Small, dense, intensely hyperchromic spheres lacking central pallor (\(\text{MCHC} > 360\ \text{g/L}\)). Loss of membrane lipid bilayer. Found in Hereditary Spherocytosis, Autoimmune Hemolytic Anaemia (AIHA), ABO Hemolytic Disease of Newborn, snake envenomation, and Clostridium perfringens sepsis.
Schistocytes / Helmet Cells (Plate 112) Fragmented, triangular, or helmet-shaped erythrocytes with sharp pointed spicules. Mechanical shearing across microvascular fibrin mesh. Found in DIC, Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP), Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS), pre-eclampsia, and severe burns.
Burr Cells / Echinocytes Erythrocytes with \(10–30\) regularly spaced, blunt, uniform surface projections. Uraemia (end-stage renal disease), severe burns, acute blood loss, pyruvate kinase deficiency.
Acanthocytes / Spur Cells (Plate 111) Irregularly shaped erythrocytes with \(2–10\) variably spaced, sharp, thorny, finger-like projections. Severe liver disease (cirrhosis), abetalipoproteinemia, post-splenectomy.
Tear Drop Cells / Dacryocytes Unipolar elongated cells resembling a droplet or pear. Myelofibrosis with myeloid metaplasia, extramedullary hematopoiesis, severe marrow infiltration by malignancy.
Half-Ghost / Blister Cells (Plate 107) Irregularly contracted cells with hemoglobin retracted to one side beneath a transparent membrane. Severe oxidative hemoglobin precipitation during G6PD Deficiency Hemolytic Crisis or dapsone/primaquine toxicity.
Rouleaux Formation (Plate 93) Red blood cells aligned face-to-face in linear stacks resembling columns of coins. Elevated plasma macromolecules (fibrinogen, monoclonal immunoglobulins) neutralizing RBC negative zeta potential. Hallmark of Multiple Myeloma & Macroglobulinemia.

Intraerythrocytic Inclusions Differential Guide

Inclusion Body Nature & Stain Diagnostic Significance
Howell-Jolly Bodies (Plate 113) Small (\(1\ \mu\text{m}\)), round, smooth, deep purple-violet nuclear DNA fragments. Visible on routine Romanowsky stain. Post-splenectomy, hyposplenism (Sickle Cell auto-splenectomy), severe Megaloblastic Anaemia, and \(\beta\)-Thalassaemia major.
Basophilic Stippling Fine to coarse blue-gray punctate granules distributed throughout the cytoplasm (precipitated ribosomal RNA). Lead poisoning (plumbism), Thalassaemia syndromes, severe megaloblastic anaemia, and sideroblastic anaemia.
Inclusion Body Nature & Stain Diagnostic Significance
Heinz Bodies Precipitated denatured hemoglobin aggregates. Invisible on routine Romanowsky stain; requires Supravital Methyl Violet / New Methylene Blue stain. G6PD deficiency oxidative crisis, unstable hemoglobinopathies, oxidant drug toxicity.
Auer Rods Needle-like pink/purple crystalline aggregates of fused azurophilic lysosomes in myeloblast cytoplasm. Pathognomonic of Acute Myeloid Leukaemia (AML) (never seen in ALL).

8.8 Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) & Plasma Viscosity

ICSH International Reference Westergren Method • Triphasic Sedimentation Kinetics (Rouleaux Aggregation \(10\ \text{min}\), Constant Velocity Fall \(40\ \text{min}\), Final Cell Packing \(10\ \text{min}\)) • Anticoagulant Ratio (\(0.4\ \text{mL}\) \(3.8\%\) Trisodium Citrate + \(1.6\ \text{mL}\) Blood \(= 1:4\)) • Westergren Tube Specifications (\(300\ \text{mm}\) Length, \(200\ \text{mm}\) Scale, \(2.55\ \text{mm}\) Bore) • Severe Physical Sources of Error: Vertical Alignment (\(3^\circ\) Tilt \(= +30\%\) Acceleration), Ambient Temperature (\(>25^\circ\text{C}\)), Bench Vibration, Direct Sunlight • Plasma Asymmetrical Macromolecules (Fibrinogen, \(\gamma\)-Globulins, CRP) vs Zeta Potential • Tropical Diagnostic Utility • Discordance in HIV-TB Co-infection • Plasma Viscosity Advantages.

Monica Cheesbrough ESR Operational Rules: (1) Westergren ESR tubes MUST be mounted absolutely vertically in a spirit-level-aligned rack away from drafts, direct sunlight, and centrifuge vibrations; a mere \(3^\circ\) tilt off vertical can falsely accelerate sedimentation by up to \(30\%\) due to side-wall streaming! (2) In tropical district practice, ESR is non-specific and elevated in many healthy individuals; in HIV/TB co-infection, ESR remains persistently elevated and fails to drop during effective anti-tuberculosis therapy due to unrelenting HIV polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia.

ICSH International Reference Westergren Method SOP

The Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) measures the distance in millimeters that red blood cells in anticoagulated, diluted whole blood sediment downward in a vertically positioned, open-ended standardized Westergren tube over exactly one hour (\(60\ \text{minutes}\)).

Standard Westergren Tube Specifications

  • Total Tube Length: \(300\ \text{mm}\) (\(30\ \text{cm}\)).
  • Graduated Scale: Millimeter scale marked from \(0\ \text{mm}\) (at the top) down to \(200\ \text{mm}\) (at the bottom).
  • Internal Bore Diameter: Uniform precision bore of \(2.55\ \text{mm} \pm 0.15\ \text{mm}\). A narrower bore impedes cell settling and retards sedimentation.
  • Rack Alignment: Spring-loaded vertical stand with neoprene/rubber leveling feet and spirit level.

Anticoagulant Preparation & Blood Dilution Ratio

Parameter Specification Functional Action
Anticoagulant Reagent \(3.8\%\ \text{w/v}\) (\(109\ \text{mmol/L}\)) Trisodium Citrate (\(\text{Na}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\)) Chelates ionized calcium while maintaining physiological plasma tonicity.
Standard Dilution Ratio \(1\ \text{part citrate} : 4\ \text{parts whole blood}\) Standardized proportion required by ICSH reference method.
Exact Volumes \(0.4\ \text{mL}\) Citrate + \(1.6\ \text{mL}\) Blood (\(= 2.0\ \text{mL}\) total) Mixed thoroughly in a clean vial; zero bubbles aspirated into pipette up to the \(0\ \text{mm}\) mark.
Specimen Stability Test within \(2\ \text{hours}\) at room temp (or up to \(6\ \text{hours}\) if EDTA blood is refrigerated at \(4–8^\circ\text{C}\) before citrate addition). Prevents in vitro spherical shape remodeling of RBCs.

Biophysics & Triphasic Sedimentation Kinetics

Under normal physiological conditions, erythrocytes maintain a net negative surface charge (zeta potential created by sialic acid residues on glycophorin A), which generates mutually repulsive electrostatic forces preventing spontaneous cell aggregation.

Plasma Macromolecules & Rouleaux Mechanism

In tissue inflammation, acute infection, or malignancy, liver and plasma cells release large, positively charged, asymmetrical acute-phase proteins into the bloodstream:

  • Fibrinogen: The single most potent plasma macromolecule accelerating ESR (elongated asymmetrical structure).
  • Immunoglobulins (\(\gamma\)-Globulins): Particularly IgG, IgM, and monoclonal paraproteins in Multiple Myeloma.
  • C-Reactive Protein (CRP) & \(\alpha_2\)-Macroglobulin: Neutralize the negative zeta potential, allowing RBCs to adhere face-to-face into cylindrical stacks (Rouleaux formation).
  • Stokes' Law: Sedimentation velocity (\(V\)) is proportional to the square of the aggregate radius (\(V \propto r^2\)). A rouleaux cluster of 10 red cells falls much faster than 10 individual isolated erythrocytes.

The Three Kinetic Phases of 60-Minute Sedimentation

1 Phase 1: Aggregation / Rouleaux (First \(10\ \text{Minutes}\))

Individual erythrocytes collide and form rouleaux stacks. Sedimentation is slow and progressive.

2 Phase 2: Fast Settling / Constant Velocity (Middle \(40\ \text{Minutes}\))

Large aggregate clusters fall at a rapid, constant downward velocity through the plasma column.

3 Phase 3: Cell Packing / Deceleration (Final \(10\ \text{Minutes}\))

Erythrocyte aggregates reach the bottom of the tube, packing tightly against each other; sedimentation decelerates to a standstill.

Physical Sources of Error & Technical Pitfalls

Because ESR depends on delicate gravity settling against upward fluid displacement, the test is extraordinarily vulnerable to environmental and technical variables.

Critical Factors Falsely Accelerating ESR (\(\uparrow \text{ESR}\))

Physical / Technical Variable Mechanism of Spurious Acceleration
Tube Tilting / Non-Vertical Rack A tilt of as little as \(3^\circ\) off true vertical accelerates ESR by up to \(30\%\)! Red cells aggregate and slide down the lower tube wall while plasma streams rapidly up the upper wall (wall effect).
High Ambient Temperature (\(>25^\circ\text{C}\)) High tropical heat lowers plasma viscosity, speeding up sedimentation. Always test in temperature-controlled room (\(18–25^\circ\text{C}\)) or apply local temperature correction nomograms.
Severe Anaemia Low hematocrit / red cell concentration decreases upward resistance from displaced plasma, allowing faster settling.
Macrocytosis Enlarged red cells possess greater mass and sediment more rapidly according to Stokes' law.

Critical Factors Falsely Retarding ESR (\(\downarrow \text{ESR}\))

Physical / Technical Variable Mechanism of Spurious Retardation
Low Ambient Temperature (\(<18^\circ\text{C}\)) Cold increases plasma viscosity, slowing sedimentation rate.
Abnormal Poikilocytosis (Sickle Cells / Spherocytes) Rigid crescentic sickle cells (\(\text{HbSS}\)) and spherical erythrocytes cannot stack face-to-face to form rouleaux. ESR is characteristically near zero (\(0–2\ \text{mm/hr}\)) even in severe sickle crisis.
Polycythaemia & Hemoconcentration High packed cell volume creates dense crowded resistance, severely retarding downward settling.
Microclots / Inadequate Mixing Fibrin entrapment consumes plasma fibrinogen and removes red cells from suspension.
Narrower Tube Bore (\(<2.4\ \text{mm}\)) Capillary wall attraction impedes settling.

Clinical Reference Ranges, Pathology Matrix & Plasma Viscosity

ESR is a non-specific screening and monitoring parameter whose results must always be correlated with the full clinical picture and acute-phase biomarkers.

Reference Ranges (Westergren, \(1\ \text{Hour}\))

Patient Demographic Normal Reference Upper Limit (\(\text{mm/1st hr}\))
Adult Males (\(<50\ \text{years}\)) \(0–10\ \text{mm/hour}\)
Adult Females (\(<50\ \text{years}\)) \(0–15\ \text{mm/hour}\)
Elderly Males & Females (\(>50\ \text{years}\)) \(0–20\ \text{mm/hour}\)
Pregnancy & Puerperium Elevated physiologically up to \(30–40\ \text{mm/hour}\) due to elevated fibrinogen.
Tropical Clinical Reality: In tropical countries, baseline ESR is often mildly elevated (\(15–25\ \text{mm/hr}\)) in asymptomatic individuals due to endemic subclinical helminthiasis, malaria exposure, and dietary variations.

Causes of Markedly Raised ESR (\(>50–100\ \text{mm/hr}\))

  • Chronic Mycobacterial Infections: Pulmonary and extrapulmonary Tuberculosis (TB).
  • Deep Visceral Protozoal Sepsis: African Trypanosomiasis (rapid dramatic rise) and Visceral Leishmaniasis (Kala-Azar) (massive hypergammaglobulinemia).
  • Malignancies: Multiple Myeloma (frequently \(>100\ \text{mm/hr}\)), Hodgkin's Lymphoma, disseminated metastatic carcinoma.
  • Autoimmune / Connective Tissue Diseases: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), Rheumatoid Arthritis, Giant Cell Arteritis / Polymyalgia Rheumatica.
  • Acute Deep Pyogenic Sepsis: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID), bacterial endocarditis, osteomyelitis, ruptured ectopic pregnancy.
TB-HIV Discordance: When monitoring tuberculosis therapy with ESR, ESR levels drop steadily as TB resolves; however, in patients co-infected with HIV, the ESR remains persistently elevated and fails to normalize, due to persistent HIV-driven B-cell hyperactivity and hypergammaglobulinemia!

Plasma Viscosity (PV) vs ESR

Plasma Viscosity (measured in mPa.s / centipoise at \(25^\circ\text{C}\)): Directly measures the frictional resistance of plasma against flow in a capillary viscometer.

  • Unaffected by Red Cell Variables: Unlike ESR, plasma viscosity is completely independent of anaemia, sickle cells, polycythaemia, or poikilocytosis.
  • Temperature Independent: Measured at fixed \(25^\circ\text{C}\) or thermostatically controlled.
  • High Precision: Reference range \(1.50–1.72\ \text{mPa.s}\). Elevated in hyperviscosity syndromes (Waldenström's macroglobulinemia, myeloma, rheumatoid arthritis).

8.9 Reticulocyte Count & Screening for Haemolytic Anaemias (G6PD)

Supravital Staining of Unfixed Live Erythrocytes (New Methylene Blue Reagent No. 61 vs Brilliant Cresyl Blue) • Ribosomal RNA / Reticulin Precipitation • 500-Cell Counting SOP & Miller Eyepiece Aperture • Relative Percentage vs Absolute Reticulocyte Count (\(\times 10^9/\text{L}\)) • Corrected Reticulocyte Count & Reticulocyte Production Index (RPI) • Intraerythrocytic Inclusions: Heinz Bodies (Supravital Methyl Violet) vs Haemoglobin H (\(\beta_4\) Golf-Ball Inclusions) • Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) Screening: Brewer's Methaemoglobin Reduction Test (Sodium Nitrite + Methylene Blue Redox Catalysis) • Strict Timing Rule: Never Test During an Acute Haemolytic Crisis.

Monica Cheesbrough G6PD & Reticulocyte Golden Rules: (1) To visualize ribosomal RNA (reticulin) in reticulocytes or oxidized Heinz bodies, blood must be stained supravitally while cells are alive and unfixed; methanol fixation dissolves RNA-dye complexes and masks Heinz bodies. (2) Never perform a G6PD screening assay during or immediately following an acute hemolytic crisis! Older, enzyme-deficient erythrocytes have already hemolyzed, and the peripheral blood is dominated by young reticulocytes containing high physiological G6PD levels, producing a dangerous false-normal result. Always re-test 2 to 3 months post-crisis.

Reticulocyte Enumeration: Supravital Staining Protocol

Reticulocytes are juvenile, non-nucleated erythrocytes that have lost their nucleus but retain residual networks of ribosomal ribonucleic acid (rRNA) and mitochondria. They remain in the marrow for \(2–3\ \text{days}\) and circulate in peripheral blood for \(1–2\ \text{days}\) before maturing into adult erythrocytes.

Supravital Stain Formulations

  • New Methylene Blue (Reagent No. 61, \(1.0\%\ \text{w/v}\)): Chemically distinct from basic methylene blue; provides superior, intense, crisp dark blue-violet precipitation of reticulin networks with clean background. Recommended standard.
  • Brilliant Cresyl Blue (Reagent No. 17, \(1.0\%\ \text{w/v}\)): Alternative supravital dye; must be dissolved in isotonic physiological saline (\(0.85\%\)) to prevent osmotic lysis.
  • Mandatory Pre-Filtration: Always filter stain immediately before use to remove precipitated dye crystals that mimic reticulin.

Step-by-Step Staining & Incubation SOP

  1. Filter \(2–3\ \text{drops}\) of supravital stain into a small test tube or vial.
  2. Add an equal volume (approx. \(2–3\ \text{drops}\) / \(1:1\) ratio) of well-mixed EDTA anticoagulated blood (or capillary blood). If patient is severely anaemic (\(\text{Hb} < 70\ \text{g/L}\)), double the volume of blood.
  3. Mix thoroughly and incubate at room temperature for \(20\ \text{minutes}\) (or \(35–37^\circ\text{C}\) for \(10–15\ \text{minutes}\)).
  4. Re-suspend red cells gently, place a drop on each of two slides, and spread thin films. Air dry rapidly. Do not fix with methanol or counterstain.

Microscopical Counting Technique & Formula

Under oil immersion (\(100\times\) objective), mature RBCs appear light pale green-blue; reticulocytes contain deep blue-violet granular reticulin networks (Plate 110):

Eyepiece Field Reduction: Insert a circular disc of black paper with a central \(5\ \text{mm}\) aperture into the microscope eyepiece to reduce field size and prevent eye fatigue.
Standard 500-RBC Count Calculation:

Count a total of \(500\ \text{erythrocytes}\) systematically across consecutive fields, tallying the number of reticulocytes (\(R\)):

\[\text{Reticulocyte Count (\%)} = \frac{R}{500} \times 100 = \frac{R \times 2}{10} = \mathbf{\frac{R}{5}}\]

Example: If \(25\) reticulocytes are seen among \(500\) RBCs: \(\text{Reticulocytes} = \frac{25}{5} = \mathbf{5.0\%}\).

Reticulocyte Mathematical Indices & Bone Marrow Kinetics

The relative percentage of reticulocytes can be misleading in severe anaemia due to fewer total circulating erythrocytes. True marrow erythropoietic capacity is accurately quantified by absolute counts and the Reticulocyte Production Index (RPI).

Absolute Reticulocyte Count (ARC)

Actual number of reticulocytes per liter of whole blood.

\[\text{ARC } (10^9/\text{L}) = \frac{\text{Reticulocytes (\%)} \times \text{RBC Count } (10^{12}/\text{L})}{100} \times 1000\] \[\text{ARC } (10^9/\text{L}) = \text{Retic (\%)} \times \text{RBC } (10^{12}/\text{L}) \times 10\]

Reference Range: \(25–100 \times 10^9/\text{L}\) (\(0.5–2.5\%\) in adults; \(2.0–5.0\%\) in newborns at birth).

Corrected Reticulocyte Count (CRC)

Adjusts relative reticulocyte percentage for the degree of anaemia.

\[\text{CRC (\%)} = \text{Retic (\%)} \times \frac{\text{Patient's PCV}}{\text{Normal Reference PCV (0.45)}}\]

Normalizes reticulocyte concentration to a standard baseline hematocrit of \(0.45\ \text{L/L}\).

Reticulocyte Production Index (RPI)

Corrects for premature release of marrow 'shift' reticulocytes.

\[\text{RPI} = \frac{\text{CRC (\%)}}{\text{Maturation Factor (Shift Days)}}\] (\(\text{PCV } 0.35 \to 1.5\ \text{d}\); \(\text{PCV } 0.25 \to 2.0\ \text{d}\); \(\text{PCV } 0.15 \to 2.5\ \text{d}\))

Interpretation: \(\text{RPI} > 2.0–3.0\) indicates an adequate hyperproliferative marrow response (hemolysis/acute hemorrhage); \(\text{RPI} < 2.0\) indicates hypoproliferation.

Supravital Intraerythrocytic Inclusions: Heinz Bodies vs HbH Golf-Balls

Supravital staining enables the definitive differential identification of unstable hemoglobin aggregates and oxidative precipitates that are invisible on conventional fixed Romanowsky films.

Heinz Bodies (Plate 108)

  • Biochemical Nature: Large (\(1–3\ \mu\text{m}\)), round precipitates of oxidized, insoluble, denatured globin attached to the inner surface of the RBC membrane.
  • Staining Requirement: Invisible on Leishman/Giemsa stains (dissolved/masked by methanol). Stained brilliantly using \(0.5\%\) Methyl Violet or Crystal Violet in isotonic saline on unfixed blood.
  • Appearance in Reticulocyte Prep: Stain light blue-violet, lying eccentrically against or protruding through the erythrocyte membrane.
  • Clinical Etiology: G6PD deficiency during acute oxidative crisis (fava beans, primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides), unstable hemoglobins (Hb Köln), and post-splenectomy.

Haemoglobin H (\(\text{HbH} / \beta_4\)) Inclusions (Plate 106)

  • Biochemical Nature: Unstable tetramers of beta globin chains (\(\beta_4\)) resulting from severe alpha chain synthesis deletion (\(\alpha\)-thalassaemia).
  • Staining SOP: Incubate whole blood with \(1.0\%\) Brilliant Cresyl Blue for \(1\ \text{hour}\) at \(37^\circ\text{C}\).
  • Characteristic 'Golf-Ball' Appearance: Erythrocytes become packed with dozens of fine, uniformly distributed, pale greenish-blue punctate precipitates, resembling a patterned golf ball.
  • Diagnostic Distinction: Present in \(>10–50\%\) of RBCs in HbH Disease (3-gene \(\alpha\)-thalassaemia deletion) and in rare cells (\(<1\%\)) in \(\alpha\)-thalassaemia trait.

Screening for G6PD Deficiency: Methaemoglobin Reduction Test (Brewer's Test)

Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) catalyzes the first committed step in the hexose monophosphate (HMP) shunt, producing \(\text{NADPH}\) to maintain reduced glutathione (\(\text{GSH}\)), which protects red cell membranes against oxidative injury.

Chemical Reaction Mechanism

Step 1: Oxidation
Sodium nitrite (\(\text{NaNO}_2\)) oxidizes hemoglobin to brown methaemoglobin (\(\text{Hi} / \text{Fe}^{3+}\)).

Step 2: Enzymatic Reduction via HMP Shunt
Methylene blue acts as an artificial electron carrier, activating the pentose phosphate pathway. In erythrocytes with normal G6PD activity, \(\text{NADPH}\) is generated via G6PD, and methaemoglobin reductase converts brown methaemoglobin back to red haemoglobin within 90 minutes. In G6PD-deficient cells, lack of \(\text{NADPH}\) prevents enzymatic reduction; the blood remains permanently brown.

Three-Tube Test Protocol (35–37°C for 90 Minutes)

Reagents Added Test Tube Normal Control Tube Deficient Control Tube
Sodium Nitrite + Glucose \(0.1\ \text{mL}\) — (Omit) \(0.1\ \text{mL}\)
Methylene Blue (\(0.4\ \text{mmol/L}\)) \(0.1\ \text{mL}\) — (Omit) — (Omit)
Patient Blood (\(\text{PCV} \approx 0.40\)) \(2.0\ \text{mL}\) \(2.0\ \text{mL}\) \(2.0\ \text{mL}\)
Incubation & Dilution Incubate at \(35–37^\circ\text{C}\) for \(90\ \text{min}\); dilute \(0.1\ \text{mL}\) in \(10\ \text{mL}\) water to read color.
Visual Color Interpretation:
  • Normal G6PD Activity: Clear RED color (matches Normal Control tube).
  • G6PD Deficiency (Hemizygous Male / Homozygous Female): Dark BROWN color (matches Deficient Control tube).
  • Heterozygous Female Carrier: Intermediate reddish-brown color.

Mandatory Post-Crisis Timing Rule

Why Testing During a Hemolytic Crisis is Contraindicated:
In G6PD-deficient individuals, erythrocytes lose enzyme activity as they age. When an acute hemolytic crisis is triggered by oxidant drugs or fava beans, the oldest, most enzyme-deficient erythrocytes undergo rapid intravascular destruction. The bone marrow mounts a brisk erythropoietic response, releasing high concentrations of young reticulocytes which possess high baseline G6PD activity. Testing blood during or immediately following a crisis yields a FALSE-NORMAL result! Always schedule G6PD screening \(8–12\ \text{weeks}\) after the hemolytic crisis has completely resolved.
