8.10 Investigation of Sickle Cell Disease & Haemoglobin Electrophoresis

Genetics of Sickle Cell Disorders (HbSS, HbAS, HbSC, HbS/\(\beta\)-Thalassaemia, HbS-D Punjab) • Rapid Screening: Sodium Metabisulfite Sickling Slide Test • Quantitative Differentiation: Sodium Dithionite HbS Solubility Filtration Test • Infant Screening Modification (\(<6\ \text{months}\)) • Confirmatory Alkaline Cellulose Acetate Electrophoresis (Tris-EDTA-Borate Buffer \(\text{pH}\ 8.5\), Mylar-Backed Titan III Plates, \(350\ \text{V}\) for \(25\ \text{minutes}\)) • Electrophoretic Mobility Hierarchy (\(\text{Anode } (+) \leftarrow \text{A} - \text{F} - \text{S/D/G} - \text{C/A}_2/\text{E/O} \rightarrow \text{Cathode } (-)\)) • Acid Citrate Agar Electrophoresis (\(\text{pH}\ 6.0\)) for Resolving Co-migrating Variants.

Monica Cheesbrough Sickle Cell Golden Rules: (1) The Sodium Dithionite Solubility Test confirms the presence of insoluble HbS (tactoid crystals), but it cannot differentiate Sickle Cell Trait (HbAS) from Sickle Cell Anaemia (HbSS) without the quantitative filtration step. (2) Standard solubility testing is falsely negative in infants \(<6\ \text{months}\) because \(\text{HbF}\) predominates and \(\text{HbS}\) concentration is below the threshold of macroscopic turbidity; in neonates, use microscopic slide sickling or definitive alkaline electrophoresis! (3) On alkaline electrophoresis (\(\text{pH}\ 8.5\)), HbS co-migrates identically with HbD and HbG, and HbC co-migrates with \(\text{HbA}_2\), HbE, and HbO, requiring acid agar electrophoresis (\(\text{pH}\ 6.0\)) for complete separation.

Sodium Metabisulfite Sickling Slide Test

The Sickle Cell Slide Test is a rapid, low-cost qualitative screening method suitable for peripheral health centres. It detects the physical capacity of erythrocytes containing Sickle Haemoglobin (\(\text{HbS}\)) to undergo morphological sickling under acute chemical deoxygenation.

Principle & Reducing Chemistry

Sodium Metabisulfite (\(\text{Na}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_5, 2.0\%\ \text{w/v}\)): A potent reducing agent that consumes dissolved oxygen in the blood suspension.

  • Under profound hypoxia (\(\text{pO}_2 \downarrow\)), deoxygenated \(\text{HbS}\) molecules polymerize into rigid, insoluble crystalline filaments (tactoids).
  • The expanding tactoid polymers deform the flexible biconcave red cell membrane into characteristic rigid crescentic, holly-leaf, or filamentous sickle shapes (drepanocytes).
  • Reagent Preparation: Prepare fresh daily (\(0.2\ \text{g}\) in \(10\ \text{mL}\) distilled water); metabisulfite rapidly auto-oxidizes to inactive sulfate on exposure to air.

Step-by-Step Slide Technique

  1. Mix \(1\ \text{drop}\) of EDTA blood (or capillary blood) with \(1\ \text{drop}\) of fresh \(2\%\) sodium metabisulfite on a clean glass slide.
  2. Apply a coverslip, taking care to avoid air bubbles.
  3. Airtight Sealing (Crucial Step): Seal the four edges of the coverslip completely with melted petroleum jelly, paraffin wax, or nail polish to prevent atmospheric oxygen re-entry.
  4. Incubate at room temperature and examine under the \(40\times\) objective at \(30\ \text{minutes}\), \(1\ \text{hour}\), and \(4\ \text{hours}\) (up to \(24\ \text{hours}\) for trait).
Limitation: The slide sickling test is strictly qualitative. It is positive in both Sickle Cell Disease (HbSS) and Sickle Cell Trait (HbAS), and cannot distinguish between them.

Sodium Dithionite HbS Solubility & Filtration Test

The HbS Solubility Test (Itano's Solubility Test) provides a rapid, robust method to detect \(\text{HbS}\) based on the unique insolubility of deoxygenated sickle hemoglobin in concentrated phosphate buffer, with quantitative filtration differentiating disease from trait.

Chemical Principle of Differential Solubility

  • Lysis & Reduction: Saponin hemolyzes the red cells, releasing hemoglobin. Sodium dithionite (\(\text{Na}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_4\)) rapidly reduces hemoglobin to the deoxygenated state.
  • High Molarity Phosphate Buffer (\(2.24\ \text{mol/L}\)): Deoxygenated normal adult hemoglobin (\(\text{HbA}\)), fetal hemoglobin (\(\text{HbF}\)), and \(\text{HbC}\) remain fully soluble, forming a clear transparent red solution.
  • HbS Insolubility: Deoxygenated \(\text{HbS}\) is virtually insoluble in high-phosphate buffer, precipitating out of solution into an opaque, cloudy, light-scattering suspension of nematic liquid crystals.
  • Macroscopic Turbidity Read: Hold tube \(2.5\ \text{cm}\) in front of a white card ruled with dark black lines. If lines cannot be seen through the solution \(\to\) Positive for HbS.

Quantitative Filtration Differentiation (Disease vs Trait)

To differentiate homozygous Sickle Cell Anaemia (\(\text{HbSS}\)) from heterozygous Sickle Cell Trait (\(\text{HbAS}\)), filter the turbid mixture through Whatman No. 1 filter paper:

Sickle Phenotype Filtration Supernatant Color Filter Paper Residue
Normal Adult (\(\text{HbAA}\)) Clear Pink-Red Filtrate No dark precipitate on filter paper
Sickle Cell Trait (\(\text{HbAS}\)) Pink-Red Filtrate (\(\text{HbA}\) passes through) Dark red-brown precipitate of insoluble \(\text{HbS}\) on paper
Sickle Cell Anaemia (\(\text{HbSS}\)) Completely Colorless / Water-Clear Filtrate (all \(\text{HbS}\) trapped) Heavy dark red precipitate containing 100% of the hemoglobin
Infant Modification (\(<6\ \text{months}\)): Due to high \(\text{HbF}\) levels, infants \(<6\ \text{months}\) yield false-negative macroscopic turbidity. Examine a drop of the reagent-blood mixture microscopically: intact unlysed cells containing insoluble \(\text{HbS}\) confirm sickle genotype.

Alkaline Cellulose Acetate Haemoglobin Electrophoresis (pH 8.5)

Alkaline cellulose acetate electrophoresis is the definitive reference method for identifying and separating abnormal hemoglobin variants. At alkaline \(\text{pH}\ 8.4–8.6\), hemoglobin molecules carry a net negative electrical charge and migrate toward the Anode (\(+\)) at velocities governed by their net surface charge density.

Modern Mylar-Backed Titan III System SOP

  • Membrane: Plastic-supported (Mylar-backed) cellulose acetate plates (Titan III, \(60 \times 76\ \text{mm}\)). Pre-soaked in buffer for \(20\ \text{minutes}\) and blotted.
  • Buffer: Tris-EDTA-Borate (TEB) Buffer Reagent No. 86 (\(\text{pH}\ 8.5\)).
  • Hemolysate Preparation: Saline-washed RBCs lysed in EDTA-KCN hemolyzing reagent (or distilled water/toluene for storage).
  • Sample Application: \(5\ \mu\text{L}\) of patient hemolysates and controls (HbAA, HbAS, HbAF, HbAC) applied simultaneously using an 8-unit multi-applicator near the Cathode (\(-\)) end.
  • Electrophoresis Run: Zip-Zone chamber powered at \(350\ \text{V}, 50\ \text{mA}\) for \(20–25\ \text{minutes}\).

Electrophoretic Migration Hierarchy (Cathode to Anode)

Because amino acid substitutions alter net surface charge, hemoglobin variants separate into distinct, predictable bands:

Cathode \((-)\) [Origin]  \(\longrightarrow\)  \(\text{C} / \text{A}_2 / \text{E} / \text{O}\)  \(\longrightarrow\)  \(\text{S} / \text{D} / \text{G}\)  \(\longrightarrow\)  \(\text{F}\)  \(\longrightarrow\)  \(\text{A}\)  \(\longrightarrow\)  \(\text{H} / \text{Barts}\)  \(\longrightarrow\)  Anode \((+)\)

Mnemonic (Fastest to Slowest toward Anode):
A • Fast • Slow • Crawl  \(\Longrightarrow\)  A > F > S > C

  • \(\text{HbA}\) (Normal Adult \(\alpha_2\beta_2\)): Migrates fastest toward the anode.
  • \(\text{HbF}\) (Fetal \(\alpha_2\gamma_2\)): Migrates immediately behind HbA.
  • \(\text{HbS}\) (Sickle \(\alpha_2\beta_2^{6\text{Glu}\to\text{Val}}\)): Loses two negative glutamic acid charges; migrates behind HbF.
  • \(\text{HbC}\) (Variant \(\alpha_2\beta_2^{6\text{Glu}\to\text{Lys}}\)): Gains two positive lysine charges; slowest migration, staying close to the cathode origin with \(\text{HbA}_2\).

Co-migrating Variants & Acid Citrate Agar Electrophoresis (pH 6.0)

A major analytical limitation of alkaline cellulose acetate electrophoresis is that several structural hemoglobin variants share identical net surface electrical charges and co-migrate within the same band.

Co-migration Clusters on Alkaline pH 8.5

Alkaline Band Position Co-migrating Hemoglobin Variants Confirmatory Differentiation Method
\(\text{HbS}\) Position \(\text{HbS}\), \(\text{HbD}\) (Punjab/Los Angeles), \(\text{HbG}\) (Philadelphia) HbS is Solubility Positive (+); HbD & HbG are Solubility Negative (-); Acid Citrate Agar separates HbS from HbD/G.
\(\text{HbC}\) Position \(\text{HbC}\), \(\text{HbA}_2\), \(\text{HbE}\), \(\text{HbO}\) (Arab) Acid Citrate Agar (\(\text{pH}\ 6.0\)) cleanly separates \(\text{HbC}\) from \(\text{HbA}_2/\text{HbE}/\text{HbO}\); DEAE cellulose chromatography for \(\text{HbA}_2\).

Acid Citrate Agar Electrophoresis (pH 6.0)

In acid citrate agar (\(\text{pH}\ 6.0–6.2\)), separation does not depend primarily on net electrical charge, but on the differential binding affinity of hemoglobin molecules for the agaropectin matrix:

Anode \((+)\)  \(\leftarrow\)  \(\text{F}\)  •  \(\text{A} / \text{D} / \text{G} / \text{E} / \text{A}_2\)  •  \(\text{S}\)  •  \(\text{C}\)  \(\rightarrow\)  Cathode \((-)\)

  • \(\text{HbF}\) migrates farthest toward the anode.
  • \(\text{HbA}\), \(\text{HbD}\), \(\text{HbG}\), and \(\text{HbE}\) remain together near the application origin.
  • \(\text{HbS}\) and \(\text{HbC}\) migrate toward the cathode, completely separated from each other and all other variants.

8.11 Investigation of Bleeding Disorders & Blood Coagulation

Physiology of Hemostasis (Primary Vascular-Platelet Plug vs Secondary Fibrin Mesh) • Screening Battery: Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT, Intrinsic/Common Pathway), Prothrombin Time / International Normalized Ratio (PT/INR, Extrinsic/Common Pathway), Thrombin Time (TT, Fibrinogen Conversion) • Fibrinolytic System & D-Dimer / FDP Rapid Assays in Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) • Tropical Coagulopathies: Obstetric Disasters, Severe Liver Disease, Sepsis, and Viper/Adder Snake Envenomation (20-Minute Whole Blood Clotting Test / 20WBCT) • Comprehensive Chart 8.7 Hemostatic Differential Diagnostic Matrix.

Monica Cheesbrough Coagulation Golden Rules: (1) All coagulation screening assays (PT, APTT, TT) strictly require \(9:1\) blood-to-citrate ratio collected in clean plastic/siliconized glass tubes; underfilled tubes contain excess free citrate that chelates reagent calcium, causing artifactual prolongation. (2) In suspected viper snake envenomation (e.g., Carpet Viper Echis ocellatus or Russell's Viper), perform the bedside 20-Minute Whole Blood Clotting Test (20WBCT): if blood in a clean dry glass tube fails to clot solidly after 20 minutes, venom-induced consumption coagulopathy is confirmed, requiring immediate antivenom therapy.

Hemostasis Physiology: Primary vs Secondary Coagulation Pathways

Hemostasis is the dynamic physiological defense mechanism that arrests blood loss from an injured vessel while maintaining blood fluidity within the intact vascular bed.

Primary Hemostasis (Vascular & Platelet Phase)

  • Vasoconstriction: Immediate reflex spasm of injured vascular smooth muscle mediated by endothelin and thromboxane \(\text{A}_2\).
  • Platelet Adhesion: Subendothelial collagen exposure allows von Willebrand Factor (vWF) to bridge platelet glycoprotein \(\text{Ib/IX}\) receptors to the vessel wall.
  • Platelet Activation & Secretion: Platelets change shape, degranulating ADP, serotonin, and calcium, synthesizing \(\text{TXA}_2\).
  • Platelet Aggregation: Fibrinogen binds to activated glycoprotein \(\text{IIb/IIIa}\) receptors across adjacent platelets, forming the temporary primary hemostatic platelet plug.
  • Clinical Manifestation of Defects: Petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses, epistaxis, and immediate bleeding after minor trauma (e.g., thrombocytopenia, vWD, platelet dysfunction).

Secondary Hemostasis (Fibrin Clot Formation)

A sequential cascade of circulating proenzymes converted into active serine proteases, culminating in thrombin-catalyzed generation of an insoluble fibrin meshwork:

Pathway Division Initiating Trigger & Factor Cascade Screening Laboratory Test
Intrinsic Pathway Surface contact activation: Factor XII \(\to\) XI \(\to\) IX (+ VIIIa, \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\), PL) \(\to\) Factor X activation. APTT
Extrinsic Pathway Vascular injury / Tissue Factor release: Tissue Factor (III) + Factor VIIa (+ \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\)) \(\to\) Factor X activation. PT / INR
Common Pathway Factor Xa (+ Va, \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\), PL) \(\to\) Prothrombin (II) to Thrombin (IIa) \(\to\) Fibrinogen (I) to Insoluble Fibrin (Ia) \(\xrightarrow{\text{XIIIa}}\) Cross-linked Fibrin. PT, APTT & TT
Clinical Manifestation of Coagulation Defects: Deep tissue hematomas, hemarthroses (bleeding into joints), and delayed, recurrent severe post-operative hemorrhage (e.g., Haemophilia A/B, severe liver failure, warfarin toxicity).

Coagulation Screening Protocols: APTT, PT/INR & Thrombin Time

Standardized coagulation testing in district laboratories provides rapid discrimination of intrinsic, extrinsic, common pathway, and fibrinogen deficiencies.

1. APTT (Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time)

Screens Intrinsic & Common pathways (Factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, I).

Principle: Citrated plasma + Kaolin (surface activator) + Platelet Substitute (cephalin phospholipid) incubated at \(37^\circ\text{C}\) for \(3–5\ \text{min}\). Clotting initiated by adding \(0.025\ \text{M}\ \text{CaCl}_2\).
  • Reference Range: \(30–45\ \text{seconds}\) (varies with reagent; patient value compared to control).
  • Key Clinical Uses: Screening for Haemophilia A (Factor VIII), Haemophilia B (Factor IX), von Willebrand Disease, monitoring unfractionated heparin therapy, and lupus anticoagulant.

2. PT / INR (Prothrombin Time)

Screens Extrinsic & Common pathways (Factors VII, X, V, II, I).

Principle: Citrated plasma incubated at \(37^\circ\text{C}\). Clotting initiated by adding Tissue Thromboplastin + \(\text{CaCl}_2\) combined reagent.
  • Reference Range: \(11–16\ \text{seconds}\).
  • INR Calculation: \[\text{INR} = \left(\frac{\text{Patient PT}}{\text{Mean Normal Control PT}}\right)^{\text{ISI}}\] (\(\text{ISI} =\) International Sensitivity Index of thromboplastin). Target INR for warfarin: \(2.0–3.0\) (\(2.5–3.5\) for prosthetic valves).
  • Causes of Prolongation: Warfarin therapy, Vitamin K deficiency, liver cirrhosis, DIC, newborn hemorrhagic disease.

3. TT (Thrombin Time)

Screens final conversion of Fibrinogen to Fibrin.

Principle: Standard bovine/human Thrombin reagent added directly to citrated plasma at \(37^\circ\text{C}\). Bypasses all upstream clotting factors.
  • Reference Range: \(12–15\ \text{seconds}\).
  • Causes of Prolongation: Severe hypofibrinogenemia / afibrinogenemia (\(<1.0\ \text{g/L}\)), presence of circulating Fibrin Degradation Products (FDPs / D-Dimers), heparin contamination, and dysfibrinogenemia.

Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) & Snake Envenomation

Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) is a devastating systemic consumptive thrombo-hemorrhagic syndrome characterized by uncontrolled microvascular fibrin deposition, exhaustion of platelets and clotting factors, and hyperfibrinolysis.

DIC Pathophysiology & D-Dimer / FDP Rapid Testing

  • Etiological Triggers in the Tropics:
    • Obstetric Emergencies: Abruptio placentae, amniotic fluid embolism, septic abortion, eclampsia, retained dead fetus.
    • Severe Infections: Meningococcal sepsis (Waterhouse-Friderichsen), Gram-negative endotoxic shock, severe Falciparum malaria.
    • Viper Snake Envenomation: Saw-scaled viper (Echis spp.), Russell's viper, Puff adder.
  • Consumptive Coagulopathy Profile: Platelets \(\downarrow (<50 \times 10^9/\text{L})\), \(\text{PT} \uparrow\), \(\text{APTT} \uparrow\), \(\text{TT} \uparrow\), Fibrinogen \(\downarrow (<1.0\ \text{g/L})\). Blood becomes completely incoagulable.
  • D-Dimer Latex Agglutination: Specific degradation products of cross-linked fibrin; \(\text{D-Dimer} > 500\ \text{ng/mL}\) confirms active intravascular microthrombosis and secondary fibrinolysis.

20-Minute Whole Blood Clotting Test (20WBCT) for Snakebite

In rural district health centres lacking centrifuges and coagulation reagents, the 20WBCT is the WHO-recommended bedside diagnostic test for venom-induced consumption coagulopathy:

Bedside 20WBCT Standard Operating Procedure:
  1. Draw approx. \(2.0\ \text{mL}\) of fresh venous blood via clean venepuncture.
  2. Dispense into a clean, dry, non-siliconized glass test tube (do not use plastic!).
  3. Leave completely undisturbed at room temperature for exactly 20 minutes.
  4. At 20 minutes, tip the tube gently:
    • Normal Result: Blood forms a firm solid clot; tube can be completely inverted without spilling.
    • Abnormal / Incoagulable Blood (Positive Test): Blood remains completely liquid or forms a fragile partial clot that breaks immediately upon tilting \(\Longrightarrow\) Confirms severe hemotoxic viper envenomation; administer antivenom immediately!

Chart 8.7: Comprehensive Hemostatic Differential Diagnostic Matrix

Adapted from Cheesbrough, Dacie & Lewis: Systematic differential diagnosis of bleeding disorders based on platelet count, Prothrombin Time (PT), Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT), and Thrombin Time (TT):

Clinical Condition / Bleeding Disorder Platelet Count (\(150–400 \times 10^9/\text{L}\)) PT (\(11–16\ \text{s}\)) APTT (\(30–45\ \text{s}\)) TT (\(12–15\ \text{s}\)) Pathophysiological Mechanism & Key Features
Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP / Onyalai) \(\downarrow\) Reduced (\(<50\)) Normal Normal Normal Isolated primary platelet destruction; intact plasma coagulation factors.
Haemophilia A (Factor VIII) & B (Factor IX) Normal Normal \(\uparrow\) Prolonged Normal X-linked recessive intrinsic defect. Normal PT/TT; deep hemarthroses and hematomas.
von Willebrand Disease (vWD) Normal (or mild \(\downarrow\)) Normal \(\uparrow\) Prolonged Normal Defective platelet adhesion + secondary Factor VIII deficiency; bleeding time \(\uparrow\).
Early Oral Anticoagulation / Factor VII Def. Normal \(\uparrow\) Prolonged Normal Normal Isolated extrinsic pathway defect (Factor VII has shortest half-life of \(4–6\ \text{hrs}\)).
Vitamin K Deficiency / Therapeutic Warfarin Normal \(\uparrow\) Prolonged \(\uparrow\) Prolonged Normal Impaired carboxylation of Factors II, VII, IX, X (PT prolonged early; APTT prolonged later).
Chronic Liver Disease (Cirrhosis) \(\downarrow\) Mild / Normal \(\uparrow\) Prolonged \(\uparrow\) Prolonged \(\uparrow\) Mild / Normal Impaired hepatic synthesis of all clotting factors (except Factor VIII/vWF from endothelium).
Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) \(\downarrow\) Severe \(\uparrow\) Prolonged \(\uparrow\) Prolonged \(\uparrow\) Prolonged Total consumptive coagulopathy; D-Dimer \(>500\ \text{ng/mL}\); blood often completely incoagulable.
Unfractionated Heparin Therapy Normal Normal (or mild \(\uparrow\)) \(\uparrow\) Markedly Prolonged \(\uparrow\) Markedly Prolonged Potentiates Antithrombin III, neutralizing thrombin (IIa) and Factor Xa.
Factor XIII Deficiency (Rare) Normal Normal Normal Normal Clot forms normally but lyses in \(5\ \text{M}\) urea / \(1\%\) monochloroacetic acid within \(24\ \text{hrs}\).

Part 2 • Chapter 9: Blood Transfusion Practice

9.1 Blood Transfusion Services at District Level & Quality Assurance

Monica Cheesbrough pp. 348–353 35 min read 8 MCQs (MCQ 585–592) Complete

Clinical Overview: Blood Transfusion in Tropical District Hospitals

At district level in tropical and resource-constrained developing countries, blood transfusion is predominantly an emergency, life-saving intervention rather than an elective procedure. Blood is a scarce, precious, and potentially hazardous biological resource that carries substantial risks of Transfusion-Transmissible Infections (TTIs) (e.g., HIV-1/2, Hepatitis B virus [HBV], Hepatitis C virus [HCV], Treponema pallidum [syphilis], and Plasmodium species) as well as life-threatening immunological adverse reactions.

Primary Emergency Indications

  • Infants & Young Children (<5 years): Severe, life-threatening anaemia with respiratory distress caused by severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria and/or protein-energy malnutrition.
  • Obstetric Emergencies: Severe maternal anaemia and acute peripartum haemorrhage (antepartum haemorrhage, placenta praevia, abruptio placentae, ruptured uterus, and primary postpartum haemorrhage).
  • Acute Major Haemorrhage: Severe surgical trauma, road traffic accidents, and visceral ruptures.

Principles of Appropriate Blood Usage

  • Strict Clinical Justification: Transfuse blood only after thorough clinical evaluation and measurement of patient haemoglobin (or PCV).
  • Fluid Resuscitation First: Manage acute hypovolaemia with crystalloid solutions (0.9% saline, Ringer's lactate) or colloids before considering blood.
  • Never Transfuse for Stable Anaemia: Chronic compensated anaemia without cardiac failure or respiratory distress must be managed by nutritional/haematinic therapy, not blood.
Key Strategy Intervention at District Level Impact on Blood Transfusion Demand
Antenatal Care & Nutrition Routine oral iron and folic acid supplementation, early detection of obstetric risks. Reduces maternal anaemia at delivery; prevents emergency peripartum transfusions.
Malaria Prevention & Control Insecticide-treated nets (ITNs), intermittent preventive treatment (IPTp), rapid artemisinin combination therapy (ACT). Prevents severe falciparum malarial anaemia in infants and children <5 years.
Surgical Blood Management Meticulous surgical haemostasis, intraoperative blood salvage for ectopic ruptures, intravenous replacement fluids. Saves homologous donor blood and eliminates allogeneic transfusion risks.

Guidelines for Blood Transfusion in Tropical Practice

Monica Cheesbrough and the WHO Blood Safety Unit set forth strict, standardized clinical and laboratory criteria for administering blood products in resource-limited district healthcare settings:

Paediatric Guidelines (<5 Years)

Blood transfusion is strictly indicated in infants and children when:

  • $\text{Hb} < 50\ \text{g/L}\ (5.0\ \text{g/dL})$ AND accompanied by clinical respiratory distress (tachypnoea, nasal flaring, subcostal recession, grunting).
  • $\text{Hb} < 40\ \text{g/L}\ (4.0\ \text{g/dL})$ complicated by malaria or severe bacterial infection, even in the absence of respiratory distress.
  • $\text{Hb} < 30\ \text{g/L}\ (3.0\ \text{g/dL})$ profound anaemia, regardless of clinical respiratory distress or obvious infection.
Paediatric Dosing & Administration: Transfuse with Whole Blood (not packed red cells) at a dose of $10\ \text{ml/kg}$ body weight. Diuretics are generally not required in children with severe anaemia if this volume is respected.

Adult & Obstetric Guidelines

Blood transfusion in adults and pregnant women is indicated when:

  • Critical Hypoxia/Heart Failure: Patient is in imminent danger of dying of anaemic heart failure or tissue hypoxia before medical therapy can raise haemoglobin.
  • Imminent Delivery: Obstetric delivery is imminent with $\text{Hb} < 70\ \text{g/L}\ (7.0\ \text{g/dL})$.
  • Emergency Major Surgery: $\text{Hb} < 80\ \text{g/L}\ (8.0\ \text{g/dL})$ with anticipated intraoperative blood loss > 500\ \text{ml}$.
Adult Dosing & Volume Overload Control: Use Concentrated (Packed) Red Cells at $10\ \text{ml/kg}$ body weight administered slowly over 4–6 hours. A rapidly acting intravenous loop diuretic (e.g., furosemide) should be administered to prevent fatal pulmonary oedema.

Acute Haemorrhage & Shock

  • Volume Loss Threshold: Transfusion indicated when acute blood loss exceeds $30\%$ of total blood volume and blood pressure / tissue perfusion cannot be restored by crystalloids (normal saline, Ringer's lactate) or colloids ($5\%$ dextran, $5\%$ hydroxyethyl starch).
  • Postpartum Haemorrhage (PPH): Transfusion indicated when hypotension, tachycardia, and altered consciousness persist after at least $50\ \text{ml/kg}$ of volume replacement fluids have been infused and local haemostatic measures executed.

Neonatal Exchange Transfusion

  • Bilirubin Threshold: Emergency exchange blood transfusion is indicated in newborn infants with severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia when serum total bilirubin exceeds $300\ \mu\text{mol/L}\ (\approx 17.5–18.0\ \text{mg/dL})$ to prevent irreversible bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus).
  • Goal: Removes circulating maternal antibodies (e.g., anti-D), sensitized infant RBCs, and unconjugated toxic bilirubin while restoring normal haematocrit.

Autologous Blood Transfusion & Intraoperative Blood Salvage

Autologous blood transfusion involves the re-infusion of a patient's own blood. This procedure completely eliminates the risk of alloimmunization, ABO incompatibility, and transfusion-transmitted viral infections.

Emergency Intraoperative Salvage in Ruptured Ectopic Pregnancy

In district hospitals where donor blood is severely limited, intraoperative blood salvage serves as an emergency life-saving technique during exploratory laparotomy for ruptured ectopic pregnancy or clean internal trauma:

  1. Blood is collected aseptically from an uncontaminated, sterile body cavity (peritoneal cavity) using a sterile scoop, dish, or bowl.
  2. The collected blood is immediately filtered through several layers (6–8 layers) of sterile surgical gauze into a sterile recipient vessel or sterile blood bottle containing Acid-Citrate-Dextrose (ACD) or Citrate-Phosphate-Dextrose (CPD) anticoagulant.
  3. The filtered anticoagulated autologous blood is re-infused back into the patient via a standard blood transfusion giving set equipped with an integral mesh filter.
  4. Contraindications: Blood contaminated with faecal matter, bowel contents, urine, amniotic fluid, or purulent exudate must never be salvaged or re-infused.

Quality Assurance (QA) in District Blood Transfusion Practice

Errors in blood grouping, crossmatching, donor screening, blood storage, or documentation can produce fatal ABO haemolytic transfusion reactions or catastrophic viral transmissions. QA in blood transfusion must be comprehensive, affordable, documented, and rigorously implemented across the entire transfusion chain.

Core Objectives of Transfusion QA

  • Prevent unnecessary and clinically inappropriate transfusions.
  • Ensure all transfused blood is safe, screened for major TTIs, traceable, and available on demand.
  • Recruit voluntary non-remunerated low-risk blood donors.
  • Standardize testing using strictly validated SOPs, controls, and calibrated equipment.
  • Eliminate patient misidentification, blood mislabelling, and clerical transcription errors.
  • Maintain unbroken cold-chain storage and secure long-term record archives.

Mandatory SOP Hierarchy

  • Clinical SOPs: Request form standards, bedside patient ID verification, calculation of pediatric infusion rates, adverse reaction management.
  • Donor SOPs: Selection criteria, confidential pre-donation health questionnaire, self-exclusion policy, aseptic phlebotomy.
  • Laboratory SOPs: ABO/Rh typing (tube & slide), antibody screening, compatibility crossmatching, TTI serological screening (HIV, HBsAg, HCV, VDRL/RPR).
  • Storage & Disposal SOPs: Refrigerator temperature logging, cold chain maintenance, quarantine protocols, biohazardous sharps and blood autoclaving/incineration.

Clinical Responsibility & External Quality Assessment (EQA)

A designated, experienced District Medical Officer holds overall administrative and clinical responsibility for the district transfusion service in close liaison with the National Blood Transfusion Service (NBTS), regional transfusion directorate, and district laboratory coordinator.

Traceability & Record Keeping: All donor registers, screening logs, blood issue logs, and crossmatch report request forms must be archived securely for a minimum of $5\ \text{to}\ 10\ \text{years}$ (or indefinitely as mandated by national blood policies) to ensure 100% full bi-directional traceability from donor to recipient. District laboratories must participate in regional EQA proficiency panels for blood grouping, antibody detection, and TTI serology.

9.2 Blood Donation and Storage of Blood

Monica Cheesbrough pp. 352–365 45 min read 8 MCQs (MCQ 593–600) Complete

Blood Donor Recruitment & Pre-Donation Health Assessment

The recruitment and retention of Voluntary Non-Remunerated Blood Donors (VNRBD) from low-risk community populations (e.g., secondary schools, universities, faith communities, and civic associations) is the cornerstone of blood safety in district hospitals. Paid commercial blood donors carry an unacceptably high prevalence of blood-borne pathogens and must be strictly excluded.

Donor Health Selection Criteria

  • Age: $16–18\ \text{years}$ up to $50–65\ \text{years}$ (as per national blood policy).
  • Body Weight: Minimum $\ge 45–50\ \text{kg}$ to safely donate $450\ \text{ml} \pm 10\%$ of blood (or $\ge 45\ \text{kg}$ for $350\ \text{ml}$ units in smaller-statured populations).
  • Donation Frequency: Minimum interval of $3\ \text{months}$ ($12\ \text{weeks}$) between whole blood donations.
  • Blood Pressure: Systolic $90–180\ \text{mmHg}$, Diastolic $50–100\ \text{mmHg}$.
  • Pulse Rate: Regular rhythm, $50–100\ \text{beats/minute}$ (counted for $\ge 30\ \text{seconds}$).
  • Body Temperature: Normal ($\le 37.5^\circ\text{C}$); donors with fever, malaria symptoms, or acute infection are deferred.

Haemoglobin Screening & $\text{CuSO}_4$ Method

  • Minimum Acceptable Haemoglobin:
    • Females: $\text{Hb} \ge 125\ \text{g/L}\ (12.5\ \text{g/dL})$ or $\text{PCV} \ge 0.38\ (38\%)$.
    • Males: $\text{Hb} \ge 135\ \text{g/L}\ (13.5\ \text{g/dL})$ or $\text{PCV} \ge 0.40\ (40\%)$.
  • Copper Sulphate ($\text{CuSO}_4$) Gravimetric Method:
    • Solution specific gravity: exactly $1.053$ (equivalent to $125\ \text{g/L}\ \text{Hb}$).
    • Procedure: A drop of capillary blood is dropped from $1\ \text{cm}$ into the solution.
    • Pass: Drop sinks to the bottom within $15\ \text{seconds}$ (donor eligible).
    • Fail: Drop floats or hesitates on surface (donor deferred due to anaemia).
  • Alternative Field Methods: WHO Haemoglobin Colour Scale (HCS) or portable photometric haemoglobinometers (e.g., HemoCue).

Confidentiality & Self-Exclusion Protocol

All pre-donation medical interviews must take place in strict privacy. Donors must be provided with an easy-to-understand questionnaire assessing medical history and high-risk behaviors (multiple sexual partners, recent STIs, sharing needles/syringes, partner with AIDS/HIV). Donors must be given the unambiguous option to self-exclude confidentially without embarrassment, and offered confidential post-test counseling.

Anticoagulant-Preservative Formulations & Red Cell Viability

Anticoagulant solutions in blood collection bags prevent coagulation and maintain red cell metabolism, ATP generation, and 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) levels during hypothermic liquid storage at $+2^\circ\text{C}\ \text{to}\ +6^\circ\text{C}$.

Preservative Solution Key Chemical Constituents Storage Shelf-Life ($+2^\circ\text{C}$ to $+6^\circ\text{C}$) Biochemical Mechanism & Characteristics
ACD (Acid-Citrate-Dextrose) Trisodium citrate, Citric acid, Dextrose (Glucose) 21 Days Citrate chelates calcium ($\text{Ca}^{2+}$) to block coagulation. Dextrose supports glycolytic ATP production. Rapid loss of 2,3-DPG after 7 days.
CPD (Citrate-Phosphate-Dextrose) Trisodium citrate, Citric acid, Dextrose, Sodium dihydrogen phosphate ($\text{NaH}_2\text{PO}_4$) 28 Days Inorganic phosphate acts as a physiological buffer, maintaining higher intracellular pH and preserving red cell 2,3-DPG (oxygen delivery capacity).
CPDA-1 (Citrate-Phosphate-Dextrose-Adenine) CPD formula + Adenine ($0.275\ \text{g/L}$) + Higher Dextrose ($31.9\ \text{g/L}$) 35 Days Adenine provides the substrate for de novo synthesis of adenine nucleotides (ATP), maintaining membrane deformability and 24-hour post-transfusion red cell survival $>75\%$.
SAGM (Saline-Adenine-Glucose-Mannitol) Saline ($150\ \text{mmol/L}$), Adenine, Glucose, Mannitol ($29\ \text{mmol/L}$) 42 Days Additive solution added to concentrated red cells after plasma separation. Mannitol stabilizes the erythrocyte membrane and prevents osmotic haemolysis.

Blood Collection Protocol, Phlebotomy & The Underfilled Bag Rule

Phlebotomy & Collection Standards

  1. Vein Selection & Cuff: Apply a sphygmomanometer cuff inflated to $40–60\ \text{mmHg}$ (comfortable venous congestion without arterial occlusion).
  2. Skin Asepsis: Disinfect antecubital fossa with $70\%\ \text{v/v}$ ethanol or chlorhexidine-alcohol using outward concentric friction; let air dry completely for $\ge 30\ \text{seconds}$.
  3. Venepuncture: Insert a sterile 16-gauge (16G) thin-wall needle bevel up to ensure rapid, non-turbulent, laminar blood flow.
  4. Continuous Mixing: Immediately mix blood with anticoagulant continuously throughout donation (manually by gentle inversion every 30–45 seconds, or via an automated oscillating blood rocker/mixer).
  5. Duration of Donation: Ideally completed in $5–10\ \text{minutes}$. Collections exceeding $12–15\ \text{minutes}$ should be discarded or excluded from platelet/plasma processing due to coagulation cascade activation.

The Underfilled Bag Safety Rule

Standard blood bags contain $63\ \text{ml}$ of CPDA-1 designed for $450\ \text{ml} \pm 10\%$ ($405–495\ \text{ml}$) of whole blood (total unit weight $\approx 500–600\ \text{g}$).

DANGER OF UNDERFILLING (<405 ml): If blood flow ceases before $405\ \text{ml}$ is collected, the unit is underfilled. The excessive proportion of anticoagulant to blood leads to severe hyperosmolarity, red cell crenation/lysis, and introduces dangerous amounts of unbound citrate into the recipient, causing hypocalcaemia, cardiac arrhythmias, and citrate toxicity. Underfilled units ($<405\ \text{ml}$) must be quarantined and discarded.

Pre-Refrigeration Holding: Keep freshly collected bags at ambient temperature ($20–25^\circ\text{C}$) for $1–2\ \text{hours}$ prior to refrigeration to permit natural bactericidal action of donor leukocytes and gradual cooling.

Mandatory Screening for Transfusion-Transmissible Infections (TTIs)

In district laboratories, every single unit of donor blood must be tested for key infectious pathogens before being released for clinical transfusion:

Viral Pathogens (HIV, HBV, HCV)

  • HIV-1 & HIV-2: Screened by highly sensitive rapid combo antigen-antibody assays or ELISA. Transmission risk from HIV-infected blood exceeds $95\%$. Window period: Early infection where antibody is undetectable highlights the critical need for pre-donation behavioral screening.
  • Hepatitis B Virus (HBV): Screened by detecting Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) using rapid immunochromatographic strips or ELISA. Adult carrier rates in tropical regions reach $6–15\%$.
  • Hepatitis C Virus (HCV): Screened by anti-HCV antibody detection. $70–80\%$ of infected individuals develop chronic carrier state, liver cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma.

Bacterial & Parasitic Pathogens

  • Treponema pallidum (Syphilis): Screened by Rapid Plasma Reagin (RPR) or VDRL. Cold Inactivation: Viable spirochaetes die off when blood is stored at $+2^\circ\text{C}\ \text{to}\ +6^\circ\text{C}$ for $48–72\ \text{hours}$, significantly lowering transmission risk in refrigerated banked blood.
  • Plasmodium species (Malaria): In hyperendemic zones where all donors have semi-immunity, routine blood screening is often impractical; high-risk recipients (infants, pregnant women) are treated with prophylactic antimalarial medication.
  • Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas Disease): Mandatory screening in endemic Central and South America.

Blood Storage Cold Chain & Refrigerator Operation

Unbroken cold-chain maintenance is vital. Red blood cells stored outside $+2^\circ\text{C}\ \text{to}\ +6^\circ\text{C}$ suffer rapid metabolic depletion, bacterial overgrowth, and fatal haemolysis.

Storage Temperature & The Refrigerator

  • Target Temperature: Maintained strictly between $+2^\circ\text{C}\ \text{and}\ +6^\circ\text{C}$ in a dedicated, compression or gas-operated blood bank refrigerator with internal fan circulation.
  • Temperature Monitoring: Monitored continuously via circular chart recorders or logged manually with a High/Low thermometer at least twice daily (morning and evening).
  • Audio/Visual Alarms: Calibrated to trigger immediately if temperature drops below $+2^\circ\text{C}$ or rises above $+6^\circ\text{C}$.
  • Shelf Organization: Strict segregation of Quarantine Stock (untested/pending) from Released Stock (tested safe, ABO/Rh grouped, crossmatched).

NEVER Freeze Whole Blood & The 30-Min Rule

FATAL DANGER OF FREEZING (<0°C): Freezing destroys erythrocyte lipid bilayers, causing massive in vitro haemolysis. If thawed haemolysed blood is transfused, massive release of free haemoglobin and potassium causes fatal acute renal tubular necrosis, hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest, and DIC.

The 30-Minute Rule: Blood issued from the blood refrigerator must be commenced within $30\ \text{minutes}$. If not initiated, it must be returned immediately to the blood bank refrigerator. The entire transfusion of a unit must be completed within $4\ \text{hours}$ to prevent bacterial proliferation.

9.3 Blood Grouping (ABO & Rh Blood Group Systems)

Monica Cheesbrough pp. 362–370 45 min read 8 MCQs (MCQ 601–608) Complete

The ABO Blood Group System & Antigen Genetics

The ABO blood group system, discovered by Karl Landsteiner in 1900, is the most critical system in transfusion medicine. Transfusing ABO-incompatible blood triggers rapid, complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis leading to acute renal failure, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and death.

Antigens & Precursor H Substance

  • H Gene & Precursor H Antigen: The *H* gene codes for a fucosyltransferase that adds L-fucose to a precursor carbohydrate chain on the RBC membrane, producing H antigen.
  • A Gene: Encodes $\alpha$-N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase, adding N-acetylgalactosamine to H substance ($\rightarrow$ A antigen).
  • B Gene: Encodes $\alpha$-D-galactosyltransferase, adding D-galactose to H substance ($\rightarrow$ B antigen).
  • O Gene: An amorph (non-functional gene); group O erythrocytes express unconverted H antigen in highest density.
  • Bombay Phenotype ($hh$): Extremely rare individuals homozygous for non-functional *h* gene. They lack H antigen, cannot express A or B antigens, and produce potent, wide-thermal-range anti-H, anti-A, and anti-B. They can receive blood only from other Bombay phenotype individuals.

ABO Antibodies (Isoagglutinins)

  • "Naturally Occurring" Regular Antibodies: Developed during the first $3–6\ \text{months}$ of life following environmental exposure to gut bacterial antigens mimicking A and B carbohydrates.
  • Group A: Has A antigen on RBCs $\rightarrow$ Anti-B in serum (predominantly IgM).
  • Group B: Has B antigen on RBCs $\rightarrow$ Anti-A in serum (predominantly IgM).
  • Group AB: Has both A and B antigens $\rightarrow$ No ABO antibodies in serum (Universal RBC Recipient).
  • Group O: Has neither A nor B antigen $\rightarrow$ Anti-A, Anti-B, and Anti-A,B in serum (Universal RBC Donor). Group O anti-A,B is predominantly IgG and can cross the placenta, causing ABO Haemolytic Disease of the Newborn (HDN).

Subgroups of A & Lectin Differentiation

Subgroup Population Frequency Reaction with Monoclonal Anti-A Reaction with *Dolichos biflorus* (Anti-$A_1$ Lectin) Serum Antibody Incidence
$A_1$ $\approx 80\%$ of Group A Strong ($4+$) Positive ($4+$ Agglutination) Anti-B only
$A_2$ $\approx 20\%$ of Group A Positive ($3+$ to $4+$) Negative (No Agglutination) $1–8\%$ produce irregular cold-reacting Anti-$A_1$
$A_2B$ Subgroup of AB Positive Negative $22–26\%$ produce irregular Anti-$A_1$

The Rhesus (Rh) Blood Group System & D Antigen

The Rhesus (Rh) blood group system is second in clinical importance only to ABO. The system comprises over 50 antigens, with D, C, c, E, and e being the five primary antigens.

Immunogenicity of the D Antigen

  • High Immunogenicity: D is by far the most immunogenic RBC antigen; over $80\%$ of Rh-negative individuals develop immune Anti-D after receiving a single unit of Rh-positive blood.
  • Rh Positive vs Rh Negative: A person is termed Rh Positive if their red cells possess the D antigen, and Rh Negative if they lack D ($dd$). (There is no "d" antigen).
  • Tropical Epidemiology: In sub-Saharan African and Asian populations, the frequency of Rh positivity is extraordinarily high ($95–99\%$), whereas in European/Caucasian populations, $\approx 15\%$ are Rh negative.
  • Rh Antibodies: Immune antibodies (principally IgG1 and IgG3) produced following transfusion or fetomaternal haemorrhage. They react optimally at $37^\circ\text{C}$ in the Antihuman Globulin (AHG) phase and cross the placenta, causing severe Rh HDN.

Weak D ($\text{D}^\text{u}$) vs Partial D ($\text{D}^\text{VI}$)

  • Weak D (formerly $\text{D}^\text{u}$): A quantitative reduction in D antigen density per red cell. Does not readily agglutinate directly with standard anti-D in immediate spin, but agglutinates strongly after incubation at $37^\circ\text{C}$ in the Indirect Antiglobulin Test (IAT).
  • Partial D (e.g., $\text{D}^\text{VI}$): A qualitative mosaic defect where specific D epitopes are missing. Individuals can produce alloanti-D against the missing epitopes if exposed to normal D+ blood.
  • Transfusion Policy:
    • Blood Donors: Must be tested for Weak D/Partial D; if positive, classified and labelled as Rh POSITIVE (to prevent sensitizing Rh- recipients).
    • Patients / Recipients: If Weak D or Partial D ($\text{D}^\text{VI}$), managed and transfused as Rh NEGATIVE.

Laboratory Protocols: Tube & Slide ABO/Rh Grouping

Accurate ABO grouping mandates both Forward (Cell) Grouping and Reverse (Serum) Grouping. Both tests must show complete reciprocal concordance before releasing blood.

Tube # Phase Contents Added Group A Group B Group AB Group O
Tube 1 Cell (Front) 1 drop Anti-A (Blue) + 1 drop $3–5\%$ patient RBCs $+$ $-$ $+$ $-$
Tube 2 Cell (Front) 1 drop Anti-B (Yellow) + 1 drop $3–5\%$ patient RBCs $-$ $+$ $+$ $-$
Tube 3 Serum (Back) 1 drop patient serum + 1 drop $3–5\%$ known A cells $-$ $+$ $-$ $+$
Tube 4 Serum (Back) 1 drop patient serum + 1 drop $3–5\%$ known B cells $+$ $-$ $-$ $+$
Tube 5 Autocontrol 1 drop patient serum + 1 drop $3–5\%$ patient RBCs $-$ $-$ $-$ $-$

Neonates & Elderly Grouping

  • Infants <4 Months: Serum reverse grouping is omitted because neonates do not produce their own isoagglutinins until $3–4\ \text{months}$ of age; any antibodies in serum are passively transferred maternal IgG. Grouping is based solely on washed red cell front grouping.
  • Elderly / Immunodeficient: Isoagglutinins may be weak or undetectable. Enhance reverse grouping by incubating tubes at $4^\circ\text{C}$ for $15–30\ \text{minutes}$ with an autologous control.

Resolving ABO Discrepancies

  • Rouleaux Formation (Pseudoagglutination): High globulin/fibrinogen levels (multiple myeloma, nephrotic syndrome) cause "stack-of-coins" stacking. Resolved by Saline Replacement Technique (true agglutination remains; rouleaux disperses).
  • Cold Autoantibodies: Causes positive reaction in Tube 5 (Autocontrol). Resolved by pre-warming cells and reagents to $37^\circ\text{C}$ and washing RBCs with warm saline.
  • Acquired B Phenomenon: Colon cancer or Gram-negative septicemia bacteria de-acetylate A antigen into pseudo-B. Patient is group A; serum contains normal anti-B.

Part 2 • Chapter 9: Blood Transfusion Practice

9.4 Compatibility Testing & Investigation of Transfusion Reactions

Monica Cheesbrough pp. 370–379 50 min read 8 MCQs (MCQ 609–616) Complete

Compatibility Testing (The Major Crossmatch)

Compatibility testing (crossmatching) is the definitive pre-transfusion laboratory barrier designed to prevent acute haemolytic transfusion reactions. The Major Crossmatch tests the Patient\'s (Recipient\'s) Serum against the Donor\'s Red Blood Cells to verify ABO compatibility and detect clinically significant irregular/atypical alloantibodies (e.g., Rh, Kell, Duffy, Kidd).

The Standard 3-Phase Crossmatch

  1. Saline Room Temperature Phase ($20–25^\circ\text{C}$): Detects potent, cold-reactive IgM agglutinins (ABO incompatibility, anti-M, anti-N, Lewis antibodies).
  2. $37^\circ\text{C}$ Incubation Phase (with LISS or Albumin): Facilitates sensitized binding of warm-reactive IgG antibodies (Rh, Kell, Duffy, Kidd) to donor RBC antigens.
  3. Indirect Antihuman Globulin (AHG / Coombs) Phase: The most sensitive and essential phase. Washes donor red cells $3–4\times$ with isotonic saline, adds AHG reagent (anti-IgG / green dye), and centrifuges. Crosslinks sensitized IgG antibodies to produce macroscopic agglutination.

LISS Acceleration & Coombs\' Control Cells

  • Low Ionic Strength Saline (LISS): Reduces ionic strength from $0.15\ \text{M}$ to $0.03\ \text{M}$, lowering the electrostatic shielding (zeta potential) between erythrocytes and accelerating antibody uptake. Shortens $37^\circ\text{C}$ incubation time from $45–60\ \text{minutes}$ down to $15\ \text{minutes}$.
  • Validation with Coombs\' Control (Check) Cells: To every tube showing a negative AHG reaction, 1 drop of IgG-sensitized red cells must be added. Macroscopic agglutination ($2+$ to $3+$) MUST occur.
    • Agglutination occurs: AHG reagent was active and un-neutralized (test valid).
    • No agglutination: AHG was omitted or neutralized by residual serum globulins from inadequate washing; test is INVALID and must be repeated.

Emergency Crossmatch Protocols

Immediate Catastrophic Haemorrhage: Issue uncrossmatched Group O Rh-negative (or Group O Rh-positive for males/postmenopausal females if O- is scarce) packed red cells with an emergency release form signed by the clinician. Rapid Emergency Crossmatch ($5–10\ \text{min}$): Saline immediate spin crossmatch to exclude ABO incompatibility while standard AHG crossmatching continues in parallel.

Adverse Transfusion Reactions: Classification & Emergency Workup

Transfusion reactions range from mild cutaneous allergy to catastrophic fatal intravascular haemolysis or endotoxic shock. Clinical vigilance and standardized investigation are mandatory.

Reaction Type Primary Mechanism Clinical Presentation Key Diagnostic Findings
Acute Haemolytic (AHTR) ABO incompatibility; IgM complement-mediated intravascular lysis Fever, chills, severe flank/back pain, hypotension, dyspnoea, dark urine, DIC, shock Pink/red post-transfusion plasma (free Hb), haemoglobinuria, positive DAT, repeat crossmatch incompatible
Delayed Haemolytic (DHTR) Anamnestic secondary IgG response (Kidd, Rh, Kell) $3–14\ \text{days}$ post-transfusion Unexplained drop in haemoglobin, mild jaundice, low-grade fever, extravascular splenic clearance Positive DAT (mixed-field), rising unconjugated bilirubin, newly detectable alloantibody in serum
Febrile Non-Haemolytic (FNHTR) Cytokines accumulated in unit or recipient anti-leukocyte/HLA antibodies Fever ($\ge 1^\circ\text{C}$ rise), chills, rigors during or shortly after transfusion No haemolysis; plasma clear; DAT negative; urine clear
Allergic & Anaphylactic Hypersensitivity to plasma proteins; Anti-IgA antibodies in IgA-deficient recipients Urticaria, rash, pruritus; in severe cases: laryngeal oedema, bronchospasm, vascular collapse No haemolysis; respond to antihistamines / adrenaline
Bacterial Contamination / Sepsis Psychrophilic Gram-negative bacilli (*Pseudomonas*, *Yersinia enterocolitica*) Sudden profound hyperpyrexia, shivering, severe hypotension, endotoxic collapse, DIC Gram stain of donor bag reveals abundant bacteria; positive donor bag blood culture

Immediate Bedside Protocol

  1. STOP TRANSFUSION IMMEDIATELY; disconnect blood set but keep IV line patent with normal saline.
  2. Check patient vital signs and verify clerical labels (wristband vs blood pack).
  3. Notify attending medical officer and transfusion laboratory immediately.
  4. Collect post-transfusion EDTA blood, clotted blood, and first-voided urine sample.
  5. Send donor blood bag with remaining contents, IV giving set, and samples to laboratory.

Laboratory Investigation Protocol

  • Visual Inspection: Centrifuge pre- and post-transfusion samples side-by-side; inspect plasma for pink/red discolouration (free haemoglobin) or icterus.
  • Direct Antiglobulin Test (DAT): Perform DAT on post-transfusion EDTA cells (detects circulating in vivo sensitized donor RBCs).
  • Repeat ABO/Rh Grouping: Re-group pre-transfusion sample, post-transfusion sample, and donor bag blood.
  • Repeat Crossmatch: Crossmatch pre- and post-transfusion serum against donor bag cells via saline, $37^\circ\text{C}$, and AHG.
  • Microbiological Screen: Gram stain and blood cultures of remaining blood in the pack.

Haemolytic Disease of the Newborn (HDN) & Exchange Transfusion

HDN occurs when maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta into the fetal circulation, targeting fetal red blood cells displaying paternal antigens.

ABO HDN vs Rh HDN

  • ABO HDN (Most Common in Tropics):
    • Setting: Mother is Group O; infant is Group A or B (maternal IgG anti-A,B).
    • Parity: Can occur in the first pregnancy without prior sensitization.
    • Clinical: Milder jaundice; rarely causes hydrops.
    • Morphology: Marked spherocytosis on infant blood film.
    • DAT: Weakly positive ($1+$ to $2+$) or occasionally negative.
  • Rh HDN (Most Severe):
    • Setting: Mother is Rh-negative; infant is Rh-positive (maternal IgG Anti-D).
    • Parity: Spares the first pregnancy; progressively worsens in subsequent Rh+ pregnancies.
    • Clinical: Severe anaemia, rapid profound jaundice, hydrops fetalis, hepatosplenomegaly.
    • Morphology: Marked polychromasia, reticulocytosis, and abundant nucleated RBCs; minimal spherocytosis.
    • DAT: Strongly positive ($3+$ to $4+$).

Exchange Blood Transfusion Protocol

Indicated when infant unconjugated serum bilirubin exceeds $300\ \mu\text{mol/L}\ (17.5–18.0\ \text{mg/dL})$ to prevent irreversible bilirubin encephalopathy (Kernicterus).

Blood Selection for Exchange Transfusion:
  • For Rh HDN: Use ABO-compatible Rh-negative blood (or Group O Rh-negative).
  • For ABO HDN: Use Group O blood of the infant\'s Rh group with low-titre anti-A/anti-B.
  • Compatibility Crossmatch: Must be crossmatched against the Mother\'s Serum (which contains the causative IgG antibody).
  • Unit Specifications: Fresh blood ($<5\ \text{days}$ old) with low plasma potassium and high $2,3\text{-DPG}$, CMV-negative.

General Principles for Reagent Preparation, Safety & Quality Control

Accurate and reproducible laboratory diagnosis depends fundamentally upon the correct preparation, purity, pH calibration, storage, and quality control of diagnostic stains and chemical reagents. All district laboratory personnel must adhere strictly to standard safety practices (Subunit 3.5 in Part 1) and standard operating procedures for chemical storage.

Universal Preparation Standards

  • Water Quality: Use clean, high-grade distilled or deionized water for all reagent preparations (never use unpurified tap water which introduces heavy metal and chlorine ions).
  • Room Temperature Defined: In tropical district laboratories, "Room Temperature" refers specifically to $20^\circ\text{C}\ \text{to}\ 28^\circ\text{C}$. Reagents requiring cold storage must be kept at $2^\circ\text{C}\ \text{to}\ 8^\circ\text{C}$ in dedicated chemical refrigerators.
  • Volumetric Accuracy: Measure liquids with calibrated glass cylinders or volumetric flasks. Ensure cylinders are held at eye level to read the bottom of the meniscus.
  • Analytical Weighing: Weigh analytical grade chemicals on a calibrated balance; use clean weighing paper/boats and clean spatulas.

Chemical Hazard & Storage Protocols

  • Corrosive Acids & Alkalis: Always add concentrated acid to water slowly down the side of the container with continuous mixing. NEVER add water to concentrated acid (causes violent boiling and dangerous splattering).
  • Flammable Solvents (Methanol, Ethanol, Acetone, Ether): Store in heavy metal safety cabinets well away from open flames, Bunsen burners, and direct sunlight.
  • Toxic / Carcinogenic Agents: Work in well-ventilated rooms or chemical fume hoods. Never mouth-pipette any reagent.
  • Clear Labelling & Expiry: Every reagent bottle must be clearly labelled with: Reagent Name, Concentration, Date of Preparation, Expiry Date, Hazard Symbol, and Initials of Preparer.

Stain B (Iodine): Iodine $6.0\ \text{g}$, KI $9.0\ \text{g}$, Water $900\ \text{ml}$.		 Room Temp in brown glass bottles; Stable for 1 year. Demonstration of metachromatic volutin granules in *Corynebacterium diphtheriae*.
No. 6 Auramine-phenol fluorescent stain Auramine O $0.3\ \text{g}$, Phenol crystals (pure) $30\ \text{g}$, Distilled water $970\ \text{ml}$. Dissolve phenol in warm water, add auramine, shake well, filter. Toxic. Store in dark amber bottle at Room Temp; Stable for 6 months. Fluorescence microscopy screening of sputum for *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*.
No. 7 Bile solubility reagent ($10\%$) Sodium deoxycholate $10.0\ \text{g}$, Sterile distilled water $100\ \text{ml}$. Dissolve and filter. Store at $2–8^\circ\text{C}$; Stable for 6 months. Differentiation of *Streptococcus pneumoniae* (bile soluble / clears) from Viridans Streptococci.
No. 9 Catalase reagent ($3\%\ \text{H}_2\text{O}_2$) Hydrogen peroxide ($30\%\ \text{w/v}$ / 100 vol) $10\ \text{ml}$, Distilled water $90\ \text{ml}$. Prepare in clean glassware. Store at $2–8^\circ\text{C}$ in dark plastic bottle; Renew monthly (check with *S. aureus* QC). Differentiating Staphylococci (catalase positive) from Streptococci (catalase negative).
No. 12 Crystal violet stain, $0.5\%\ \&\ 1\%$ Crystal violet powder $5.0\ \text{g}$, Distilled water $1\ \text{L}$ ($0.5\%$), or $10\ \text{g}$ with $100\ \text{ml}$ ethanol and $900\ \text{ml}$ water ($1\%$). Filter. Room Temp; Stable for 2 years. Filter before dispensing. Primary basic stain in Gram's staining method for bacterial morphology.
No. 20 Gram's iodine solution Potassium iodide $20.0\ \text{g}$, Iodine crystals $10.0\ \text{g}$, Distilled water $1\ \text{L}$. Dissolve KI in $50\ \text{ml}$ water, dissolve iodine crystals, dilute to $1\ \text{L}$. Store in dark amber glass bottle at Room Temp; Stable for 1 year. Mordant in Gram staining (forms insoluble crystal violet-iodine complex).
No. 24 India ink (Nigrosin wet mount) Commercial Pelikan waterproof drawing ink or $10\%\ \text{w/v}$ Nigrosin in distilled water with $0.5\%\ \text{w/v}$ formalin preservative. Filter before use. Room Temp in clean dropper bottle; Stable indefinitely. Negative background capsule staining of *Cryptococcus neoformans* in CSF.
No. 25 Kovac's indole reagent p-Dimethylaminobenzaldehyde $5.0\ \text{g}$, Isoamyl or pure amyl alcohol $75\ \text{ml}$, Concentrated $\text{HCl}$ $25\ \text{ml}$. Dissolve aldehyde in alcohol, slowly add acid. Pale yellow colour. Store at $2–8^\circ\text{C}$ in dark glass bottle; Stable for 1 year. Discard if turns dark brown. Testing bacterial tryptophanase activity (red rosindole ring indicates indole positive, e.g., *E. coli*).
No. 27 Kovac's oxidase reagent ($1\%$) Tetramethyl-p-phenylenediamine dihydrochloride $0.1\ \text{g}$, Sterile distilled water $10\ \text{ml}$. Dissolve fresh in sterile container. Protect from light. Prepare FRESH; Auto-oxidizes rapidly. Stable for 1 week if frozen at $-20^\circ\text{C}$ in foil wrap. Detection of cytochrome oxidase in *Pseudomonas*, *Neisseria*, *Vibrio*, and *Campylobacter* (deep purple within $10\ \text{s}$).
No. 28 Lactophenol cotton blue (LPCB) Cotton blue (aniline blue) $0.05\ \text{g}$, Phenol crystals $20.0\ \text{g}$, Glycerol $40\ \text{ml}$, Lactic acid $20\ \text{ml}$, Water $20\ \text{ml}$. Dissolve with gentle heat. Corrosive. Store in dark amber bottle at Room Temp; Stable indefinitely. Mounting and staining fungal hyphae, conidia, and sporangia from fungal cultures.
No. 32 McFarland turbidity standards ($0.5–4.0$) $0.5\ \text{McFarland}:$ Add $0.05\ \text{ml}$ of $1.175\%\ \text{w/v}\ \text{BaCl}_2\cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to $9.95\ \text{ml}$ of $1\%\ \text{v/v}\ \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$. Density $\approx 1.5 \times 10^8\ \text{CFU/ml}$. Seal tube with wax/parafilm. Store in dark at Room Temp; Stable for 6 months. Vortex vigorously before matching. Standardization of bacterial inocula for disk diffusion Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (AST).
No. 38 ONPG reagent ($\beta$-galactosidase) o-Nitrophenyl-$\beta$-D-galactopyranoside $80\ \text{mg}$, Monopotassium phosphate buffer ($0.25\ \text{M}$, pH $7.5$) $15\ \text{ml}$, Water $5\ \text{ml}$. Dissolve and store. Store at $2–8^\circ\text{C}$ in dark bottle; Stable for 1 month (or freeze at $-20^\circ\text{C}$ for 6 months). Detection of late/slow lactose fermenters (*Shigella sonnei*, *Citrobacter*) lacking permease. Yellow = positive.
No. 47 Safranin counterstain, $0.5\%\ \text{w/v}$ Safranin O $5.0\ \text{g}$, Distilled water $1\ \text{L}$. Dissolve and filter. (Or Neutral Red $1.0\ \text{g/L}$). Room Temp; Stable for 2 years. Gram stain counterstain for Gram-negative bacteria (stains pink/red).
No. 53 Voges-Proskauer reagents (VP-A & VP-B) VP-A: $\alpha$-Naphthol $5.0\ \text{g}$, Absolute ethanol $100\ \text{ml}$.
VP-B: Potassium hydroxide ($\text{KOH}$) $40.0\ \text{g}$, Distilled water $100\ \text{ml}$.		 Store at $2–8^\circ\text{C}$ in dark dropper bottles; Stable for 6 months. Detection of acetoin (acetylmethylcarbinol) in glucose metabolism (*Klebsiella/Enterobacter* positive; *E. coli* negative).
No. 55 Ziehl-Neelsen Carbol Fuchsin Basic fuchsin $10.0\ \text{g}$, Phenol crystals $50.0\ \text{g}$, Absolute ethanol $100\ \text{ml}$, Distilled water $900\ \text{ml}$. Dissolve basic fuchsin in alcohol, dissolve phenol in water, combine, mix well, filter. Store at Room Temp in amber bottle; Stable for 1 year. Filter before use. Primary stain for Acid-Fast Bacilli (AFB) in sputum, CSF, and tissue smears (*M. tuberculosis*, *M. leprae*).

Appendix 2: Master Compendium of Bacteriological Culture Media & QC

Monica Cheesbrough Part 2 pp. 381–410 35 Culture Media Formulations ATCC QC Battery & Sterility Protocols Complete

Preparation, Sterilization & Quality Control Standards for Culture Media

Culture media provide the nutritional and environmental requirements for isolating, enumerating, and identifying pathogenic microorganisms. High-quality media preparation demands rigorous adherence to rehydration, autoclaving parameters, heat-sensitive additive handling, pouring temperatures, and quality control with reference ATCC strains.

Preparation & Pouring Protocols

  • Rehydration & Dissolution: Weigh dehydrated powder accurately; add to distilled water and soak for 5 min. Heat with frequent agitation until completely dissolved before autoclaving.
  • Autoclaving Parameters: Standard sterilization is $121^\circ\text{C}\ (15\ \text{psi}\ /\ 103\ \text{kPa})$ for $15\ \text{minutes}$. Do not over-autoclave (causes caramelization of sugars and precipitation of phosphates).
  • Heat-Labile Media: Media containing selective bile salts and brilliant green (e.g., TCBS, XLD, DCA, Selenite F) must NEVER be autoclaved; heat only to boiling point with swirling.
  • Pouring Temperature: Cool molten agar in a water bath to $45^\circ\text{C}\ \text{to}\ 50^\circ\text{C}$ before adding blood, antibiotics, or pouring into sterile Petri dishes ($15–20\ \text{ml}$ per 90 mm dish, giving a depth of $4\ \text{mm}$).

Sterility & Performance QC Testing

  • Sterility Testing: Incubate $3–5\%$ of each prepared batch of plates at $35^\circ\text{C}\ \text{to}\ 37^\circ\text{C}$ for $24–48\ \text{hours}$. The batch passes only if there is zero microbial growth.
  • Performance Testing (Growth & Selectivity): Inoculate positive and negative control ATCC reference strains to verify colony morphology, haemolysis, selective inhibition, and biochemical indicator color shifts.
  • Storage & Shelf-Life: Seal solidified plates in plastic bags to prevent moisture loss; store at $2^\circ\text{C}\ \text{to}\ 8^\circ\text{C}$ inverted (lid down) to prevent condensation droplets from falling onto the agar surface. Shelf-life: Plain media $4–6\ \text{weeks}$; Blood/Chocolate agar $2–3\ \text{weeks}$.

Master Compendium of Bacteriological Culture Media (Media No. 1 to No. 35)

Formulations, Sterilization Modes, Selective Agents, and QC Strains from Part 2 Appendix I.

No. Culture Medium Name Formulation (per Litre) & Preparation Sterilization Target Pathogens & QC Strains
Media 1 Blood Agar (BA) Nutrient / Columbia agar base $40\ \text{g}$, Distilled water $1\ \text{L}$. Autoclave, cool to $45–50^\circ\text{C}$, add $50–100\ \text{ml}$ ($5–10\%$) sterile defibrinated sheep or horse blood. Mix gently; pour plates. Base: Autoclave $121^\circ\text{C}$, 15 min. Blood: Aseptic addition. Enriched medium for fastidious bacteria; detects haemolysis ($\alpha, \beta, \gamma$). QC: *S. pyogenes* ($\beta$), *S. pneumoniae* ($\alpha$).
Media 2 Chocolate (Heated Blood) Agar Nutrient/GC agar base $40\ \text{g}$, Water $1\ \text{L}$. Autoclave, cool to $75^\circ\text{C}$, add $70\ \text{ml}$ sterile blood. Hold at $75^\circ\text{C}$ with gentle swirling until chocolate brown ($10–15\ \text{min}$). Cool to $50^\circ\text{C}$, pour plates. Base: Autoclave. Heat lyses RBCs, releasing Factor X (hemin) and Factor V (NAD). Isolation of *Haemophilus influenzae* and *Neisseria meningitidis*. QC: *H. influenzae* ATCC 49247.
Media 3 MacConkey Agar (with salt) Peptone $20\ \text{g}$, Lactose $10\ \text{g}$, Bile salts $5\ \text{g}$, $\text{NaCl}$ $5\ \text{g}$, Neutral red $0.075\ \text{g}$, Agar $12\ \text{g}$, Water $1\ \text{L}$. pH $7.4$. Autoclave $121^\circ\text{C}$, 15 min. Selective/differential for Enterobacteriaceae. Lactose Fermenters (pink/red, e.g., *E. coli*); Non-Lactose Fermenters (pale/colourless, e.g., *Salmonella*).
Media 4 Xylose Lysine Deoxycholate (XLD) Agar Xylose $3.5\ \text{g}$, L-Lysine $5.0\ \text{g}$, Lactose $7.5\ \text{g}$, Sucrose $7.5\ \text{g}$, $\text{NaCl}$ $5.0\ \text{g}$, Yeast extract $3.0\ \text{g}$, Phenol red $0.08\ \text{g}$, Sodium deoxycholate $2.5\ \text{g}$, Sodium thiosulphate $6.8\ \text{g}$, Ferric ammonium citrate $0.8\ \text{g}$, Agar $13.5\ \text{g}$, Water $1\ \text{L}$. pH $7.4$. DO NOT AUTOCLAVE. Heat to boiling point with swirling; cool to $50^\circ\text{C}$, pour. Selective isolation of *Salmonella* (red colonies with black $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ centers) and *Shigella* (translucent red colonies). QC: *S. typhimurium*, *S. flexneri*.
Media 5 Thiosulphate Citrate Bile Salts Sucrose (TCBS) Yeast extract $5\ \text{g}$, Peptone $10\ \text{g}$, Sucrose $20\ \text{g}$, Sodium thiosulphate $10\ \text{g}$, Sodium citrate $10\ \text{g}$, Ox bile $8\ \text{g}$, $\text{NaCl}$ $10\ \text{g}$, Ferric citrate $1\ \text{g}$, Bromothymol blue $0.04\ \text{g}$, Thymol blue $0.04\ \text{g}$, Agar $14\ \text{g}$, Water $1\ \text{L}$. pH $8.6$. DO NOT AUTOCLAVE. Heat to boiling point only; cool to $50^\circ\text{C}$, pour plates. Selective isolation of *Vibrio cholerae* (sucrose-fermenting yellow colonies) and *V. parahaemolyticus* (green colonies). QC: *V. cholerae* ATCC 14035.
Media 6 CLED Agar (Cystine Lactose Electrolyte Deficient) Peptone $4\ \text{g}$, Tryptone $4\ \text{g}$, Beef extract $3\ \text{g}$, Lactose $10\ \text{g}$, L-Cystine $0.128\ \text{g}$, Bromothymol blue $0.02\ \text{g}$, Agar $15\ \text{g}$, Water $1\ \text{L}$. pH $7.3$. Electrolyte deficient to prevent swarming of *Proteus*. Autoclave $121^\circ\text{C}$, 15 min. Quantitative urine culture for UTIs. Prevents *Proteus* swarming; Lactose fermenters (*E. coli*) yellow; Non-fermenters blue.
Media 7 Lowenstein-Jensen (LJ) Medium Mineral salts solution (potassium phosphate, magnesium sulphate, magnesium citrate, asparagine, glycerol) $600\ \text{ml}$, Malachite green ($2\%$ aqueous) $20\ \text{ml}$, Fresh whole homogenized hens' eggs $1\ \text{L}$. Mix aseptically, dispense into sterile screw-cap bottles. Inspissation: Heat at $85^\circ\text{C}$ in slanted position for $45\ \text{minutes}$ (coagulates egg protein). Primary isolation of *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* (buff, rough, "breadcrumb" colonies in 2–6 weeks). QC: *M. tuberculosis* H37Rv.
Media 8 Mueller-Hinton Agar (MHA) Beef infusion $300\ \text{g}$, Acid hydrolysate of casein $17.5\ \text{g}$, Starch $1.5\ \text{g}$, Agar $17\ \text{g}$, Water $1\ \text{L}$. pH $7.2–7.4$. Pour plates to uniform depth of exactly $4\ \text{mm}$ ($25\ \text{ml}$ per 90 mm plate). Autoclave $121^\circ\text{C}$, 15 min. Standard CLSI/EUCAST medium for disk diffusion Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (AST). QC: *E. coli* ATCC 25922, *S. aureus* ATCC 25923.
Media 11 Selenite F Broth Sodium hydrogen selenite $4\ \text{g}$, Peptone $5\ \text{g}$, Lactose $4\ \text{g}$, Disodium hydrogen phosphate $9.5\ \text{g}$, Sodium dihydrogen phosphate $0.5\ \text{g}$, Water $1\ \text{L}$. pH $7.0$. Dispense into sterile tubes. DO NOT AUTOCLAVE. Heat in boiling water or steam for 10 min. Toxic. Enrichment broth for isolating *Salmonella enterica* from faecal specimens. Subculture to XLD/DCA at 12–18 h.
Media 13 Triple Sugar Iron (TSI) Agar Peptone $20\ \text{g}$, Glucose $1\ \text{g}$ ($0.1\%$), Lactose $10\ \text{g}$ ($1\%$), Sucrose $10\ \text{g}$ ($1\%$), $\text{NaCl}$ $5\ \text{g}$, Ferrous sulphate $0.2\ \text{g}$, Sodium thiosulphate $0.3\ \text{g}$, Phenol red $0.024\ \text{g}$, Agar $13\ \text{g}$, Water $1\ \text{L}$. pH $7.4$. Slant with deep butt. Autoclave $121^\circ\text{C}$, 15 min; Slant tubes to give 1 inch butt and 1.5 inch slant. Biochemical identification of Enterobacteriaceae (Carbohydrate fermentation, gas $\text{CO}_2/\text{H}_2$, and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ blackening).
Media 18 Castaneda Diphasic Blood Culture Medium Solid Phase: Tryptic soy / BHI agar ($2.5\%$) poured on bottle side. Liquid Phase: BHI broth ($50\ \text{ml}$) containing $0.025–0.05\%\ \text{w/v}$ Sodium Polyanethol Sulphonate (SPS). Gas phase flushed with $5–10\%\ \text{CO}_2$. Autoclave bottles $121^\circ\text{C}$, 15 min. SPS added filter-sterilized. Diphasic blood culture for isolation of *Brucella*, *Salmonella Typhi*, and fastidious septicaemia pathogens without opening bottles.
Media 19 Sabouraud Dextrose Agar (SDA) Peptone $10\ \text{g}$, Dextrose (Glucose) $40\ \text{g}$, Agar $15\ \text{g}$, Distilled water $1\ \text{L}$. pH $5.6$. Add Chloramphenicol ($0.05\ \text{g/L}$) to suppress bacteria, and Cycloheximide ($0.5\ \text{g/L}$) for dermatophytes. Autoclave $121^\circ\text{C}$, 15 min (Avoid overheating due to high sugar content). Cultivation of medical fungi, yeasts (*Candida albicans*), dermatophytes, and dimorphic systemic fungi. Incubate at $25–30^\circ\text{C}$.
Media 20 Modified New York City (MNYC) Medium GC agar base, Lysed horse blood ($5\%$), Yeast dialysate, Starch, Vancomycin ($3\ \text{mg/L}$), Colistin ($7.5\ \text{mg/L}$), Nystatin ($12,500\ \text{IU/L}$), Trimethoprim ($5\ \text{mg/L}$). Base autoclaved. Blood and selective antibiotic supplement added aseptically at $50^\circ\text{C}$. Primary selective isolation of *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* and *Neisseria meningitidis* from contaminated urogenital/throat sites.
Media 21 Christensen's Urea Agar Peptone $1\ \text{g}$, Dextrose $1\ \text{g}$, $\text{NaCl}$ $5\ \text{g}$, $\text{KH}_2\text{PO}_4$ $2\ \text{g}$, Phenol red $0.012\ \text{g}$, Agar $15\ \text{g}$, Water $900\ \text{ml}$. Autoclave, cool to $50^\circ\text{C}$, add $100\ \text{ml}$ of $20\%$ filter-sterilized urea. Slant with deep butt. Base autoclaved; Urea solution is heat-labile (must be membrane filter-sterilized $0.22\ \mu\text{m}$). Detection of urease enzyme (*Proteus* rapid positive bright pink/magenta in 2–4 h; *Klebsiella* delayed positive; *E. coli/Salmonella* negative).

High-Priority Critical (Panic) Laboratory Alert Values

Critical (Panic) values represent laboratory test results that signal an immediate, life-threatening medical emergency. When a critical value is obtained, the laboratory scientist must immediately verify the result and telephone the attending medical officer directly, recording the call details in the laboratory Critical Value Logbook.

Diagnostic Analyte Low Critical Alert Limit High Critical Alert Limit Clinical Threat & Emergency Escalation
Haemoglobin ($\text{Hb}$) $< 50\ \text{g/L}\ (5.0\ \text{g/dL})$ $> 200\ \text{g/L}\ (20.0\ \text{g/dL})$ Severe hypoxia, high-output heart failure / Hyperviscosity stroke
Platelet Count $< 20 \times 10^9\text{/L}\ (20,000\text{/\mu L})$ $> 1000 \times 10^9\text{/L}$ Spontaneous fatal intracranial / gastrointestinal haemorrhage / Thrombosis
Total White Blood Cells $< 1.5 \times 10^9\text{/L}$ (Neutrophils $<0.5$) $> 30.0 \times 10^9\text{/L}$ (or Blasts present) Agranulocytosis, overwhelming sepsis / Acute leukemia, leukostasis
Serum Potassium ($\text{K}^+$) $< 2.8\ \text{mmol/L}\ (2.8\ \text{mEq/L})$ $> 6.2\ \text{mmol/L}\ (6.2\ \text{mEq/L})$ Lethal ventricular arrhythmias, peaked T waves, cardiac arrest
Serum Sodium ($\text{Na}^+$) $< 120\ \text{mmol/L}$ $> 160\ \text{mmol/L}$ Cerebral oedema, intractable seizures, brain herniation, coma
Blood Glucose $< 2.5\ \text{mmol/L}\ (45\ \text{mg/dL})$ $> 25.0\ \text{mmol/L}\ (450\ \text{mg/dL})$ Severe neuroglycopenia, hypoglycaemic coma / Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
Neonatal Total Bilirubin - $> 300\ \mu\text{mol/L}\ (17.5\ \text{mg/dL})$ Kernicterus (irreversible toxic bilirubin encephalopathy); Exchange transfusion needed
Prothrombin Time (INR) - $\text{INR} > 5.0$ Critical coagulopathy, spontaneous major internal haemorrhage

Appendix 4: Global Health Directory & District Training Curriculum

Monica Cheesbrough Part 1 (pp. 414–435) & Part 2 (pp. 411–418) International Reference Centers & EQA Bodies District Laboratory Training Curriculum Blueprint Complete

International Diagnostic Directory, Reference Bodies & EQA Schemes

District health networks rely on national blood transfusion services, external quality assessment (EQA) schemes, non-governmental humanitarian agencies, and specialized diagnostic manufacturers to ensure unbroken supply chains, valid standards, and technical proficiency.

International Health Organizations & EQA

  • World Health Organization (WHO):
    • Essential Health Technologies & Blood Safety Unit (Geneva, Switzerland).
    • WHO Regional Offices (AFRO, AMRO/PAHO, EMRO, EURO, SEARO, WPRO).
  • Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC): Division of Parasitic Diseases and Malaria; Global AIDS Program (Atlanta, USA).
  • External Quality Assessment (EQA) Schemes:
    • UK NEQAS (United Kingdom National External Quality Assessment Service) — Haematology, Clinical Chemistry, Microbiology, Parasitology.
    • RIQAS (Randox International Quality Assessment Scheme).
  • Humanitarian Diagnostic Support:
    • International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC).
    • Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF / Doctors Without Borders).

Tropical Equipment & Cold Chain Suppliers

  • Solar-Powered Systems: Solar photovoltaics and deep-cycle battery banks for rural microscopy and centrifugation.
  • Cold Chain Refrigeration:
    • Dometic / Electrolux — Absorption kerosene/gas and solar direct drive blood bank refrigerators.
    • Vestfrost — WHO PQS-certified blood bank and vaccine storage units.
  • Diagnostic Point-of-Care Instruments:
    • HemoCue AB (Sweden) — Microcuvette dual-wavelength haemoglobinometers ($570/880\ \text{nm}$) and glucose analyzers.
    • Olympus / Nikon / Leica — Tropicalized anti-fungal coated microscopes with mirror/LED lighting.

Supplement: Planning a Training Curriculum for District Laboratory Personnel

Monica Cheesbrough outlined a competency-based curriculum blueprint designed to equip district laboratory scientists with practical, problem-solving diagnostic skills matched directly to tropical disease burdens.

Core Competency Modules

  1. Pre-Analytical Competencies: Aseptic phlebotomy, specimen collection protocols, transport cold chains, rejection criteria, and barcode/register transcription.
  2. Analytical Diagnostic Skills:
    • Parasitology: Rapid thick/thin malaria film microscopy, quantification, stool concentration techniques, urine filtration for schistosomes.
    • Microbiology: Aseptic plating, Gram/ZN staining, reading biochemical TSI/urease batteries, Kirby-Bauer AST zone measurement.
    • Haematology: HiCN spectrophotometry, microhaematocrit centrifugation, differential WBC counts, peripheral film pathology.
    • Blood Transfusion: Tube ABO/Rh grouping, major crossmatching with AHG, Coombs check cell validation, donor screening.
  3. Post-Analytical & QA: Levey-Jennings QC plotting, Westgard rules, panic value communication, biosafety waste autoclaving.

Practical Assessment & CPD

  • Objective Structured Practical Examinations (OSPE): Timed diagnostic stations testing slide identification, unknown culture isolation, and pipetting precision.
  • Proficiency Panels (Blind Testing): Regular quarterly blind slide panels (malaria density, AFB smear grading, unknown serum grouping) administered through regional EQA coordinators.
  • Continuous Professional Development (CPD): Mandatory annual refreshers on emerging pathogens (Ebola, Marburg, Dengue, Chikungunya, drug-resistant MDR/XDR-TB, MRSA, CRE).
  • Leadership & Inventory Management: Stock buffer calculations, cold chain contingency planning, SOP drafting, and equipment preventive maintenance.
